representative.title: How Tania stopped her own child marriage | Prothom Alo
representative.author: Zahin Jaimah Kabir

snapshot.title: How Tania stopped her own child marriage
snapshot.evidenceText: <p>While other students were preparing to enrol in college after completing secondary school, Tania of Satkhira was struggling to stop her own marriage. Meanwhile, the results of the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examination were published. Astonishing everyone, she achieved not only a GPA of 5 but also A+ grades in every subject. She scored 100 out of 100 in chemistry and 99 in physics.</p><p>Yet she felt no joy at her remarkable achievement. Her mind was consumed by anxiety over her impending marriage and uncertainty about her future. Ultimately, thanks to the support of her teachers and her outstanding SSC results, the determined Tania managed to escape child marriage this time.</p><p>Today, Sunday, is the International Day of the Girl Child. This year’s theme is “End Child Marriage, Invest in Girls’ Rights”. The situation in Bangladesh, however, seems to tell a somewhat different story.</p>.<p>The latest Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF, shows that the rate of child marriage has fallen from 51.4 per cent in 2019 to 47.2 per cent. Nevertheless, among women aged 20–24, 47.2 per cent were married before turning 18, while 13.4 per cent were married before the age of 15.</p><p>The survey also found that the proportion of married women aged 15–19 rose from 32.9 per cent in 2019 to 38.9 per cent over the seven-year period. The adolescent birth rate has also increased. In 2019, there were 83 births a year for every 1,000 adolescent girls; by 2025, the figure had risen to 92.</p>.One in every two girls subjected to child marriage.<p>Tania Khatun is 17. Just before her SSC examinations, she learnt that a marriage proposal had come for her. Neither she nor her mother wanted the marriage, but other family members put considerable pressure on them. They cited the family’s financial hardship, concerns about girls’ safety in society and various other reasons.</p><p>Tania did not know what to do. Under pressure, she eventually said she might agree on one condition: she must be allowed to continue her education after marriage. But the prospective groom’s family refused to accept even that condition.</p><p>News of Tania’s proposed marriage spread through her school and the surrounding area. Her hopes began to fade. But the story took a turn when Tania and her mother visited Akleema Khatun, the school’s information and communication technology teacher, with sweets to celebrate Tania’s excellent results.</p><p>Tania recalled that the teacher told her mother, “She has achieved such good results. How can you marry her off like this? We have taught your daughter for five years. We also have a claim on her future.”</p>.<p>The teacher, along with fellow teacher Foyezul Haque and local human rights activist Sakibur Rahman, then began trying to persuade Tania’s family to abandon the marriage plan.</p><p>Eventually, they took Tania to the upazila nirbahi officer (UNO), or upazila executive officer. The UNO spoke to her family, and mounting pressure from the authorities ultimately led them to withdraw the marriage decision.</p><p>Sakibur Rahman told Prothom Alo that the greatest source of strength in Tania’s struggle was her mother, who holds a master’s degree. She had opposed the marriage from the outset. An educated mother, he said, can provide the greatest courage in such adverse circumstances.</p><p>Tania has enrolled in the first year of higher secondary education in the science stream at Satkhira Government College. Her excellent SSC results have also earned her the opportunity to receive private tuition free of charge.</p>.I was deprived of everything: Global report hears from over 250 girls who experienced child marriage.<p>Tania’s story is an inspiring one. But very different stories are also common. The main causes of child marriage are said to include school dropout, financial hardship within families, social customs and weak enforcement of the law. Inadequate birth registration is also seen as a major obstacle. A 2025 survey found that only 59.2 per cent of children under five had been registered at birth.</p><p>Under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, the minimum legal age for marriage is 18 for women and 21 for men. However, exceptions are allowed in certain circumstances. If a marriage involving a minor takes place in the best interests of the minor, with a court order and parental consent and in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the rules, it is not considered an offence under the Child Marriage Restraint Act.</p>

representative.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph | Longform | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Lina Abu Zayed

snapshot.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
snapshot.evidenceText: Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph. Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them. Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work. For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems. Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems. She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities. Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone. While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom. “I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.” In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard. Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera. All are smiling. They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Sara Rayan took it, holding out the phone so everyone fit in the frame. The girls were 17 and 18. Like many teenagers their age, they worried about exams and university places, talked about what they wanted to become, and imagined the lives that lay ahead. Four months later, Israel's war on Gaza began. Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Four have left Gaza. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended. Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined, and to see whether they could be brought together again for a photograph in the same schoolyard. Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Some classrooms still bear the marks of the war: holes left by quadcopter gunfire, windows damaged by shelling and soot stains where families cooked over open fires. On the walls, children have drawn kites, flowers and a Palestinian flag. Some have written their names: Haya, Marah, Mohammed and Khaled. Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them. It's just past 10am on a Thursday in late September when Yasmin Abu Zaid arrives. Then Aya Adnan arrives, quickening her pace when she sees Yasmin and pulling her into an embrace. “I haven’t seen you for three years,” she says. “Where have you been? You never show up.” Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader arrives a few minutes later, carrying a plastic bag of books for Aya’s younger sister, who is preparing for the Tawjihi, Gaza’s national secondary school graduation exams. Aya and Lina have seen each other since leaving school. Their families have been friends for years, and they still live in the same neighbourhood of Nuseirat. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. With the fighting making it difficult to meet, neither has seen her for three years. The three have also kept in touch with Ghaida Zaqout, who now lives in Egypt. Together, they have a private WhatsApp group where they chat regularly and check on one another. When Maha finishes teaching, she greets "my girls" with arms wide open. They erupt into chatter, talking over one another and trying to catch up. In time, Maha pulls up the old photograph on her phone. The girls huddle around her, then point at the tree behind them, recognising it from the photograph. Now, they begin recalling the school days they shared. There were the ordinary intimacies of teenage friendship: who would lend you a pen, who would explain homework you didn't understand, who whispered through lessons and who worried for days about an exam. Ghaida was the girl whose laughter could be heard before she entered the classroom, and who rarely stopped talking, even when teachers moved her to another desk. Sara and her twin sister Fatima were forever taking selfies, while Lina al-Hour was quieter, often bringing novels to read during breaks. The girls talked about clothes, television programmes and football. They bought food together during breaks and wondered aloud about university and what they might become. Some dreamed of studying medicine; another wanted to design buildings. Their futures still seemed to turn on exams, marks, university places and what their families could afford. Maha remembers Sara Rayan laughing, and Ghaida, she says, is in Egypt now, studying dentistry. Here, she pauses, enlarges Lina’s face on the screen and falls silent. Her smile has disappeared. When she speaks again, her voice is quieter and catches slightly. “This is my well-mannered student, Lina,” she says softly. “She is a martyr.” On November 17, 2023, Lina was killed in an Israeli air strike. She was 18. For a moment, the girls wrap their arms even tighter around one another in silence. Standing in the same schoolyard three years later, they tell one another they wish they could return to those days. But most of the girls in the photograph are missing at this reunion. Aya takes out her phone and holds it at arm's length, trying to recreate the selfie Sara took three years earlier. “Sara should have been here to take it,” she says. But Sara cannot come. She now works for an NGO, using her wages to help pay her university fees and contribute to her family's income. Aya Adnan stands with the three in the new photograph, tall, with a dimple in her chin and her hijab falling behind her shoulders. Three years earlier, she had been looking forward to university. She wanted to become a doctor, preferably a neurosurgeon. Aya enjoyed studying. She arrived early for extra physics lessons and worked through difficult material until she understood it. She had also noticed how few female surgeons there were in Gaza and disliked hearing that surgery was too demanding a profession for women. Her interest in neurology had become personal in the 11th grade, when she suffered a severe headache and dizziness that lasted 24 hours. “It felt like my head was heavier than my body,” she recalls, “as if it might fall off.” After undergoing scans and seeing a neurologist, she was told pressure from the vertebrae in her neck was affecting her spinal cord. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology. When her final school results came, she had scored 96 percent. But studying medicine was expensive, and the family - her father was an UNRWA social worker - could not comfortably afford the fees. representative.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
representative.author: Tom Bateman

snapshot.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
snapshot.evidenceText: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Roofs were ripped off buildings after Isaias barrelled into the US on Friday evening, before it weakened to a post-tropical cyclone. All but one of those who died, including the gunman, were related, police say. A motive for the shooting is not yet known. The US president's said President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world". Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".

snapshot.title: US sanctions International Criminal Court in major escalation
snapshot.evidenceText: Latest action seeks to stem resources to international tribunal Trump administration has vowed to dismantle. Washington, DC – United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced a new set of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), this time targeting the entity itself, as opposed to the tribunal’s officials or groups that provide support. The announcement on Friday represented a major escalation from the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has vowed an “all of government” approach to dismantling the court. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on social media. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” As justification for its actions, the administration has pointed to the court’s ongoing investigation into abuses committed in Afghanistan, which could ensnare US military and intelligence personnel, as well as the ICC’s arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes committed in Gaza. Before Friday’s actions, the US had sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, a UN special rapporteur focusing on the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian rights groups that have provided evidence to the court. Several rights groups have challenged those sanctions in US federal court, saying restricting how US citizens interact with the court treads on their constitutional freedoms. Sanctioned ICC judges have also launched legal challenges in the US. Speaking to the Reuters news agency on Friday, deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said the sanctions “must be condemned”. “The sanctions are intended to undermine ⁠⁠⁠⁠the rule of ⁠⁠⁠⁠law internationally and the work that an ⁠⁠⁠⁠independent judicial institution ⁠⁠⁠⁠is doing,” ⁠⁠⁠⁠Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our ‌‌‌‌situations, our investigations and our ‌‌‌‌prosecutions.” In a statement, the ICC called on member states to redouble support. “History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it said. The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the founding treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, the court has long ruled that abuses committed by US or Israeli citizens in the territories of countries that are ICC members can be prosecuted. Israel was among those cheering the Trump administration’s latest action. “Thank you for your leadership,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement posted on social media. To date, the court has not sought to prosecute any US citizens. A US law dating back to 2002, amid the so-called “Global War on Terror”, already prohibits extradition of US citizens to be tried by the ICC. It further authorises the use of military force in the event that a US citizen is held in detention while being prosecuted by the court, in what critics have dubbed the “Hague invasion clause”. Nevertheless, some US administrations, particularly those led by Democrats, have sought to provide support for the court and have espoused its founding principles. Rights observers have said that the US pressure campaign could have wide-ranging implications for the court’s investigations, particularly the network of local organisations and fact-finders upon which it relies to build cases. Mark Kersten, an international law expert and professor at the University of Fraser Valley in British Columbia, Canada, said ICC advocates have feared direct sanctions on the court itself since Trump took office for his second term in January last year. “This was the number one concern: the possibility not only that individuals would be sanctioned, but that the court itself would be sanctioned,” he told Al Jazeera. “That should give people a sense of the significance of this…the worst-case scenario has come about”. The US has also urged other countries to withdraw from the court, suggesting it would assess allies’ relationship with the court when determining foreign assistance. The appeal has dovetailed with wariness from some ICC members over what they have called the unequal application of international law, with offenders in the Global South more likely to face accountability. In July, Chad and Venezuela moved to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The years ahead, Kersten said, will be a test of support from ICC members, who will need to intervene to circumvent the US sanctions. Most of Europe, Latin America and large areas of Africa remain members of the tribunal, as do Canada and Australia. “Only with the support and concrete action of those states will the court really ultimately survive,” he said. The latest round of sanctions means that companies that provide services to the court could be penalised. Sanctioning the entire entity, which has about 900 staff, as opposed to individual officials, will make it more difficult for the court to insulate itself from such sanctions. The sanctions block “all property and interests in property” the court has in the US, while prohibiting “making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit” of the court. The sanctions included several temporary exemptions, including for services providing maintenance, technology and pension plans. The State Department said the exemptions are meant to “provide time for States Parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental US concerns regarding the ICC”. William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, said it was not immediately clear how impactful the sanctions would be. He said the court had been preparing for the eventuality for over a year. “They have been developing a plan B on how to get around this,” Schabas told Al Jazeera. That has included migrating some US-made software to European alternatives and recently ending its relationship with the French health and life insurance company Axa, which does business with the US. “How significant this will be remains to be seen,” he said. “Obviously for the institution it’s going to complicate things considerably.” Friday’s announcement came just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist and former ICC judge Navi Pillay. Pillay also oversaw the 2025 UN Human Rights report that found Israel’s actions in Gaza constituted a genocide. Schabas drew a connection to the timing of the State Department’s announcement and Trump’s ire towards the Nobel Committee, which he has maintained should award him the Peace Prize. “The prize is a recognition more generally of the international institutions with which Pillay was affiliated, in particular the International Criminal Court and also a kind of polite endorsement of the report that she wrote last year for the United Nations condemning Israel for genocide,” he said. “There’s often a political message lurking behind the award of the Nobel Peace Prize and I think this year is no exception,” he said. The Nobel judges said the prize comes at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack”. “An international legal system in which war ⁠⁠⁠⁠criminals are held to account, and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world,” they said.

snapshot.title: Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court?
snapshot.evidenceText: The sanctions targeting the ICC, which prosecutes humanitarian crimes, are the latest move by the US against the court. The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), hours after one of its former judges was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in what the Nobel committee said was, in part, a show of support for institutions under attack. South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who is currently a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also in The Hague, was announced winner of the prize on Friday. Nobel Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”. “In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice,” the committee said. The US move follows sanctions it has already imposed this year on judges and other personnel at the ICC. On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the latest set of US sanctions targeting the ICC, this time focusing on the court itself, which was established in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” he said in a video shared on social media. The Trump administration claims that the ICC has gone beyond its remit by pursuing non-member countries. In 2024, the Trump administration condemned the court when it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for suspected war crimes in Gaza. It also previously opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan. The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, abuses committed by citizens of non-statute states in ICC territories or countries can still be prosecuted. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement, adding that if the US allies failed to “rein in the court”, the US would “continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”. These sanctions are just the latest in the US’s campaign against the ICC. Previous measures have targeted dozens of ICC judges and prosecutors , the UN special rapporteur for Palestine, Francesca Albanese, and Palestinian rights groups which have provided evidence of war crimes committed by Israel to the court. In August, ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior lawyer Abdoulaye Sey were also sanctioned by the US, in what Rubio said was the US’s unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court”. Any assets they hold in the US are frozen, and US companies are limited in conducting transactions with them. The sanctions targeting the court could see companies that provide services to it penalised. They will also freeze any ICC assets held in US territories. However, they have given US companies a six-month grace period to wrap up any existing business with the court. There are also some other exemptions allowing for certain transactions. William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, told Al Jazeera that the court has been “developing a plan B” to get around potential sanctions for more than a year. This includes migrating to European alternatives to US software, and ending its relationship with insurance company Axa, which does business with the US. “How significant this will be remains to be seen,” he said. “Obviously for the institution, it’s going to complicate things considerably.” “What Trump is trying to do is to make the world safe for American and Israeli war criminals,” Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University and former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera. The ICC itself released a statement condemning the US move, which it said was an attempt to “obstruct the course of justice” and intimidate those who work or cooperate with the court. “It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” it said, calling on its 125 states parties to take action to ensure it can continue its work. “History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it added. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply alarmed” by the decision, adding that it was “a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice”. The foreign ministers of the UK, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan all said they “strongly disagree” with the sanctions, and warned of the significant impact they would have on the court. Netanyahu thanked Trump for his leadership on social media, and accused the ICC of being a “political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide”. The US targeting of the ICC threatens the rule of law, as international courts and tribunals must be able to operate without the threat of sanctions. The US itself has repeatedly ignored international law under President Trump. Its joint attack on Iran with Israel in February was criticised by observers as being in violation of both US law and Article 2(4) of the UN Charter , while the US military abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from Caracas in January was also condemned as illegal. The Trump administration has also launched strikes against alleged drug smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific, killing more than 200 people in what UN human rights experts warn are “ extrajudicial and unlawful “. Under Trump, the US has also pulled out of international organisations and agreements, from the Iran nuclear deal (the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action) and the Paris Climate Agreement during Trump’s first term, to the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, more recently. “What Trump is doing is obstructing justice,” Roth said of the ICC sanctions. “If you look at Article 70 of the Rome Statute, it makes it a crime to intimidate or threaten court officials because of their official duties.” “But the court remains strong, it is very capable of doing its work,” he said, adding, “there’s important work for the court to do to protect victims in places like Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Afghanistan, the Philippines. This is work that should continue, and it will.”

snapshot.title: The US just sanctioned the International Criminal Court. What’s next?
snapshot.evidenceText: Our programs and centers deliver in-depth, highly relevant issue briefs and reports that break new ground, shift opinions, and set agendas on public policy, with a focus on advancing debates by integrating foundational research and analysis with concrete policy solutions. When major global news breaks, the Atlantic Council’s experts have you covered—delivering their sharpest rapid insight and forward-looking analysis direct to your inbox. Reports from the front lines of global policy—by the experts shaping it. A weekly column by Atlantic Council President and CEO Frederick Kempe, Inflection Points focuses on the global challenges facing the United States and how to best address them. UkraineAlert is a comprehensive online publication that provides regular news and analysis on developments in Ukraine’s politics, economy, civil society, and culture. UkraineAlert sources analysis and commentary from a wide-array of thought-leaders, politicians, experts, and activists from Ukraine and the global community. MENASource offers the latest news from across the Middle East, combined with commentary by contributors, interviews with emerging players, multi-media content, and independent analysis from fellows and staff. Econographics provides an in-depth look at trends in the global economy utilizing state-of-the-art data visualization tools. Translate the page or open accessibility tools from the same menu. Adjust text size, contrast, link visibility, and motion from the same menu. Translate the page or open accessibility tools from the same menu. Adjust text size, contrast, link visibility, and motion from the same menu. Washington has issued its own verdict. On Friday, the Trump administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), extending a yearslong campaign beyond individual judges and prosecutors to the tribunal itself. The new sanctions threaten to disrupt the court’s access to essential banking, insurance, and technology services. What’s behind the US decision? And can the ICC continue to operate? Our experts weigh in below. Gissou Nia is the director of the Strategic Litigation Project at the Atlantic Council. A human rights lawyer, she started her career in The Hague, where she worked on war crimes and crimes against humanity trials at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Criminal Court. Today’s announcement from the US Department of State that the International Criminal Court has been sanctioned as an entity is a complete inversion of the intended use of sanctions. The sanctions designation places the ICC on the US Department of the Treasury’s financial blacklist and represents a measure normally used against global militant networks, drug cartels, and transnational gangs—not the lawyers, judges, and bureaucrats investigating and prosecuting them. The designation cuts the court off from the global financial system and, without aggressive countermeasures from supporting countries, will grind the court’s daily work to a halt. This risks depriving thousands of survivors and victims of the world’s most serious crimes—including murder, rape, torture, and mass starvation—of one of their last remaining paths to much-needed justice. The ICC is a court of last resort, meaning that it only steps in when a country is unwilling or unable to investigate or prosecute crimes committed within its borders or by its nationals. While US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claims that the sanctions are intended to prevent US service members from being charged by the court, the reality is that US personnel are not the subject of any current investigation, nor have they ever been a primary focus. In the past year alone, the court has convicted a Sudanese militia chief for crimes in Darfur, unsealed arrest warrants against top Taliban leaders in Afghanistan for crimes against humanity including gender persecution, confirmed charges against Ugandan warlord Joseph Kony, prepared for the trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte for widespread extrajudicial killings in a sweeping “war on drugs,” begun proceedings against a suspect accused of crimes against prison detainees in Libya, convicted a Central African Republic rebel leader for crimes against humanity, and more. This activity covers a range of global crimes—and none of these cases involves US perpetrators. A June 2026 statement from the ICC presidency described the body as “one of the most significant achievements of human civilisation.” The claim—coming from one of the court’s formal organs—could seem hyperbolic. But there is truth in those words. It is almost inconceivable in today’s polarized world that delegations from 120 countries could vote “yes” to establish an institution and voluntarily submit themselves to an accountability framework beyond their domestic justice systems for the greater good. The threatened destruction of what took decades to build should steel the determination of the court’s supporters to take the bold actions needed to save it. Matthew Kroenig is a senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security, and a former US defense and intelligence official. The ICC has always been fraught strategically and geopolitically. The strategic vision was to deter and hold accountable tyrants engaged in grievous crimes. This is a noble goal. In practice, it may have had the opposite effect, incentivizing dictators engaged in civil wars, for example, to employ any means necessary to cling to power. A defeated Napoleon received an island exile; today’s defeated dictators are hauled off to The Hague. Geopolitically, the court has wrongly pursued powerful democracies engaged in legal wars consistent with the law of armed conflict, including US soldiers in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders in Gaza. Washington has never been a fan of and never signed the Rome Statute that established the ICC. Then-National Security Advisor John Bolton threatened sanctions in President Donald Trump’s first term, and Rubio is doubling down in the second. Multilateral institutions cannot survive without the backing of powerful states. The ICC may learn this lesson soon. Mark Klamberg is a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Strategic Litigation Project. The latest US sanctions against the ICC are fundamentally more serious than previous measures. Until now, sanctions have targeted individual representatives; the new sanctions target the court as an entity. In concrete terms, this means it will become more difficult—or even impossible—for the court to pay its employees, settle bills, and rely on essential services. The court had already anticipated this risk and taken some precautionary measures. Last year, it decided to replace Microsoft Office with a European software alternative, amid mounting concerns about dependence on US technology. These sanctions appear to come in direct response to the ICC’s decision to issue arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. However, this case is just one among many that the court is currently pursuing. The ICC is simultaneously investigating the situation in Ukraine, where it has issued an arrest warrant against Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as ongoing cases related to Sudan, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Venezuela, and the Philippines. This range of situations illustrates that the court’s mandate extends across vastly different geopolitical contexts, applying the same legal standards regardless of the power or alliances of the states involved—a fact that underscores, rather than undermines, its claim to impartiality. Supporters of the ICC, such as the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada, should consider using their blocking statutes to help companies withstand the risks of continuing to do business with the ICC. In short, blocking statutes contain provisions designed to counter the effects of foreign sanctions and trade restrictions. They not only prohibit persons and companies within their jurisdictions from complying with specified foreign sanctions, but also allow individuals and companies to recover damages through legal action for losses caused by the extraterritorial application of these foreign sanctions—as is the case under the EU blocking statute. More fundamentally, the US should reconsider its current adversarial stance toward the ICC. Since the Nuremberg trials, the US has played a key role in advancing international justice. There may be legitimate disagreement over individual decisions, but the court operates on core principles of judicial independence, complementarity, and fair-trial guarantees—principles the US itself has long championed. Lize de Kruijf is an assistant director within the GeoEconomics Center’s Economic Statecraft Initiative As the threat of US sanctions against the ICC has grown, the EU blocking statute has frequently been floated as a way to protect the court and allow it to continue its work. The statute essentially nullifies the effect of designated foreign sanctions within the EU. Adding the ICC sanctions to the blocking statute would mean that EU persons and entities would be prohibited from complying with them, and US court rulings enforcing them would be unenforceable in the EU. The Netherlands—which hosts the ICC in The Hague and is legally bound by its Headquarters Agreement to ensure the court’s continued operation—has so far prioritized working behind the scenes, seeking a resolution with Washington. However, in an interview during this year’s UN General Assembly, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen stated that the Netherlands “will do everything it can to protect the court” and that it had asked the European Commission to prepare to activate a blocking statute in case sanctions were imposed on the entire ICC. Given the EU’s strong support for the court, activation of the blocking statute is a real possibility. However, even with the blocking statute, keeping the court operational may still prove challenging. Banks will risk losing access to the US financial system, a risk that large Dutch banks with international operations, in particular, may be unwilling to take. The statute also does not offer compensation for companies that lose US business as a result of complying with it. Their only recourse is to sue whoever caused the harm. The private sector’s tolerance for sanctions risk is typically very low. AXA, the France-based health insurance provider for the ICC, for example, recently cut ties with the ICC amid the growing threat of sanctions. As a result, there is a risk that companies may seek exemptions from the statute or quietly wind down their business with the court instead. Celeste Kmiotek is a senior staff lawyer for the Strategic Litigation Project at the Atlantic Council. The preamble of the ICC’s Rome Statute states that, in agreeing to establish the ICC, state parties were: “Mindful that during this century millions of children, women and men have been victims of unimaginable atrocities that deeply shock the conscience of humanity, Recognizing that such grave crimes threaten the peace, security and well-being of the world.” The ICC’s mandate is and always has been strictly tailored to address only these situations. Its jurisdiction is principally limited to four categories of crimes : war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and aggression. There are preconditions for the ICC to exercise jurisdiction: Generally, either the state on whose territory the conduct occurred or the state of which the accused is a national must be a party to the Rome Statute or have otherwise accepted the ICC’s jurisdiction. The ICC’s authority narrows again through conditions governing the opening of investigations and the selection of cases. For example, it is a “ court of last resort ,” generally admitting cases only when a state is unable or unwilling to investigate and prosecute. The Office of the Prosecutor only prosecutes those alleged to be “ most responsible ” for a given crime. The system is then undergirded by procedural safeguards , such as the requirement that a Pre-Trial Chamber review the Office of the Prosecutor’s applications before issuing arrest warrants. In short, only an extremely select group of people have reason to fear ICC prosecution. In the twenty-four years since its establishment, there have been sixty-eight arrest warrants, twenty-three detentions, and fifteen convictions. In stark contrast, as of 2023 , 10,900 victims had participated in court proceedings, 2,500 had received court-ordered reparations, and over 130,000 survivors were supported by the ICC’s Trust Fund for Victims. In other words, a person is far more likely to interact with the ICC as a victim than as a defendant. The Trump administration’s apparent fear of the ICC is telling. These sanctions and the broader campaign against the ICC appeal to the legal concept of “sovereignty,” even as the US repeatedly carries out actions that seem to violate international law. snapshot.title: US announces sanctions on the International Criminal Court
snapshot.evidenceText: The US has announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. It's the latest in a series of steps by the Donald Trump administration as it seeks to "dismantle" the intergovernmental organization. US President Donald Trump 's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize. This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court." The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said in a statement . "That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said. Rubio said that both US political parties had long agreed that the ICC should not have jurisdiction over US citizens, but said "only President Trump" resolved to take action. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said. "If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer." The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an independent international court supported by more than half of the UN's members. "The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane, who already faces US sanctions . The ICC called the Rome Statute, which underpins membership of the court, a "collective promise" that the most serious international crimes must not go unpunished. "That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it," the court said. It appealed to members to take "concrete actions" to ensure the court would still have the necessary means to continue its work. "No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice," it said. "History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an insitution created to protect them came under attack." A collection of US allies that are full members of the ICC including Germany issued a joint statement reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC." "As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," the governments of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the UK said . They said that, despite the ICC's best efforts to prepare and mitigate their effect, the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked the US government for its "leadership" in issuing the sanctions. "The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," he said. The State Department released the announcement a few hours after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, who was an ICC judge from 2003 to 2012. Last year Trump repeatedly complained that he should have won the accolade for promoting world peace, prompting Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to present him with her trophy as a gift . Without naming names, the Nobel Committee clearly referenced US sanctions against the ICC when announcing Pillay as this year's laureate. "The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently," the Committee wrote. It said judges like Pillay "guard the thin red line between order and chaos," but lamented that "today ... these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked." The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague. It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide , crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression. The ICC was established in 2002 and is governed by the Rome Statute. More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it. Several of the world's most significant powers, including China, India, Israel, Russia and the United States, do not recognize the court's jurisdiction and are not parties to the statute. A grey area, however, remains since the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize it. That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians. The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term. Rubio has often led the charge. In July, he wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution." He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe." Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC. A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC following a US request. The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan , who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court. In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court. representative.author: Tom Bateman

snapshot.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
snapshot.evidenceText: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Roofs were ripped off buildings after Isaias barrelled into the US on Friday evening, before it weakened to a post-tropical cyclone. All but one of those who died, including the gunman, were related, police say. A motive for the shooting is not yet known. The US president's said President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world". Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".

snapshot.title: Hurricane Isaias kills at least four, leaves thousands without power in US
snapshot.evidenceText: A backyard is flooded in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Destin, Florida, US. ( Reuters: Marco Bello ) Hurricane Isaias has killed at least four people, leaving hundreds of thousands without power across three US states. Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared emergencies. Hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes were expected across parts of the US, the National Hurricane Center said. At least four people have died and 800,000 Florida, Alabama and Georgia residents were without power after Hurricane Isaias made landfall. Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. However, hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US were expected, the National Hurricane Center said. The tornado threat is expected to continue today across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared emergencies. The hurricane has left damage in multiple states. ( Reuters: Marco Bello ) In Florida, power restoration was marked as priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. "They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," Mr DeSantis said. He also warned that casualties might follow "in the days after". Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the storm, he said. More than 430,000 customers in Florida, over 280,000 in Alabama and some 100,000 in Georgia lost power as the storm hit shore, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. In Alabama and Florida, three people were killed by falling trees, according to local media and authorities. Sheriff Chip W Simmons of Escambia County, Florida has confirmed two "storm-related fatalities" via social media. "A tree fell on a house and unfortunately took the life of a lady," he said, and later confirmed that a man died from carbon monoxide poisoning. Alabama's emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. "Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. Isaias rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season. It is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said. The clean up will begin in coming days across the affected states. ( Reuters: Marco Bello ) Oil and gas producer Shell has said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito, and Appomattox assets in the Gulf. President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was "under control." Earlier, emergency declarations were approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X. "There's also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of," DeSantis told FOX News. "But so far, we've had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on." A second hurricane has developed into a powerful category 4 system which is expected to make landfall "near or just inland" of Mexico's west-central coast on Sunday, local time. The National Hurricane Centre in Miami said Hurricane Simon's maximum sustained winds increased to 240km/h. A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane. The centre said the hurricane could bring as much as 25-50 centimetres of rain over parts of south-western Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 76cm. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the centre warned in a bulletin that also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare as tropical-storm conditions were expected to arrive Saturday afternoon. representative.title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama : NPR
representative.author: Bill Chappell

snapshot.title: At least 4 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
snapshot.evidenceText: A driver look at his overturned truck in a flooded parking lot on Saturday morning in Tiger Point, Fla., close to where Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday night. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage and power outages wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least four people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed. Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland. One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office. "The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email. A person also died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a room, according to Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons. Four others were hospitalized in the same incident. Many people use generators when they lose connection to the electricity grid. An uprooted tree is seen in Gulf Breeze, Fla., on Saturday. The southeastern U.S. faced a high risk of flooding as Isaias, weakened from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone, moved northward. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham. "We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence." A fourth death was confirmed by Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey's office, which told NPR that a person died in Barbour County, southeast of Montgomery. They did not provide details about the circumstances. More than 390,000 people across the state and Florida were without power as of Sunday morning. At least 95% of outages across the state are expected to be restored by midnight, Alabama Power said on Sunday. In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference. The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners. "Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges. Hurricane Isaias forced a Waffle House restaurant to shut down when it passed through Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane. Joe Raedle/Getty Images hide caption Florida Power & Light Company said it hopes to have power restored to 95% of those impacted by Isaias by end of day Monday. Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin. Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama. "Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service." But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as the Florida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast. On Sunday, there were tornado warnings in North Carolina, as well as high risk of flooding. Other parts of the rest of the East Coast, including Virginia, also saw heavy rain. NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
