representative.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft | Longform | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Aatif Ammad

snapshot.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft
snapshot.evidenceText: Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted. The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts. For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place. Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s. Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh. “Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842. “They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added. Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike. “Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.” Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand. “In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.” There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs. Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees). “We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. We never imagined that one day we would struggle even to run our household.” Over the past year, however, the orders have vanished with the rise in silver prices. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers. Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran. In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. But this year, amid the conflict with Iran, silver prices briefly soared as high as $4,670 (450,000 rupees) per kg before easing after the ceasefire. Even now, after some decline, prices are hovering around $2,600 (250,000 rupees) per kg, more than three times their levels just a few years ago. Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets. “When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.” The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery. He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options. “The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.” The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves. “India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said. These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said. Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver. India more than doubled its effective import taxes on gold and silver in May. That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years. High silver prices are now forcing Lucknow’s brides to make tough, sometimes devastating, decisions. For 28-year-old Lucknow resident Uzma Siddique, who is set to marry in December, owning and wearing a pair of silver nagras on her big day has always topped her wedding wishlist. “My mother wore silver nagras at her wedding in 1992. So did my grandmother and so did my great-grandmother,” Siddique said. “I always imagined myself wearing them and taking my wedding photographs in them and posting them on Instagram. It was never just footwear; it was an emotion and a family tradition.” But when she visited the market with plans to order a pair, the prices stunned her. “A pair that cost around $156 to $208 (15,000 to 20,000 rupees) just a few years ago is now selling for nearly $673 (65,000 rupees),” she said. Determined to have a pair, she decided to give up on other wedding luxuries instead. “I had to cut back on many other wedding expenses. I bought a lighter lehenga (long skirt), reduced the number of suits I planned to purchase, and trimmed my budget in several places, just so I could afford these nagras.” Despite the financial strain, she says giving up the footwear tradition was never an option. “They have become incredibly expensive, but our emotions are attached to them. That’s why I still bought them,” she said. But many of her friends have had to go without. “Some had dreamed of wearing silver nagras on their wedding day, but they had to let go of that dream because they simply couldn’t afford them. They are deeply hurt by it,” she said. Not far from Siddique’s home lives her friend, 25-year-old Safiya Khan, who is also getting married in December. Unlike Siddique, Safiya has not been able to buy silver nagras for her wedding. From a lower middle-class family, she says soaring prices put upholding that tradition out of reach. “My entire wedding shopping budget is around $1,250 (120,000 rupees). I simply cannot spend more than half of it on a pair of shoes,” Khan said, noting that she was sad to end the family tradition. “I think this tradition will end with my generation,” she said. “My mother had a pair of silver nagras, but she had to sell them last year because of financial difficulties. We always believed we would buy another pair for my wedding. Had we known silver prices would rise so dramatically, we would never have sold them.” She has been shocked by how a distant war has so negatively affected this beloved local tradition. “I know the recent conflicts have pushed silver prices higher, but I never imagined that a war thousands of km away could take away a tradition so close to my heart,” she said. “I had always dreamed of taking my wedding photographs in silver nagras. Now that dream will never come true.” Naseem Jahan, a Lucknow resident in her late seventies, still treasures the pair of silver chappals her mother gave her for her wedding in 1972. “I remember my mother paid around $2.50 (250 rupees) for this pair,” Jahan recalled. “We had to wait nearly seven months after placing the order before it was finally ready. Those were beautiful days.” More than five decades later, the silver slippers remain one of her most cherished possessions. She has them polished every three years and proudly wears them to weddings and other important family gatherings, as do many of the older women in Lucknow. “Every time I wear them, people come to admire them and praise their beauty. That makes me so happy,” she said with a smile. But Jahan fears the tradition may not continue into the next generation. “Today, very few people can afford such footwear,” she said. When she recently visited the market to buy a similar pair for her granddaughter, the soaring price of silver made it unaffordable. Still, she wants her granddaughter to have traditional bridal footwear, so she has made a tough decision. “I have decided to gift her my own pair,” she said. “Let these slippers adorn her feet now. I want them to continue their journey.” As the only precious keepsake she has preserved from her wedding, Jahan knows how connected brides feel to the shoes. “I have developed an emotional bond with them. They remind me of my mother, my wedding day and the Lucknow I grew up in. snapshot.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft
snapshot.evidenceText: Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted. The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts. For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place. Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s. Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh. “Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842. “They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added. Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike. “Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.” Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand. “In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.” There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs. Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees). “We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. We never imagined that one day we would struggle even to run our household.” Over the past year, however, the orders have vanished with the rise in silver prices. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers. Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran. In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. But this year, amid the conflict with Iran, silver prices briefly soared as high as $4,670 (450,000 rupees) per kg before easing after the ceasefire. Even now, after some decline, prices are hovering around $2,600 (250,000 rupees) per kg, more than three times their levels just a few years ago. Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets. “When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.” The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery. He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options. “The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.” The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves. “India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said. These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said. Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. That’s why I still bought them,” she said. snapshot.title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades
snapshot.evidenceText: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but his work as a codebreaker has finally been recognised "My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything." From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two. Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort. But research into the life story of Vanke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers. About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945. After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow. The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile. Fred fled Poland after a happy childhood in Krakow Believed to be the last surviving member of these Polish codebreakers, Ferdynand Stanislaw Vanke grew up in Krakow, but fled at the age of 16 when war arrived on his doorstep in 1939. He said: "I did wake up in the morning hearing the planes. I ran to the window and I could see Germans coming over but I thought it was Polish Air Force training. "People were screaming and falling to the ground and we could hear machine gun fire. My father burst in and said 'in to the cellar, the Germans are coming'. That's how my war started." Fred, his sister and a friend travelled east in a Polish Army Hospital van, to his grandparents' home, avoiding Nazi gunfire on the roads. "I could see people coming from all over the place, masses of people," he said. "When Germans would come, my sister said to me 'under the van, under the van'. That's the first time I've seen people being injured to that extent." Fred and his father served together in the Middle East After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. "Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing. "One day my commanding officer, Colonel Mayer, called me and explained 'you're young, I've got a son like you, you volunteer to be dropped in Poland you will last four or five months on average and that's the end of you. I've got something better'. Fred served in the Middle East before his service took an unexpected turn Instead, a captain visited from Bletchley Park, the then-secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School, the forerunner of GCHQ, and the base for Allied codebreaking. "He gave us all a lecture and a little puzzle," said Fred. After cracking the first, he was given a second which he also deciphered. "He said, 'you've got a gift which very few people have'," Fred recalled. So despite being in his early 20s, several years younger than anyone else on the unit, Fred was recruited to work at The Arches in Boxmoor, a Polish sigint station near Hemel Hempstead which supported Bletchley Park. The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators. One of dozens of Polish codebreakers based there, Fred would work in a team listening to German signals and attempting to decode them. Poles like Fred worked in secret under the guidance of Bletchley Park Fred said: "You start with the simple things. You've got to learn the language, how it is built, and what is the quirk in that language, and you base your guessing on that. "When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday." However outside of The Arches, life was tougher for Fred. He said: "The people in Hemel Hempstead, because we had uniforms with Poland, they spat on you and called 'why don't you eff off to fight Germans instead'. "You couldn't say what you're doing, so that was a little bit upsetting." But what Fred and his Polish compatriots were doing, both before the war and during it, was pivotal in the Allied war effort. Bletchley Park was the secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School Among those identified during the research were Marian Rejewski and Henryk Zygalski, two of the three Polish mathematicians who alongside Jerzy Różycki first broke the German military Enigma cipher before the war, and who continued codebreaking work in Britain after escaping occupied Europe. At the Pyry Conference near Warsaw in 1939, Polish cryptologists invited French and British counterparts, including Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox, to share their pioneering success in breaking the German Enigma machine cipher. Dr David Kenyon, the research historian at Bletchley Park Trust who investigated Fred's story, said: "This meeting was important because it laid the groundwork for partnership between the British and the Polish and significantly helped the subsequent British attack on Enigma." Fred said: "I was very pleased when I received a letter from the British government for what I've done. But I was very proud of Zygalski, Rejewski and Różycki - that's our three real codebreakers." Fred and Patricia met in Nottingham after the war After the war, Fred moved to Nottingham where he started a photography firm with a fellow Polish ex-paratrooper. "I met my wife in Jessops in one of the shops," he said. "She was a model there, once I saw her, I said 'this is my wife'." The couple raised three children, and were together until her death in 1996 - but Fred never told her about his wartime role. "My wife died and she still didn't know what I was doing. I never told anybody," he said. "In fact, she always complained - 'all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell, you never tell anything'. "You were sworn not to tell, so I kept that." Having reached the age of 103, Fred puts his long life down to luck, whiskey and stopping smoking in 1963, and believes he must now be the last surviving Polish codebreaker. "I'm bound to be, I am 103-and-a-half, and I was the youngest by two years," he said. Fred and 26 other Poles who served under Bletchley Park have been added to its Roll of Honour Kenyon said: "Due to the secrecy of the work at Bletchley Park, so much of this work remained classified for decades - the full scale of Polish involvement in Britain's WW2 codebreaking effort is still being pieced together. "Adding these Polish names to our Roll of Honour pays tribute to the contribution made by Polish citizens in the wider Allied effort in WW2, not only on the fighting fronts, but also at Bletchley Park, and in other secret intelligence work, a contribution which may have been overlooked in the past." Rafał Wiśniewski, Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in London, said: "The work of Polish cryptologists, well before and during WW2, was instrumental in cracking the Enigma cypher and, ultimately, in the Allied victory, which helped save countless lives. "The evidence proving direct links to Bletchley Park and other secret intelligence work is truly important and shows the depth of our co-operation, which needs to be recognised." Caroline Whelan said her father's story showed the importance of intelligence and the role it can play in bringing about peace Fred's daughter Caroline Whelan, 60, said: "We've had a very happy, normal life, considering dad had a really traumatic start to his. "It is unbelievably fantastic that he is able to witness the acknowledgement that so many people haven't been able to," she said. "He's one of the people that you never get bored of talking to, and he's always got a story to tell now." Fred and his father served together in the Middle East After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. "Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing. "One day my commanding officer, Colonel Mayer, called me and explained 'you're young, I've got a son like you, you volunteer to be dropped in Poland you will last four or five months on average and that's the end of you. I've got something better'. Fred served in the Middle East before his service took an unexpected turn Instead, a captain visited from Bletchley Park, the then-secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School, the forerunner of GCHQ, and the base for Allied codebreaking. "He gave us all a lecture and a little puzzle," said Fred. After cracking the first, he was given a second which he also deciphered. "He said, 'you've got a gift which very few people have'," Fred recalled. So despite being in his early 20s, several years younger than anyone else on the unit, Fred was recruited to work at The Arches in Boxmoor, a Polish sigint station near Hemel Hempstead which supported Bletchley Park. The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators. One of dozens of Polish codebreakers based there, Fred would work in a team listening to German signals and attempting to decode them. Poles like Fred worked in secret under the guidance of Bletchley Park Fred said: "You start with the simple things. You've got to learn the language, how it is built, and what is the quirk in that language, and you base your guessing on that. "When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday." However outside of The Arches, life was tougher for Fred. He said: "The people in Hemel Hempstead, because we had uniforms with Poland, they spat on you and called 'why don't you eff off to fight Germans instead'. "You couldn't say what you're doing, so that was a little bit upsetting." But what Fred and his Polish compatriots were doing, both before the war and during it, was pivotal in the Allied war effort. Bletchley Park was the secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School Among those identified during the research were Marian Rejewski and Henryk Zygalski, two of the three Polish mathematicians who alongside Jerzy Różycki first broke the German military Enigma cipher before the war, and who continued codebreaking work in Britain after escaping occupied Europe. At the Pyry Conference near Warsaw in 1939, Polish cryptologists invited French and British counterparts, including Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox, to share their pioneering success in breaking the German Enigma machine cipher. Dr David Kenyon, the research historian at Bletchley Park Trust who investigated Fred's story, said: "This meeting was important because it laid the groundwork for partnership between the British and the Polish and significantly helped the subsequent British attack on Enigma." Fred said: "I was very pleased when I received a letter from the British government for what I've done. But I was very proud of Zygalski, Rejewski and Różycki - that's our three real codebreakers." Fred and Patricia met in Nottingham after the war After the war, Fred moved to Nottingham where he started a photography firm with a fellow Polish ex-paratrooper. "I met my wife in Jessops in one of the shops," he said. "She was a model there, once I saw her, I said 'this is my wife'." The couple raised three children, and were together until her death in 1996 - but Fred never told her about his wartime role. "My wife died and she still didn't know what I was doing. I never told anybody," he said. "In fact, she always complained - 'all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell, you never tell anything'. "You were sworn not to tell, so I kept that." Having reached the age of 103, Fred puts his long life down to luck, whiskey and stopping smoking in 1963, and believes he must now be the last surviving Polish codebreaker. "I'm bound to be, I am 103-and-a-half, and I was the youngest by two years," he said. Fred and 26 other Poles who served under Bletchley Park have been added to its Roll of Honour Kenyon said: "Due to the secrecy of the work at Bletchley Park, so much of this work remained classified for decades - the full scale of Polish involvement in Britain's WW2 codebreaking effort is still being pieced together. "Adding these Polish names to our Roll of Honour pays tribute to the contribution made by Polish citizens in the wider Allied effort in WW2, not only on the fighting fronts, but also at Bletchley Park, and in other secret intelligence work, a contribution which may have been overlooked in the past." Rafał Wiśniewski, Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in London, said: "The work of Polish cryptologists, well before and during WW2, was instrumental in cracking the Enigma cypher and, ultimately, in the Allied victory, which helped save countless lives. "The evidence proving direct links to Bletchley Park and other secret intelligence work is truly important and shows the depth of our co-operation, which needs to be recognised." Caroline Whelan said her father's story showed the importance of intelligence and the role it can play in bringing about peace Fred's daughter Caroline Whelan, 60, said: "We've had a very happy, normal life, considering dad had a really traumatic start to his. "It is unbelievably fantastic that he is able to witness the acknowledgement that so many people haven't been able to," she said. "He's one of the people that you never get bored of talking to, and he's always got a story to tell now." representative.title: Meet “Noo-Noo”: A 99-Million-Year-Old Insect with a Surprising Secret | Tel Aviv University | Tel Aviv University

snapshot.title: Meet “Noo-Noo”: A 99-Million-Year-Old Insect with a Surprising Secret
snapshot.evidenceText: TAU researchers discover a new insect species from the age of the dinosaurs, revealing an unusual feeding mechanism that has disappeared from the insect world today. • Tel Aviv University researchers identified a previously unknown insect species preserved in 99-million-year-old amber from the age of the dinosaurs. • The new species, Cretodorus noonoo, nicknamed “Noo-Noo,” had exceptionally long, flexible mouthparts reaching nearly twice its body length. • Researchers believe these mouthparts helped the insect reach sugar-rich fluids deep inside cracks in tree bark. • The discovery reveals an ancient evolutionary adaptation with almost no modern equivalent and offers new insights into the ecosystems of Cretaceous forests. Some 99 million years ago, during the age of the dinosaurs, a tiny insect belonging to a species previously unknown to science became trapped in tree resin. The resin hardened and turned into amber, and the fossil preserved within it has now enabled a team of researchers from the School of Zoology and The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History to identify and describea new species: Cretodorus noonoo, or “Noo-Noo.” Alongside the description of the new species, the study reveals an extraordinary biological adaptation that characterized Noo-Noo and its close relatives: exceptionally long and flexible mouthparts, which in Noo-Noo reached nearly twice the length of its body. The researchers believe that this unusual structure enabled the insects to reach food sources that were inaccessible to insects with more rigid mouthparts, deep inside cracks and crevices in tree bark. The study, published in the journal Insects, was conducted by Dolev Fabrikant and Dr Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of the School of Zoology, Wise Faculty of Life Sciences, The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History and New Environmental School at Tel Aviv University, in collaboration with Dr Yanzhe Fu of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The newly described species - Cretoduros noonoo, Photo credit: Dolev Fabrikant The researchers examined insect fossils belonging to Neazoniidae, an ancient family of planthoppers, including 13 specimens preserved in Kachin amber from Myanmar. In their modern relatives, the mouthparts are structured like a simple needle, allowing them to pierce plant tissues and suck fluids from them. The ancient insects examined in the study, however, were found to possess extremely elongated mouthparts, the surface of which was densely covered with transverse folds. Using high-resolution micro-computed tomography, the researchers were able to reconstruct their internal structure. The scans showed that the folds were not merely external ornamentation, but part of the structure itself. They likely gave the mouthparts flexibility while preventing them from kinking or collapsing — much like a bendy drinking straw or a corrugated flexible hose. Further evidence comes from the fossils themselves: in several specimens, the mouthparts were preserved in a bent position. Because the amber froze the insects in place when they became trapped in the resin, the researchers view this as further evidence that the mouthparts were also flexible during the insect’s lifetime. Such a structure is unknown among their living relatives today, pointing to an ancient evolutionary solution that has since disappeared. The new species’ unusual appearance also inspired by its name: Cretodorus noonoo. The epithet “Noo-Noo” was chosen after the friendly vacuum cleaner from the children’s television series Teletubbies, whose long, flexible hose resembles the mouthpart of the ancient insect. But why would an insect need such long mouthparts? Butterflies might immediately come to mind, as they use a flexible proboscis to drink nectar, but the researchers believe that the resemblance is only superficial. The mouthparts of “Noo-Noo” pointed backward and functioned as a piercing-and-sucking system, which like those of their modern relatives are less suitable for feeding on nectar. Moreover, despite examining numerous fossils, the researchers found no convincing evidence of pollen accumulating on their bodies — a sign that would have indicated a role as pollinators. The explanation proposed by the researchers is that these insects were specialists in sucking sap from trees. Their long, flexible mouthparts could have snaked through narrow cracks in the bark and guided the piercing organs toward the deep vascular tissues. At the tip was another unusual feature: a structure with two grooved lobes that likely opened during feeding, helping to anchor the mouthpart to the walls of the crack — much like a wall plug expanding inside a drilled hole. The researchers’ discovery may also have broader significance for our understanding of Cretaceous forests. Long or corrugated feeding structures appeared in several unrelated insect groups during this period, raising the possibility that forests rich in thick-barked trees provided an advantage for insects capable of reaching deeper tissues. The study notes that resin-producing forests of the Cretaceous period were also associated with evidence of recurrent fires, and that trees in fire-prone environments often develop thicker bark. The researchers cautiously suggest that such conditions may have created ecological opportunities for unique feeding strategies — strategies that are almost entirely absent among planthoppers today. Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou stated: “The discovery of ‘Noo-Noo,’ a new species that lived approximately 99 million years ago, gives us an extraordinary glimpse into the insect world of the age of the dinosaurs. This is not merely an insect previously unknown to science, but an animal that developed an evolutionary solution with almost no modern equivalent: a long, flexible, and durable feeding organ that likely enabled it to reach food deep within tree bark. The fact that similar structures appeared in several insect groups during the Cretaceous period suggests that ancient forests created ecological conditions and opportunities very different from those we know today. The discovery of a new species like this is therefore not simply the addition of another name to the tree of life, but another piece of the puzzle that enables us to reconstruct what ecosystems looked like and how they functioned tens of millions of years ago.” Lead Authors of the study. Dolev Fabrikant (right), Dr. Leonidas Romanos Davranoglau (left), Photo credit: Dolev Fabrikant

snapshot.title: Scientists found a 9-million-year-old capybara relative's tooth in Chile's Atacama Desert, one of Earth's driest places; the water-loving animal adds evidence that the region once supported wetlands and a much wetter climate
snapshot.evidenceText: The Atacama Desert is a landscape where water is measured in millimetres, not rivers. Today, parts of this vast Chilean desert receive almost no rain, making the discovery of an animal that depended on plentiful freshwater all the more surprising. Buried in an ancient deposit, a single tooth has now offered scientists another glimpse of a very different Atacama, one with wetlands, vegetation and enough water to support a large, semi-aquatic rodent.According to a report by Live Science, researchers identified the roughly 9-million-year-old tooth as belonging to an extinct relative of today's capybaras, adding to growing evidence that the Atacama was not continuously hyperarid throughout its long geological history.A surprising fossil in the desertThe Atacama occupies northern Chile and is considered one of the oldest and driest deserts on Earth. Its hyperarid core receives less than 2 millimetres of rainfall per month in some areas. The region's extreme dryness is partly linked to its geography. The Chilean Coast Range blocks moisture arriving from the Pacific, while the Andes restrict moisture from the Atlantic. However, geological research suggests that the desert's aridity began taking shape millions of years before the Andes reached their present heights, adds the online report by Live Science.The newly discovered tooth provides another reason to reconsider how the region looked in the distant past, the report claims.As per Live Science, the fossil belonged to a large capybara relative identified as Hydrochoerus and Cardiatherium, which lived during the late Miocene. Modern capybaras are the world's largest rodents and depend heavily on stable freshwater environments. They feed on vegetation that also requires sufficient water to grow. Finding one in today's Atacama therefore points towards an environment dramatically different from the barren landscape visible now.Evidence of an ancient wetlandThe tooth was discovered in a geological layer containing evidence of a shallow marine environment that existed between about 7 million and 10 million years ago, claims the report. It was not an isolated clue. Researchers have also found microscopic plant remains known as phytoliths, indicating that palms, grasses, gingers and other flowering plants once grew in the region. Together, these discoveries paint a picture of a landscape that periodically supported far more water and vegetation than the Atacama does today.Other fossil evidence from the region has pointed to freshwater fish and crocodiles, strengthening the possibility that wetlands and waterways periodically spread across parts of the desert. The capybara relative adds another piece to that ecological puzzle because its semi-aquatic lifestyle would have required access to dependable water.How did capybaras get there?According to Live Science, the discovery also raises a geographical mystery. The Andes presented a formidable barrier between the animal's likely habitats farther east and the fossil site in northern Chile, with elevations reaching around 5,500 metres. Researchers suggest the animals may have travelled instead along South America's western coast, moving between wetlands, rivers and other freshwater habitats. The tooth itself also makes long-distance transport an unlikely explanation. Its size makes it difficult to imagine being carried hundreds of kilometres by wind, while a waterway capable of transporting such material would itself point towards a wetter environment.A changing picture of the AtacamaThe fossil does not mean the entire Atacama was once a lush landscape. Rather, it strengthens the case that the region experienced periods of significantly wetter conditions during the late Miocene. For a desert famous for its extreme dryness, the tiny fossil offers a surprisingly big lesson: landscapes that appear permanently hostile today can have remarkably different histories. The capybara tooth is another fragment of that history, revealing a time when water-loving mammals could survive in a place that now seems almost entirely defined by its absence.Images Courtesy: istock and Science Alert

representative.title: ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war | Primatology | The Guardian
representative.author: Gloria Dickie

snapshot.title: ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war
snapshot.evidenceText: John Mitani spent years studying a huge community of chimpanzees in Uganda. But then things took a dark turn – and his findings stunned the scientific world John Mitani spent years studying a huge community of chimpanzees in Uganda. But then things took a dark turn – and his findings stunned the scientific world J ohn Mitani can still remember the first time he set foot in Uganda’s Kibale national park. The old-growth east African rainforest enveloped him, its canopy stretching to heights of 40 metres. Fruit trees bowed under the weight of African star apples and bountiful Ficus mucuso figs. And then there were the chimpanzees. Furry black blobs darted through the jungle, their raucous calls often deafening. It was the summer of 1995, and Mitani, a primatologist from northern California, had just come from working with the chimps living in the Mahale mountains of Tanzania. At the time, Mahale was home to the largest known population of chimps, with about 100 individuals. But there were rumours that this section of Kibale – only accessible via a 12-hour drive from the capital, Kampala – might host an even more unusual abundance of apes. “It only took a few days to realise that something weird was going on at this place,” Mitani, now 72, recalls. “There were chimps everywhere.” He was then a professor at the University of Michigan, and with his colleagues would eventually count nearly 200 chimpanzees living together peacefully in the forests of Ngogo, a research area in the central section of Kibale first established in the 1970s for the study of red colobus monkeys. Such a large chimp troop was then unheard of in primatology. Later that year, Mitani co-founded the Ngogo Chimpanzee Project with the Yale university primatologist David Watts , using a $500,000 (£380,000) award from the US National Science Foundation. Three decades on, the project is one of just 12 long-term studies worldwide of chimpanzees in their natural environment, and has transformed what we know about one of our closest relatives. It took years to build trust with the population, Mitani says. The chimps were not accustomed to human presence and were quick to run away whenever researchers approached. Days were spent chasing them over hills and down valleys. “It was fun, exciting and exhilarating. It was also a challenge.” The first ape to break the ice was a 25-year-old male with an easily identifiable cleft palate that Mitani would later name Hare . During his second year at Ngogo, Mitani was observing chimpanzees in a massive fig tree when Hare descended. Mitani assumed he would run away as he had done in the past. Instead, the chimp walked slowly toward the next fruit tree, permitting Mitani to follow. “When I realised what was happening, I almost started to cry. After working so hard for so long, it was tremendously gratifying to have gained Hare’s trust,” Mitani wrote in the 2022 anthology Chimpanzee Memoirs. Mitani estimates he has spent 85 months of his life hiking the forests of Ngogo, or approximately seven years. What began as a few basic structures and tents has grown into a large – albeit rustic – research camp that has housed the nearly 90 researchers who have worked with the Ngogo project over three decades. The findings that have emerged from Ngogo over the years have stunned the scientific world, similar to the discoveries first made at Gombe in Tanzania by Jane Goodall in the 1960s and 1970s. Mitani and his colleagues documented the lowest mortality ever recorded for a wild chimp population, suggesting that good habitat conditions could lengthen life expectancy to close to that of human hunter-gatherers. They found that unrelated males could form strong alliances and cooperate , moving beyond the accepted paradigm that only close kin would work together. Hunting and meat-eating (particularly munching on the red colobus monkeys) were found to be important for male social bonding, not just nutrition. But the most notable – and disturbing – finding of Ngogo began on a June day in 2015. Mitani and his fellow researchers were observing a cluster of the group when the chimps began to display nervous behaviour and scattered at the sounds of approaching group members. “All of a sudden, the individuals I was following just ran down the hill for no apparent reason,” Mitani says. “Chaos erupted. They started to run around and chase each other.” That moment, in retrospect, was the first sign of what would become a years-long bloody conflict – chronicled in the 2023 Netflix series Chimp Empire – between a once close-knit group of chimps. In a study published this April in the journal Science, Mitani and his colleagues describe what may be the first “ civil war ” among wild chimps. By 2018, two distinct chimp groups had formed in Ngogo. Nine males and 19 infants have been killed during the conflict. Scientists later found that the unexpected result of this lethal aggression was that female fertility doubled and offspring survival increased substantially at Ngogo. But for Mitani, who has spent much of his life among the Ngogo chimps, witnessing the split was far more personal. “I was in denial. I was still in this mindset that they were doing so well together as a big group,” he recalls. “It’s been hard to watch. In the first 20 years, going back to see the chimps was fun. I always looked forward to these visits. But it’s gotten to be increasingly difficult to go back and see this, to see these killings continue.” So much so, he adds, that it took him more than a decade to write the paper on the dark events they had borne witness to in the forests of Ngogo. “I think I was dragging my heels because maybe I didn’t really want to write about this.” Still, Mitani pushes back against the takeaway that the civil war says anything about humans’ evolutionary propensity for violence and in-fighting. This behaviour, he adds, has not been witnessed among bonobos, with whom we also share a common ancestor dating back approximately 8m years. “Many of us who study chimps emphasise the similarities , and for good reason,” Mitani says. “But when it comes to the behavioural similarities, sometimes I think my colleagues stretch things a bit too much. If there is one thing I’ve learned from studying chimps all these years, it is that they are not us.” Though the greatest threat the Ngogo chimps now face is, in a way, themselves, Mitani says the presence of researchers on the ground over many decades has helped to conserve these populations. Researchers work with the wildlife authority to remove snares for other wild game that occasionally trap a chimp by mistake, for example. But Mitani, who now lives between Michigan and Arizona, worries for the future of research at Ngogo. The project has received the bulk of its funding from the US National Science Foundation’s behavioural and cognitive sciences division. Under the Trump administration’s proposed 2027 budget, that funding is due to be eliminated. “The chimps there have many more important stories to tell us,” Mitani says. “This is one of the reasons I am so concerned about the war on science and truth in this country.” He will return again to Ngogo this month – and for as long as he is able. “The funny thing is that the hills at Ngogo get increasingly steeper every year. And the distance between the trails seems to get longer. But I feel blessed that I still can do it.” If there is any legacy to his life’s work, he hopes that being able to impart some knowledge of the complex lives of these animals will give people a better appreciation of the chimpanzees. That maybe that will inspire people to ensure we continue living on a planet alongside them. “That would be the grand, big hope.” Find more age of extinction coverage here , and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe , Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features.

But there were rumours that this section of Kibale – only accessible via a 12-hour drive from the capital, Kampala – might host an even more unusual abundance of apes. “It only took a few days to realise that something weird was going on at this place,” Mitani, now 72, recalls. “There were chimps everywhere.” He was then a professor at the University of Michigan, and with his colleagues would eventually count nearly 200 chimpanzees living together peacefully in the forests of Ngogo, a research area in the central section of Kibale first established in the 1970s for the study of red colobus monkeys. Such a large chimp troop was then unheard of in primatology. Later that year, Mitani co-founded the Ngogo Chimpanzee Project with the Yale university primatologist David Watts , using a $500,000 (£380,000) award from the US National Science Foundation. Three decades on, the project is one of just 12 long-term studies worldwide of chimpanzees in their natural environment, and has transformed what we know about one of our closest relatives. It took years to build trust with the population, Mitani says. The chimps were not accustomed to human presence and were quick to run away whenever researchers approached. Days were spent chasing them over hills and down valleys. “It was fun, exciting and exhilarating. It was also a challenge.” The first ape to break the ice was a 25-year-old male with an easily identifiable cleft palate that Mitani would later name Hare . During his second year at Ngogo, Mitani was observing chimpanzees in a massive fig tree when Hare descended. Mitani assumed he would run away as he had done in the past. Instead, the chimp walked slowly toward the next fruit tree, permitting Mitani to follow. “When I realised what was happening, I almost started to cry. After working so hard for so long, it was tremendously gratifying to have gained Hare’s trust,” Mitani wrote in the 2022 anthology Chimpanzee Memoirs. Mitani estimates he has spent 85 months of his life hiking the forests of Ngogo, or approximately seven years. What began as a few basic structures and tents has grown into a large – albeit rustic – research camp that has housed the nearly 90 researchers who have worked with the Ngogo project over three decades. The findings that have emerged from Ngogo over the years have stunned the scientific world, similar to the discoveries first made at Gombe in Tanzania by Jane Goodall in the 1960s and 1970s. Mitani and his colleagues documented the lowest mortality ever recorded for a wild chimp population, suggesting that good habitat conditions could lengthen life expectancy to close to that of human hunter-gatherers. They found that unrelated males could form strong alliances and cooperate , moving beyond the accepted paradigm that only close kin would work together. Hunting and meat-eating (particularly munching on the red colobus monkeys) were found to be important for male social bonding, not just nutrition. But the most notable – and disturbing – finding of Ngogo began on a June day in 2015. Mitani and his fellow researchers were observing a cluster of the group when the chimps began to display nervous behaviour and scattered at the sounds of approaching group members. “All of a sudden, the individuals I was following just ran down the hill for no apparent reason,” Mitani says. “Chaos erupted. They started to run around and chase each other.” That moment, in retrospect, was the first sign of what would become a years-long bloody conflict – chronicled in the 2023 Netflix series Chimp Empire – between a once close-knit group of chimps. In a study published this April in the journal Science, Mitani and his colleagues describe what may be the first “ civil war ” among wild chimps. By 2018, two distinct chimp groups had formed in Ngogo. Nine males and 19 infants have been killed during the conflict. Scientists later found that the unexpected result of this lethal aggression was that female fertility doubled and offspring survival increased substantially at Ngogo. But for Mitani, who has spent much of his life among the Ngogo chimps, witnessing the split was far more personal. “I was in denial. I was still in this mindset that they were doing so well together as a big group,” he recalls. “It’s been hard to watch. In the first 20 years, going back to see the chimps was fun. I always looked forward to these visits. But it’s gotten to be increasingly difficult to go back and see this, to see these killings continue.” So much so, he adds, that it took him more than a decade to write the paper on the dark events they had borne witness to in the forests of Ngogo. “I think I was dragging my heels because maybe I didn’t really want to write about this.” Still, Mitani pushes back against the takeaway that the civil war says anything about humans’ evolutionary propensity for violence and in-fighting. This behaviour, he adds, has not been witnessed among bonobos, with whom we also share a common ancestor dating back approximately 8m years. “Many of us who study chimps emphasise the similarities , and for good reason,” Mitani says. “But when it comes to the behavioural similarities, sometimes I think my colleagues stretch things a bit too much. If there is one thing I’ve learned from studying chimps all these years, it is that they are not us.” Though the greatest threat the Ngogo chimps now face is, in a way, themselves, Mitani says the presence of researchers on the ground over many decades has helped to conserve these populations. Researchers work with the wildlife authority to remove snares for other wild game that occasionally trap a chimp by mistake, for example. But Mitani, who now lives between Michigan and Arizona, worries for the future of research at Ngogo. The project has received the bulk of its funding from the US National Science Foundation’s behavioural and cognitive sciences division. Under the Trump administration’s proposed 2027 budget, that funding is due to be eliminated. “The chimps there have many more important stories to tell us,” Mitani says. “This is one of the reasons I am so concerned about the war on science and truth in this country.” He will return again to Ngogo this month – and for as long as he is able. “The funny thing is that the hills at Ngogo get increasingly steeper every year. And the distance between the trails seems to get longer. But I feel blessed that I still can do it.” If there is any legacy to his life’s work, he hopes that being able to impart some knowledge of the complex lives of these animals will give people a better appreciation of the chimpanzees. That maybe that will inspire people to ensure we continue living on a planet alongside them. “That would be the grand, big hope.” Find more age of extinction coverage here , and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe , Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features.

representative.title: Falling catches threaten Ho Chi Minh City’s oldest fishing village | DTiNews

snapshot.title: Falling catches threaten Ho Chi Minh City’s oldest fishing village | DTiNews
snapshot.evidenceText: Dawn comes early in Phuoc Hai, in Ho Chi Minh City’s Vung Tau area. At around 6 am, small round basket boats return to shore after a night at sea, carrying catches of fish, squid, shrimp and crabs. The sight of the little circular boats against the blue water has become a defining feature of the fishing village beneath Minh Dam Mountain. As the boats reach shore, fishermen hurry to untangle their nets and sort their seafood to keep it fresh before taking it to market. Nguyen Ngoc Chau, 55, was visibly disappointed after returning from a night at sea with only a few crabs. “Seafood catches have fallen significantly in recent years,” he said. “We used to earn an average of VND 500,000 (about USD 19) a night. Now we make only around VND 200,000 (about USD 7.70).” Nguyen, 46, who has been part of the village since childhood, said about 80 per cent of residents depended on fishing for their livelihoods. “Things are different now. There are fewer fish. Those who can afford it have replaced their basket boats with larger vessels equipped with GPS, fish-finding equipment and radios so they can fish farther offshore. Those of us who fish close to shore earn very little,” he said. More than a century after its establishment, Phuoc Hai continues to follow the rhythms of life at sea. After selling their catch, fishermen return home to mend nets and rest before preparing their gear for the next trip in the late afternoon or evening. Le Huu Duc, 58, said basket boats used relatively little fuel but yielded smaller catches. On calm days, he might bring home several dozen kilos of fish; in rough seas, the catch could fall to just 5-7kg. He said he had to make two trips a day to earn enough to support his three-member household. representative.title: ‘They searched my bag, and my Israeli passport was inside’: An extraordinary journey
representative.author: Assaf Kamar

snapshot.title: ‘They searched my bag, and my Israeli passport was inside’: An extraordinary journey through Saudi Arabia
snapshot.evidenceText: The religious police officers began rummaging through his bag. Hidden deep inside an inner pocket was the last thing he wanted anyone in Saudi Arabia to find: his Israeli passport. "They caught me in Medina, the city sacred to Muslims," adventurer Adam Jano, a resident of the northern Israeli community of Klil, told ynet. "They're not particularly pleasant people. They started searching through my things, and I was an idiot for bringing it with me," he recalled. "I had to move between hotels, so I thought, fine, I'll take it along. I hid it, and luckily they didn't see it." The encounter took place in the courtyard of the Prophet Muhammad's Mosque in Medina, one of Islam's holiest cities. "The religious police asked me, 'Are you Muslim?' I said, 'No, I'm not Muslim.' Then they started saying, 'Give us your bag.' They began searching, and my heart just sank." Fortunately for the Israeli traveler, whose identity could have landed him in serious trouble, the officers never opened the inner pocket, and his Israeli passport remained undiscovered. "It was a pretty frightening moment," Jano said. "Your heart starts racing, the adrenaline kicks in, and I have a wife and a child. Looking back, I think, wow, that was really stupid and dangerous. I should have handled things a little differently." It was Jano's second trip to Saudi Arabia, which he entered using a foreign passport. This time, he was determined to explore far beyond the modern capital, Riyadh. He embarked on long drives deep into the country's wild desert landscapes, reaching even the region bordering Yemen. One stretch of road that left a particularly strong impression followed the Red Sea coastline. "It's a beautiful road, and when you're driving north, the sea is always on your left, just like driving through Sinai, only from the other side." Most of the men Jano encountered wore the traditional white thobe, while the few women he saw were dressed in black. "They dressed me in a robe, and they were very proud of it," he laughed. "There are so many laundries on practically every corner. Because they constantly have to wash all those white clothes, it looks like the dry cleaners are making an absolute fortune." Ironically, it was the relative absence of tourists that made Jano's challenging journey so rewarding. "You meet people, you make friends," he said enthusiastically. "Suddenly, someone you met the day before calls you and says, 'I want to introduce you to my friend.' "Why did I meet so many people specifically in Saudi Arabia? If I went to Thailand, I'd just be another tourist, and the locals wouldn't find me particularly interesting. In Saudi Arabia, there aren't many tourists, so when you're a different face, you attract attention." One memorable encounter took place at a Western-style coffee shop in Riyadh, where several Saudi women approached him. "I'm standing in line, and these women wearing veils come up to me. You can only see their eyes. They ask, 'Where are you from?'" It was a perfectly ordinary question with an answer he could not afford to give. "I don't say Israel," he laughed. "Then they ask, 'Can we please pay for your coffee?' They were closed off for so many years, and now things are opening up. When unfamiliar faces start appearing, it sparks curiosity, and it's funny. "They take selfies with me while wearing their veils, and I'm thinking, wait a minute, what's going on here? You're taking a picture with someone whose face is covered, so what exactly can you see in the photo?" One of the highlights of Jano's journey was AlUla, one of Saudi Arabia's leading tourist destinations. Located in the country's northwest, the region is surrounded by dramatic sandstone cliffs, canyons and an ancient oasis. It was once an important stop along the Nabataean incense trade route connecting the Arabian Peninsula with the East and the Mediterranean. In recent years, AlUla has become a flagship project of Saudi Arabia's tourism ambitions, with luxury hotels, cultural attractions and extraordinary architecture emerging amid the desert landscape. Jano checked into one of the region's luxury resorts and discovered a swimming pool in the middle of the desert, gourmet restaurants, golf carts and impeccable five-star service. Almost everything was there, except the guests. "I was alone. There was nobody there," he laughed. "I was sitting alone in the restaurant, surrounded by waiters, and you're the only person there. They have golf carts to take you around because the hotel isn't just one building, it's an entire complex. "They ask you, 'Which restaurant would you like? There's a Thai restaurant or a Middle Eastern restaurant.' And whichever one you choose, you're the only guest. Everything is five-star. It's the top of the top." The hotel itself was designed to blend seamlessly into the surrounding desert. "The rooms are built into the mountain, and the swimming pool is there too. Even the stairs blend into the rocks. It's a very impressive, very special hotel, but being the only guest there feels strange." So where were all the tourists? "The employees tell me, 'Oh, they're coming.' They're coming. We want tourists." And what about the sightseeing bus? "I was the only passenger. Why would they even send out a bus? Can you imagine? An entire bus, and I'm riding in it alone." Beyond the luxurious hotels, the region is home to Nabataean archaeological sites and ancient tombs carved directly into the rock. "These are the same people who built what you see in Petra," Jano explained. "They carved straight into the rock, and it's incredibly impressive. Absolutely amazing." In AlUla, Jano also encountered a striking symbol of Saudi Arabia's ambitious transformation: Maraya, an enormous mirrored building that seems almost to disappear into the surrounding landscape, like a mirage reflecting the desert. "You can't see it," the veteran traveler said enthusiastically. "When you're walking through the desert and suddenly come across it, it tricks your eyes. It's like an optical illusion. It's a huge, square mirrored building, surrounded by mountains and desert, and the building reflects all the colors." Outside AlUla's lavish resorts, some of Jano's most memorable experiences took place around the dinner table. "Saudi food is very delicate and very good," he declared with the confidence of someone who has sampled plenty of it. "Think of Bedouin food, but imagine having a five-star chef prepare the meal and refine it," he laughed. "I particularly loved the lamb, slow-cooked with rice and spices." But the meal that stayed with him most was at the home of a Saudi friend he had met during his travels. "Arab hospitality is hospitality done properly," Jano said appreciatively. "When you're under someone's protection and they're responsible for you, you're treated like royalty." To protect his host's personal safety, we'll limit the description to the fact that he lives on a magnificent estate with a separate area designed specifically for entertaining guests. "He has this tent outside for visitors, and that's where they serve the food. He shows you photographs and things. He loves hunting, so he has stuffed animals and things from Africa. You sit on the carpet and eat with your hands." Yet beyond the hypnotic desert landscapes and luxury hotels, Jano had arrived in the mysterious kingdom with another, more discreet mission. "The Jewish story, wherever it exists, fascinates me," he said. "Everywhere I go, I try to put together another piece of the puzzle of Jewish history. And the very idea that there are 'hidden Jews' in Saudi Arabia made me curious to go looking for them and meet them." In a country where he himself had been forced to conceal his Israeli passport, the search for Jewish roots took on an entirely different level of significance. "You arrive there, you meet someone, and it's as if you're bringing them treasure," he said excitedly, recalling a discreet meeting with a person who identified as a secret Jew in Saudi Arabia. "You're bringing something into a place where it doesn't exist. And then they say, 'Wow, thank you for the siddur and the tefillin. How did you manage to bring those in?' It was incredibly moving." A siddur is a Jewish prayer book, while tefillin are small leather boxes containing biblical passages, traditionally worn during weekday morning prayers. The dusty city of Tabuk recently made headlines in Israel following the emergency landing of a flydubai aircraft carrying Israeli passengers. Jano, however, had traveled to the remote city for an entirely different reason: information about a Saudi citizen who secretly maintained a Jewish identity. After a four-hour drive to the edge of the desert, the man apparently got cold feet, and the much-anticipated meeting was called off. From there, the Israeli adventurer continued to an intriguing archaeological site near Al-Bad, known as the Split Rock of Horeb. The unusual natural formation is identified by proponents of the theory that Mount Sinai is located in Saudi Arabia as the rock from which Moses brought forth water for the Israelites, according to the biblical account. The identification is disputed and is not an established archaeological finding. "I felt, wow, if the Israelites really were here, and I've managed to make it all the way here, what now? What am I supposed to do?" Jano recalled. "So I said, let's do the Jewish thing. I put on tefillin in front of the rock, and I felt something incredibly powerful there. You're in a different desert, and you feel that you're different." Through connections he developed during his travels, the energetic Israeli also managed to meet Saudi citizens who introduced him to a contemporary Jewish story in the kingdom. One encounter was with a wealthy couple in Riyadh. "There are people living in Saudi Arabia who say they have Jewish connections," he said with a smile. "They say they're Jewish and that there's a Jewish community in Saudi Arabia. These are very wealthy people who lived in England and Europe and then returned to Saudi Arabia, but their Jewish identity is still hidden." Outwardly, he explained, they are part of mainstream Saudi society. "They live like modern people in Saudi Arabia," he said. "The man wears the traditional white clothing, and I didn't ask whether he goes to pray at the mosque. He looks like a modern person dressed in traditional clothes, but he's secretly Jewish." Then came the most emotional part of the encounter. "And then you bring him a gift, a Hebrew prayer book," Jano said, struggling to conceal his excitement. "It's as though you're unexpectedly bringing someone a treasure. 'Wow, thank you so much, a siddur.' The couple understood the value of the gift and what I had gone through to bring it to them. It was incredibly moving." Jano's search for Jewish roots in Saudi Arabia also brought him to an abandoned Jewish cemetery in the city of Al-Hofuf. "You imagine you're going to see gravestones, but all there was was this white sand that had been packed down by sandstorms," he recalled. "You're actually walking over the graves and can't see anything because the desert has covered everything. But the local Muslims still respect the place and don't build on it. It's still fenced off and recognized as a Jewish cemetery, a no-go zone." For Jano, visiting the cemetery was more than another stop on an extraordinary journey. "I'm not a religious person," he explained. "But if there's a hidden Jewish cemetery that really hasn't been visited in a very long time, then I feel that part of my responsibility is to go there and pay my respects."

snapshot.title: Pakistan imposes emergency rule over Imran Khan's provincial government
snapshot.evidenceText: ISLAMABAD, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Pakistan's president declared a state of emergency and suspended a provincial government led by the party of jailed former Prime MinisterImran Khan on Sunday, which the federal government said had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan. The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in theprovince intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan's release. The party’s last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces and Khan’s 2023 arrest sparked nationwide riots that threatened the military’s standing. Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters have been detained ahead of the planned march, in what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years. Pakistan's constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency, and Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months. Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed.The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province. The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs. Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters. Khan's aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government's move "more of a coup disguised as emergency," adding that it risks leading to further bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest. The government has expanded the military's powers and PTI accuses the army of dominating politics, which the military denies. Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. "Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy," he told a news conference in Islamabad. The government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces in Islamabad and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament. Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say the military rigged the vote against him, which the military denies. Cases against Khan range from concerns over state gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing. President Asif Ali Zardari declared the emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said. Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.” Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathized with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge. (Reporting by Asif Shahzad and Ariba Shahid in Islamabad; Additional reporting by Mubasher Bukhari in Lahore; Editing by Jamie Freed, Elaine Hardcastle, Alexandra Hudson) Our correspondents are already on the next chapter.
