representative.title: New large docodont fossil sheds light on Jurassic mammaliaform diversity-Xinhua

snapshot.title: New large docodont fossil sheds light on Jurassic mammaliaform diversity
snapshot.evidenceText: SHENYANG, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- An international team led by Chinese scientists has discovered a new docodont mammaliaform species, the largest known of its kind, in Jurassic strata dating back about 160 million years, enriching scientific understanding of Jurassic mammaliaform diversity. The new species has been named Megacauda sungei. Its fossil specimen, discovered in Ningcheng, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, measures roughly 52 centimeters in length and is estimated to have weighed around 2 kilograms, making it the largest known docodont mammaliaform. Its skull is clearly preserved, its trunk is robust, and its most striking feature is an unusually long, coiled tail. The specimen also retains well-preserved pelvic bones, hind limbs and tail vertebrae, suggesting it was adapted for swimming. Based on its distinctive teeth, researchers believe it could have hunted small animals living in the same environment, with a lifestyle possibly similar to that of the modern platypus. The study also sheds light on the animal's throat structure. The bones in its throat are similar to those of modern mammals, suggesting that behaviors such as swallowing, lapping and suckling may have already existed in the early ancestors of mammals, long before modern mammal groups appeared. "Mammaliaforms from the Mesozoic are often imagined as tiny creatures under dinosaur feet, but Megacauda sungei clearly raises the size limit of this group," said Li Yikun, an associate professor at Shenyang Normal University in northeast China. The study was published online in the journal Nature on Oct. 7. ■

representative.title: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk
representative.author: Ohio University

snapshot.title: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk
snapshot.evidenceText: edited by Sadie Harley , reviewed by Robert Egan This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: An international team of researchers has uncovered new evidence illuminating the evolutionary origins of one of the defining features of mammals: the ability to suckle and consume milk during infancy. Their findings, published in Nature , suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals. The findings describe a newly discovered species called Megacauda sungei, a large mammaliaform that lived during the Middle Jurassic Period in what is now Inner Mongolia, China. The research was led by scientists from the University of Chicago, Shenyang Normal University, Shandong University of Science and Technology, the University of Bonn and Ohio University. Using high-resolution microCT imaging, the team reconstructed the skull and skeletal anatomy of the fossil. They discovered an unexpected combination of traits. Megacauda had specialized blade-like cheek teeth resembling those of modern seals, a platypus-like pelvis and an otter-like tail, indicating it was likely a semiaquatic predator that hunted small vertebrates and invertebrates in freshwater environments. More significantly, the researchers identified a pair of small bony projections on the roof of the mouth that closely resemble features found in living therian mammals, a group that includes marsupials (such as kangaroos and opossums) and placental mammals (such as elephants and humans). In modern mammals, these structures help support the soft palate and muscles involved in suckling, swallowing and protecting the airway. Because soft tissues are rarely preserved in fossils, scientists have long struggled to determine when these important feeding structures first evolved. "The anatomy of Megacauda suggests that structures involved in coordinating swallowing and sucking had already begun to evolve by the Middle Jurassic. This discovery helps us better understand the biological foundations of one of the defining characteristics of mammals: feeding young with milk," said Zhe-Xi Luo, Ph.D., professor of organismal biology and anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of the study. The researchers also found highly specialized hyoid bones in the throat region. In living mammals, these bones help anchor muscles for swallowing. Together, the evidence suggests that Megacauda likely possessed an early version of the coordinated muscular system used by modern mammals to move milk and food safely from the mouth to the esophagus. The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about how these structures evolved. Researchers found that the newly identified therian-like bony hooks existed alongside more primitive bony ridges known from earlier mammaliaforms and mammalian ancestors. Their coexistence in the same animal suggests the modern structures did not evolve directly from the primitive ridges as previously believed. "This fossil captures an important stage in mammalian evolution," said Luo. "For decades, scientists have wanted to know when the soft-tissue structures necessary for suckling and complex swallowing first appeared. Megacauda provides some of the clearest evidence yet that many of these innovations emerged well before the rise of modern mammals." The research also has important implications for understanding living mammals. While therian mammals use a sophisticated suckling mechanism supported by the soft palate and constrictor muscles, monotremes such as platypuses and echidnas use a different method for obtaining milk and lack some of these anatomical features. The new evidence suggests that monotremes likely lost elements of the ancestral suckling apparatus during their evolutionary history and developed an alternative method of milk intake. Beyond feeding biology, Megacauda highlights the remarkable ecological diversity of mammaliaforms living alongside dinosaurs. At approximately the size of a modern otter, it is among the largest known Jurassic mammaliaforms and represents one of the earliest examples of adaptation to a semiaquatic lifestyle. "These discoveries continue to reveal that the age of dinosaurs was also a time of extraordinary evolutionary innovation among early mammals," said Peishu Li, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine and a co-author of the study. representative.title: Retracing the steps of Mark Dennis, the 'brilliant' barrister with a dark side - ABC News
representative.author: Charlotte Grieve, Kyle Taylor, Daryna Zadvirna

snapshot.title: Mark Dennis went from top silk and charity 'big boss' to accused predator
snapshot.evidenceText: Mark Dennis built a reputation defending accused criminals before he himself became the accused. ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon ) Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide. There is a small terrace house in Sydney's inner west that always gave builder Chad Loxsom an uneasy feeling. "I've been in thousands and thousands of people's houses," he said, but this one "was a little bit strange". The Leichhardt property belonged to Mark Dennis SC, a criminal defence barrister, who Loxsom said had a "weird demeanour" and was "just odd". But what he saw inside is what gnawed at him for years. "All over the walls of his house, he had dozens upon dozens upon dozens of pictures of him with little kids," he said. In some photos, Loxsom said Dennis was hugging shirtless children. Loxsom shared his suspicions with an electrician. "His gut was this guy was doing something bad with kids as well," he said. The electrician first noticed the "come back with a warrant" doormat, and then the large mirror fixed to the ceiling above Dennis's bed. But, like Loxsom, what really alarmed him was the sheer volume of photographs in almost every room, even the kitchen. "It was just disturbing. Like, these kids weren't happy," he said. Dennis was found dead in his home in Sydney's inner west in February. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) Eventually, Loxsom decided to make a report with the child protection hotline. "I didn't do it straight away, which now I regret," he said. In January, Dennis came onto the police's radar again when he was searched at Sydney Airport as he returned from a trip to Cambodia. What was found on his devices led to his arrest, a raid of his house, and child abuse material charges from evidence prosecutors described as "disturbing". Dennis was released on bail, and soon after, was found dead in his home . Last week, Background Briefing and ABC Investigations revealed his death did not bring the police investigation to an end . Codenamed Operation Queenstown, Cambodian and Australian national police have been quietly probing Dennis's network and links to famous children's charity Sunrise Cambodia all year. The ABC travelled to Cambodia in June to retrace Dennis's steps to reveal the inside story of how an accused predator accumulated power within a high-profile charity and gained access to vulnerable children. In an investigation that combines a tranche of internal documents with dozens of interviews, the ABC can reveal allegations that Dennis sexually harassed a former Sunrise staff member and made teenage girls feel uncomfortable by excessive touching. Listen to Dark Menace , a new three-part investigative podcast from Background Briefing and ABC Investigations, via the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts. The claims raise important questions for all children's charities that must balance the need to fundraise with child safety, as multiple former Sunrise staff say they saw Dennis's bad behaviour but felt they could not report it. "They saw this," one former staff member told the ABC through a translator. "But they could not do anything because he's a big sponsor." A spokesperson for Sunrise said they were never aware of any complaints about Dennis and police had told them no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of his victims. The charity defended its child protection policies, saying the children always came first. Dennis grew up in a large family on Sydney's northern beaches, and by 2001, was a criminal defence barrister with a room at the prestigious Forbes Chambers. "You don't get to go to Forbes unless you are absolutely brilliant," says one solicitor who briefed Dennis. "He was one of those people who was married to the profession." His nickname was "Dark Menace" — a play on words that several acquaintances said reflected his personality and black sense of humour, exemplified by his "WASNTME" personalised number plate. Across his career, Dennis was known to have mentored junior lawyers and published papers under provocative titles and on topics like defending accused paedophiles and cross-examining child witnesses. Some of the legal papers authored by Dennis. ( ABC News / supplied ) "You need to watch the child witness carefully and assess matters such as intelligence, level of vocabulary and articulation, degree of self-confidence, general demeanour," he wrote in 2017. One lawyer who knew Dennis for more than a decade said he was "not shocked" by the charges because he had a reputation for sexual harassment and aggression towards women. "It's one of those situations where, and I know I'm not the only person who's thought about this, I think a lot of us in retrospect are like, 'This was actually f***ing obvious,'" he said. Three lawyers told the ABC about an incident where Dennis was intoxicated at the 2012 Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS) Christmas party in Sydney, when he lunged at a woman with an open fist. He was then banned from ALS Christmas parties. Barrister Charles Waterstreet, who worked at Forbes alongside Dennis for more than a decade until facing his own sexual misconduct allegations, described his former colleague as "very ambitious" but "an oddball". "He loved a drink, especially on Friday nights," he said. "He sort of became another personality." Forbes Chambers is on the 11th floor of a building overlooking Sydney's Hyde Park. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) In 2011, Dennis began hosting legal conferences to raise funds for his charity, Reasonable Cause, that pledged to help "disadvantaged young Cambodians to further their education". Tickets cost $450, and the guest list included magistrates, silks and politicians, according to the 2024 invitation. In interviews with more than 20 sitting Forbes barristers, some were quick to defend their late colleague — insinuating the evidence was thin, based on industry rumours, and one said they did not think his charity work should be "smeared". "It did such good work. I don't think it was connected … to some sexual interest," they said. However, despite some celebrating his work and attending his legal conferences, many could not name the charity the money went to. The largest recipient of Dennis's fundraising was Sunrise Cambodia — a high-profile children's charity founded by Adelaide-born Geraldine Cox. Cox has spent decades crisscrossing the globe, and according to her 2011 report, delivering speeches to company executives in the United Arab Emirates, government officials in Australia, private schools, and lawyers like Dennis. "I flew to Sydney to address a group of lawyers at an event arranged by sponsor Mark Dennis, where over $14,000 was raised. Who said lawyers do not have hearts!" Cox wrote. Her work has been celebrated internationally. She has won awards, been praised by Australian media and rubbed shoulders with Hollywood celebrities and Australian prime ministers. Geraldine Cox's work has brought her into contact with the likes of Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt and Anthony Albanese. ( ABC News / supplied ) Starting in 2008, Dennis personally sponsored a handful of children at Sunrise whom he visited in the orphanages each year. Over time, he backed the whole organisation — raising at least $340,000 in seven years through the legal conferences. In 2010, he also began funding and attending Sunrise's annual beach holidays to Sihanoukville, a once-sleepy Cambodian coastal town now filled with scam compounds and casinos. Itineraries for these trips obtained by the ABC show the children played football, shared meals, performed concerts and socialised with sponsors, including Dennis. Photographs from these trips show Dennis on the beach, and hugging and playing with young children at the hotel. There is no suggestion the photographs are sexual. Dennis playing with children during one of the Sunrise trips to Sihanoukville. ( ABC News / supplied ) A spokesperson for Sunrise said sponsors were not permitted to initiate contact with children. "However, if a child comes running at a sponsor for a hug, the sponsor is not expected to push them away as this can be very emotionally damaging to a kid who may actually feel safe for the first time in his/her life," they said. A former Sunrise employee told the ABC it was during one of these beach trips that Dennis was swimming when he went under the water and touched her leg in a sexual manner. "I felt really afraid," she said. "I kicked Mark off. I was very terrified. He apologised later." A Sunrise spokesperson said the charity did not know about this allegation and was "very sorry to hear this". "Had they reported this, we could and would have dealt with it at the time," the spokesperson said. The woman did not complain formally, but said staff were concerned about Dennis's behaviour and agreed they needed to be "careful" around him to "protect the kids". Geraldine Cox (second from left) and Dennis (seated with arms crossed) on a beach at Sihanoukville. ( Supplied ) The same former employee said she was also concerned about Dennis's behaviour towards an autistic teenage girl living in Sunrise, whom he regularly tried to come close to, and touched her breasts. She said she saw Dennis entering the girls' and boys' bedrooms at Sunrise, but staff felt there was nothing they could do "because he's a big sponsor" and therefore did not report this. Eng Sopheak, who lived at Sunrise from the age of five and then worked as Cox's personal driver, also said he witnessed Dennis regularly entering the girls' dormitories. "I was personally worried," he said, because men were typically not allowed to enter the dormitories. Eng Sopheak became Cox's personal driver after living at Sunrise as a child. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Sopheak said there needed to be greater separation between sponsors and children. "My recommendation to sponsors is just that they donate the money, but they don't need to have a relationship with the child," he said. A spokesperson for Sunrise said dormitories were private areas and as of last year, sponsors were no longer invited to Sihanoukville. They said they had plans to phase out individual child sponsorship but did not specify when. However, Sunrise's website still allows sponsors to preference the age and gender of children whom they can visit for $50 per month. By 2018, Dennis was appointed chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered Australian charity managing donations for Sunrise at the time. In this role, Dennis was involved in almost every aspect of Sunrise's operations — managing redundancies, approving wages, signing off on hiring policies and even becoming a 49 per cent shareholder of Sunrise's Sihanoukville property, which was valued at more than $US3 million in 2017. "He was the big boss," said Yi Soksan, who held senior positions at Sunrise between 2011 and 2018. Soksan said staff were told by Cox to "just trust" Dennis because he was a donor and lawyer, and recalls her saying: "He's my friend, he's one of the big donors and sponsors. He loves Sunrise." Yi Soksan says he knew Dennis as "the big boss". ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) "She advised us, 'He's also the lawyer, so he understands, you know, the rules, the laws. So, just trust him.'" Cox said she had no recollection of discussing Dennis with staff. While she considered him a friend, she said she had no knowledge of his personal life and never witnessed any bad behaviour. While chairman, Dennis wielded power over Cox. In an email sent in November 2019, Cox asked for his approval for Sunrise to cover personal expenses. "Since I offered to reduce my salary … around the time you took over, Mark, I am finding it increasingly difficult to have any sort of normal life," she wrote. While their relationship was financial and social, it was also fractious. Emails show Dennis privately described Cox as an "unreliable historian" and "something of a compulsive spender" — descriptions Cox said she could not comment on. snapshot.title: Mark Dennis went from top silk and charity 'big boss' to accused predator
snapshot.evidenceText: Mark Dennis built a reputation defending accused criminals before he himself became the accused. ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon ) Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide. There is a small terrace house in Sydney's inner west that always gave builder Chad Loxsom an uneasy feeling. "I've been in thousands and thousands of people's houses," he said, but this one "was a little bit strange". The Leichhardt property belonged to Mark Dennis SC, a criminal defence barrister, who Loxsom said had a "weird demeanour" and was "just odd". But what he saw inside is what gnawed at him for years. "All over the walls of his house, he had dozens upon dozens upon dozens of pictures of him with little kids," he said. In some photos, Loxsom said Dennis was hugging shirtless children. Loxsom shared his suspicions with an electrician. "His gut was this guy was doing something bad with kids as well," he said. The electrician first noticed the "come back with a warrant" doormat, and then the large mirror fixed to the ceiling above Dennis's bed. But, like Loxsom, what really alarmed him was the sheer volume of photographs in almost every room, even the kitchen. "It was just disturbing. Like, these kids weren't happy," he said. Dennis was found dead in his home in Sydney's inner west in February. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) Eventually, Loxsom decided to make a report with the child protection hotline. "I didn't do it straight away, which now I regret," he said. In January, Dennis came onto the police's radar again when he was searched at Sydney Airport as he returned from a trip to Cambodia. What was found on his devices led to his arrest, a raid of his house, and child abuse material charges from evidence prosecutors described as "disturbing". Dennis was released on bail, and soon after, was found dead in his home . Last week, Background Briefing and ABC Investigations revealed his death did not bring the police investigation to an end . Codenamed Operation Queenstown, Cambodian and Australian national police have been quietly probing Dennis's network and links to famous children's charity Sunrise Cambodia all year. The ABC travelled to Cambodia in June to retrace Dennis's steps to reveal the inside story of how an accused predator accumulated power within a high-profile charity and gained access to vulnerable children. In an investigation that combines a tranche of internal documents with dozens of interviews, the ABC can reveal allegations that Dennis sexually harassed a former Sunrise staff member and made teenage girls feel uncomfortable by excessive touching. Listen to Dark Menace , a new three-part investigative podcast from Background Briefing and ABC Investigations, via the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts. The claims raise important questions for all children's charities that must balance the need to fundraise with child safety, as multiple former Sunrise staff say they saw Dennis's bad behaviour but felt they could not report it. "They saw this," one former staff member told the ABC through a translator. "But they could not do anything because he's a big sponsor." A spokesperson for Sunrise said they were never aware of any complaints about Dennis and police had told them no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of his victims. The charity defended its child protection policies, saying the children always came first. Dennis grew up in a large family on Sydney's northern beaches, and by 2001, was a criminal defence barrister with a room at the prestigious Forbes Chambers. "You don't get to go to Forbes unless you are absolutely brilliant," says one solicitor who briefed Dennis. "He was one of those people who was married to the profession." His nickname was "Dark Menace" — a play on words that several acquaintances said reflected his personality and black sense of humour, exemplified by his "WASNTME" personalised number plate. Across his career, Dennis was known to have mentored junior lawyers and published papers under provocative titles and on topics like defending accused paedophiles and cross-examining child witnesses. Some of the legal papers authored by Dennis. ( ABC News / supplied ) "You need to watch the child witness carefully and assess matters such as intelligence, level of vocabulary and articulation, degree of self-confidence, general demeanour," he wrote in 2017. One lawyer who knew Dennis for more than a decade said he was "not shocked" by the charges because he had a reputation for sexual harassment and aggression towards women. "It's one of those situations where, and I know I'm not the only person who's thought about this, I think a lot of us in retrospect are like, 'This was actually f***ing obvious,'" he said. Three lawyers told the ABC about an incident where Dennis was intoxicated at the 2012 Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS) Christmas party in Sydney, when he lunged at a woman with an open fist. He was then banned from ALS Christmas parties. Barrister Charles Waterstreet, who worked at Forbes alongside Dennis for more than a decade until facing his own sexual misconduct allegations, described his former colleague as "very ambitious" but "an oddball". "He loved a drink, especially on Friday nights," he said. "He sort of became another personality." Forbes Chambers is on the 11th floor of a building overlooking Sydney's Hyde Park. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) In 2011, Dennis began hosting legal conferences to raise funds for his charity, Reasonable Cause, that pledged to help "disadvantaged young Cambodians to further their education". Tickets cost $450, and the guest list included magistrates, silks and politicians, according to the 2024 invitation. In interviews with more than 20 sitting Forbes barristers, some were quick to defend their late colleague — insinuating the evidence was thin, based on industry rumours, and one said they did not think his charity work should be "smeared". "It did such good work. I don't think it was connected … to some sexual interest," they said. However, despite some celebrating his work and attending his legal conferences, many could not name the charity the money went to. The largest recipient of Dennis's fundraising was Sunrise Cambodia — a high-profile children's charity founded by Adelaide-born Geraldine Cox. Cox has spent decades crisscrossing the globe, and according to her 2011 report, delivering speeches to company executives in the United Arab Emirates, government officials in Australia, private schools, and lawyers like Dennis. "I flew to Sydney to address a group of lawyers at an event arranged by sponsor Mark Dennis, where over $14,000 was raised. Who said lawyers do not have hearts!" Cox wrote. Her work has been celebrated internationally. She has won awards, been praised by Australian media and rubbed shoulders with Hollywood celebrities and Australian prime ministers. Geraldine Cox's work has brought her into contact with the likes of Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt and Anthony Albanese. Dennis playing with children during one of the Sunrise trips to Sihanoukville. ( ABC News / supplied ) A spokesperson for Sunrise said sponsors were not permitted to initiate contact with children. "However, if a child comes running at a sponsor for a hug, the sponsor is not expected to push them away as this can be very emotionally damaging to a kid who may actually feel safe for the first time in his/her life," they said. "I felt really afraid," she said. "I kicked Mark off. I was very terrified. He apologised later." A Sunrise spokesperson said the charity did not know about this allegation and was "very sorry to hear this". "Had they reported this, we could and would have dealt with it at the time," the spokesperson said. Geraldine Cox (second from left) and Dennis (seated with arms crossed) on a beach at Sihanoukville. She said she saw Dennis entering the girls' and boys' bedrooms at Sunrise, but staff felt there was nothing they could do "because he's a big sponsor" and therefore did not report this. Eng Sopheak, who lived at Sunrise from the age of five and then worked as Cox's personal driver, also said he witnessed Dennis regularly entering the girls' dormitories. "I was personally worried," he said, because men were typically not allowed to enter the dormitories. Eng Sopheak became Cox's personal driver after living at Sunrise as a child. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Sopheak said there needed to be greater separation between sponsors and children. "My recommendation to sponsors is just that they donate the money, but they don't need to have a relationship with the child," he said. A spokesperson for Sunrise said dormitories were private areas and as of last year, sponsors were no longer invited to Sihanoukville. They said they had plans to phase out individual child sponsorship but did not specify when. However, Sunrise's website still allows sponsors to preference the age and gender of children whom they can visit for $50 per month. By 2018, Dennis was appointed chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered Australian charity managing donations for Sunrise at the time. In this role, Dennis was involved in almost every aspect of Sunrise's operations — managing redundancies, approving wages, signing off on hiring policies and even becoming a 49 per cent shareholder of Sunrise's Sihanoukville property, which was valued at more than $US3 million in 2017. "He was the big boss," said Yi Soksan, who held senior positions at Sunrise between 2011 and 2018. Yi Soksan says he knew Dennis as "the big boss". ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) "She advised us, 'He's also the lawyer, so he understands, you know, the rules, the laws. So, just trust him.'" representative.title: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner
representative.author: Asharq Al Awsat

snapshot.title: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner
snapshot.evidenceText: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner Thousands of residents of Syria’s Hasakah province rallied after Friday prayers to demand state authority across the province and the release of detainees and people forcibly disappeared in prisons run by the dissolved Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). In scenes described as the “greatest celebration” and the “Hasakah flood,” protesters gathered in Freedom Square in the city center under the slogan “Friday of the Syrian Flag.” They called for state sovereignty and a stronger presence for its institutions, a day after the national flag was raised on the square’s tallest flagpole before a large gathering of residents and officials. The protests capped a week of rapid developments in Hasakah over the implementation of a Jan. 29, 2026, agreement between the Syrian government and the SDF. The deal called for the former Kurdish Autonomous Administration’s civilian, security and military institutions to be integrated into state structures. Arabs, who make up the province’s population majority, have complained that the SDF remains dominant despite its announced dissolution in late August. Residents began arriving early in the morning from Hasakah’s al-Aziziya, al-Kallasa and al-Nashwa neighborhoods and from other towns, including al-Shaddadi, Markada, al-Hol and al-Arisha. They gathered outside Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Mosque in Ghweiran before marching after Friday prayers to the city’s main square, known as Liberation Square, carrying Syrian national flags. Government internal security forces reinforced their presence across the city from midnight Thursday to protect protesters, residents and public and private property. The deployment followed indiscriminate gunfire by “outlaw” gunmen in several neighborhoods. Activists accused a Kurdish group referred to as “Revolutionary Popular” of stirring tensions to impose a curfew and block the demonstrations. Internal security forces restored calm that night, Syria’s Al-Ikhbariya television channel reported. Protesters carried national flags, photographs of SDF detainees and pictures of “martyrs of the Syrian revolution.” They chanted, “One, one ... the Syrian people are one,” seeking to reassure the province’s Arab, Kurdish and Christian communities that all were subject to the law and equal in rights and duties. Their demands included extending state sovereignty and authority across Hasakah, restoring state institutions and making them operational, releasing detainees forcibly disappeared in SDF prisons, and allowing their sons to join the internal security forces. They also called for an end to the province’s dual authorities and the presence of Revolutionary Youth. Videos posted on social media showed protesters removing Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and SDF flags and banners from streets and buildings. Sohaib al-Yaarubi, an activist from the province’s Arab tribes and one of those who called for the protests, said the message was clear: the overwhelming majority in Hasakah supported the Syrian state, wanted its sovereignty extended across the province and wanted only the flag of the Syrian Arab Republic flown there. Yaarubi told Asharq Al-Awsat the demonstrations were “successful” and the demands “patriotic and legitimate.” He said there were no tensions or provocations apart from one incident involving Revolutionary Youth members, which protesters defused. Ibrahim al-Halabi, another activist from the province’s Arab tribes, described the crowds in Liberation Square as “awe-inspiring, beautiful and truly wonderful.” The peaceful demonstrations lasted about two hours. He said the raising of the national flag brought overwhelming joy, stirring emotions that recalled the early days of the Syrian revolution against the former government in 2011. “Some described the demonstrations and the crowds in Liberation Square as the greatest celebration in Hasakah, a city denied the chance to celebrate the victory achieved when the ousted government fell nearly two years ago,” Halabi said. Delegations from other provinces, including Deir Ezzor, joined the Hasakah protests. Similar demonstrations took place in several provinces in support of its residents’ demands. The Friday rallies followed Thursday’s raising of the national flag on the tallest flagpole in central Hasakah before a large gathering of residents and officials. Government officials also inspected the courthouse to “create suitable conditions for making the judicial system operational.” Internal security forces had deployed around the courthouse after members of the dissolved SDF vacated their positions there, while the government strengthened its security presence across the city. On Tuesday, the SDF’s counterterrorism forces had handed over their positions to internal security forces. Maj. Gen. Abdul Qader Tahhan, head of Syria’s General Intelligence Service, and Brig. Gen. Abdul Rahman al-Dabbagh, head of foreign intelligence, subsequently arrived in Hasakah with a large security delegation. The developments followed mass peaceful protests after prayers the previous Friday in several towns and cities across Hasakah province, demanding state authority and a stronger presence for its institutions throughout the province. Washington Targets Hezbollah’s Alternative Funding Networks The United States is stepping up efforts to track alternative financing channels used by Hezbollah as tighter sanctions threaten its traditional sources of funding, particularly Iranian money that has long underpinned the group’s military and security capabilities and political influence in Lebanon. Washington’s campaign extends beyond restricting Iranian transfers to tracing foreign funding networks and cross-border commercial activities that Hezbollah could use to compensate for any decline in Tehran’s support. A Reuters report last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million in cash from Iran the previous month to assist tens of thousands of families displaced by the war prompted a response from the US State Department. The department expressed doubt that the money had reached Hezbollah but reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining pressure on the group’s funding sources through sanctions, while supporting the legitimate Lebanese government’s efforts to rebuild southern Lebanon. Sami Nader, director of the Middle East Institute for Strategic Affairs, described the measures as part of a new round of US sanctions aimed at tightening financial pressure on Iran and its regional affiliates. “The issue is not specifically Hezbollah, but primarily Iran,” Nader told Asharq Al-Awsat, pointing to a recent US announcement describing Hezbollah as an integral part of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps. Nader said Tehran had developed alternative channels to circumvent financial restrictions, particularly through gold and cryptocurrencies. He described an expanding network of such activities across the region, with links to Iran and Hezbollah. The latest sanctions are designed to target these alternative mechanisms, he explained. Nader added that if cryptocurrency offices linked to these networks are found to exist, Lebanese authorities would likely be asked to shut them down and take action against them, while also tightening oversight of gold transactions. Hezbollah has long relied on multiple funding sources, particularly under previous Lebanese administrations that turned a blind eye to billions of dollars reaching the group, including through official border crossings. Economist Antoine Farah identified four principal sources of financing: The first was direct Iranian support, provided through regular transfers from Tehran. The second involved illicit activities, particularly drug smuggling and the Captagon trade, which Farah said Hezbollah had engaged in both inside Lebanon and abroad, notably in several Latin American countries. The third consisted of substantial donations from Shiite financiers and supporters around the world. The fourth was a network of front businesses established to generate additional revenue, launder money and conceal the origins and destinations of funds. Farah told Asharq Al-Awsat that Hezbollah’s ability to draw on most of these sources had declined considerably, while the group faced mounting pressure from legislative and regulatory measures being strengthened in Lebanon. Farah highlighted amendments being introduced to Law No. 44 on combating money laundering and terrorist financing, particularly provisions requiring the identification of the ultimate beneficial owners of companies and commercial enterprises. Identifying who ultimately benefits from commercial activities, while tracing the origins and destinations of funds, would help restrict the operations of front businesses established by Hezbollah, he explained. Farah also pointed to measures being taken by Banque du Liban, Lebanon’s central bank, to regulate currency exchange dealers and money transfer companies. He said the measures were making it increasingly difficult to exploit these sectors to transfer money and channel financing to Hezbollah. Syrian Security Forces Step Up anti-ISIS Operations, Pursue Former Regime Loyalists Syrian security forces have intensified operations against ISIS cells following a deadly September bus attack near Masyaf in central Syria, while separately pursuing former regime operatives accused of crimes against civilians. Within a week, authorities announced the dismantling of an ISIS cell in Homs province, following the arrest of the group’s alleged military commander there. Seven former regime suspects were also detained as part of transitional justice efforts. The Internal Security Forces announced that raids in the Houla area of northern Homs, conducted with the General Intelligence Directorate, had dismantled an ISIS-linked cell and foiled planned attacks on places of worship and security patrols. Two suspects were arrested and two explosive devices were seized. Preliminary investigations indicated that the detainees had received and transported explosives and monitored potential targets as part of plans to incite unrest and undermine security. One suspect was caught attempting to plant an explosive device on a railway track, authorities reported. Investigations are continuing to identify other cell members and their connections. The operation followed the arrest about three days earlier of Khaled Raed Bayrouni, known as Abu Hassan Doshka, in Hujayra, near Damascus. The Interior Ministry described him as ISIS’s operational arm in Homs and the group’s overall military commander in its so-called Homs province. Bayrouni is accused of planning and overseeing bombings and sectarian attacks, including an explosion at an Alawite mosque in Homs that killed eight people in late 2025. Authorities also launched raids and arrests following a Sept. 27 attack on a bus transporting workers near the Masyaf bypass bridge, on the road linking Masyaf and Homs, that killed seven civilians. Despite ISIS’s territorial defeat in Syria and Iraq, its small cells remain a security threat, exploiting instability and security gaps, particularly in remote areas. In early October, the international coalition against ISIS pledged more than $75 million to support Syria’s counterterrorism efforts, including measures to address security vulnerabilities and dismantle dormant cells. Separately, the Defense Ministry reported Saturday that a Syrian army soldier had died of wounds sustained in a shooting by unidentified gunmen Tuesday evening in Buqrus, eastern Deir Ezzor province. Two customs patrol members were also wounded when unidentified attackers opened fire near Izraa bridge in Daraa province as officers escorted a transit convoy, the General Authority for Ports and Customs announced Saturday. In a parallel operation, security forces detained seven former regime suspects in Masyaf, Hama province, accusing them of serious abuses against civilians. Nabil Adnan Ismail and Ghazi Mohammed Ismail allegedly commanded groups within militias affiliated with the former Air Force Intelligence Directorate and participated in kidnappings, looting and massacres, including violence in Aqrab village. They also face extortion allegations. Brothers Taher Youssef al-Mohammed and Talal Youssef al-Mohammed, who served in Air Force Intelligence and the Scientific Studies and Research Center, are accused of repression, arrests and exploiting access to detainees’ files to extort their families. Faisal Badour, nicknamed “Tiger Cub” for his alleged brutality toward civilians, joined armed militias in 2012 and participated in former regime military operations in Hama and Aleppo provinces. Another detainee, Assef Salameh, served as a noncommissioned officer at defense factories until 2018. Authorities had earlier arrested Shaheen Hamdan al-Shaheen, a founder of the Air Force Intelligence-linked Shaheen Regiment militia. He is accused of involvement in massacres in eastern Hama and along the Athriya–Raqqa road in 2017. His militia allegedly committed killings, arrests, torture and destruction in Palmyra and Deir Ezzor province through 2019. representative.title: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner
representative.author: Asharq Al Awsat

snapshot.title: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner
snapshot.evidenceText: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner Thousands of residents of Syria’s Hasakah province rallied after Friday prayers to demand state authority across the province and the release of detainees and people forcibly disappeared in prisons run by the dissolved Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). In scenes described as the “greatest celebration” and the “Hasakah flood,” protesters gathered in Freedom Square in the city center under the slogan “Friday of the Syrian Flag.” They called for state sovereignty and a stronger presence for its institutions, a day after the national flag was raised on the square’s tallest flagpole before a large gathering of residents and officials. The protests capped a week of rapid developments in Hasakah over the implementation of a Jan. 29, 2026, agreement between the Syrian government and the SDF. The deal called for the former Kurdish Autonomous Administration’s civilian, security and military institutions to be integrated into state structures. Arabs, who make up the province’s population majority, have complained that the SDF remains dominant despite its announced dissolution in late August. Residents began arriving early in the morning from Hasakah’s al-Aziziya, al-Kallasa and al-Nashwa neighborhoods and from other towns, including al-Shaddadi, Markada, al-Hol and al-Arisha. They gathered outside Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Mosque in Ghweiran before marching after Friday prayers to the city’s main square, known as Liberation Square, carrying Syrian national flags. Government internal security forces reinforced their presence across the city from midnight Thursday to protect protesters, residents and public and private property. The deployment followed indiscriminate gunfire by “outlaw” gunmen in several neighborhoods. Activists accused a Kurdish group referred to as “Revolutionary Popular” of stirring tensions to impose a curfew and block the demonstrations. Internal security forces restored calm that night, Syria’s Al-Ikhbariya television channel reported. Protesters carried national flags, photographs of SDF detainees and pictures of “martyrs of the Syrian revolution.” They chanted, “One, one ... the Syrian people are one,” seeking to reassure the province’s Arab, Kurdish and Christian communities that all were subject to the law and equal in rights and duties. Their demands included extending state sovereignty and authority across Hasakah, restoring state institutions and making them operational, releasing detainees forcibly disappeared in SDF prisons, and allowing their sons to join the internal security forces. They also called for an end to the province’s dual authorities and the presence of Revolutionary Youth. Videos posted on social media showed protesters removing Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and SDF flags and banners from streets and buildings. Sohaib al-Yaarubi, an activist from the province’s Arab tribes and one of those who called for the protests, said the message was clear: the overwhelming majority in Hasakah supported the Syrian state, wanted its sovereignty extended across the province and wanted only the flag of the Syrian Arab Republic flown there. Yaarubi told Asharq Al-Awsat the demonstrations were “successful” and the demands “patriotic and legitimate.” He said there were no tensions or provocations apart from one incident involving Revolutionary Youth members, which protesters defused. Ibrahim al-Halabi, another activist from the province’s Arab tribes, described the crowds in Liberation Square as “awe-inspiring, beautiful and truly wonderful.” The peaceful demonstrations lasted about two hours. He said the raising of the national flag brought overwhelming joy, stirring emotions that recalled the early days of the Syrian revolution against the former government in 2011. “Some described the demonstrations and the crowds in Liberation Square as the greatest celebration in Hasakah, a city denied the chance to celebrate the victory achieved when the ousted government fell nearly two years ago,” Halabi said. Delegations from other provinces, including Deir Ezzor, joined the Hasakah protests. Similar demonstrations took place in several provinces in support of its residents’ demands. The Friday rallies followed Thursday’s raising of the national flag on the tallest flagpole in central Hasakah before a large gathering of residents and officials. Government officials also inspected the courthouse to “create suitable conditions for making the judicial system operational.” Internal security forces had deployed around the courthouse after members of the dissolved SDF vacated their positions there, while the government strengthened its security presence across the city. On Tuesday, the SDF’s counterterrorism forces had handed over their positions to internal security forces. Maj. Gen. Abdul Qader Tahhan, head of Syria’s General Intelligence Service, and Brig. Gen. Abdul Rahman al-Dabbagh, head of foreign intelligence, subsequently arrived in Hasakah with a large security delegation. The developments followed mass peaceful protests after prayers the previous Friday in several towns and cities across Hasakah province, demanding state authority and a stronger presence for its institutions throughout the province. Washington Targets Hezbollah’s Alternative Funding Networks The United States is stepping up efforts to track alternative financing channels used by Hezbollah as tighter sanctions threaten its traditional sources of funding, particularly Iranian money that has long underpinned the group’s military and security capabilities and political influence in Lebanon. Washington’s campaign extends beyond restricting Iranian transfers to tracing foreign funding networks and cross-border commercial activities that Hezbollah could use to compensate for any decline in Tehran’s support. A Reuters report last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million in cash from Iran the previous month to assist tens of thousands of families displaced by the war prompted a response from the US State Department. The department expressed doubt that the money had reached Hezbollah but reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining pressure on the group’s funding sources through sanctions, while supporting the legitimate Lebanese government’s efforts to rebuild southern Lebanon. Sami Nader, director of the Middle East Institute for Strategic Affairs, described the measures as part of a new round of US sanctions aimed at tightening financial pressure on Iran and its regional affiliates. “The issue is not specifically Hezbollah, but primarily Iran,” Nader told Asharq Al-Awsat, pointing to a recent US announcement describing Hezbollah as an integral part of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps. Nader said Tehran had developed alternative channels to circumvent financial restrictions, particularly through gold and cryptocurrencies. He described an expanding network of such activities across the region, with links to Iran and Hezbollah. The latest sanctions are designed to target these alternative mechanisms, he explained. Nader added that if cryptocurrency offices linked to these networks are found to exist, Lebanese authorities would likely be asked to shut them down and take action against them, while also tightening oversight of gold transactions. Hezbollah has long relied on multiple funding sources, particularly under previous Lebanese administrations that turned a blind eye to billions of dollars reaching the group, including through official border crossings. Economist Antoine Farah identified four principal sources of financing: The first was direct Iranian support, provided through regular transfers from Tehran. The second involved illicit activities, particularly drug smuggling and the Captagon trade, which Farah said Hezbollah had engaged in both inside Lebanon and abroad, notably in several Latin American countries. The third consisted of substantial donations from Shiite financiers and supporters around the world. The fourth was a network of front businesses established to generate additional revenue, launder money and conceal the origins and destinations of funds. Farah told Asharq Al-Awsat that Hezbollah’s ability to draw on most of these sources had declined considerably, while the group faced mounting pressure from legislative and regulatory measures being strengthened in Lebanon. Farah highlighted amendments being introduced to Law No. 44 on combating money laundering and terrorist financing, particularly provisions requiring the identification of the ultimate beneficial owners of companies and commercial enterprises. Identifying who ultimately benefits from commercial activities, while tracing the origins and destinations of funds, would help restrict the operations of front businesses established by Hezbollah, he explained. Farah also pointed to measures being taken by Banque du Liban, Lebanon’s central bank, to regulate currency exchange dealers and money transfer companies. He said the measures were making it increasingly difficult to exploit these sectors to transfer money and channel financing to Hezbollah. Within a week, authorities announced the dismantling of an ISIS cell in Homs province, following the arrest of the group’s alleged military commander there. Seven former regime suspects were also detained as part of transitional justice efforts. The Internal Security Forces announced that raids in the Houla area of northern Homs, conducted with the General Intelligence Directorate, had dismantled an ISIS-linked cell and foiled planned attacks on places of worship and security patrols. Two suspects were arrested and two explosive devices were seized. Preliminary investigations indicated that the detainees had received and transported explosives and monitored potential targets as part of plans to incite unrest and undermine security. One suspect was caught attempting to plant an explosive device on a railway track, authorities reported. Investigations are continuing to identify other cell members and their connections. Bayrouni is accused of planning and overseeing bombings and sectarian attacks, including an explosion at an Alawite mosque in Homs that killed eight people in late 2025. Authorities also launched raids and arrests following a Sept. 27 attack on a bus transporting workers near the Masyaf bypass bridge, on the road linking Masyaf and Homs, that killed seven civilians. Despite ISIS’s territorial defeat in Syria and Iraq, its small cells remain a security threat, exploiting instability and security gaps, particularly in remote areas. In early October, the international coalition against ISIS pledged more than $75 million to support Syria’s counterterrorism efforts, including measures to address security vulnerabilities and dismantle dormant cells. They also face extortion allegations. His militia allegedly committed killings, arrests, torture and destruction in Palmyra and Deir Ezzor province through 2019. Students of Sri Ramana Vidyalaya Matriculation School in Tambaram tend to the plants at the terrace garden Every second Sunday, Sri Ramana Vidyalaya Matriculation School in Tambaram turns into a mini-market with the management opening its gates for farmers to come and sell their organic produce. For the last three months, Thalir Karima Velaan Santhai has enabled at least 30 farmers from different villages to sell their bounty, parents of the school and neighbours being their biggest patrons. The school management looks at this initiative as an extension of its eco-club activities where it operates a terrace garden maintained by the students. The garden has evolved with every passing year and currently has a good variety of vegetable growing plants. Students of classes VII to IX have one period a week allotted in their timetable to engage in terrace garden work, where they till the soil, plant saplings in used containers that serve as pots, water them and do all other things to ensure they grow. Workshops and other engaging activities are conducted at the farmers market “This time, our produce has not been great, but whatever we get is shared among students who take it home. Recently, when we got a decent amount of lady’s finger and cluster beans, we left it to the students to decide who wants to take it,” says V. Selvamani, correspondent of the school. When students have a free period, they are encouraged to spend time in the terrace garden. Traditional rice varieties, cold-pressed oils, pulses, organic gardening inputs and local pottery are among the stalls at the market. Selvamani says they charge a nominal amount for arranging tables and chairs, and the larger goal is to eliminate middle men. To encourage visitors to understand what goes into their plate, the organisers conduct various knowledge sharing sessions. For example, in the last few months, they had a session on tips for terrace gardening and free seed sharing, and another on making seed Ganesha using clay. This time, there’s a special workshop, “21 Plate Balanced Meal for 7 Days,” from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. by culinary artisan Akila Kunalan. Like other farmers market happening in the city, visitors are encouraged to bring cloth bags. For registration, call 97909 72612 or 99403 37100. representative.title: Phantom land, false signature: How agents allegedly duped migrant worker quota system | Malaysiakini
representative.author: B Nantha Kumar

snapshot.title: Phantom land, false signature: How agents allegedly duped migrant worker quota system | Malaysiakini
snapshot.evidenceText: In a small office near Jalan Makbar Darat, Kuantan, Nazlan Mokhtar, 57, sits in his chair as usual. The secretary of Koperasi Kijang Mas Negeri Pahang Berhad has spent years managing the affairs of the cooperative’s thousands of members. However, for the past few months, that chair has felt much heavier to sit in. This is no ordinary tale of a village cooperative. This is the story of how a quota of 1,125 migrant workers, allegedly worth millions of ringgit on the black market of labour trading, was approved under the name of an Orang Asli cooperative - without the full knowledge of those who were supposed to sign off on it, through questionable methods, and with the possibility that the quota was misused. A Malaysiakini investigation revealed application documents built upon non-existent land acreage, agreements with an unlicensed company, the cooperative chairperson's signature allegedly being forged, and conflicting marriage records for a company director between two government agencies. In a small office near Jalan Makbar Darat, Kuantan, Nazlan Mokhtar, 57, sits in his chair as usual. The secretary of Koperasi Kijang Mas Negeri Pahang Berhad has spent years managing the affairs of the cooperative’s thousands of members. However, for the past few months, that chair has felt much heavier to sit in. This is no ordinary tale of a village cooperative. This is the story of how a quota of 1,125 migrant workers, allegedly worth millions of ringgit on the black market of labour trading, was approved under the name of an Orang Asli cooperative - without the full knowledge of those who were supposed to sign off on it, through questionable methods, and with the possibility that the quota was misused. A Malaysiakini investigation revealed application documents built upon non-existent land acreage, agreements with an unlicensed company, the cooperative chairperson's signature allegedly being forged, and conflicting marriage records for a company director between two government agencies. Meanwhile, the approved quota never brought a single worker to the cooperative’s land. "I’m stressed out," Nazlan said, half-joking, half-serious, during an interview with Malaysiakini . This story begins not with success, but with failure. The roots of Koperasi Kijang Mas can be traced back to the late 1980s, when it was known as Korporasi Orang Asli Maju Rompin. It was subsequently administered under the Orang Asli Affairs Department (JHEOA) and later the Orang Asli Development Department (Jakoa). According to Nazlan ( above ), in 2023, the cooperative applied for a migrant worker quota on its own through its committee member, but the application failed. For a cooperative already struggling with financial difficulties while its membership continued to shrink, any opportunity for an injection of manpower and new income looked like a way out. It was during that critical situation, according to Nazlan, that two individuals emerged in the cooperative's affairs. They were an Indian national man and a Malaysian woman. In the interview, Nazlan referred to the man as “Mr G” as the main agent, and the woman as "Ms K", stressing that these were not their real names. According to Nazlan, after the two came into the picture, the quota matters slipped out of the cooperative’s full control. "First, we applied for a migrant worker quota but were rejected. Then, they came in as agents to assist us. They handled everything, including preparing the application documents until more than 1,100 quotas were approved," he said. According to Nazlan, Mr G handled the second application entirely. As a result, a quota of 1,125 migrant workers was approved under the name of Koperasi Kijang Mas. However, there were several suspicious matters in the process. A document Malaysiakini sighted showed that an "Agreement Deed" was signed on Aug 1, 2024, between the cooperative and Agensi Pekerjaan Uni Jobs Sdn Bhd - a company with an address at Plaza Prima, Jalan Klang Lama, Kuala Lumpur. In the document, Uni Jobs was named the "contractor" while the cooperative was named the "landowner". The agreement appeared to give Uni Jobs the right to bring in migrant workers, manage them, and fulfil all rules, requirements, and welfare of the migrant workers, including all government regulations and wages. In return, the contractor was required to harvest rubber from the cooperative’s land. However, a check with the Human Resources Ministry revealed that Uni Jobs did not possess a valid Private Employment Agency (APS) Licence. This licence is a mandatory requirement under the law for any entity wishing to operate as an employment agency. Meanwhile, Nazlan claimed that the signature appearing above the cooperative chairperson’s name on the document was not his. In a police report lodged by Nazlan on behalf of the cooperative, he accused Mr G and Ms K, among other things, of forging the signature. Malaysiakini could not independently verify the signature forgery allegations. Additionally, Nazlan said the cooperative chairperson had never attended any interview session with the authorities for the migrant worker quota application. Another anomaly in the agreement document was the land size claimed to be owned by the cooperative. The document stated that the cooperative owned 4,500ha of land. The same figure is believed to have been used in the application handled by Uni Jobs to obtain the quota. However, that land size does not exist. Instead, Nazlan said, the actual size of the land cultivated by the cooperative for vegetable crops was only around 300 to 400 acres (121.4 to 161.9ha) - as seen by Malaysiakini when visiting the area. Besides the migrant worker quota issue, there were other anomalies surrounding the case. A search with the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM) found that Uni Jobs has two directors, both Malaysian citizens. Based on official documents from the Immigration Department, one of them is Mr G’s wife. However, a check by Malaysiakini with the National Registration Department (NRD) showed that the Malaysian woman was also married to a man of another nationality, and that marriage remained valid as they were not divorced. Malaysiakini has submitted official queries to the Home Ministry to clarify this discrepancy in records. Malaysiakini had also contacted Mr G, Ms K, both directors of Uni Jobs (including the woman alleged to be Mr G’s wife), and her lawful husband on Sept 1, 2026, to seek comments regarding the allegations against them, but has yet to receive a response. According to Nazlan, the real trouble began after the cooperative received approval for the quota. The cooperative waited for the workforce to arrive to develop their land, but days passed without certainty. When the cooperative tried to get the latest status on the workers, Ms K allegedly offered various excuses, including claiming that there were issues on the immigration side. As time went on without a single worker setting foot on the cooperative’s land, suspicions grew stronger. The cooperative eventually suspected that the two agents had illegally sold the quota to third parties and abused the cooperative’s name and status without any authorisation or legal power. "The quota of 1,125 migrant workers that was supposed to be used to develop the cooperative's land was issued and sold to third parties as a standalone commodity. "While the cooperative was merely a name on paper to validate the approval of the quota," he said. The real shock came when the Home Ministry itself contacted the cooperative. According to Nazlan, Home Ministry officers, together with Immigration Department officers, first came to Kuantan, and later requested cooperative representatives to attend a detailed interrogation session in Putrajaya. "When Home Ministry came to the office, they asked me, 'Do you know that these migrant workers have already entered the country?'" Nazlan asked, recalling the moment that changed everything. In Putrajaya, officers showed documents and interrogated the cooperative representatives. After determining that the cooperative had likely been duped, Home Ministry officers advised the cooperative to lodge a police report as a step to protect its own standing. On Jan 19, Nazlan lodged a report at the Travers police station in Brickfields, Kuala Lumpur. In the report, he denied the cooperative’s link to any involvement in the fraudulent activities, while also reporting the misuse and forgery of the cooperative's documents. He emphasised that the cooperative was not involved, did not sign any agreement, and received no payment or profit from the management or sale of the quota linked to the cooperative's name. Nazlan also requested the police to conduct a thorough investigation into Mr G, Ms K, and any other parties involved, as well as take legal action for offences of cheating, document forgery, breach of trust, and abetment. According to him, the actions caused reputational damage and legal risks to the cooperative. representative.title: Phantom land, false signature: How agents allegedly duped migrant worker quota system | Malaysiakini
representative.author: B Nantha Kumar

snapshot.title: Phantom land, false signature: How agents allegedly duped migrant worker quota system | Malaysiakini

The secretary of Koperasi Kijang Mas Negeri Pahang Berhad has spent years managing the affairs of the cooperative’s thousands of members. However, for the past few months, that chair has felt much heavier to sit in. This is no ordinary tale of a village cooperative. This is the story of how a quota of 1,125 migrant workers, allegedly worth millions of ringgit on the black market of labour trading, was approved under the name of an Orang Asli cooperative - without the full knowledge of those who were supposed to sign off on it, through questionable methods, and with the possibility that the quota was misused. A Malaysiakini investigation revealed application documents built upon non-existent land acreage, agreements with an unlicensed company, the cooperative chairperson's signature allegedly being forged, and conflicting marriage records for a company director between two government agencies. A Malaysiakini investigation revealed application documents built upon non-existent land acreage, agreements with an unlicensed company, the cooperative chairperson's signature allegedly being forged, and conflicting marriage records for a company director between two government agencies. Meanwhile, the approved quota never brought a single worker to the cooperative’s land. "I’m stressed out," Nazlan said, half-joking, half-serious, during an interview with Malaysiakini . This story begins not with success, but with failure. The roots of Koperasi Kijang Mas can be traced back to the late 1980s, when it was known as Korporasi Orang Asli Maju Rompin. It was subsequently administered under the Orang Asli Affairs Department (JHEOA) and later the Orang Asli Development Department (Jakoa). According to Nazlan ( above ), in 2023, the cooperative applied for a migrant worker quota on its own through its committee member, but the application failed. For a cooperative already struggling with financial difficulties while its membership continued to shrink, any opportunity for an injection of manpower and new income looked like a way out. It was during that critical situation, according to Nazlan, that two individuals emerged in the cooperative's affairs. They were an Indian national man and a Malaysian woman. In the interview, Nazlan referred to the man as “Mr G” as the main agent, and the woman as "Ms K", stressing that these were not their real names. According to Nazlan, after the two came into the picture, the quota matters slipped out of the cooperative’s full control. "First, we applied for a migrant worker quota but were rejected. Then, they came in as agents to assist us. They handled everything, including preparing the application documents until more than 1,100 quotas were approved," he said. According to Nazlan, Mr G handled the second application entirely. As a result, a quota of 1,125 migrant workers was approved under the name of Koperasi Kijang Mas. However, there were several suspicious matters in the process. A document Malaysiakini sighted showed that an "Agreement Deed" was signed on Aug 1, 2024, between the cooperative and Agensi Pekerjaan Uni Jobs Sdn Bhd - a company with an address at Plaza Prima, Jalan Klang Lama, Kuala Lumpur. In the document, Uni Jobs was named the "contractor" while the cooperative was named the "landowner". The agreement appeared to give Uni Jobs the right to bring in migrant workers, manage them, and fulfil all rules, requirements, and welfare of the migrant workers, including all government regulations and wages. In return, the contractor was required to harvest rubber from the cooperative’s land. However, a check with the Human Resources Ministry revealed that Uni Jobs did not possess a valid Private Employment Agency (APS) Licence. This licence is a mandatory requirement under the law for any entity wishing to operate as an employment agency. Meanwhile, Nazlan claimed that the signature appearing above the cooperative chairperson’s name on the document was not his. In a police report lodged by Nazlan on behalf of the cooperative, he accused Mr G and Ms K, among other things, of forging the signature. Malaysiakini could not independently verify the signature forgery allegations. Additionally, Nazlan said the cooperative chairperson had never attended any interview session with the authorities for the migrant worker quota application. Another anomaly in the agreement document was the land size claimed to be owned by the cooperative. The document stated that the cooperative owned 4,500ha of land. The same figure is believed to have been used in the application handled by Uni Jobs to obtain the quota. However, that land size does not exist. Instead, Nazlan said, the actual size of the land cultivated by the cooperative for vegetable crops was only around 300 to 400 acres (121.4 to 161.9ha) - as seen by Malaysiakini when visiting the area. Besides the migrant worker quota issue, there were other anomalies surrounding the case. A search with the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM) found that Uni Jobs has two directors, both Malaysian citizens. Based on official documents from the Immigration Department, one of them is Mr G’s wife. However, a check by Malaysiakini with the National Registration Department (NRD) showed that the Malaysian woman was also married to a man of another nationality, and that marriage remained valid as they were not divorced. Malaysiakini has submitted official queries to the Home Ministry to clarify this discrepancy in records. Malaysiakini had also contacted Mr G, Ms K, both directors of Uni Jobs (including the woman alleged to be Mr G’s wife), and her lawful husband on Sept 1, 2026, to seek comments regarding the allegations against them, but has yet to receive a response. According to Nazlan, the real trouble began after the cooperative received approval for the quota. The cooperative waited for the workforce to arrive to develop their land, but days passed without certainty. When the cooperative tried to get the latest status on the workers, Ms K allegedly offered various excuses, including claiming that there were issues on the immigration side. As time went on without a single worker setting foot on the cooperative’s land, suspicions grew stronger. The cooperative eventually suspected that the two agents had illegally sold the quota to third parties and abused the cooperative’s name and status without any authorisation or legal power. "The quota of 1,125 migrant workers that was supposed to be used to develop the cooperative's land was issued and sold to third parties as a standalone commodity. "While the cooperative was merely a name on paper to validate the approval of the quota," he said. The real shock came when the Home Ministry itself contacted the cooperative. "When Home Ministry came to the office, they asked me, 'Do you know that these migrant workers have already entered the country?'" Nazlan asked, recalling the moment that changed everything. In Putrajaya, officers showed documents and interrogated the cooperative representatives. After determining that the cooperative had likely been duped, Home Ministry officers advised the cooperative to lodge a police report as a step to protect its own standing. On Jan 19, Nazlan lodged a report at the Travers police station in Brickfields, Kuala Lumpur. In the report, he denied the cooperative’s link to any involvement in the fraudulent activities, while also reporting the misuse and forgery of the cooperative's documents. He emphasised that the cooperative was not involved, did not sign any agreement, and received no payment or profit from the management or sale of the quota linked to the cooperative's name. Nazlan also requested the police to conduct a thorough investigation into Mr G, Ms K, and any other parties involved, as well as take legal action for offences of cheating, document forgery, breach of trust, and abetment. According to him, the actions caused reputational damage and legal risks to the cooperative. "The ministry has also conducted oversight inspections and further investigations, and found that there were parties involved in document forgery as well as elements of human trafficking. "This case also serves as another proof of how important it is for the Home Ministry to conduct transparent and comprehensive oversight inspection processes to ensure any misuse of migrant worker quotas can be detected and contained at an early stage," they added. At the end of the interview, when asked what his actual demands to the government were, Nazlan did not ask for compensation or drastic action. His request was much simpler. "I ask the government to pay attention to the relevant departments, whether regarding migrant labour or other matters, and take good care of them. "The Orang Asli, if no one guides them, they don't know about these things," he said. "We didn't even know we were walking into a trap and getting scammed. "We hope Home Ministry returns our quota so that we can bring in migrant workers to cultivate our land," Nazlan added.
