representative.title: US Sanctions on ICC Put Global Justice at Risk | Human Rights Watch

snapshot.title: US Sanctions on ICC Put Global Justice at Risk
snapshot.evidenceText: Member Countries Should Renew Support for Court, Minimize Harm Share this via Bluesky Share this via Facebook Share this via X Share this via WhatsApp Share this via Email More sharing options Share this via LinkedIn Share this via Reddit Share this via Telegram Share this via Printer (New York) – The Trump administration’s decision to sanction the International Criminal Court (ICC) is an unprecedented assault on global justice and the rule of law, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 9, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the imposition of sanctions on the ICC. “The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court,” said Philippe Bolopion , executive director of Human Rights Watch. “By attacking the court, the US government is threatening justice for victims of abuses from Palestine to Ukraine, Myanmar, and Sudan.” The ICC is a permanent international court created to try people, including senior officials, accused of war crimes , crimes against humanity , genocide, and the crime of aggression. Following the genocides in the mid-1990s in Rwanda and in the former Yugoslavia, the international community created the ICC to prevent those most responsible for serious crimes from evading justice. Nearly two-thirds of UN member countries have joined the court. In addition to its Palestine investigation, the court has opened investigations into alleged crimes in 17 situations , including in Afghanistan , Darfur in Sudan , Bangladesh/Myanmar , Ukraine , and Venezuela . The US government’s decision to sanction the ICC was announced on the same day that the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay , a former ICC judge and renowned international lawyer, in recognition of her central role “in ensuring that war crimes , crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” In his October 9 announcement, Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza. Palestine became an ICC member in 2015 and gave the court a mandate to address serious crimes committed on its territory or by its nationals since June 13, 2014. The Trump administration has already sanctioned ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges, three prominent Palestinian human rights groups, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and called on ICC member countries to leave the court. US sanctions have serious effects on those targeted, including frozen or closed bank accounts, rejected financial transactions, denied access to digital services, and US entry bans. US sanctions also have a chilling effect on non-US banks and other companies outside of US jurisdiction that could themselves lose access to the US banking system if they do not adhere to the sanctions. This means that the ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for everyday functions, from banking to information, technology to travel. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed a lawsuit in US federal court on August 11, 2026, seeking to have the sanctions regime previously used to authorize court-wide sanctions struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit. ICC member countries , including the Netherlands which hosts the ICC in The Hague, the leadership body of the court’s Assembly of States Parties , the European Union , UN human rights experts , the UN secretary-general , the UN high commissioner for human rights , civil society organizations , and the ICC itself have repeatedly spoken out against the sanctions. The ICC and its member countries have also taken important steps to insulate the court from the potential impact of sanctions, but more action is needed to protect the court’s ability to continue its critical work. The EU should immediately activate its blocking statute , which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions. The Trump administration’s sanctions targeting international justice are part of a broader attack on the laws, institutions, and organizations created to protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said. The United States has also withdrawn from the Paris Climate Accords and the World Health Organization , while disengaging from the UN Human Rights Council . President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have also expressed contempt for international law , and threatened to commit war crimes . “The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, can escape justice for the worst crimes,” Bolopion said. “Governments everywhere should take every available measure to counter the effects of the US sanctions and stand with the court and those relying on it to obtain justice.” UK and US Forced Displacement of the Chagossians and Ongoing Colonial Crimes Share this via Bluesky Share this via Facebook Share this via X Share this via WhatsApp Share this via Email More sharing options Share this via LinkedIn Share this via Reddit Share this via Telegram Share this via Printer Human Rights Watch defends the rights of people in close to 100 countries worldwide, spotlighting abuses and bringing perpetrators to justice Get updates on human rights issues from around the globe. snapshot.title: China Unveils First Nationwide Labor Rules to Protect Gig Economy Workers
snapshot.evidenceText: China’s labor ministry on Thursday released draft rules that would set nationwide protections for workers in the fast-growing gig economy, including minimum-pay safeguards, limits on algorithmic decision-making and stronger obligations for internet platforms. The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is seeking public comment through Nov. 8 on the 54-article draft, which would be China’s first ministerial regulation specifically governing the rights of workers in new forms of employment, such as food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers and truck drivers. China Proposes Sweeping E-Commerce Overhaul to Protect Gig Workers, Counter Foreign Curbs Pioneering Injury Lawsuit Could Finally Hold China’s Gig Platforms Liable 1. China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security has released a 54-article draft rule, open for public comment until Nov. 8, that would establish the country’s first ministerial regulation specifically protecting workers in the gig economy, including food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers, and truck drivers. The proposal reflects Beijing’s effort to extend labor protections to a workforce that has grown rapidly alongside internet platforms but often falls outside conventional labor-law definitions due to flexible and complex employment arrangements. [para. 1 ] [para. 2 ] [para. 3 ] 2. The draft determines employment relationships based on whether a platform exercises “controlling labor management” over workers. Workers subject to such control and meeting employment-relationship conditions must receive labor contracts; the same applies when a platform’s partner company recruits and manages workers in an employment relationship. If the relationship does not meet the formal threshold, platforms must sign a written work agreement—or a three-party agreement when both platform and partner jointly manage the worker. The rules do not apply to independent business operators or freelancers using platforms. Platforms must vet partners, bear employer responsibility for unqualified partners, and are prohibited from encouraging workers to register as sole proprietors or using multilayer subcontracting to evade obligations. In disputes, workers may name both platform and labor-service partner as joint parties. [para. 7 ] [para. 8 ] [para. 9 ] [para. 10 ] [para. 11 ] [para. 12 ] 3. The proposal sets detailed pay protections: minimum-wage calculations must subtract workers’ costs for providing their own equipment or tools, ensuring net earnings do not fall below local minimum wage. Workers can withdraw compensation on the agreed cycle without fees. The draft encourages positive incentives and prohibits abuse of fines and punitive measures, addressing complaints about arbitrary deductions. It also requires transparent rules and breaks to protect rest rights, as well as labor protections in severe weather, given the outdoor nature of much gig work. [para. 13 ] [para. 14 ] [para. 15 ] 4. The draft restricts platforms’ handling of worker data. Personal information may be processed only lawfully, properly, necessarily, in good faith, and only to the extent required for work management. Platforms must establish accurate work records that workers can conveniently view and download through apps or other channels, and companies must retain records for at least two years after a worker leaves. [para. 16 ] [para. 17 ] 5. A prominent section targets algorithmic management. Platforms must explain the basic principles and operating mechanisms of their algorithms to workers and are barred from algorithmic discrimination. Decisions with major consequences—such as suspending order assignments or banning accounts—cannot be made automatically by an algorithm and require human review. Wang Tianyu, deputy director of the social-law research division at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Law, said this provision addresses public concern that delivery riders and other platform workers have become trapped by algorithmically imposed targets. [para. 18 ] [para. 19 ] [para. 20 ] 6. The ministry noted existing labor laws do not always apply directly to platform work, but experience since a 2021 policy guideline on protecting gig workers allowed mature policies to be turned into binding institutional rules and address gaps. Wang said platform work has become an important part of China’s employment landscape, with complaints including withheld compensation, excessively long hours, inadequate safety protections, opaque algorithmic rules, and lack of occupational-injury coverage. Shen Jianfeng, a law professor at the Central University of Finance and Economics, said parts of the draft adapt traditional labor standards to platform conditions, while provisions on data protection and algorithm rules represent institutional innovations. Public comments can be submitted via the ministry’s website, mail, or email. If the relationship does not meet the formal threshold, platforms must sign a written work agreement—or a three-party agreement when both platform and partner jointly manage the worker. The rules do not apply to independent business operators or freelancers using platforms. Platforms must vet partners, bear employer responsibility for unqualified partners, and are prohibited from encouraging workers to register as sole proprietors or using multilayer subcontracting to evade obligations. In disputes, workers may name both platform and labor-service partner as joint parties. [para. 7 ] [para. 8 ] [para. 9 ] [para. 10 ] [para. 11 ] [para. 12 ] 3. The proposal sets detailed pay protections: minimum-wage calculations must subtract workers’ costs for providing their own equipment or tools, ensuring net earnings do not fall below local minimum wage. Workers can withdraw compensation on the agreed cycle without fees. The draft encourages positive incentives and prohibits abuse of fines and punitive measures, addressing complaints about arbitrary deductions. It also requires transparent rules and breaks to protect rest rights, as well as labor protections in severe weather, given the outdoor nature of much gig work. [para. 13 ] [para. 14 ] [para. 15 ] 4. The draft restricts platforms’ handling of worker data. Personal information may be processed only lawfully, properly, necessarily, in good faith, and only to the extent required for work management. Platforms must establish accurate work records that workers can conveniently view and download through apps or other channels, and companies must retain records for at least two years after a worker leaves. Platforms must explain the basic principles and operating mechanisms of their algorithms to workers and are barred from algorithmic discrimination. representative.title: ACC Elections Department accidentally sends more than 1,000 duplicate absentee ballots - Now Georgia
representative.author: McClain Baxley

snapshot.title: ACC Elections Department accidentally sends more than 1,000 duplicate absentee ballots - Now Georgia
snapshot.evidenceText: ATHENS, Ga. ( WUGA ) — The Athens-Clarke County elections department distributed a second absentee ballot to 1,154 registered voters for the November 3 general election. The first group of mail-in ballots were sent out on Monday through a state-authorized print vendor. The elections department was alerted on Wednesday that two absentee ballots were received by some Athens-Clarke County voters. The issue was the mailing list provided to the printer included addresses that were on an earlier list, too. The elections department is now asking voters who received a second ballot to only complete and mail in one of the ballots. Voters should either shred the extra ballot or bring it blank to 155 East Washington Street. ACCGov Elections Department director Pam Long understands the concern of voters after receiving multiple ballots but ensures that the election will still be secure. “We understand that receiving two absentee ballots can be concerning to voters,” Long said in a statement. “We want our community to know that we identified the issue, are tracking the affected ballots, and have procedures in place to ensure that each eligible voter has only one ballot accepted. We remain committed to transparency and to maintaining the accuracy, security, and integrity of our elections.” ACCGov Elections Department staff informed the Georgia Secretary of State’s office of the error, and they accepted Athens-Clarke County’s response.

representative.title: Election officials settle on fix to 'Coco' train ballot error
representative.author: Marianne Goodland

snapshot.title: Election officials settle on fix to 'Coco' train ballot error
snapshot.evidenceText: State officers on Friday met with their local counterparts in four counties affected by the error and together set testing protocols in the voting system to ensure only those eligible votes within the passenger rail district are counted for the question called Issue 7A. Voters within the boundaries of the Front Range Passenger Rail District face a decision this November whether to establish a new 0.333% sales and use tax in order to generate $295 million a year and permit the jurisdiction to take on $580 million in debt to build a passenger rail line connecting several communities along the Front Range. But not every voter in the 13 counties of the proposed rail line should have Issue 7A on their ballots. Only voters within the rail district’s boundaries should see that question. Instead, some 800,000 voters in Adams, Arapahoe, Douglas and Weld counties have been sent ballots with the sales tax hike question. The rail district, which admitted to failing to communicate the new electoral boundaries to the counties, has apologized for the error. The question before election officers is how to separate out Issue 7A ballots from the rest. On Thursday, the Secretary of State’s Office sent guidance to the county clerks in the four counties on how to tabulate votes for Issue 7A and distinguish eligible voters in that contest. The protocol likely will include a hand count for a few precincts. In a statement, Josh Zygielbaum of Adams County, Sheri Davis of Douglas County and Carly Koppes of Weld County said their primary goal is to ensure voting is secure, transparent and accurate. Arapahoe County Clerk Joan Lopez added, “The most important thing our voters need to know is that their votes will be counted accurately, securely, and transparently and results will be reported in a timely fashion.” The state election office and Colorado County Clerks Association echoed that statement and urged voters to simply fill out the ballot they were sent — and officers would sort them out. The 800,000 ballots in question are tied to the original map for the rail district. But legislators revised those boundaries this year to narrow the district’s borders, a request backed by the Front Range Passenger Rail. The district’s narrowed “bubble” boundaries, set by the 2026 legislation, have focused voting on municipalities near planned stations, while excluding some corridor communities between Littleton and Colorado Springs, according to project documents. Front Range Passenger Rail District General Manager Sal Pace had defended the approach as tied to requirements by the Federal Railroad Administration to qualify as passenger rail based on distance between stations and train speed. Critics said the move had cut out more conservative communities, thereby arguing that the vote boundaries, as now constituted, favor the sales tax hike’s passage. Ballot processing does not begin until Oct. 19. snapshot.title: Inside Thailand’s cyanide murders and the search for its ‘most prolific serial killer’ in history
snapshot.evidenceText: When healthy people suddenly began dying, grieving families struggled to get answers. The series, Death Loans, retraces how a dogged investigator looking into a friend’s death helped police connect 15 cases to one woman eventually. BANGKOK: When her friend gave her some herbal medicine for her cough, Kantima “Pla” Paesaard did not think too much about it. She wasn’t to know it would turn out to be an alleged murder attempt. Less than 10 minutes after they went their separate ways, Pla started feeling short of breath. So she turned on the air-conditioner in her car and got a strong draught blowing at her face. “But no matter how I tried to breathe, I still couldn’t,” she recalled. After she called an ambulance, her hands started to stiffen. When the ambulance arrived a few minutes later, only her little finger could move a bit, she said. And once she was in the ambulance, “everything just went black”. Loading Hours went by before she started to awake. “After I regained consciousness, my husband told me, ‘Do you know that earlier, your heart had actually stopped beating?’” she recounted. “The doctor told me they did a brain scan. They checked my blood and examined my whole body, and there was nothing abnormal. So I thought it was an allergic reaction to the herbal medicine.” Her friend, Sararat “Aem” Rangsiwuthaporn, checked on her in hospital, seemingly worried for her health. Pla did not suspect anything. They had known each other for about 10 years. Their husbands — or ex-husband, in Aem’s case — were from the same police academy class. “I felt like Aem was part of the family. We’d always visit each other,” she said. Two months later, in November 2022, when the two friends went to a gathering together, Pla’s mum asked Aem (also spelt as Am) why she looked thinner. Weight-loss pills, she replied. “So my mum said, ‘If that’s the case, bring some for Pla to try so she can lose weight too,’” Pla recounted. After the gathering ended, Aem brought over the pills to their house in Thailand’s Kanchanaburi province. But Pla chose not to take them. She still did not have any suspicions of her friend, not until she heard the news about a woman who had been poisoned with cyanide months later, with Aem present at the scene. Pla, then 36, started googling the symptoms of cyanide poisoning and found that they included difficulty breathing and stiff hands. “At that moment, I was very shocked,” she said. She was the only survivor out of 15 victims identified by the police in what has become a historic set of cases, involving a pattern of deaths in different provinces starting as far back as 2015. Aem, now 39, is the “most prolific serial killer in Thai history”, according to Surachate Hakparn, the deputy police chief from 2022 to 2024. “She’s killed more people than Jack the Ripper, the Zodiac and BTK (did individually),” he charged. Only one of those three — BTK (Bind, Torture, Kill), the moniker for American killer Dennis Rader — was caught. And it took one of the largest investigations ever conducted in Thailand for the Royal Thai Police to catch their killer better known as Aem Cyanide. The series, Death Loans , tells how the country’s cyanide murders finally ended. WATCH PART 1: ‘She didn’t go alone’ — This CCTV footage helped expose Thai serial killer (46:57) Most of the victims were in their 30s and healthy. All died under mysterious circumstances. In Mukdahan province, Sawitree “Nim” Budsrirak, 40, had just given birth to a baby girl, “exactly as we’d hoped”, said her husband, Nitipon “Ta” Nuchit. A month later, in November 2020, he was back at work in Bangkok, 650km away. Nim was taking care of the children — their newborn and their five-year-old son — and cleaning the house. One day when he was on his break, he tried video-calling Nim. She did not answer. Then he sent her a message. It was left unread. So he video-called his son, Neo. “I asked him, ‘Who are you with? Where’s Mummy? I want to talk to Mummy.’ Neo turned the camera towards the mattress. I saw Nim lying face down, with her face resting on the edge of the mattress,” he recounted. Thinking that Nim was tired and had taken a nap, he decided to end the call. “After no more than 30 minutes, I tried video-calling again,” he continued. “Neo answered as before and turned the camera towards Nim, who was still lying in the same position. That’s when I realised something was wrong.” He immediately called a neighbour to check on Nim. Her lips had turned dark bluish, a trickle of blood was oozing from her mouth, and her body was covered in sweat. “Nim was found dead on the bed while our daughter was sleeping only a few feet away,” Ta said. “Nim was playing just fine with the children. It’s impossible that she’d then die. How could something like this happen?” At that time, he wasn’t to know the answer lay in Thailand’s money-sharing circles. These are rotating savings groups whose members save together. The money they contribute regularly is pooled, which members can borrow when needed. These loans are not free. Members pay a monthly interest — setting the rate themselves beforehand — on loans taken out from the group’s fund. They must also continue their regular contributions as they repay the loans. “It’s estimated that millions of Thais participate in share groups, with billions of baht estimated to be in circulation,” said Piriya Pholphirul, an economics professor at the National Institute of Development Administration. Nim was one of them, joining in as a way of earning additional income, said Ta. Sharing circles have existed for generations, built on friendship and trust. But the problem was that she joined an online sharing group with Aem. For another victim, Surat “Bee” Toraphap, 35, his friendship with Aem went back to childhood. They had been schoolmates. In January 2021, his brother “Koon” was at a temple when a neighbour in Kanchanaburi’s Tha Maka district called to say that Bee was in the bathroom and turning blue. Koon hurried over. “There were police all over the house. I saw my younger sibling sitting on the toilet in the bathroom, leaning to the right. I realised my sibling was no longer with me,” he said. “My younger brother was healthy, didn’t drink and didn’t smoke. His death was abnormal. I started getting suspicious and unlocked my brother’s phone and wondered why this friend named ‘Aem’ wasn’t responding to him.” It turned out that Bee had lent her money: 50,000 baht (US$1,500) at first and then another 10,000 baht. But for all of Koon’s suspicions, his brother’s death was classified as natural, as was the case for Nim and other victims. Aem’s victims could be categorised in a few groups, such as those in savings groups where she was the organiser, those whom she borrowed money from and those who loaned her money to lend out to others. One of the people she invited to lend money through her was her friend Siriporn “Koy” Khanwong, 32. On Apr 14, 2023, Koy told her mother she was going to run an errand. “She told me to wait,” recalled Thongpin Kiatchanasiri. “She said she’d come back in the evening and take me shopping. But she never came back.” Koy had two phones. “If one phone was off, the other one would still be on,” said her elder sister, Nipawan “Som” Khanwong. “But that day, both phones were off at the same time. I was so anxious, wondering why.” As Koy’s family tried to figure out where she was, a friend of hers, independent investigator Rapee Chamnanrua, received a photo of a person the police in Ratchaburi province were trying to identify. It was Koy. She had fainted and died by the Mae Klong River, 80km west of Bangkok. The police cited the official cause of death as a heart attack. But her mother “didn’t believe that her heart would fail”. “My daughter was only 32, healthy and strong,” said Thongpin, now 65. “I was shocked. I felt I was losing my sanity. … I kept asking where her bag went, where her phone went, because they were all gone.” Som also “felt something was wrong”, but the police “wouldn’t listen”, she recounted. The family’s request for a further probe into Koy’s death was turned down. Her body was returned to them the next day for Buddhist rites and cremation. The first person who listened to the family and thought her death was unnatural was Rapee. “How could someone so young just die so suddenly?” he questioned. “Because I knew her, this case was special (to me).” But at first, his investigation went down the wrong path. The family suspected a former boyfriend who had allegedly threatened her. This was a police officer named Navin — whose alibi ruled him out, according to the police. Doubting that the police would implicate one of their own, Rapee “asked people to go check on Navin”. He reasoned: “Navin had an intimate relationship with Koy.” Above all else, however, he wanted “someone in authority” to hear the family out before her cremation. So they met the police general Surachate, who is known in Thailand by his nickname, “Big Joke”. “I put all the evidence in front of him and asked him if he felt the local police had done their job,” recounted Rapee, who cited Koy’s missing belongings, among other things. “A heart attack doesn’t make belongings disappear.” Surachate gave credit to Rapee for getting him involved in the case. His own suspicions were aroused when Rapee showed him the autopsy report, which recorded that Koy was healthy. “This was unusual,” he said, adding that Navin’s alleged threats were also “concerning”. Things started moving “much faster” after Surachate got involved in the case, said Som. For example, the police called her in to watch the footage from the closed-circuit television cameras pointed towards the walkway along the river. Rapee said they were “very lucky” because the cameras had been recently repaired after being “broken for a long time”. Meanwhile, a second, more detailed autopsy was performed on Koy. When the toxicology results came out, forensic pathologist Smith Srisont, who ran the test, “was very shocked”. It was a cyanide poisoning case. His colleague at Ramathibodi Hospital, internal medicine doctor Sahaphume Srisuma, had “never seen this before” in his practice in Thailand. “Cyanide is one of the most lethal chemical compounds known to mankind. It’s virtually untraceable,” said Sahaphume. “The most dangerous thing is cyanide is lethal either by ingestion or inhalation. All it takes is a tiny dose, maybe smaller than a grain of rice.” That was not the only evidence that “changed the case immediately” as Surachate described. CCTV footage showed that when Koy went to release fish at the Mae Klong pier, she did not go alone. She was with Aem. It turned out Koy had transferred 300,000 baht to Aem for her to invest “because she was a friend and we trusted her”, said Som, who shared that she herself first met Aem at age 16. “Aem was very chatty, and she got along with people easily,” Som added. “But her personality changed when it came to money. She started getting involved with money matters, talking about it, pushing it, things like that.” Aem’s financial motives led the police to follow the money trail, which eventually led to gambling websites and gambling dens. “I’ll give one example. She was travelling from Kanchanaburi to Nakhon Pathom. She found a gambling den along the way. She goes straight in, plays and loses 10 million baht,” cited Surachate. “Whose money was that? Money she’d just borrowed from people.” Online savings groups and instant bank transfers — plus misplaced trust — allowed money to move with ease and feed her gambling addiction. “When asked to repay, if there’s no money to clear debts, what do you do?” remarked Surachate. Citing what he learnt from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, he added: “Serial killers, if they’re men, will commit crimes outside the city, and the motive is sexual in nature. But if it’s a woman, the motive must be money.” Prior to Aem, there was the case of serial killer Somkid Phumphuang, who raped and killed his victims — six of them — between 2005 and 2019. There are “many contributing factors”, however, in cases like Aem, according to Somdet Chaopraya Institute of Psychiatry deputy director Winyoo Chanakul, who has over 20 years’ experience in caring for psychiatric patients who have committed violent acts or even homicide. “Someone who has financial problems to the point of being able to kill others, and to do so repeatedly, can’t be explained by financial reasons alone. Otherwise, everyone in debt would be killing people,” he said. “The person must have certain personality traits that allow them to commit serious wrongdoing for their own benefit without feeling guilt. This includes a lack of empathy and a disregard for social rules.” Thinking back on Aem’s personality, Som remembered her once saying that if anyone were to fight with her or say something bad, “she wouldn’t let it go” and would “go as far as killing”. When the police arrested Aem, however, senior staff writer Pravit Rojanaphruk at news outlet Khaosod English remembers that “everyone was confused” by this woman from a middle-class background. “She looks just like anyone from an average neighbourhood,” he said. It became a major news story that many people have followed. “No one person has caused this much of an uproar before,” he added, citing the 14 murder charges. She has contested all the charges so far. One of her lawyers, Thannicha “Pat” Aeksuwannawat, said it was “impossible that Aem committed all 14 murders”. “The police want to dump the murder cases onto Aem so they don’t have to find the real perpetrator. It was clear that she was being targeted,” said Pat. “It’s media-driven momentum more than facts. “They said death was due to cyanide. … That cyanide mightn’t have come from Aem. This is the weakness of the case.” Buying cyanide in Thailand is not suspicious on its own. It is used in factories in metal-related industries, such as for metal plating and electroplating. It is used in gold shops and in research. And what the police found was that Aem “never used her own name to order cyanide”, said Surachate. “She had others order it, and then it reached her.” One of the cyanide bottles that the police seized had been sold by a company that called Grab to do the delivery. And the rider took a photo when delivering the cyanide to Aem in her Toyota Fortuner, recounted Rapee. “In that photo, a small pink Hello Kitty bag was visible beside the gear stick. Once the police … impounded the bag, we found this bottle,” he said, adding that the bottle had a registration number showing who the importer was. “Aem used her phone number to contact the company. All the evidence pointed directly to Aem. Game over.” Although Rapee said it was Aem’s “own mistakes that brought her down”, his involvement led to a breakthrough in the case in more ways than one. After he and Koy’s family appealed publicly for information once Aem was fingered as a suspect, his phone began ringing nonstop. Families across Thailand told of similar stories: sudden deaths, missing money and a connection to savings groups. One of those who came forward was Pla. She said Aem had asked for a loan to repay a fund, so she gave her 250,000 baht. “She was my friend. Why would I refuse?” said Pla. But she was lending the money only for a month. Then she asked Aem to return the entire amount as agreed because she had to pay for her car. “Reliving my ordeal wasn’t easy,” said Pla, who did it so that Aem “won’t be able to hurt anyone else again”. Pravit described her role as the “nail in the coffin” for Aem, who was sentenced to death in November 2024 for the murder of Koy. WATCH PART 2: ‘She tried to kill me twice’ — The witness who survived a serial killer (46:59) It is a penalty she deserves, said Thongpin, who was “very close” to Koy. “We’d travel together, perform Buddhist rituals together.” Koy and her sister were also close. Som called her the “pillar of the family” who took care of everyone. “Koy only had one child, so she doted on her. She loved her so much. Whatever the child wanted, she got,” said Som, referring to Koy’s daughter, now 13. “Everything she built, she built it for her daughter.” The murders of Nim and Bee, meanwhile, have not gone to trial yet. Koon said he thinks about his younger brother every day. “And whenever I do, my heart feels as if it’s going to break,” he lamented. As for Ta, if he had the chance, he would want to speak to Nim — whom he lovingly described as “good-hearted” and “always willing to help others” — one more time. “I’d want to thank her for coming into my life as my wife and as the mother of our children, for making my life better and helping me grow and become more mature,” he said. As of Sep 22, the criminal court has delivered three death sentences and two life imprisonments for Aem’s string of cyanide murders, plus acquittals in three cases where the court cited a lack of evidence in her favour. Since the end of 2009, Thailand has carried out only one execution, in 2018, even as several death sentences have been imposed. Aem’s next trial date is Nov 25, for the attempted murder of Pla. Her lips had turned dark bluish, a trickle of blood was oozing from her mouth, and her body was covered in sweat. “Nim was found dead on the bed while our daughter was sleeping only a few feet away,” Ta said. “Nim was playing just fine with the children. It’s impossible that she’d then die. How could something like this happen?” At that time, he wasn’t to know the answer lay in Thailand’s money-sharing circles. These are rotating savings groups whose members save together. The money they contribute regularly is pooled, which members can borrow when needed. These loans are not free. Members pay a monthly interest — setting the rate themselves beforehand — on loans taken out from the group’s fund. They must also continue their regular contributions as they repay the loans. “It’s estimated that millions of Thais participate in share groups, with billions of baht estimated to be in circulation,” said Piriya Pholphirul, an economics professor at the National Institute of Development Administration. Nim was one of them, joining in as a way of earning additional income, said Ta. Sharing circles have existed for generations, built on friendship and trust. But the problem was that she joined an online sharing group with Aem. For another victim, Surat “Bee” Toraphap, 35, his friendship with Aem went back to childhood. They had been schoolmates. In January 2021, his brother “Koon” was at a temple when a neighbour in Kanchanaburi’s Tha Maka district called to say that Bee was in the bathroom and turning blue. Koon hurried over. “There were police all over the house. I saw my younger sibling sitting on the toilet in the bathroom, leaning to the right. I realised my sibling was no longer with me,” he said. “My younger brother was healthy, didn’t drink and didn’t smoke. His death was abnormal. I started getting suspicious and unlocked my brother’s phone and wondered why this friend named ‘Aem’ wasn’t responding to him.” It turned out that Bee had lent her money: 50,000 baht (US$1,500) at first and then another 10,000 baht. But for all of Koon’s suspicions, his brother’s death was classified as natural, as was the case for Nim and other victims. Aem’s victims could be categorised in a few groups, such as those in savings groups where she was the organiser, those whom she borrowed money from and those who loaned her money to lend out to others. One of the people she invited to lend money through her was her friend Siriporn “Koy” Khanwong, 32. On Apr 14, 2023, Koy told her mother she was going to run an errand. “She told me to wait,” recalled Thongpin Kiatchanasiri. “She said she’d come back in the evening and take me shopping. But she never came back.” Koy had two phones. “If one phone was off, the other one would still be on,” said her elder sister, Nipawan “Som” Khanwong. “But that day, both phones were off at the same time. I was so anxious, wondering why.” As Koy’s family tried to figure out where she was, a friend of hers, independent investigator Rapee Chamnanrua, received a photo of a person the police in Ratchaburi province were trying to identify. It was Koy. She had fainted and died by the Mae Klong River, 80km west of Bangkok. The police cited the official cause of death as a heart attack. But her mother “didn’t believe that her heart would fail”. “My daughter was only 32, healthy and strong,” said Thongpin, now 65. “I was shocked. I felt I was losing my sanity. … I kept asking where her bag went, where her phone went, because they were all gone.” Som also “felt something was wrong”, but the police “wouldn’t listen”, she recounted. The family’s request for a further probe into Koy’s death was turned down. Her body was returned to them the next day for Buddhist rites and cremation. The first person who listened to the family and thought her death was unnatural was Rapee. “How could someone so young just die so suddenly?” he questioned. “Because I knew her, this case was special (to me).” But at first, his investigation went down the wrong path. The family suspected a former boyfriend who had allegedly threatened her. This was a police officer named Navin — whose alibi ruled him out, according to the police. Doubting that the police would implicate one of their own, Rapee “asked people to go check on Navin”. He reasoned: “Navin had an intimate relationship with Koy.” Above all else, however, he wanted “someone in authority” to hear the family out before her cremation. So they met the police general Surachate, who is known in Thailand by his nickname, “Big Joke”. “I put all the evidence in front of him and asked him if he felt the local police had done their job,” recounted Rapee, who cited Koy’s missing belongings, among other things. “A heart attack doesn’t make belongings disappear.” Surachate gave credit to Rapee for getting him involved in the case. His own suspicions were aroused when Rapee showed him the autopsy report, which recorded that Koy was healthy. “This was unusual,” he said, adding that Navin’s alleged threats were also “concerning”. Things started moving “much faster” after Surachate got involved in the case, said Som. For example, the police called her in to watch the footage from the closed-circuit television cameras pointed towards the walkway along the river. Rapee said they were “very lucky” because the cameras had been recently repaired after being “broken for a long time”. Meanwhile, a second, more detailed autopsy was performed on Koy. When the toxicology results came out, forensic pathologist Smith Srisont, who ran the test, “was very shocked”. It was a cyanide poisoning case. His colleague at Ramathibodi Hospital, internal medicine doctor Sahaphume Srisuma, had “never seen this before” in his practice in Thailand. “Cyanide is one of the most lethal chemical compounds known to mankind. It’s virtually untraceable,” said Sahaphume. “The most dangerous thing is cyanide is lethal either by ingestion or inhalation. All it takes is a tiny dose, maybe smaller than a grain of rice.” That was not the only evidence that “changed the case immediately” as Surachate described. CCTV footage showed that when Koy went to release fish at the Mae Klong pier, she did not go alone. She was with Aem. It turned out Koy had transferred 300,000 baht to Aem for her to invest “because she was a friend and we trusted her”, said Som, who shared that she herself first met Aem at age 16. “Aem was very chatty, and she got along with people easily,” Som added. “But her personality changed when it came to money. She started getting involved with money matters, talking about it, pushing it, things like that.” Aem’s financial motives led the police to follow the money trail, which eventually led to gambling websites and gambling dens. “I’ll give one example. She was travelling from Kanchanaburi to Nakhon Pathom. She found a gambling den along the way. She goes straight in, plays and loses 10 million baht,” cited Surachate. “Whose money was that? Money she’d just borrowed from people.” Online savings groups and instant bank transfers — plus misplaced trust — allowed money to move with ease and feed her gambling addiction. “When asked to repay, if there’s no money to clear debts, what do you do?” remarked Surachate. Citing what he learnt from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, he added: “Serial killers, if they’re men, will commit crimes outside the city, and the motive is sexual in nature. But if it’s a woman, the motive must be money.” Prior to Aem, there was the case of serial killer Somkid Phumphuang, who raped and killed his victims — six of them — between 2005 and 2019. There are “many contributing factors”, however, in cases like Aem, according to Somdet Chaopraya Institute of Psychiatry deputy director Winyoo Chanakul, who has over 20 years’ experience in caring for psychiatric patients who have committed violent acts or even homicide. “Someone who has financial problems to the point of being able to kill others, and to do so repeatedly, can’t be explained by financial reasons alone. Otherwise, everyone in debt would be killing people,” he said. “The person must have certain personality traits that allow them to commit serious wrongdoing for their own benefit without feeling guilt. This includes a lack of empathy and a disregard for social rules.” Thinking back on Aem’s personality, Som remembered her once saying that if anyone were to fight with her or say something bad, “she wouldn’t let it go” and would “go as far as killing”. When the police arrested Aem, however, senior staff writer Pravit Rojanaphruk at news outlet Khaosod English remembers that “everyone was confused” by this woman from a middle-class background. “She looks just like anyone from an average neighbourhood,” he said. It became a major news story that many people have followed. “No one person has caused this much of an uproar before,” he added, citing the 14 murder charges. She has contested all the charges so far. One of her lawyers, Thannicha “Pat” Aeksuwannawat, said it was “impossible that Aem committed all 14 murders”. “The police want to dump the murder cases onto Aem so they don’t have to find the real perpetrator. It was clear that she was being targeted,” said Pat. “It’s media-driven momentum more than facts. “They said death was due to cyanide. … That cyanide mightn’t have come from Aem. This is the weakness of the case.” Buying cyanide in Thailand is not suspicious on its own. It is used in factories in metal-related industries, such as for metal plating and electroplating. It is used in gold shops and in research. And what the police found was that Aem “never used her own name to order cyanide”, said Surachate. “She had others order it, and then it reached her.” One of the cyanide bottles that the police seized had been sold by a company that called Grab to do the delivery. And the rider took a photo when delivering the cyanide to Aem in her Toyota Fortuner, recounted Rapee. “In that photo, a small pink Hello Kitty bag was visible beside the gear stick. Once the police … impounded the bag, we found this bottle,” he said, adding that the bottle had a registration number showing who the importer was. “Aem used her phone number to contact the company. All the evidence pointed directly to Aem. Game over.” Although Rapee said it was Aem’s “own mistakes that brought her down”, his involvement led to a breakthrough in the case in more ways than one. After he and Koy’s family appealed publicly for information once Aem was fingered as a suspect, his phone began ringing nonstop. Families across Thailand told of similar stories: sudden deaths, missing money and a connection to savings groups. One of those who came forward was Pla. She said Aem had asked for a loan to repay a fund, so she gave her 250,000 baht. “She was my friend. Why would I refuse?” said Pla. But she was lending the money only for a month. Then she asked Aem to return the entire amount as agreed because she had to pay for her car. “Reliving my ordeal wasn’t easy,” said Pla, who did it so that Aem “won’t be able to hurt anyone else again”. Pravit described her role as the “nail in the coffin” for Aem, who was sentenced to death in November 2024 for the murder of Koy. WATCH PART 2: ‘She tried to kill me twice’ — The witness who survived a serial killer (46:59) It is a penalty she deserves, said Thongpin, who was “very close” to Koy. “We’d travel together, perform Buddhist rituals together.” Koy and her sister were also close. Som called her the “pillar of the family” who took care of everyone. “Koy only had one child, so she doted on her. She loved her so much. Whatever the child wanted, she got,” said Som, referring to Koy’s daughter, now 13. “Everything she built, she built it for her daughter.” The murders of Nim and Bee, meanwhile, have not gone to trial yet. Koon said he thinks about his younger brother every day. “And whenever I do, my heart feels as if it’s going to break,” he lamented. As for Ta, if he had the chance, he would want to speak to Nim — whom he lovingly described as “good-hearted” and “always willing to help others” — one more time. “I’d want to thank her for coming into my life as my wife and as the mother of our children, for making my life better and helping me grow and become more mature,” he said. As of Sep 22, the criminal court has delivered three death sentences and two life imprisonments for Aem’s string of cyanide murders, plus acquittals in three cases where the court cited a lack of evidence in her favour. Since the end of 2009, Thailand has carried out only one execution, in 2018, even as several death sentences have been imposed. Aem’s next trial date is Nov 25, for the attempted murder of Pla. But some of these links are so-called "affiliate links" to products that we recommend. First and foremost, because we believe that they add value to you. For example, when we wrote a post about the environmental impact of long showers, we came across an EPA recommendation to use WaterSense showerheads. So we linked to where you can find them. Or, for many of our posts, we also link to our favorite books on that topic so that you can get a much more holistic overview than one single blog post could provide. First, and most importantly, we still only recommend products that we believe add value for you. When you buy something through one of our affiliate links, we may earn a small commission - but at no additional costs to you. And at this point in time, all money is reinvested in sharing the most helpful content with you. This includes all operating costs for running this site and the content creation itself. You may have noticed by the way Impactful Ninja is operated that money is not the driving factor behind it. It is a passion project of mine and I love to share helpful information with you to make a positive impact on the world and society. However, it's a project in that I invest a lot of time and also quite some money. Eventually, my dream is to one day turn this passion project into my full-time job and provide even more helpful information. But that's still a long time to go. 📰 The quick summary : A tiny volcanic hamlet in Sicily reopened what Italian media call the smallest school in Europe after more than 20 years, welcoming one six-year-old girl and helping her family stay together in their remote island community. 📈 One key stat : Italy is projected to lose around one million pupils by 2034, dropping from 6.91 million to 5.90 million, making Ginostra’s school reopening a rare bright spot in a national trend of shrinking classrooms. 💬 One key quote : “It was neither easy nor a given, but we made it. A victory for our whole community, which has followed this adventure of ours from the very beginning,” said Monica Abbate, Aysha’s mother. 1️⃣ The big picture : On September 10, 2026, a six-year-old named Aysha became the only pupil at Ginostra’s newly reopened school on the island of Stromboli in Sicily, Italy, after a more than 20-year closure. Ginostra is one of Europe’s most isolated communities, with only a few dozen winter residents, no cars, and sea as its only link to the outside world. Her parents fought for months to get the school reopened, writing letters to local officials and the regional school office, and Italian law had to make a special exception since the school has just one pupil instead of the legally required 15 . Without the reopening, the family faced an impossible choice: send Aysha on unreliable sea crossings to reach schools on other islands, opt for homeschooling, or split the family apart. The classroom is a renovated room in a local church, and the teacher was given a full-year appointment to give Aysha stability that hard-to-reach schools have rarely been able to offer. 2️⃣ Why is this good news : Reopening the school kept one close-knit family whole, allowing Aysha’s father to continue his work in Ginostra while her mother stayed on the island she loves. For a community of just a few dozen winter residents, the school serves as more than a classroom, acting as a symbol of belonging and a reason for families to stay rather than leave. Italy loses tens of thousands of pupils per year as its birth rate falls and rural communities empty out, so even one school reopening sends a signal that remote communities can hold on and attract new residents. Aysha’s father publicly voiced hope that the achievement could reverse the trend of families leaving Ginostra because of schooling concerns, and her mother expressed a wish that other families move to the hamlet or enroll their children there. At a time when thousands of Italian school buildings face closure, this story shows that targeted exceptions and community collaboration can keep education alive even in the most isolated corners of the country. 3️⃣ What’s next : Whether the school stays open beyond Aysha’s first year depends on how many pupils enroll in the years ahead, since a full primary cycle requires steady attendance numbers. Families on nearby islands such as Filicudi still face serious schooling gaps, showing that Ginostra’s success has not yet spread across the region. Officials have been clear that the current setup meets one family’s specific need, and broader policy changes for isolated communities remain an open question. Read the full story here : Ecoticias – A village of a few dozen winter residents on Stromboli reopened what Italian media call the smallest school in Europe for one 6-year-old girl, and her mother says the alternative was splitting the family

representative.title: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus
representative.author: Manisha Caleb, Themiya Nanayakkara

snapshot.title: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus
snapshot.evidenceText: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created. The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky. But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint. So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst. We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars . At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin. However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them. The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself. As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access. This includes how electrons are distributed through the cosmic web, as well as information on magnetic fields that pervade the universe. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years. FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history. Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint. With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article . Lead image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Themiya Nanayakkara (USYD), Joseph DePasquale (STScI), CC BY Manisha Caleb is a senior lecturer in astrophysics at the University of Sydney. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years. FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history. Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint. With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time. representative.title: The animal kingdom may be 800 million years old: Mongolia removes a ceiling from the molecular clock
representative.author: Guido Donati

snapshot.title: The animal kingdom may be 800 million years old: Mongolia removes a ceiling from the molecular clock
snapshot.evidenceText: A team from Oxford, Berkeley, Zurich and Yale places the origin of animals between 800 and 700 million years ago, 126 to 226 million years before the oldest animal fossils. The argument rests on an absence in a Mongolian rock, not on a new fossil. The study appeared in Science Advances on 2 October 2026. The dates in play for the origin of animals, in millions of years ago: the molecular-clock estimate of Lole Durbin et al., the deposits proposed as a maximum limit, the Kheseen Biota, the biomarkers, the Weng’an Biota and the earliest animal fossils. Ages and localities marked with an asterisk come from the University of Oxford press release. Chart produced by ScienceOnline from data in Lole Durbin O.M. et al., Science Advances 2026, doi 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289.Image file: 2026-10-08_02_grafico_en.png In Mongolia there is a rock that preserves microfossils exceptionally well. It is called the Kheseen Biota and it formed between 550 and 526 million years ago, when animals certainly existed. It holds no definite animal.That absence is the starting point of a study by Orin Lole Durbin, Eliel Anttila, Derek Briggs, Francis Macdonald and Ross Anderson, published in Science Advances on 2 October 2026. Lole Durbin is first author. Anderson, of the Museum of Natural History at the University of Oxford, leads the work. The team includes researchers from Berkeley, ETH Zurich and Yale.The problem is one of dates. Lipid biomarkers, fossil molecules left by cell membranes, point to animals before 635 million years ago. Body fossils go back no further than 574 million. Between the two lies a gap of about sixty million years with no visible animal. Molecular clocks are meant to bridge it. Differences in the DNA of living species build up over time, and counting them dates the split between two lineages. The clock has to be calibrated with fossils. A fossil fixes a group’s minimum age, because the group existed when that organism died. A maximum age is harder to set. It needs a deposit where animals would have been preserved had they been there, and where they are missing.For years that role went to the Weng’an Biota in China, dated by the University of Oxford press release to about 590 million years. Weng’an preserves microfossils in fine detail and contains no definite animals. Many analyses took it as a ceiling, with no animals before Weng’an. The team compared Weng’an with Kheseen. The two sites share similar preservation and similar microfossils, and neither shows a definite animal. Kheseen, though, is more than 40 million years younger and dates from a time when animals were undoubtedly around. If they are invisible at Kheseen, their absence at Weng’an proves nothing. The ceiling goes.In its place the authors propose several older deposits from the Tonian period that preserve both non-animal fossils and biomarkers. According to the press release these are the Svanbergfjellet Formation in Norway, the Bitter Springs Group in Australia and the Chuar Group in Arizona, between 850 and 730 million years old. The same names appear in the files the authors deposited in Dryad, the public data archive. With these limits the clock, run in the MCMCTree software, places the origin of animals between the late Tonian and the mid-Cryogenian, roughly 800 to 700 million years ago.That window precedes or overlaps the great Cryogenian glaciations, the so-called Snowball Earth, which began about 720 million years ago. If the estimate holds, animals appeared before that ice or during it. The authors do not claim 800-million-year-old animals. Lole Durbin says so in the press release: the analysis “does not prove that animals existed”. The paper is an argument about calibrating the clock. The date it produces depends on the rock chosen as the limit, and the article discusses that uncertainty. The release adds that early animals were probably small and soft-bodied, poor candidates for fossilisation.ScienceDaily’s headline speaks of 200 million years earlier than thought. The figure holds only as a loose estimate. Between the clock’s window and the oldest body fossils lie 126 to 226 million years, depending on which end is taken. Against the biomarkers the gap is 65 to 165 million. Funders include NASA, the Royal Society and the ETH Zurich Foundation. Anderson concedes that the birth date of the animal kingdom will stay uncertain until older fossils turn up. ReferencesLole Durbin O.M., Anttila E.S.C., Briggs D.E.G., Macdonald F.A., Anderson R.P., "Re-evaluating molecular clock maximum age calibrations revives pre-Ediacaran divergence estimates for animals", Science Advances, 12, 40, published online 2 October 2026, open access (CC BY). doi: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289Lole Durbin O.M., Anttila E.S.C., Briggs D.E.G. et al., "Data from: Re-evaluating molecular clock maximum age calibrations revives pre-Ediacaran divergence estimates for animals", Dryad, 20 August 2026. doi: 10.5061/dryad.tqjq2bwfdUniversity of Oxford, press release "New study suggests animals may have evolved vastly earlier than fossil evidence suggests", 2026.*Board Member, SRSN (Roman Society of Natural Science)Past Editor-in-Chief Italian Journal of Dermosurgery

representative.title: Treasury Imposes First Civil Penalty Under the Outbound Investment Rule | Covington & Burling LLP
representative.author: Devin DeBacker, David N. Fagan, Heather L. Finstuen, Mark E. Plotkin, Jonathan R. Wakely

snapshot.title: Treasury Imposes First Civil Penalty Under the Outbound Investment Rule
snapshot.evidenceText: Covington & Burling LLP operates as a limited liability partnership worldwide, with the practice in England and Wales conducted by an affiliated limited liability multinational partnership, Covington & Burling LLP, which is formed under the laws of the State of Delaware in the United States and authorized and regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority with registration number 77071.. On October 7, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury (“Treasury”) announced its first enforcement action under the Outbound Investment Security Program (“OISP”), imposing a $200,000 civil penalty on Amidi, LLC (“Amidi”), a U.S. investor, for failing to submit a required notification for an investment by its controlled Chinese subsidiary in a Chinese artificial intelligence company. The penalty is notable not only because it is the first, but also because it suggests Treasury is prepared to bring enforcement actions that target investments undertaken by U.S. persons’ controlled foreign entities, even where the investments are relatively small and arguably may not implicate the core policy concerns that motivated the OISP. The importance of these early enforcement signals goes beyond compliance with the current OISP: they will carry increased importance in light of Treasury’s forthcoming regulations to strengthen and update the OISP under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (“COINS”) Act of 2025, especially given the National Security Science and Technology Strategy’s recent indication that the “Trump Administration will expand Outbound to encompass additional restrictions on U.S. investments in other areas implicated by China’s military-civil fusion strategy.” According to Treasury, on April 19, 2025, a Chinese investment fund controlled by Amidi invested approximately $92,478 in Shanghai Qiongche Intelligent Technology Company Limited (“Noematrix”), a private Chinese company that develops artificial intelligence systems for robotics applications. Treasury concluded that the investment was subject to the OISP’s notification requirements and imposed a $200,000 civil penalty after determining that Amidi did not submit the required post-closing notification. Treasury’s announcement emphasizes that the violation involved a transaction undertaken by a controlled foreign entity of a U.S. person. As discussed in our prior client alert , the OISP prohibits or requires notification for certain transactions by U.S. persons involving Chinese or Chinese-linked entities engaged in specified activities related to semiconductors, quantum information technologies, and artificial intelligence. The rule applies not only to direct U.S. person investments but also includes certain anti-circumvention provisions that carry extraterritorial effect. One of those provisions relates to controlled foreign entities: The OISP requires a U.S. person to submit a notification of any transaction undertaken by its controlled foreign entity if the transaction would have been notifiable had it been undertaken by the U.S. person directly. Treasury’s press release highlighted the OISP’s requirement that U.S. persons (here, Amidi) take “all reasonable steps to prohibit and prevent” transactions by their controlled foreign entities (Amidi’s Chinese fund subsidiary) that would constitute prohibited transactions if undertaken by the U.S. person itself. The OISP also requires U.S. persons to file notifications with Treasury for any transaction by a controlled foreign entity that would be a notifiable transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person. Treasury’s press release also notes that Amidi is the parent entity of the organization that does business as Plug and Play Tech Center. Publicly available announcements indicate that Plug and Play China participated in financing rounds involving Noematrix before the OISP took effect, meaning that the transaction underlying Treasury’s enforcement action was a follow-on investment in a company in which Amidi, through Plug and Play China, had previously invested. representative.title: Toronto approves 2026 budget with historic capital plan | The Canada Voice
representative.author: Toronto Voice Staff

snapshot.title: City Council approves Toronto's 2026 budget with $63.1-billion capital plan, frozen TTC fares
snapshot.evidenceText: The Canada Voice network · 13 local news sites across Ontario Toronto City Council has signed off on an $18.9-billion operating budget and the largest 10-year capital plan in the city's history, including frozen TTC fares and a property tax increase below inflation. October 10, 2026 at 6:18 p.m. · Updated October 11, 2026 at 2:10 p.m. · 2 min read Toronto City Council has approved the city's 2026 budget, signing off on an $18.9-billion operating plan and a 10-year capital budget that the city says is the largest in its history. The budget — Mayor Olivia Chow's third since her election in 2023 — was passed at a special meeting of council on Tuesday, according to a statement from Councillor Paula Fletcher , who represents Toronto-Danforth and published a budget breakdown on her website. The centrepiece of the plan is a $63.1-billion capital budget and plan covering 2026 to 2035, which Fletcher described as the biggest 10-year capital commitment the city has ever made. Fletcher said the budget's affordability measures — including frozen TTC fares and free meals for students — would save a working family with two children about $1,200 a year on groceries and transportation costs alone. The property tax increase for 2026 is set at 2.2 per cent, which Fletcher noted is below the rate of inflation. The budget also proposes what she called a fairer approach to funding city services, asking "empty home speculators and luxury property buyers" — the top 2 per cent of all buyers — to contribute more. The budget also includes $788 million in new savings and efficiencies, according to Fletcher, who said the city's financial position has improved over the past two years under Chow's leadership. Among the service investments, the budget funds seven-day-a-week library access and increases funding for tenant supports, home upgrade grants, flood protection, and programs that help seniors stay in their homes. On public safety, Fletcher said shootings, youth violence and 911 wait times have all significantly decreased. The budget builds on that trend, she said, by investing in more firefighters, paramedics, police officers and mental health workers, while boosting crime prevention programs. More than 25,000 residents took part in budget consultations held in October 2025, including telephone town halls and local events such as Fletcher's own budget town hall, ensuring the final plan reflected residents' priorities, her statement said. "I was pleased to support Mayor Chow's budget and her progressive vision of a more affordable, caring and safe Toronto," Fletcher wrote in her post. The budget vote came during a busy final stretch of the 2022-2026 council term. According to Fletcher's update, councillors also dealt with a maximum heat bylaw to protect tenants during extreme heat, a new funding deal to build more housing, and the provincial upload of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway. Other items on the agenda included Fletcher's motion about odours from the Ashbridges Bay sewage treatment plant, a redevelopment plan for Ookwemin Minising, and increased support from the mayor's office for vulnerable youth and low-income tenants. representative.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war? | Explainer News | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Al Jazeera Staff

snapshot.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
snapshot.evidenceText: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on. Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea. So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war? Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty. In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”. He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”. The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea. Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”. “The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera. Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years. Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts. “Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said. “The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.” Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city. In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force. Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi. It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting. Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement.
