snapshot.evidenceText: Get the latest headlines, discounts for the military community, and guides to maximizing your benefits Ethiopia and Eritrea have taken their escalating border confrontation to the United Nations Security Council, each accusing the other of aggression and seeking international action. Eritrea appealed to the Council on October 10, a day after Ethiopia invoked its right to self-defence over an alleged Eritrean invasion of Tigray. The competing appeals came as Ethiopian forces entered the strategic border city of Adigrat and UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for an immediate end to hostilities. Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos notified the Security Council on October 9 that Eritrean forces, including mechanised units, had advanced as far as 60 kilometres into northern Ethiopia. Addis Ababa invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a state’s inherent right of self-defence following an armed attack. Eritrea denied invading Ethiopian territory and accused its neighbour of using the allegations to justify military action. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh responded by asking the Council to condemn Ethiopia and take deterrent measures under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. Asmara characterised Ethiopia’s accusations as preparation for a war of aggression. Reuters reviewed the letter, which did not specify what measures Eritrea wanted the Council to adopt. Chapter VII gives the Security Council authority to address threats to international peace and security, including through sanctions and, in certain circumstances, military action. Article 51, which forms part of the same chapter, separately recognises the right of individual or collective self-defence. Eritrea is seeking action by the Council, while Ethiopia is asserting its right to respond to an alleged armed attack. Neither government’s appeal establishes the legality of its military conduct or automatically triggers UN enforcement measures. The UN Secretary-General expressed grave concern about renewed fighting in Tigray, Amhara and Afar in a statement dated October 9 and published the following day. Guterres called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to dialogue under the African Union-brokered Pretoria peace agreement of 2022. He also expressed concern about reports of Eritrean forces inside Ethiopia and urged regional governments to respect territorial integrity and refrain from actions that could intensify the conflict. The competing diplomatic appeals coincided with significant military developments. On October 10, Ethiopian government troops and allied Tigrayan militia entered Adigrat, approximately 30 kilometres from Eritrea’s border. Reuters verified footage showing pro-government militia members in the city, while three residents confirmed seeing Ethiopian soldiers and military vehicles. The agency did not independently establish complete government control. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) reported that Eritrean forces crossed the border near Zelambesa on October 7 and subsequently withdrew from Adigrat. Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted vehicles carrying Eritrean personnel and equipment during the withdrawal. Eritrea continues to deny that its forces invaded Ethiopia, and the full scale of the reported incursion remains independently unverified. The confrontation follows renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia that began on September 23. Ethiopian federal forces have since recaptured several major towns from a rebel alliance led by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Ethiopia and Eritrea fought together against the TPLF during the devastating 2020–2022 war but later became adversaries. Their relations have also deteriorated over Ethiopia’s pursuit of direct access to the Red Sea. Landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, Ethiopia regards maritime access as a strategic necessity, while Eritrea fears that Addis Ababa’s ambitions could threaten its sovereignty and coastline. The Security Council now faces competing requests from two neighbouring states whose forces have reportedly engaged in cross-border military operations. Guterres has offered UN assistance in resolving the crisis, but no binding Council response to the latest appeals has been established. Further troop movements, drone strikes and diplomatic initiatives will indicate whether the confrontation can be contained or develops into sustained interstate warfare. snapshot.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?

Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. snapshot.title: Rooppur Unit-1 achieves first nuclear chain reaction
snapshot.evidenceText: The first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was achieved today (11 October), marking a major milestone in Bangladesh's first nuclear power project as the reactor entered its initial criticality stage ahead of electricity generation. The chain reaction marks the first of four stages before the plant can generate electricity. The subsequent stages involve thermal energy transfer, mechanical energy conversion, and finally electricity generation and supply to the national grid. Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, confirmed the development to The Business Standard, saying the reaction was initiated after the required compliance procedures, technical parameters and external certifications had been completed. "Today at 3:34pm, we were able to achieve the chain reaction smoothly. By the grace of Allah, the parameters were within the desired ranges, and the reactor was very stable," he said. Inside a nuclear reactor, a controlled chain reaction splits uranium atoms through nuclear fission, releasing energy as heat. That heat is used to generate steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity. Russian specialists, Bangladeshi experts and other technical specialists were present to observe the process and assess the reactor's performance, Anwar added. He said nuclear fuel had already been loaded into the reactor and the fission process had now begun. Anwar said technical teams were working to complete the remaining processes as quickly as possible, while stressing that every stage must comply with the required procedures and safety standards. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Ishwardi, Pabna, is being built with two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units using Russian technology supplied by Rosatom. snapshot.title: Rooppur Unit-1 crosses hurdle to get going in Dec
snapshot.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy Bangladesh has cleared a major regulatory hurdle for commissioning its first nuclear power plant, with the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) approving the "first criticality" process for Unit-1 of the 2,400-MW Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant (RNPP). "We have issued the approval named B2 for Unit-1 to move forward in the second stage of rigorous scrutiny before initiation of its commercial operation," BAERA Chairman Mahmudul Hasan told The Financial Express on Thursday. The unit will require two more certifications, C and D, before commercial operation can begin, he said. The B2 approval clears the way for the reactor's physical start-up, during which it will achieve a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction for the first time -- a key prerequisite for generating electricity. Project officials said the approval had been delayed due to technical complications involving the reactor's pilot-operated relief and safety valves, a critical component of the plant's safety systems. Russian experts were brought in to resolve the issue, following which the system passed a series of tests, paving the way for regulatory approval. Officials now expect Unit-1 to start supplying electricity to the national grid on a trial basis by the end of December. First criticality has long been regarded as one of the most challenging milestones for the Rooppur project. During the process, the reactor will transition from a static installation to an operating nuclear facility through the initiation of a stable and self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. As part of the physical start-up, the reactor will initially operate at less than 1.0 per cent of its designed thermal capacity. Engineers and regulators will closely monitor reactor parameters, safety systems, control equipment and overall performance. The entire physical start-up process, including initial criticality, is expected to take between 30 and 40 days. If test results prove satisfactory, reactor power will be gradually increased in successive stages. Following completion of the physical start-up phase, the project will enter the power start-up stage, during which reactor output will be increased progressively, turbine synchronisation will be carried out and the generator will ultimately be connected to the national grid. Before entering this phase, the operating organisation will have to obtain a trial operational licence from BAERA. Electricity generation is expected to begin at around 3.0 per cent of capacity and gradually rise to 20-30 per cent, when power can be supplied to the national grid. Trial generation is expected to continue for seven to eight months after the reactor starts producing electricity. Project officials said the power start-up phase would involve significant technical and organisational challenges, requiring coordination among the reactor, turbine and safety systems, along with strict regulatory oversight and cooperation with external agencies. Once Rooppur starts supplying power to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world's 33rd nuclear power-producing nation, opening a new chapter in the country's energy security and technological advancement. The long-awaited achievement is also expected to strengthen Bangladesh's efforts to diversify its energy mix and ensure a more stable long-term electricity supply.

Officials concerned with the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) said the initiation of heat production through nuclear fission in the first unit had initially been planned for September. However, technical defects identified during safety valve testing delayed the next stage of work. Following two rounds of high-pressure testing, the results were submitted to the regulatory authority, which approved them last Thursday, the project officials said. The tests assessed whether the control valves were functioning according to prescribed standards. Fire safety and radiation protection arrangements were also examined as part of the process. The approval allows the project to proceed with further reactor commissioning activities. However, the officials said that achieving first criticality, gradually increasing reactor power, starting the turbine and supplying electricity to the national grid are separate stages, each requiring the completion of relevant technical and safety checks. The next major milestone is 'first criticality', when a controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction is established inside the reactor. A series of tests and observations will follow - a process that could take around a month. Reactor power will then be increased gradually. Initially, the plant is expected to supply around 300 MW to the national grid on a trial basis. Further testing and technical assessments will be required before the facility reaches commercial operation. Built with technical assistance from Russia, Rooppur uses third-generation VVER-1200 reactor technology. Project estimates suggest that the plant could meet around 10 percent of Bangladesh's electricity demand when both units are operational at full capacity. Its actual contribution will depend on national demand, plant performance, maintenance schedules and grid conditions. Unlike coal-, oil- or gas-fired power plants, nuclear facilities generate heat through the fission of uranium atoms rather than by burning fossil fuels. The heat produces steam, which drives a turbine connected to an electricity-generating system. Rooppur is designed for an operational life of 60 years, potentially extendable by another 20 to 30 years, subject to technical upgrades, safety assessments and regulatory approval. Routine maintenance and fuel replacement will remain essential, with refuelling potentially required approximately every 18 months. Sheikh Mohammad Touhidul Islam, joint secretary (Nuclear Power Wing) of the Ministry of Science and Technology, told BSS that Rooppur was not merely an electricity generation project but also a major opportunity to strengthen Bangladesh's technological capabilities and develop skilled human resources. He said the first unit was in the final stages of preparation for generation, while uranium for the second unit had also arrived at the project site. He expressed hope that work could be completed ahead of schedule. representative.author: Mohiuddin

snapshot.title: Rooppur nuclear power plant begins fission, moves closer to electricity generation
snapshot.evidenceText: <p>The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has begun a nuclear fission reaction, bringing Bangladesh’s only nuclear power plant closer to starting electricity generation and supplying power to the national grid.</p><p>The reaction is the process through which nuclear energy is released and marks a crucial stage in the final preparations for electricity generation and supply. The plant is scheduled to supply 300 megawatts of electricity to the national grid in December.</p><p>According to sources at the Rooppur plant, the process of generating energy through nuclear fission was initially scheduled to begin in September. However, the schedule was delayed after defects were detected during tests of safety valves. The valves were tested under high pressure in two rounds last week. After reviewing the test results, the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) approved the start of the reaction last Thursday. Nuclear fission began at 3:34pm on Sunday.</p><p>The Rooppur project in Pabna is the largest single project in Bangladesh’s history in terms of cost. The Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, under the Ministry of Science and Technology, is implementing the project. The state-owned Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL), under the commission, is responsible for operating the plant.</p><p>Russian contractor Atomstroyexport is constructing two units at Rooppur, each with a capacity of 1,200 megawatts.</p> .<p>NPCBL Managing Director Md Zahedul Hasan told Prothom Alo that the final process leading to the start of the nuclear reaction began on Saturday after three days of preparation. The controlled reaction successfully started on Sunday.</p><p>“This brings to an end the long wait following the beginning of Bangladesh’s journey towards the peaceful use of nuclear energy in 1961. This is a major milestone for the country’s science sector,” he said.</p><p>Sources at the plant said the reactor vessel of the first unit had achieved criticality for the first time. This is a significant milestone for Bangladesh’s nuclear power programme. Following criticality, all key reactor parameters have remained within the prescribed limits, and the process is being conducted under controlled conditions.</p><p>Officials involved in the project said the start of the nuclear reaction was a major step towards connecting the plant to the national grid. The next stages will involve reactor physics tests, verification of safety systems, a gradual increase in reactor power and the completion of tests and preparations required for grid connection, in accordance with the approved commissioning programme.</p><p>Each stage must comply with the highest safety standards, approved procedures and regulatory requirements.</p><p>According to plant officials, achieving reactor criticality is not merely a technical success but also a historic recognition of Bangladesh’s capabilities in science, engineering and nuclear technology. After years of effort, the country has reached a crucial stage in connecting its first nuclear power plant to the national grid.</p> .<p>Sources at the Rooppur plant said a series of tests would be conducted following the start of the nuclear reaction. The entire process could take 30 to 40 days.</p><p>The reactor’s power output will then be increased gradually. Nuclear fuel fission will generate heat, which will be used to produce steam and drive a turbine to generate electricity.</p><p>Once the reactor begins producing energy, electricity can be supplied to the national grid when its output reaches 30 per cent of capacity. At that stage, the plant is expected to supply 300 megawatts of electricity, potentially in December.</p><p>Plant officials said trial operations could continue for seven to eight months after the initial start-up. Once electricity is supplied to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world’s 33rd country to generate nuclear power.</p><p>Rooppur was recognised as a nuclear installation after nuclear fuel arrived at the project site in October 2023. With the receipt of the fuel, Bangladesh also joined the group of countries possessing nuclear energy capabilities.<br>According to plant sources, once operational, the nuclear power plant will be able to supply electricity continuously at a steady rate, 24 hours a day.</p><p>The reactor will require refuelling every 18 months. A unit may remain shut down for up to two months for the removal of spent fuel, loading of fresh fuel and maintenance.</p><p>The sources said that once one unit of Rooppur became operational, it could save USD 1 billion annually in fuel imports. However, the project has already been delayed by three and a half years.</p>.<p><br>The Rooppur project was originally scheduled to run until December 2025. Its deadline has been extended twice, with the latest completion date set for June 2028.</p><p>Although the deadline has been extended under the agreement with the contractor, there is no provision to increase the project cost under that agreement. However, the rise in the dollar exchange rate has increased the project's expenses by Tk 260 billion.</p><p>The total cost of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant is now expected to reach Tk 1.39 trillion.</p>

snapshot.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy The first controlled fission reaction started today (Sunday) at Unit-1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, marking Bangladesh's entry into nuclear power generation. The reactor achieved first criticality — a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — after the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) granted the B-2 licence on Thursday. BAERA Chairman Md Mahmudul Hasan confirmed that the regulator approved the unit to proceed to the criticality stage after resolving recent safety valve issues. The approval had been delayed due to failure of two automatic pressure relief valves (PORV/POSV) during commissioning. A Russian technical team spent the last month at the site to resolve the problem and all tests were successfully completed. Officials said two more licences — C and D — will be required before the 1,200 MW VVER-1200 reactor can be synchronized to the national grid. Heat generated through nuclear fission will turn water into high-pressure steam to drive turbines. “Simply put, we have now received approval to start the nuclear reaction needed to generate heat,” he said. Once first criticality is achieved, power will be raised gradually. When the reactor reaches about 37 percent thermal power, it can move toward power generation, initially supplying around 300 MW on a trial basis. If all stages are completed successfully, trial electricity supply to the national grid is expected by the end of December this year. Rooppur is Bangladesh’s first nuclear power plant, being built at a cost of $11 billion with Russian financial and technical assistance. snapshot.title: Rooppur Unit-1 achieves first nuclear chain reaction
snapshot.evidenceText: The first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was achieved today (11 October), marking a major milestone in Bangladesh's first nuclear power project as the reactor entered its initial criticality stage ahead of electricity generation. The chain reaction marks the first of four stages before the plant can generate electricity. The subsequent stages involve thermal energy transfer, mechanical energy conversion, and finally electricity generation and supply to the national grid. Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, confirmed the development to The Business Standard, saying the reaction was initiated after the required compliance procedures, technical parameters and external certifications had been completed. "Today at 3:34pm, we were able to achieve the chain reaction smoothly. By the grace of Allah, the parameters were within the desired ranges, and the reactor was very stable," he said. Inside a nuclear reactor, a controlled chain reaction splits uranium atoms through nuclear fission, releasing energy as heat. That heat is used to generate steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity. Russian specialists, Bangladeshi experts and other technical specialists were present to observe the process and assess the reactor's performance, Anwar added. He said nuclear fuel had already been loaded into the reactor and the fission process had now begun. Anwar said technical teams were working to complete the remaining processes as quickly as possible, while stressing that every stage must comply with the required procedures and safety standards. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Ishwardi, Pabna, is being built with two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units using Russian technology supplied by Rosatom. Each unit has a planned generation capacity of 1,200 megawatts, giving the plant a combined capacity of 2,400MW. energy / Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant / RNPP / neuclear energy While most comments will be posted if they are on-topic and not abusive, moderation decisions are subjective. representative.title: Wasauksing First Nation works to bring back wild rice — and youth are at the centre of efforts - MBC Radio
representative.author: MBC News

snapshot.title: Wasauksing First Nation works to bring back wild rice — and youth are at the centre of efforts - MBC Radio
snapshot.evidenceText: Photo: Group photo of Wasauksing Manoomin Youth and Survey Tour on Wasauksing August 2026 Wasauksing First Nation partnered with the Anishinabek/Ontario Fisheries Resource Centre (A/OFRC) this summer to assess the health and potential of manoomin (wild rice) habitats in the community. Close up shot of manoomin (wild rice). Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The aim of the project is to follow the community’s lead in restoring a food source that is central to Anishinaabe culture, food sovereignty and identity. In spring 2026, Wasauksing submitted a proposal to A/OFRC to support the revival of manoomin beds through scientific expertise and state-of-the-art tools while remaining grounded in the community’s own local knowledge. For Wasauksing’s Lands and Resources Office, success means more than ecological recovery — it also means “restoring personal and community well-being and self-determination; being able to manage and harvest traditional foods, strengthening our Nation’s food sovereignty.” The project aims to support the reclamation of cultural practices and traditional knowledge surrounding manoomin, while deepening community connection to land, water, and cultural identity. Through A/OFRC, Wasauksing has visited communities like Alderville to learn from Elders like Jeff Beaver, whose community has been running a wild rice reintroduction project since the 1990s. Gabrielle Perugini, A/OFRC’s lead fisheries biologist, said much of what they have learned as an organization and what makes these sort of restoration projects possible comes from knowledge keepers like Jeff Beaver from Alderville First Nation. Youth from the community spent a week alongside the A/OFRC team exploring local waters, learning the history of manoomin in their territory and getting hands-on experience with the monitoring and surveying of identified sites. “There were lots of smiles and laughing, lots of knowledge transfer and storytelling while we were out in the canoes checking in on the sites,” said Perugini. Monitoring turbidity and water quality at manoomin sites. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The fieldwork encouraged the youth to be part of the restoration efforts by learning how to use equipment to measure water quality at potential manoomin sites. They measured and recorded pH, turbidity, sediment composition, and water levels. They also learned to identify and document optimal growing conditions: slow-moving, clear water; lakes with inflow and outflow; depths between 0.5 and three feet; minimal water level fluctuations; and silty sediment. “I think it’s important not only from the stewardship side of things, but crucial for their spiritual connection to the land,” Perugini said of the youth’s involvement. “If you get the youth involved, they start to develop a personal relationship with the manoomin, and having some personal stake in the matter fuels their stewardship. People will protect what they love and value. The hope is that it spreads to more youth and, in the blink of an eye, you have manoomin guardians at the ready.” Gabrielle Perugini from A/OFRC teaching youth how to take soil samples. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland While it is too early for a final report — A/OFRC still needs to compile and analyze the data — the early assessments were encouraging. Existing manoomin beds and habitats were found to be not beyond recovery, and the surveys affirmed the community’s memory of where wild rice once grew. A manoomin habitat located around Wasauksing First Nation. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The final survey report will be released to Wasauksing once A/OFRC has had a chance to thoroughly review and format the data after the busy summer season. The report will be kept confidential for community members and will include information on suitable wild rice habitats across various locations, insights into community participation, and plans for long-term monitoring and sustainability. Surveying the water level of a manoomin habitat near Wasauksing First Nation. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland A project update poster is expected soon, and both organizations plan to present the work at the Wasauksing Lands and Resources Open House this spring. “Manoomin restoration goes beyond stewardship,” Perugini said. “It encourages community connectedness, strengthens food security, and fortifies spiritual and cultural connections.” For the youth who spent August surveying Wasauksing’s waters, this is just the beginning. They’ve seen what’s possible — that something lost can be brought home — and they’ve become part of a legacy that will extend far beyond their own lifetimes. “Youth bring passion with them, and it is contagious. They will be the ones with the option to continue to keep and build on that legacy,” said Neil Canvin, the natural resources co-ordinator with Wasauksing’s Lands and Resources Office. Once restoration is underway, Wasauksing plans to bring the whole community into the process. “Our desire is that, for next year and future years, we will host community events that will involve community members in the harvesting and planting processes for wild rice at the identified sites,” said Canvin. The community also plans to host workshops on the cultural dances that precede manoomin harvest and the traditional methods of processing wild rice for consumption. Manoomin (wild rice) habitat. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The Anishinabek/Ontario Fisheries Resource Centre is a not-for-profit organization established in 1995 through the Anishinabek Conservation and Fishing Agreement. It serves Anishinabek communities as an independent source of fisheries information, evaluating stresses on fish and their habitats and promoting sustainable management. A/OFRC has conducted fisheries research for more than 30 years and has been involved in at least three manoomin projects since 2011 — recognizing wild rice restoration as integral to healthy aquatic ecosystems. “Manoomin beds provide important nursery habitat for juvenile fish, shelter and grazing for waterfowl and mammals, and stabilize sediment — supporting the overall health of the ecosystem,” Perugini said. Community members with questions, suggestions or feedback can contact Neil Canvin or Gabrielle Perugini at gperugini@aofrc.org . CORRECTION (OCT. 5/2:28PM): This story was edited to correct the name of the Lands and Resources Office.

representative.title: Nearly 600 Floyd County, Ind. voters receive incorrect ballots
representative.author: Aprile Rickert

snapshot.title: Nearly 600 Floyd County voters receive incorrect ballots
snapshot.evidenceText: Floyd County election officials say nearly 600 voters received incomplete ballots, and they’re reaching out to people affected to help them cast their full vote. The Floyd County Election Board met for an emergency meeting Friday afternoon to address a programming error that omitted the Floyd County Commissioners District 1 race from four precincts: Franklin, Greenville, Georgetown and Lafayette. The race is between Republican incumbent Al Knable and Democratic challenger Ellen Morrison Kelley. The board said Friday afternoon they had identified 572 impacted voters. They include people who voted early in-person between Tuesday, Oct. 6 through Thursday, Oct. 8. Absentee ballots were also impacted. “The Election Board’s immediate priority is to provide each identified voter a lawful opportunity to vote in the omitted race,” according to a news release provided by the board. “The Election Board recognizes the importance of providing every voter a complete and accurate ballot and apologizes to the affected voters for this error.” The board, which includes Floyd County Clerk Danita Burks, did not speak to news media following the meeting. Officials say they have corrected the error and that early voting resumed Friday with the corrected ballot styles on voting machines. Voters who got the incomplete ballots will receive a written explanation and ABS-5 form, officials said. That is a “statement concerning defective, lost, destroyed, or spoiled absentee ballot.” After that is processed, they'll receive instructions and a chance to vote a corrected ballot. Susan Lockhart and her husband Jerry voted Tuesday, the first day of early voting, at the Floyd County 4-H Fairgrounds. She told LPM News this week they started questioning their ballots after they left. “It wasn't until we left that I said, ‘Hey, did you vote for Ellen?’ And he said, ‘There was no place to vote for Ellen,’” Lockhart said Thursday. She questioned how the faulty ballots were issued in the first place, and said it shouldn't be up to the voters to catch it. “There's no reason for the ballot to go out incomplete if that many people have their eyes on it,” she said. “And the Floyd County clerk, the buck stops with her.” Kelley, the Democratic candidate, said after the meeting she learned about the error when she started getting text messages from people saying her name hadn’t been on their ballots. And she’s not confident the process to address the problem will work. “I know that for the average person, getting out to vote once is can be a big deal when you're trying to get to work and go to soccer practice and make sure the laundry's done,” she said. ‘“And to receive a letter in the mail that says something very weird like this, I don't think people are gonna have the time, maybe.” Knable, the Republican incumbent, said after the meeting he had concerns about people who might be out of town or have trouble getting around. “That's a great concern because I want to make sure that those people do have a chance to be heard,” he said. He also said he was concerned about the whole situation. He said he doesn’t think this incident will affect the outcome of the race. “But even if it does, that's a meager consideration when you consider the fact that we might potentially disenfranchise some of these 572 folks,” he said. Election officials did not provide a reason for the error. They said that ballot information and styles are usually reviewed and proofed before going out to voters, and they’re reviewing the process to see what happened. Voters with questions or concerns can contact the Floyd County Election Division at (812) 948-5419. Coverage of Southern Indiana is funded, in part, by Samtec Inc., the Hazel & Walter T. Bales Foundation, and the Caesars Foundation of Floyd County.
snapshot.imageAlt: The Floyd County Election Board held an emergency meeting Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, after discovering hundreds of incomplete ballots issued to voters.

representative.title: Why this Canadian farmer is letting his land grow wild - North Bay News
representative.author: Danielle Tocker Photo/Be Giant

snapshot.title: Why this Canadian farmer is letting his land grow wild
snapshot.evidenceText: Lorne Scott calls his farm an island. Given that it’s in the prairie pothole region of southern Saskatchewan – a sweep of shallow wetlands left by glaciers – this is a metaphor, but it works: in all directions from where we stand, on a sunny day in June, are cultivated croplands. They’ve been planted to within an inch of their lives with canola, wheat, lentils. Except for a few shelterbelts, there are no trees from here to the horizon. Then there’s Scott’s land, thick with trees, shrubs and grasses. Parts of his farm grow wild, or “never broke,” as he puts it, with aspen, snowberry, starflower, Solomon’s seal and northern bedstraw, from which the Cree, who were here before settlement, made red dye. The bedstraw seeds, when roasted, work as a coffee substitute. Scott doesn’t drink coffee. Nor does he harvest any of the Indigenous plants on his land, which sits about nine kilometres south of Indian Head and about 75 kilometres southeast of Regina. They’re just here, left to grow any which way. His land is wild on purpose. It’s fair to call Scott a conservationist, one of the most respected in the province, still active in the community at 79. Soft-spoken and gentle, he is still a farmer: he grows wheat and oats, albeit on a small patch – 32 hectares planted this year. His grandfather was a farmer too, on a property two kilometres east, where Scott grew up. Letting more than a quarter of his farm grow wild is a radical act. Scott wouldn’t say so. He does it “for nature,” he says, to protect the life that’s disappearing, from insects to owls to moose. The day before we met, he saw two yearling moose, as well as a whitetail doe with a fawn and a mule deer. There are bluebird nesting boxes all over the property. What makes all of this radical is the context. Modern agriculture is a high-tech, data-driven industry that uses autonomous field equipment that relies on AI, drones and satellite imagery to maximize resources – land – for profit. “Only a wild man could be so reckless as to let a valuable thing like land go free,” says Andrea Olive, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, a friend of Scott’s and the author of Protecting the Prairies: Lorne Scott and the Politics of Conservation . “It must bother his neighbours, who only see cash crops where Lorne sees true growth.” It does, and some have asked, politely, to rent those perfectly good hectares of his, to plow them under, get things going as God and the commodities markets intended. He tells them no, that their equipment is too big, “and they shake their heads and walk away.” There’s a sign at the entrance to his farm that says, “This Property Is Forever Protected.” That means there’s a conservation easement on part of the property to preserve its natural state. Scott still owns the land and can pass it to his children or whoever he wants, but the restrictions on development are permanent. Scott knows about easements: he served as Saskatchewan’s minister of environment and resource management for four years in the late ‘90s, in Roy Romanow’s NDP government, and was responsible for the Conservation Easements Act, aimed at restricting development of wild land on private property. Under the act, the farmer still owns the land but enters into an agreement with a non-profit, like Ducks Unlimited, to keep it wild, as, say, wetland or grassland. There are thousands of hectares under easement in Saskatchewan. Some ranchers find them useful for protecting natural grasslands for grazing. Grazing is good for grasslands. It disturbs the plants (as does wildfire) in ways that help them grow. A conservative estimate is that 80 per cent of the grassland in Saskatchewan has been lost since commercial agriculture began, most recently through the sale of Crown lands after Ottawa dismantled the 74-year-old Prairie Farm Rehabilitation program in 2009. In the first 20 years of the 21st century, the average farm size increased by about 20 per cent, while the number of farms shrank by 23 per cent. Farms are getting bigger, land prices are rising, and while most farms are owned by the families that work them, one to two per cent are owned by investors and 2.4 per cent by large-scale private landowners. From Manitoba to the Cypress Hills, southern Saskatchewan was once grassland where bison grazed and First Nations hunted. It’s now mostly agricultural, and many farms are dotted with oil wells and pumpjacks, sometimes called “nodding donkeys.” To Scott and groups like the Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation, a non-profit he used to head, the mixed grasslands and fescue prairie are home to more than 30 species at risk, including the greater sage-grouse, and are valuable for that fact alone. Ottawa and the private sector (including Mosaic, a potash mining company, and the Weston family, which backs Be Giant ) have donated millions of dollars to prairie habitat preservation. “Everything gets bigger and better, supposedly,” says Scott, a man of few words until he gets wound up. “The biggest impact I see is on the natural environment. The wetlands, the bush are being cleared, and with equipment and technology, everything is workable these days for growing canola or wheat, whatever, and it's really made a big impact on the natural environment, and consequently some bird species have declined by 90 per cent or more, and largely due to agriculture, intensive farming.” According to Environment and Climate Change Canada, burrowing owl numbers declined 90 per cent from 1990 to 2000, then another 64 per cent between 2005 and 2015. They are small, oddball birds with long legs for running that live underground in tunnels dug by badgers. There are now fewer than 800 pairs left in Saskatchewan and Alberta. “Out in the country and the wild west, I call it, anything goes as long as it benefits you,” Scott says. Scott is not a born politician. He’s not an ideologue. He ran for office as a New Democrat, but in the 1980s, he joined the Progressive Conservative Party. As a boy on the farm, he was more interested in birds than politics, particularly the bluebirds that nested near sloughs and aspen bluffs, in grain bins and any natural cavity, including tractor wheel wells. On a farm, bluebirds bring good luck. But as early as the 1920s, they lost habitat to industrial agriculture and urban spread, and Scott took to building simple wood houses and tacking them up on farm fences to give them a place to nest. In 1969, he got a licence to band bluebirds and tree swallows, and in the first year banded nearly 1,000. Since then, he has banded tens of thousands of birds. With other volunteers, he built a “bluebird trail” of nesting boxes, from Brandon, Manitoba, to Raymore, Saskatchewan, north of Regina. He would drive 800 kilometres four times a year to check on the nests. It was, he says, the longest bluebird trail in the world. Then everything changed: the climate, and the business of agriculture. Large grain farms replaced natural aspen bluffs, wetlands and grasslands. Extreme weather in the bluebirds’ Texas breeding grounds changed migration patterns. By 2014, only six came back to nest near Indian Head, and the next year, none. Scott hasn’t seen bluebirds on his property since. To get to the wild acreage on Scott’s farm, we drive there in a Dodge Caravan (licence plate: BLUEB1RD), not by road but over the hummocky farmland itself . He points to an eastern kingbird on the fence. “From central South America,” he says. The place is home to bees and other insect pollinators, owls, hawks, moose and songbirds. Tree swallows have taken to nesting in the old bluebird houses, and we pull up next to one on a fencepost. He opens the top to show me five white eggs in a nest. Past the fence is a new project: a tree and shrub sanctuary with dozens of species, planted on four hectares when the federal sanctuary in Indian Head was shut down in 2012 following cuts by the Stephen Harper government. Scott is growing sea buckthorn, snowberry, high bush cranberry, apples, crabapples, buffalo berry, chokecherry and poplar – 80 different species – to serve as a seed bank. There is an easement on this land, too. Meanwhile, researchers and neighbours are welcome to take cuttings from the trees. His house is cluttered with school pictures of grandchildren and paintings of ducks and birdhouses. Below a picture of a meadowlark is a small, framed photo of Scott in a suit and Canada-flag tie, receiving the Order of Canada in 2008 from Governor General Michaëlle Jean. The Governor General’s website cites his volunteer work, his political life and his reputation “throughout Western Canada as a staunch defender of wildlife and natural habitats.” I ask him why he practises what he preaches on his own farm, whether this kind of “rewilding,” as it’s called, is more than a gesture. After all, a few hectares of aspen and bedstraw won’t save the planet. “That's the way the land was when I grew up on my dad's farm, you know,” he says. “Back then, people lived more in harmony with nature. They didn't feel it necessary to cultivate every acre, and they relied on the sloughs [for water] and the grass for pasture for hay, the aspen bluffs for wood and [the shrubs for] berry picking.” That’s not radical. He’s talking about an idea of land use that accommodates wildlife alongside a less destructive form of agriculture, not either-or. He’s a farmer. But he paraphrases Teddy Roosevelt: wildlife in its habitat can’t speak, so we must and we will. “Somebody has to,” Scott says. Tom Jokinen is a Winnipeg writer and broadcaster. He writes for The Walrus, Literary Review of Canada and is a regular contributor to CBC Radio Ideas. He's won a National Magazine Award, a New York Festivals Gold Award for audio documentary, and his book Curtains , about the funeral industry, was a Canadian bestseller. snapshot.title: OrbitalHub » CHIME detects cosmic hydrogen on its own
snapshot.evidenceText: Domain is for sale. $50,000,000.00 USD. Direct any inquiries to contact@orbitalhub.com. The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, run out of a low-slung cluster of wire-mesh cylinders near Penticton, British Columbia, has just done something the rest of cosmology has been waiting on for the better part of two decades. In a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal on 28 September 2026 and posted to arXiv as 2511.19620, the CHIME Collaboration reports the first standalone detection of the cosmological 21-centimeter signal, the faint radio glow of neutral hydrogen from an era when the universe was roughly five billion years old. The result reached a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.5 across 94 nights of observing, a clean confirmation that intensity mapping can carry cosmological information without leaning on any other telescope. The detection matters because it removes a crutch that earlier 21cm cosmology work could not do without. To pick a faint hydrogen signal out of the radio sky, every previous CHIME result had to be cross-correlated with an external galaxy or quasar catalog, so that any structure showing up in both maps could be trusted. That technique works, but it ties a hydrogen experiment to the schedule and depth of someone else’s survey. The new measurement is an auto-correlation, meaning the team trusted only CHIME’s own data and still recovered a statistically unambiguous clustering signal. Splitting the 608.2 to 707.8 megahertz frequency window in two yields independent detections at 8.7 and 9.2 sigma. Two independent confirmations in a single dataset is the kind of robustness that turns a hint into a measurement. The reason this is exciting rather than merely incremental comes down to what intensity mapping is meant to do. Galaxy surveys like DESI, Euclid, and the Vera Rubin Observatory’s LSST build their maps by detecting and counting individual galaxies, a process that consumes enormous telescope time and tends to miss the dim, hydrogen-rich galaxies where most of the universe’s atoms actually live. CHIME does something different. Its four 100-metre cylindrical reflectors look at the whole northern sky every day, with no moving parts, and instead of resolving individual galaxies they sum the faint 21cm emission from millions of unresolved sources inside each patch of sky. The result is a low-resolution three-dimensional map of where the neutral hydrogen is, calibrated by redshift because cosmic expansion has stretched the original 21cm line into longer and longer wavelengths the further back in time one looks. CHIME’s full operating band runs from 400 to 800 megahertz, which corresponds to redshifts between roughly 2.5 and 0.8, an epoch the collaboration describes as substantially younger than the one surrounding Earth today but old enough to capture the period when dark energy began to dominate the cosmic energy budget. The new paper uses only the cleaner half of that window, between 608.2 and 707.8 megahertz, which corresponds to redshifts of 1.34 down to 1.01, with a mean redshift of 1.16. That is exactly the slice where the universe had finished its early formative fireworks but had not yet been completely taken over by the accelerating expansion driven by dark energy. Why this matters comes down to what the team can now attempt to do with the rest of the CHIME archive. The instrument has been collecting data continuously since first light in 2017 and the collaboration says it now has nearly seven years of observations in hand, most of which has not yet been analyzed. The Sept 28 paper uses 94 nights from 2019 only. If the new processing pipeline can keep extracting the auto-power spectrum cleanly from older data, CHIME should be able to push the measurement to higher redshifts, into the period when the universe was only about three billion years old, and to lower redshifts, where the dark-energy signal is strongest. That spans almost the entire window during which dark energy transitioned from negligible to dominant. Tracing the universe’s expansion history across that span, with a single instrument and a single tracer, is the prize the collaboration has been working toward since construction finished in 2017. The first detection was a 2023 paper that cross-correlated CHIME’s hydrogen maps with optical galaxy and quasar catalogs from eBOSS. That cross-correlation approach was scientifically productive but also exposed. The hydrogen experiment needed a second, much larger optical survey to confirm any signal. The new result flips that around: CHIME is now the primary instrument, and any cross-correlation with another survey becomes an optional consistency check rather than a requirement. Co-author Dr. Mark Halpern, a University of British Columbia physicist and CHIME principal investigator, called the result a fundamentally new way of probing the cosmos, built on an instrument conceived, paid for, and operated entirely by Canadian institutions. The technical work that made this possible is what most readers will not see and what most of the team spent the most time on. The 21cm cosmological signal at these frequencies is buried under several layers of brighter noise. Galactic synchrotron emission from our own Milky Way dominates by orders of magnitude. Distant radio galaxies and active galactic nuclei add another, structured layer on top. Human radio-frequency interference from satellites, radar, and cell towers adds a moving, partly unpredictable foreground. And small imperfections in CHIME’s receivers and correlator can mix otherwise smooth foreground signals into patterns that look like cosmological structure. Pulling the hydrogen out required the team to develop new radio-frequency interference detection algorithms, achromatic beamforming techniques that keep the telescope’s synthesized beam stable across frequency, and a foreground-filtering step that runs before time-averaging so that spectral leakage does not smear bright foregrounds into faint cosmological modes. Independent sub-band splits, null tests on the data, and many alternative processing choices were all checked before the team trusted the result, a process Chakraborty described as working very hard to convince ourselves that this was not a false alarm. The team’s analysis goes one step beyond the headline detection. In a companion paper they take the auto-power spectrum at face value as a measurement of how strongly neutral hydrogen clusters at redshift 1.16, and they compare it with predictions from the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations. The observed hydrogen clustering disagrees with the simulated clustering by about 3.1 standard deviations for the TNG100 simulation volume and 4.0 standard deviations for the larger TNG300. That is not a crisis. The team reads the gap between observation and simulation as a clue about how tightly hydrogen is packed at the small, non-linear scales the new measurement is most sensitive to, not as evidence that the total hydrogen inventory is wrong. It shows that CHIME’s standalone data can test models of how gas actually populates galaxies and dark-matter halos, not just deliver a number for dark-energy cosmology. The long-term target is still baryon acoustic oscillations, the imprint of pressure waves from the hot early universe that act as a cosmic standard ruler. Tracking how that ruler stretches at different redshifts is one of the cleanest ways to measure how the universe’s expansion rate has changed over time, and therefore to test competing models for what dark energy is doing. The current measurement does not yet deliver BAO. Foreground-removal eliminates some of the largest-scale modes the BAO analysis needs, and the detected power spectrum occupies smaller non-linear scales where gravitational clustering has already scrambled the clean linear signal. What the Sept 28 paper establishes is the prerequisite: a telescope designed to map the universe through hydrogen can isolate that hydrogen without another survey pointing out where to look. The next step is to apply that capability across more of the CHIME archive and across the wider redshift range the telescope was built for. For a community that has spent more than a decade waiting for a 21cm cosmology result that does not need a galaxy survey attached, the message from the Okanagan Valley this week is that the wait is over, and the next decade of dark-energy measurements just got a new instrument. The observed hydrogen clustering disagrees with the simulated clustering by about 3.1 standard deviations for the TNG100 simulation volume and 4.0 standard deviations for the larger TNG300. That is not a crisis. The team reads the gap between observation and simulation as a clue about how tightly hydrogen is packed at the small, non-linear scales the new measurement is most sensitive to, not as evidence that the total hydrogen inventory is wrong. It shows that CHIME’s standalone data can test models of how gas actually populates galaxies and dark-matter halos, not just deliver a number for dark-energy cosmology. The long-term target is still baryon acoustic oscillations, the imprint of pressure waves from the hot early universe that act as a cosmic standard ruler. Tracking how that ruler stretches at different redshifts is one of the cleanest ways to measure how the universe’s expansion rate has changed over time, and therefore to test competing models for what dark energy is doing. The current measurement does not yet deliver BAO. Foreground-removal eliminates some of the largest-scale modes the BAO analysis needs, and the detected power spectrum occupies smaller non-linear scales where gravitational clustering has already scrambled the clean linear signal. What the Sept 28 paper establishes is the prerequisite: a telescope designed to map the universe through hydrogen can isolate that hydrogen without another survey pointing out where to look. The next step is to apply that capability across more of the CHIME archive and across the wider redshift range the telescope was built for. For a community that has spent more than a decade waiting for a 21cm cosmology result that does not need a galaxy survey attached, the message from the Okanagan Valley this week is that the wait is over, and the next decade of dark-energy measurements just got a new instrument. representative.title: Mississauga election 2026: Mayoral candidates talk redeveloping Living Arts Centre, platform policy planks
representative.author: Nick Westoll

snapshot.title: Mississauga mayoral candidates talk redeveloping Living Arts Centre, platform policy planks
snapshot.evidenceText: With two-and-a-half weeks to go until Mississauga election day, talk about potentially redeveloping a notable chunk of the city’s downtown entered into the campaign on Thursday as mayoral candidates put forward various policy ideas and focuses. While unveiling the remaining parts of her campaign platform, Bonnie Crombie said she wants to put a stop to studying the potential demolition of the Living Arts Centre as part of a massive redevelopment project. “I will cancel Carolyn Parrish’s proposed redevelopment of the Living Arts Centre and surrounding civic lands, a $2.5-billion vanity project at a time when residents are struggling with everyday bills; this is the wrong priority,” she told reporters, arguing any potential municipal funding should be redirected to other priorities and initiatives. The Living Arts Centre, located just north of Mississauga city hall and west of Square One, opened in 1997. It has a 1,300-seat main auditorium along with various meeting rooms and exhibition spaces. Earlier in 2026, Mississauga city council voted to begin a study and consultation process that could ultimately result in a downtown transformation. The major part of the planning centres around potentially replacing the Living Arts Centre and a nearby park, which totals around 12 acres, with a new convention centre, hotel, music hub, offices, apartments and retail spaces. It is not clear when a possible vote on whether or not to proceed with that vision could be held. While making an announcement on providing additional infrastructure and supports for Ridgeway Plaza as part of a broader small business plan, Alvin Tedjo rejected the idea of proceeding with the potential massive redevelopment. “The mayor’s plan to build a $2.5-billion convention centre is a terrible idea; no one is asking for this. They’re also going to be taking out the parkland and the parking in the area. That green space is so valued for the residents who live in that area,” he said, adding he wants residents to help determine the future for the area and is open to potentially renovating the Living Arts Centre. Dipika Damerla also rejected the idea, saying she wants to proceed with a vision for downtown Mississauga that is focused on a health care innovation district. “[It] will bring young talent and make Mississauga the Silicon Valley of commercializing health care innovation,” she said, pointing to existing and upcoming hospital and education infrastructure in the city and region. Speaking with CityNews ahead of an apartment groundbreaking in Port Credit Thursday afternoon, Parrish said she backs the proposed redevelopment concept. She said a majority of the required funding would come from the private sector and noted there would be an elevated park for residents to use. “I think it’s a fabulous job creator. I think it’s a wonderful way to increase our income and taxes at the City and to enliven our city centre, it’s perfect,” she said. “We’re a modern city and we’re looking at modern ideas.” Parrish said if the plan proceeded, the Living Arts Centre would not be torn down until a new building gets erected. She also said the convention centre could be as big as 300,000 square feet and added she would like to see a five-star hotel opened to support the redevelopment. As advance voting continues in Mississauga until the end of Sunday , the leading Mississauga mayoral candidates continue to put forward policy ideas and focuses. During her announcement Thursday afternoon, Crombie touted various policy proposals on a variety of areas. “I will put the priorities of Mississaugans first and they’re clear: To bring taxes under control, protect jobs, attract investment, get Mississauga moving again and make our neighbourhoods safer,” she said. Damerla told CityNews she plans to keep campaigning and promoting the key themes of her campaign. “Here [are] the highlights of my plan: Freeze property taxes in 2027 and thereafter keep them at or below inflation, stop the waste at city hall (and) hire an independent auditor general, stop the $100 million that we’re bleeding every year to Brampton by fixing the unfair policing formula, (and) allowing ‘six-plexes’ as of right on certain arterial roads to make housing more affordable and realistic for young families,” she said Thursday afternoon. When asked what she wanted to accomplish if she gets elected for a full term, Parrish said she was focused on two areas. “Housing, I want to keep that up. I was at a topping-off ceremony yesterday for three towers on the other side of Port Credit. This is a ground-breaker, and it’s all because of the incentive that we brought in as a council,” she said Thursday afternoon, adding the changes have resulted in support from developers. “We’ve got to work on the taxes, that’s a big one. Step one was getting the road maintenance moved down from the region so we don’t have to subsidize Caledon $30 million next year, another $18 million or so on waste that we’ve moved down from the region. “Of course I’m working on the police budget, which is a 38 (per cent)-62 (per cent) split (with Brampton) and I do have a commitment from the premier that he is going to do it (addressing the funding disparity between the two cities).” Tedjo, speaking outside of Ridgeway Plaza Thursday morning, talked about his small business policy plank, which is part of his broader overall campaign platform. He said initiatives include a new 100-day guarantee for “qualified small-business permits,” small business hubs with “more affordable commercial space,” and expanded youth opportunities. He also said he would pursue bringing a Peel Regional Police substation to the plaza, which has seen crackdowns by officers amid concerns over nuisance gatherings , and extra parking at a nearby site to support the plaza. “Local entrepreneurs are spending too much time navigating city hall, small businesses are struggling to stay afloat and younger people are having a harder time getting a foot in the door. My plan will transform the City of Mississauga from a barrier into a partner,” Tedjo said. Click here for a list of all 14 candidates running for mayor. Election day in Mississauga and all of Ontario’s municipalities is on Oct. 26. representative.title: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender. | The Seattle Times
representative.author: Sophia Solano

snapshot.title: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender.
snapshot.evidenceText: Irvin E. Koch, at 103, has been perfecting his one-liners for decades. He deals them out quickly, with a half smile that reveals the four remaining teeth on his top gums and a flash of mischief in his clear blue eyes. After 63 years tending bar, he has his setup-pause-punch line down to a science. When a patron on a recent evening asks him whether he is the oldest bartender in the world, he doesn’t miss a beat. “Don’t ask me,” he says. “I haven’t been around the world yet.” By many unofficial accounts, Irv (as he is widely known) is indeed the world’s oldest bartender. And since 1963, he has been bartending at Club Sunset Knoll, a dive in a Baltimore suburb that is better known as Irv’s Basement Bar because, well, it’s in Irv’s basement. The waterfront house that Irv bought when John F. Kennedy was president sits at the end of a gravel driveway in Pasadena, Maryland. It has plastic-wrapped windows and a sliver of red above the gray exterior siding, as if the painter went off to fetch a ladder and never came back. When we, two Post reporters, pull into a small, otherwise empty lot on a September afternoon, Irv’s stepgrandson Jason Cook walks outside and ushers us down a concrete staircase. We step through a nondescript door. Irv’s Basement Bar looks today as it has for decades: a retro redoubt from the rest of the world above. The drinks are cheap, the lights are dim, and the jukebox is playing. Scrawled messages cover every surface at Irv’s, from its cracked bathroom walls to its tiled ceilings to its leathery chairs. (“Raise Hell, Praise Irv” reads one note not far from a haphazardly inked phallus. But mostly, people just write their names.) The bar’s round card tables are scuffed. Underneath one, a stray cheetah-print slipper lies forgotten. There are nude Polaroid photos hung next to police department patches from across the country. The pool table takes quarters, and the Smith Corona cash register is about as old as Irv himself. A large banner with his smiling face on it lords above his subterranean kingdom: “Drinking where the sun don’t shine,” it reads. The bar’s most notable feature, however, is the ever-growing collection of bras — padded, underwire, lace — that hang from the ceiling tiles like a tree canopy. They’re mostly graffitied, too, with the names of the women who left them there. The first of them, decades ago, was named Amy. “She did it, I didn’t do it,” Irv says. “Most of the girls want to do it. You probably want to do it yourself.” Cook, who is sitting nearby, has come to expect these sorts of comments. “He don’t hold back anything,” Cook, 43, says later. “That’s for sure.” Nothing here is formal, and the bar only operates on Irv time. “The hours are very simple,” he tells us later. “When the first one gets here, that’s when it opens up.” He closes whenever patrons leave, or when he gets tired. Over a few hours at Irv’s, we learn about many of his dislikes: tattoos, bar covers, the church, babies, naps (“wasting your life away”), cities (“too many people”) and credit cards (“the government can trace everything you do”). He hasn’t had a dog since he was a kid and never bought a cellphone. Irv’s penchant for “telling everybody what he thinks,” Cook says, is one of two qualities that generations of regulars appreciate most about him. The other, according to Cook, is that Irv is a genuinely kind man. When Cook was a toddler, he says, his mother became unable to care for him, and Irv and his wife took him in. Cook recently moved back to the house (with his wife and four children) to care for Irv. Born in 1923, Irv grew up poor in a south Baltimore neighborhood, largely during the Great Depression. As a teenager, he joined the Navy and served in the Philippines during World War II. His younger brother Harry followed him into the armed forces. After the war, Irv worked as a builder for Sears and as a plumber with Harry. Going into the bar business just sort of happened. The house he now lives in was built in 1912 as a summer home for a prominent Baltimore meatpacking family, and later became an inn before Irv bought it in 1963. “This was up for sale,” Irv says unsentimentally. “We needed a house, so we bought the house — and guess what? The bar came with it.” Not everyone who discovers that their new digs come with a fully functioning tavern would opt to leave their career for bartending. Irv did. “Well, I was gifted it, so I took it,” he says. “When I was born and all, everything was pennies, nickels and dimes. Now it’s twenties, fifties, hundreds. So that’s why I opened up the bar. For the money!” He says this line with a well-rehearsed flourish that shows he has delivered it countless times. Cook doubts its veracity. For one, the cash-only bar makes just enough for Irv to live off. He’s pretty sure Irv doesn’t just do it for the profit. “He loves the interaction, socializing with people,” Cook says. “He likes the attention, too. It definitely seems to keep him alive.” Around 6 p.m., people begin trickling in, a lone regular here, a group of four police officers there. They order bottles of Coors Light from Irv and flip through the jukebox offerings: Buddy Holly, Dean Martin, Billboard’s Top Country Hits of 1960. People used to come to Irv’s just for its cold beer and low prices. Many now come to reach back in time to before the digital age. When patrons line up for photos with Irv, their cellphones look out of place. Kathleen Hooper, 48, is there celebrating her 17th wedding anniversary with her husband, Robert. “It’s almost like Ripley’s Believe It or Not meets ‘Coyote Ugly’ meets your neighbor,” she remarks about the space. She has lived in the area for years but never before made the trip. “This is a thing that people put on their bucket list,” she says. “We just felt like we had to do it before we didn’t have the chance. … Once it’s gone, it’s gone.” Hooper was nervous before her visit because of the lack of information available about Irv’s. No website, no phone number, no firm business hours. But the adventure, the not knowing, is the fun of it, she says. She grabs a Sharpie and scrawls on a doorframe “Love! Rob + Katie 4evah,” leaving her small mark on this storied place the same scribbling way thousands of others have before. Since starting his bar, Irv has never worked another job and has never thought about quitting his basement tavern. And after Irv’s wife and brother died, “he never stopped,” Cook says. “He is very good at taking emotions and feelings and somehow either getting rid of them or just pushing them down and hiding them away.” Like his bar, Irv is a product of a different era. He doesn’t spend much time thinking about the past, and second-guessing isn’t in his makeup. “If I could go backwards?” He considers the question. “There ain’t too much I would change.” Once a party ends, Irv is looking to the next one, he says. Right now, he’s excited for his 104th birthday party in August. “Who knows if this place will exist once he goes?” Cook says. “But everybody should come on down and check us out while they still can. And meet the famous Irv.” Stay secure and make sure you have the best reading experience possible by upgrading your browser!

snapshot.title: Georgia's grape harvest surges as quality hits 99 per cent
snapshot.evidenceText: Georgia is enjoying one of its biggest and highest-quality grape harvests since independence. By 6 October, growers in the country's main wine-producing region, Kakheti, had delivered 182,210 tonnes of grapes, with 99 per cent rated medium or high quality, despite recent protests over prices. Georgia's grape harvest is in full swing, with between 13,000 and 14,000 tonnes being processed daily in Kakheti, the heart of the country's wine industry. The state-backed Harvest Management Company is collecting grapes at 22 sites across the region, helping growers sell their produce as the harvest accelerates. Saperavi, Georgia's signature red grape variety, accounts for 92,100 tonnes, while Rkatsiteli, a widely grown white variety, has contributed up to 77,400 tonnes. The standout figure, however, is the quality of the crop. Agriculture Minister Davit Songhulashvili has attributed the strong results to a new grading system introduced this year, which rewards growers with higher payments for better-quality grapes. Just one per cent of the harvest has been classified as rotten or low quality. Price protests prompt government intervention The bumper harvest has not been without challenges. Last month, grape growers in Kvareli and Gurjaani staged protests over prices, amid concerns that an abundant harvest could lead to oversupply and lower earnings. In response, the government introduced a guaranteed purchase scheme to protect growers from being left with unsold grapes. Under the scheme, the Harvest Management Company purchases surplus grapes that private wineries cannot absorb, with prices determined by grape variety and sugar content. AI graphic by AnewZ AnewZ With around 13,200 growers having delivered grapes by 6 October, the scheme is providing a safety net during one of the country's busiest harvest seasons. Why Georgia's grape harvest matters Beyond its economic importance, the grape harvest holds a special place in Georgian culture. Known locally as rtveli, the annual harvest is a tradition that brings families and communities together. Relatives return to their villages, neighbours help gather grapes, and the hard work is often followed by communal feasts filled with traditional food, toasts and singing. For many families, winemaking remains closely tied to centuries-old techniques, including fermenting grapes in large clay vessels known as qvevri, which are traditionally buried underground. The harvest is also a vital source of income. Wine is one of Georgia's best-known exports, supporting thousands of rural households whose livelihoods depend on grape production and fair prices. The country's winemaking heritage stretches back around 8,000 years, according to archaeological evidence, while traditional qvevri winemaking is recognised by UNESCO as part of humanity's intangible cultural heritage. More than just wine Not every grape harvested in Georgia ends up in a wine bottle. Some are distilled into chacha, a strong traditional spirit made from grape pomace, while others are pressed into juice. Grapes are also used to make churchkhela, a popular Georgian sweet made by dipping strings of nuts into thickened grape juice, creating a distinctive candle-shaped snack commonly found in local markets. From traditional delicacies to internationally recognised wines, Georgia's grape harvest remains central to the country's culture, economy and rural communities.
