representative.title: How a rebel force held the world to ransom in a single night of chaos and panic
representative.author: Vivian Nereim, Saeed Al-Batati, Shuaib Almosawa

snapshot.title: How a rebel force held the world to ransom in a single night of chaos and panic
snapshot.evidenceText: In a matter of hours, an Iran-allied militia trounced Saudi-backed forces to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. No one was able – or willing – to stop them. You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: In the weeks before the Iran-backed Houthi militia fanned out along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, sending their foes into a frenzied retreat, a Yemeni government commander called for help. It was obvious to the commander, Lieutenant General Tariq Saleh, that the Houthis wanted to seize his territory to reach the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important waterways in the world. According to three Yemeni officials, he tried to warn his powerful allies in Saudi Arabia and the United States. About 10 per cent of global trade goes through the strait. Amid the US-Israeli war with Iran, both countries had an interest in preventing an Iran-linked militia from winning a perch beside it. Yet last month – when the Houthis did just that – no one was able, or willing, to stop them. The militia’s stunning triumph over the Bab el-Mandeb, which unfolded in a single night of chaos and panic, set off a cascade of events that plunged Yemen back into a war with global reverberations. This month, Saudi Arabia began a bombing campaign to help the Yemeni government reclaim the territory it lost , with intelligence and targeting assistance from the US military. Government-allied forces claimed to have since made significant gains, besieging the Houthi fighters who held the strait. It is unclear whether the Houthis’ advance will hold, or where they will stop if it does. The Saudi government has pledged to help the Yemeni government “eliminate” the Houthis. The last time they took up that mantle, a decade ago, it devolved into a bloody quagmire. This is the inside story of the battle that reignited Yemen’s war and the dark lessons it imparts for the next phase of fighting. The Houthi victory on September 10 showed how a ragtag militia transformed itself into a formidable force with advanced technology. It was a major defeat for the Yemeni government and its Saudi patrons, demonstrating that they were plagued by internal strife and unable to fight cohesively. This article is based on interviews with more than 15 people who participated in the fighting or were briefed on what happened, including soldiers, Yemeni military officers, officials with Yemen’s internationally recognised government, US officials and Houthi officials. Almost all of them spoke on condition of anonymity, either because they feared retribution from the Houthis or Saudi Arabia, or because they were not authorised to discuss what happened. Their accounts make it clear that while the Houthis’ victory last month surprised many, it was foreseeable. For months, the US military and intelligence agencies had warned Saudi Arabia about a resurgent threat from the Houthis and urged Saudi officials to unify the fractious forces of the Yemeni government, according to two senior US officials and one former senior US official. In the lead-up to his defeat, Saleh had reached out to Saudi and US officials, seeking greater support in holding back the Houthis, according to a Yemeni government official and two senior Yemeni military officers. The officers said he had asked the Saudis for air cover and the Americans for electronic jamming of Houthi communications. Saleh received little from either country, the three officials said. Even some in his own government seemed disinclined to intervene. US officials offered assistance with planning and intelligence – including on Houthi troop movements – but emphasised that their aid was limited and would not include airstrikes, the current and former US officials said. It is unclear why Saudi Arabia, equipped with US fighter jets and bombs, did not step in more intensively on its own. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, nor did the White House. The Houthis, who survived a US bombing campaign last year, gained international attention during the war in the Gaza Strip by launching missiles and drones at Israel and vessels in the Red Sea. Holding territory along the Red Sea would make it even easier for the group to disrupt shipping, analysts say. Whether any foreign military campaign could have held back the militia remains an open question. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a Houthi political official, attributed their victory to progress they had made in developing their military capabilities throughout years of war. The Houthis are fighting “to liberate Yemen from occupation”, he said, dismissing their foes as Saudi “mercenaries”. Two Yemeni government soldiers interviewed by The New York Times said they ultimately blamed their own feckless leaders for their defeat. It was just after sundown on September 9 when everything crumbled, according to one of their comrades, who spoke on condition of anonymity, fearing retribution. He recalled how he had been stationed with other soldiers outside Mokha, a historic port city near the Bab el-Mandeb, when they received reports of Houthi fighters advancing from multiple directions. Suddenly, their communications went dark, he said, severing contact with other units. They heard shouting. “Retreat! Retreat! Retreat!” he remembered his comrades yelling. “The Houthis are already here!” The Houthis’ recent conquest belies their simpler origins. The group began in the 1990s as a religious movement focused on Zaydism, an offshoot of Shiite Islam. Its leaders later mounted an armed rebellion against Yemen’s government, saying that they were battling corruption and foreign influence. Scholars debate when Iran began supporting them, but the Houthis eventually became a key Iranian ally. In 2014, they took over Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, routing the government and starting a civil war. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates began a disastrous military campaign to restore the government. Hundreds of thousands of people died from violence, hunger and disease. The Houthis survived, cementing their rule over northern Yemen. After a truce in 2022, the Houthis used the lull in fighting to become stronger and more self-sufficient, expanding their arsenal, analysts say. The Yemeni government did not. During the war, it had become increasingly fragmented and weak, beholden to its Saudi and UAE patrons – which were often at odds with each other. “The Yemeni government is basically a fiction at this point,” said Gregory Johnsen, a non-resident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington. “They spend more time fighting one another than they do the Houthis.” One of the key players in this government was Saleh. The nephew of Yemen’s former authoritarian leader, he had made plentiful enemies over the years as he seesawed from one alliance to another – siding with the Houthis, then joining the government. In Mokha, with UAE backing, he formed his own armed faction. His soldiers, numbering about 50,000, served as a bulwark against the Houthis pushing south towards the Bab el-Mandeb. Then, in January, the UAE withdrew from Yemen amid a feud with Saudi Arabia. Saudi officials consolidated their control over the government’s many factions. Once again, Saleh found himself with a new sponsor: Saudi Arabia. When the US and Israel attacked Iran in February , the Houthis appeared willing at first to sit out the war. But behind the scenes, Yemen’s truce had become a brittle stalemate. Talks aimed at a long-term peace deal – from which the Houthis hoped to gain greater authority and access to oil revenue – had stalled. Poverty in Houthi territory was dire, putting pressure on the group. They blamed Saudi Arabia and bristled at Saudi restrictions on Yemeni airspace. The tensions came to a head in July. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. They declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, now a crucial route for oil exports during the Iran war. They launched missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, and the kingdom launched airstrikes on Yemen. This escalation dovetailed with the interests of Iran, where officials were pushing to widen the war with the US, raising its costs for President Donald Trump. As the Houthis put pressure on oil markets, some Yemeni government officials sensed an opportunity to solicit foreign support to fight the Houthis. Clashes reignited inside Yemen, and Houthi officials accused Saudi Arabia and their Yemeni allies of preparing a new offensive against them. Quietly, the militia readied its own plans. On August 9, the Houthis began to shower Mokha with missiles and drones, damaging the port and seeking to cut off the city’s supply line from the sea, according to two Yemeni military officers. Then, on September 3, the Houthis began a huge ground offensive. A 39-minute video released by the Houthis, which they said was filmed during fighting for control of the Red Sea coast, shows their militiamen scaling rugged mountains on foot and waving guns in jubilation. The video, which the Times was unable to independently verify, also shows the bodies of what appear to be Yemeni government fighters slumped inside vehicles. At the end, a toothless Houthi fighter vows to “pursue the enemy into their very lairs”. For more than five days, the government force held off the militia, battling in the mountains above Mokha. Eventually, the Houthis were able to push forward, with an onslaught of missiles, drones and shelling. Saudi Arabia carried out only minimal airstrikes to assist its Yemeni allies, according to the two Yemeni military officers. On the evening of September 9 and into the next morning, the government forces collapsed. In a flurry of confusion, they beat a rapid and disorganised retreat. The Houthis seized a major military camp in the foothills east of Mokha – leaving their enemies on the coastal plain exposed and vulnerable. Instead of reorganising, the government’s soldiers withdrew all the way to the southern city of Aden, handing the entire Red Sea coast, including an island inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, to the Houthis. Overnight, Yemen’s government had lost more than 4500 square kilometres of territory. At least 500 of Saleh’s fighters were killed and more than 1500 wounded, according to a statement by his group. The Houthi death toll is unknown. Soon after Mokha fell, Saleh and several of his comrades flew to the Saudi capital of Riyadh, according to one of the Yemeni government officials and two of the military officers. There, they decamped to a five-star hotel, where easy listening music echoed through a cavernous lobby and servers brought tea with madeleines. One of the military officers, who is close to Saleh, told a Times reporter that he was now focused on regrouping his forces and treating the wounded. Eventually, there will be an investigation into what went wrong, he said. In Yemen, Saleh’s soldiers have scattered. Some were left stranded outside Aden after fighters from other factions – ostensibly their allies – barred them from the city, according to the officer close to Saleh and another soldier. Speaking by phone from their makeshift encampment, that soldier said that they had gone days without food. In public statements, the Houthis sought to reassure the international community that they posed no threat to maritime security – only to Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest exporters of oil. As oil prices surged above $US100 a barrel, the Houthis began pushing to expand their territory further, promising to “liberate” all of Yemen. Last weekend, the Yemeni government’s leader, Rashad al-Alimi, declared a full-blown war against the militia. The government’s goal, he said, was to reclaim all the territory lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years. For Yemeni civilians, already facing dire poverty and hunger, the war’s return portends deeper suffering. More than 180,000 people have been displaced in recent weeks, often piling onto pick-up trucks and motorcycles as they rushed to escape. “The moment felt like doomsday, with everyone looking out for themselves,” said Hassan Sughair, a civilian who fled from a town near Mokha. “We did not even say goodbye to our neighbours, and we do not know what happened to them.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times . They launched missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, and the kingdom launched airstrikes on Yemen. This escalation dovetailed with the interests of Iran, where officials were pushing to widen the war with the US, raising its costs for President Donald Trump. As the Houthis put pressure on oil markets, some Yemeni government officials sensed an opportunity to solicit foreign support to fight the Houthis. Clashes reignited inside Yemen, and Houthi officials accused Saudi Arabia and their Yemeni allies of preparing a new offensive against them. Quietly, the militia readied its own plans. On August 9, the Houthis began to shower Mokha with missiles and drones, damaging the port and seeking to cut off the city’s supply line from the sea, according to two Yemeni military officers. Then, on September 3, the Houthis began a huge ground offensive. A 39-minute video released by the Houthis, which they said was filmed during fighting for control of the Red Sea coast, shows their militiamen scaling rugged mountains on foot and waving guns in jubilation. The video, which the Times was unable to independently verify, also shows the bodies of what appear to be Yemeni government fighters slumped inside vehicles. At the end, a toothless Houthi fighter vows to “pursue the enemy into their very lairs”. For more than five days, the government force held off the militia, battling in the mountains above Mokha. Eventually, the Houthis were able to push forward, with an onslaught of missiles, drones and shelling. Saudi Arabia carried out only minimal airstrikes to assist its Yemeni allies, according to the two Yemeni military officers. On the evening of September 9 and into the next morning, the government forces collapsed. In a flurry of confusion, they beat a rapid and disorganised retreat. The Houthis seized a major military camp in the foothills east of Mokha – leaving their enemies on the coastal plain exposed and vulnerable. Instead of reorganising, the government’s soldiers withdrew all the way to the southern city of Aden, handing the entire Red Sea coast, including an island inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, to the Houthis. Overnight, Yemen’s government had lost more than 4500 square kilometres of territory. At least 500 of Saleh’s fighters were killed and more than 1500 wounded, according to a statement by his group. The Houthi death toll is unknown. Soon after Mokha fell, Saleh and several of his comrades flew to the Saudi capital of Riyadh, according to one of the Yemeni government officials and two of the military officers. There, they decamped to a five-star hotel, where easy listening music echoed through a cavernous lobby and servers brought tea with madeleines. One of the military officers, who is close to Saleh, told a Times reporter that he was now focused on regrouping his forces and treating the wounded. Eventually, there will be an investigation into what went wrong, he said. In Yemen, Saleh’s soldiers have scattered. Some were left stranded outside Aden after fighters from other factions – ostensibly their allies – barred them from the city, according to the officer close to Saleh and another soldier. Speaking by phone from their makeshift encampment, that soldier said that they had gone days without food. In public statements, the Houthis sought to reassure the international community that they posed no threat to maritime security – only to Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest exporters of oil. As oil prices surged above $US100 a barrel, the Houthis began pushing to expand their territory further, promising to “liberate” all of Yemen. Last weekend, the Yemeni government’s leader, Rashad al-Alimi, declared a full-blown war against the militia. The government’s goal, he said, was to reclaim all the territory lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years. For Yemeni civilians, already facing dire poverty and hunger, the war’s return portends deeper suffering. More than 180,000 people have been displaced in recent weeks, often piling onto pick-up trucks and motorcycles as they rushed to escape. “The moment felt like doomsday, with everyone looking out for themselves,” said Hassan Sughair, a civilian who fled from a town near Mokha. “We did not even say goodbye to our neighbours, and we do not know what happened to them.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times . snapshot.title: A ‘spunky’ orphaned polar bear’s new life at the Winnipeg zoo | The Narwhal
snapshot.evidenceText: Eva Wasney is The Narwhal\u2019s Manitoba reporter, a role that\u2019s part of a partnership with the Winnipeg Free Press . Eva is based in Winnipeg and previously worked as a reporter and editor with the Free Press, where she covered everything from food and music to women\u2019s health and the rise of AI-generated news. She was named a National Newspaper Award finalist in 2022, and won an EPPY Award while reporting for The Brandon Sun . She is also the author of an award-winning community cookbook. Outside of work, Eva can be found making a mess in the kitchen and exploring Manitoba\u2019s many campgrounds. Eva has been reporting on environmental issues in Manitoba since joining The Narwhal in 2026. Her role is part of a partnership with the Winnipeg Free Press. It’s a grey September afternoon, and a small group is gathered for a special behind-the-scenes visit with Assiniboine Park Zoo’s newest resident. “Heeeeere, bubba,” animal-care specialist Caitlin Gordon-Hall hollers from between a double layer of chain-link fencing. After a beat, a small white face appears at the entrance of the private enclosure. The polar bear cub sniffs the air before trundling toward the fence, where his keepers have been working to encourage calm behaviour around humans ahead of his public debut today. Gordon-Hall offers sing-song affirmations while the cub, who is nearly 200 pounds and 10 or 11 months old, observes the fawning strangers with guarded curiosity. The young bear is objectively cute. With his round, fluffy frame and oversized paws, he looks more like a gift-shop stuffie than an apex predator. A low, persistent growl, however, is a reminder that his natural instincts are still intact. “In the wild, his mama would have taught him: if there’s people there, make yourself big, make noise,” Gordon-Hall says. But his mama isn’t here. The cub, whose official zoo name will be chosen by public voting, is an orphan. It’s been an intensive period of relearning for the cub, who, prior to arriving at the zoo in August, spent his days roaming the tundra near Churchill, Man. Today’s 20-minute visit is part of a series of exposure sessions designed to desensitize the bear to the zoo’s forthcoming crowds. A few minutes into the exercise and the cub is busy scratching his back on the fence, seemingly content that the nearby photojournalist’s long lens and camera shutter pose no threat. This isn’t the first polar bear cub to make the trek from the shore of Hudson Bay to a zoo enclosure. And he won’t be the last. The plight of polar bears in the face of climate change has been well-documented, and the fate of bears with less sea ice has meant they get into trouble with humans more often, with bears usually paying the price. Policy has shifted over the decades, but young orphan cubs still stand little chance of survival in the wild. Life in a zoo may be an imperfect solution — but it’s one that keeps the bear alive. As the session ends, the group heads through the locked gate of the cub care centre, where a pair of zoo visitors are peering through the slats. They pepper the staff with questions: How is the cub doing? Will he be rooming with the other six bears? When will we be able to see him? It’s been nine years since the last orphaned cub was transferred from Churchill, the “Polar Bear Capital of the World,” to the Winnipeg zoo. Public excitement in the south is palpable, while some northern residents are wary of a previously wild animal spending the rest of its life in captivity. Kelsey Eliasson, a Churchill polar bear guide and filmmaker, encountered the bear and his mother when they lived in the wild. He knew them by the nicknames “Marrón” or “Maury” and “Blanca” — Spanish for brown and white, respectively. “She was a super clean, super white bear, and then Marrón was kind of dirty and muddy, like every cub,” Eliasson says over the phone. Eliasson spent several days documenting the pair this summer as they hunkered down in the rocks along the shore of Hudson Bay. During the warmer months, bears can often be found in an area east of town hunting for seals while trying to beat the heat and bugs. Blanca, who was recognizable by a scar on her ear, looked healthy while she wrestled and rested with her cub, Eliasson says. But in mid-August, the mother bear was found dead roughly a kilometre from the Churchill garbage dump. Her cause of death remains unknown, and the results of a necropsy are still pending, a provincial spokesperson said in an emailed statement. Bears have been visiting the dump with more frequency since the spring of 2024, when the town’s enclosed waste transfer facility was destroyed in a fire. “Last year it was non-stop,” Geoff York, vice-president of science and policy for Polar Bears International, a non-profit research and conservation organization, says over a video call. For a long time, there were few rules governing the lives of polar bears in Manitoba. The provincial government frequently exported orphaned cubs and problem bears to zoos around the world until the late 1990s, when three Churchill-born bears were discovered performing in a travelling Mexican circus. The bears had been purchased from a zoo in Germany and were living in sweltering conditions without access to water. Widespread media coverage and public condemnation led to the creation of Manitoba’s Polar Bear Protection Act , which regulates the care and treatment of polar bears in captivity. Under the legislation, the province retains ownership of captive bears sent elsewhere, and their offspring, in perpetuity. The act changed Assiniboine Park Zoo’s relationship with the charismatic predators as well. The zoo has housed polar bears since at least 1939, when an orphaned seven-week-old cub, dubbed Charmichael, arrived via train after his mother was shot by a trapper on the shore of Hudson Bay, according to a Winnipeg Tribune article from the time. Bears remained a popular fixture at the zoo until the death of Debby, the world’s oldest known polar bear, in 2008 at the age of 41. Her concrete enclosure was deemed too small and ill-equipped by Manitoba Conservation standards to host a new bear without significant renovations. Amendments to the Polar Bear Protection Act created rules for rescuing orphaned cubs and paved the way for the Leatherdale International Polar Bear Conservation Centre. The $4.5-million research lab and cub transition centre opened at the zoo in 2012, followed by three new polar bear habitats at the 10-acre Journey to Churchill exhibit in 2014. Decisions to send an orphaned cub to Winnipeg are made on a case-by-case basis with input from an advisory committee of provincial appointees, zoo administrators and polar bear experts. Age is a significant consideration since polar bear cubs typically spend two years with their mothers learning to hunt and navigate. Orphans less than a year old stand little chance of survival in the wild. Eleven cubs were transferred to the zoo between 2013 and 2017 — a pace that sparked public outrage in Churchill and pushed the Winnipeg facility’s capacity to the limit. The zoo is currently home to seven rescued polar bears, including the new cub. “There’s definitely been times when we were worried about our ability to take new bears,” Stephen Petersen, Assiniboine Park Conservancy’s director of conservation and research, says, referring to space constraints. There are few other options. The province has conducted two foster parenting studies with the Born Free Foundation, a British animal welfare organization, to determine if mother polar bears with one healthy cub would adopt a second. The project was cancelled due to lack of success. A rare case of wild adoption was observed in Manitoba last year , when a mother polar bear was seen travelling with a second cub. It was the 13th documented case of adoption in the western Hudson Bay subpopulation. Orphaned cubs raised in captivity can’t currently be returned to the wild because they lack hunting skills and natural instincts. That leaves the zoo. The province has updated its cub management policy since the first influx of orphans and the zoo now only takes bears whose mothers have died through suspected conflict with humans , Petersen says. One of those points of conflict can come from garbage dumps. Dealing with municipal garbage in a northern community like Churchill, which is surrounded by rocky, intermittently frozen ground and hundreds of polar bears, poses challenges. While the previous facility allowed for indoor garbage sorting and storage, the 2024 fire forced the Town of Churchill to return to an open-dump system with an electrified fence. “The trash doesn’t just sit nicely inside this little fenced-in area. It gets pulled out by animals, and it gets blown out by the wind. So it’s created quite an attractant,” York, who specializes in reducing conflict between bears and humans, says. Dozens of bears were able to break into the dump site when the electric fence failed during a storm, he adds. The barrier has since been upgraded with funding from Polar Bears International. The group plans to install new bear-deterrent technology in the town and dumpsite. Churchill is in the process of rebuilding its garbage facility and is developing a long-term waste management strategy, a municipal spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The town also plans to revisit the feasibility of trash incineration — a concept that was shelved following the fire but has proven beneficial in other northern communities, like Nuuk, Nvt. , where the energy generated from burning household garbage is used to heat homes. Eliasson thinks incineration should be given higher priority. “Churchill has been talking about an incinerator [for a long time] and … we’re just not building one. It’s the only solution,” he says. “Polar bears will break into everything else.” The western Hudson Bay subpopulation, which includes Churchill and ranges from Chesterfield Inlet in Nunavut to the Manitoba-Ontario border, is the most researched group of polar bears in the world, according to Polar Bears International . There are roughly 800 bears living in the territory today, representing a 30 per cent population decline over the last 46 years due to shrinking sea ice caused by climate change, Evan Richardson, a polar bear research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada, says. “This is one of the most southern polar bear populations in the world, and it was among the first to show impacts of reduced sea ice availability on individual body condition, growth, reproduction and survival,” Richardson says. Polar bears make their living on the ice, using the frozen platforms to hunt for seals. Open water makes the speedy prey increasingly harder to catch. The Hudson Bay population is experiencing an era of relative stability thanks to several good ice seasons, Richardson says. While this gives current generations of bears a positive start, the survival of the species is dependent on the long-term health of their environment. “Polar bears don’t occur anywhere where there’s not persistent annual sea ice, and so as the habitat melts, it threatens the bears’ existence,” he says. Climate change is further straining the coexistence of bears and humans in northern Manitoba. “It’s a bit of a perfect storm,” York says. “Less ice means the area is more accessible to more human activity. At the same time, more bears are spending more time on shore.” As the ice-free season grows longer, Hudson Bay is seeing more traffic, whether it be freight, tourism or research. In Manitoba, the provincial and federal governments are keen to expand operations at the Port of Churchill to include year-round shipping, an all-weather road, an upgraded rail line and a liquefied natural gas terminal — all of which will bring more people and disturbance to the region. To ease the pressure on residents — bears and humans alike — York believes the governments should focus on shoring up local infrastructure, including Churchill’s garbage facility, before embarking on major national projects in remote northern communities. “Take a quick step back and say, ‘Hey, what’s needed here today for the people who are there now?’ ” he says. “This waste management need has been acute, and we haven’t had the best luck getting the attention we think it merits, from the human-health side, but also the environmental-health and wildlife-health side.” There have been 159 bear sightings and encounters reported so far this year in Churchill to the province’s Polar Bear Alert Program — a 24-hour hotline designed to minimize dangerous interactions while the animals move ashore from mid-July to mid-November. If a bear is reported near the town or dump, Manitoba Conservation officers will chase them away with non-lethal scaring devices, such as noisemakers or flares. “Problem bears” that return repeatedly or refuse to leave the area are placed in the province’s polar bear holding facility near the Churchill airport and relocated more remotely via helicopter. Seven bears have been flown out of town this year. The holding facility, colloquially known as polar bear jail , is also where orphaned cubs begin their journey to Winnipeg. After his mother died, the zoo’s new cub was captured by conservation officers and held in polar bear jail while decisions were made about his future. Within a week, he was on a plane to Winnipeg accompanied by veterinary staff from the zoo. His first 30 days were spent in medical quarantine at the cub care centre, which includes indoor and outdoor enclosure space with a shallow pool, foliage and natural ground cover for digging. The cub’s introduction to captivity has been closely managed by a small circle of trainers. “It has gone through a traumatic event of losing its mother,” Jackie Enberg, the zoo’s curator of animal care, says. “We’re here to offer a safe home and daily care. … A lot of that is relationship building and a good diet.” Enberg has overseen the transitions for all of the cubs transferred to the zoo. Unsurprisingly, food is the fastest way to a polar bear’s heart. Once the cub’s stomach adjusted to his new diet of ground meat, fish and “marine mammal chow” — a kind of dry kibble — his trainers added tong-feeding sessions to the menu. The goal is to associate humans with food delivery and reward calm behaviour, which can help with future vet checkups. Visitor exposure sessions were added post-quarantine. Over several weeks, the cub’s trainers paid close attention to his behaviour as larger groups of zoo staff and patrons stopped by his enclosure for longer periods of time. If he showed signs of distress, such as charging the fence or growling, the process was slowed, Enberg says. So far, the cub has adapted to captivity as well as expected. (A fecal cortisol study conducted on bears at the zoo, and published in the Canadian Journal of Zoology earlier this year, found orphaned cubs can adjust to living under human care within two weeks of relocation.) “I’m really impressed with how far he’s gotten. He’s just a really smart little bear, and he’s doing very well,” Enberg says. “And he’s spunky.” That spunky temperament may come into play when the cub is big enough to integrate with the zoo’s adult polar bears. Staff use personality assessments developed in the onsite research lab to determine which bears will mesh well together. The cub joins a long line of Assiniboine Park polar bears involved in local and international research programs — from non-invasive tracking techniques to whiskerprint identification to thermal imaging. Scientists at the zoo are also studying how climate change is impacting denning in the Arctic and how stress affects a bear’s DNA. “We really want the bears in our care to participate in as much research that contributes to wild bear and bear welfare overall as possible,” Petersen says. For the zoo, the new cub promises to boost ticket sales as a novel attraction while serving as an ambassador for his northern brethren. It’s a tough sell for Eliasson, the Churchill polar bear guide, who would rather see orphaned cubs returned to the wild or paired with adoptive mothers. “It’s 2026, and Manitoba has a polar bear cub rehabilitation centre where the only option is to fly the cub to Winnipeg and put it in a zoo. To me, that doesn’t sound like rehabilitation,” he says. Petersen, however, says release isn’t a viable option. “Putting a grown, healthy bear that has relied on humans for all its food back on the landscape is just a huge risk to communities further north,” he says. Meanwhile, the cub is spending his days climbing logs and splashing in the pool of his enclosure as visitors watch from beyond the fence. And soon, he’ll have a new name. The public can vote for Duke, Marly, Fletcher or Mantayo — ideas compiled by students from the Duke of Marlborough School in Churchill that speak to landmarks in the North. To ease the pressure on residents — bears and humans alike — York believes the governments should focus on shoring up local infrastructure, including Churchill’s garbage facility, before embarking on major national projects in remote northern communities. “Take a quick step back and say, ‘Hey, what’s needed here today for the people who are there now?’ ” he says. “This waste management need has been acute, and we haven’t had the best luck getting the attention we think it merits, from the human-health side, but also the environmental-health and wildlife-health side.” There have been 159 bear sightings and encounters reported so far this year in Churchill to the province’s Polar Bear Alert Program — a 24-hour hotline designed to minimize dangerous interactions while the animals move ashore from mid-July to mid-November. If a bear is reported near the town or dump, Manitoba Conservation officers will chase them away with non-lethal scaring devices, such as noisemakers or flares. “Problem bears” that return repeatedly or refuse to leave the area are placed in the province’s polar bear holding facility near the Churchill airport and relocated more remotely via helicopter. Seven bears have been flown out of town this year. The holding facility, colloquially known as polar bear jail , is also where orphaned cubs begin their journey to Winnipeg. After his mother died, the zoo’s new cub was captured by conservation officers and held in polar bear jail while decisions were made about his future. Within a week, he was on a plane to Winnipeg accompanied by veterinary staff from the zoo. His first 30 days were spent in medical quarantine at the cub care centre, which includes indoor and outdoor enclosure space with a shallow pool, foliage and natural ground cover for digging. The cub’s introduction to captivity has been closely managed by a small circle of trainers. “It has gone through a traumatic event of losing its mother,” Jackie Enberg, the zoo’s curator of animal care, says. “We’re here to offer a safe home and daily care. … A lot of that is relationship building and a good diet.” Enberg has overseen the transitions for all of the cubs transferred to the zoo. Unsurprisingly, food is the fastest way to a polar bear’s heart. Once the cub’s stomach adjusted to his new diet of ground meat, fish and “marine mammal chow” — a kind of dry kibble — his trainers added tong-feeding sessions to the menu. The goal is to associate humans with food delivery and reward calm behaviour, which can help with future vet checkups. Visitor exposure sessions were added post-quarantine. Over several weeks, the cub’s trainers paid close attention to his behaviour as larger groups of zoo staff and patrons stopped by his enclosure for longer periods of time. If he showed signs of distress, such as charging the fence or growling, the process was slowed, Enberg says. So far, the cub has adapted to captivity as well as expected. (A fecal cortisol study conducted on bears at the zoo, and published in the Canadian Journal of Zoology earlier this year, found orphaned cubs can adjust to living under human care within two weeks of relocation.) “I’m really impressed with how far he’s gotten. He’s just a really smart little bear, and he’s doing very well,” Enberg says. “And he’s spunky.” That spunky temperament may come into play when the cub is big enough to integrate with the zoo’s adult polar bears. Petersen, however, says release isn’t a viable option. “Putting a grown, healthy bear that has relied on humans for all its food back on the landscape is just a huge risk to communities further north,” he says. Meanwhile, the cub is spending his days climbing logs and splashing in the pool of his enclosure as visitors watch from beyond the fence. And soon, he’ll have a new name. The public can vote for Duke, Marly, Fletcher or Mantayo — ideas compiled by students from the Duke of Marlborough School in Churchill that speak to landmarks in the North. representative.title: Concerns as Residents Eat Fish From Fuel-hit River Nyando Following Leak | Dawan Africa | Dawan Africa
representative.author: Hassan Wekesa

snapshot.title: Concerns as Residents Eat Fish From Fuel-hit River Nyando Following Leak
snapshot.evidenceText: Kenya, 11 October 2026 - Some residents of the villages neighbouring the riverbanks of the River Nyando in Kisumu County are eating fish caught after fuel leaked into the water from a Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) line. Health concerns are mounting, while Kisumu Governor Prof Anyang’ Nyong’o on Friday demanded an impartial investigation into the fuel leak. The leak, reported on 8 October 2026, occurred on the Sinendet-Kisumu petroleum pipeline, which runs beside the river near Muhoroni, Kibigori and Ahero. Some locals risked their lives trying to collect fuel floating on the water. Others have since been catching and eating fish from the affected stretch. In their initial response, KPC officials suspected that the leak was caused by intentional interference with the line. They have since alerted detectives from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) and the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) to investigate and arrest any culprits. Accounts of what exactly happened differ. It was first reported that the pipeline was damaged while workers dug to build gabions on the riverbank to curb erosion ahead of the El Niño rains. However, on Friday last week, other residents near the affected section claimed that Kenya Railways workers maintaining the railway line struck the pipe with an excavator, exposing it to leakage. Detectives will be able to establish what exactly happened, whether it was the result of gabion construction, accidental breakage by railway workers or intentional tampering with the line. On 9 October 2026, Governor Nyong’o called for impartial investigations and fair compensation for residents around Kibigori and Muhoroni. He said the reported spill from KPC infrastructure poses serious risks to public health, the environment, livelihoods and critical national infrastructure. He urged the agencies to establish the facts quickly and professionally, without prejudging the outcome, and to ensure accountability where wrongdoing is proved. He insisted that containment, clean-up, environmental assessments and remediation proceed without delay. The extent of contamination and the risks to water sources, ecosystems, public health and livelihoods must be established, he said, with clear public guidance on precautions. All affected individuals, households, farmers and businesses should receive fair compensation for verified losses, in a process that is transparent, accessible and sensitive to vulnerable households, the governor added. He commended KPC’s initial response but said the company and relevant agencies must strengthen safeguards through better surveillance, routine integrity inspections, detection of unauthorised interference, prompt reporting and coordinated emergency response. He urged residents to remain calm, cooperate with authorities and share credible information with investigators. One thing is clear: the residents are facing a chemical incident, which the World Health Organization (WHO) describes as an uncontrolled release of a toxic substance, potentially resulting in harm to public health and the environment. WHO further explains that chemical incidents can occur as a result of natural events or as a result of accidental or intentional events. “These incidents can be sudden and acute or have a slow onset when there is a ‘silent’ release of a chemical. They can also range from small releases to full-scale major emergencies,” WHO states. These chemical incidents can be caused by anthropogenic or technological events. Besides oil spills and leaks from storage units during transportation, other chemical incidents include explosions at factories that store or use chemicals, contamination of the food or water supply with a chemical, deliberate release of chemicals in conflict or terrorism, and outbreaks of disease associated with chemical exposure. Between 2009 and 2018 alone, about 65,000 people died as a result of technological events. A fuel leak poses a major health risk because crude oil contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and these carry over into refined products such as diesel, super petrol and jet fuel, which the Sinendet-Kisumu line transports. Several PAHs are genotoxic and carcinogenic. Fuels also contain benzene, for which Kenya’s Onshore National Contingency Plan sets a worker exposure limit of 1 part per million over eight hours. The plan also notes that light products such as diesel and jet fuel are more acutely toxic than heavier oils. River Nyando is a freshwater, non-navigable water body, and most of the fish there are teleosts, or bony fish. According to scientific researchers, teleost fish can metabolise PAHs efficiently, breaking them down and excreting them. This typically leaves lower residues in their edible flesh than in shellfish and, in principle, reduces the risk to people who eat them. That does not make fish from fuel-affected water safe. representative.title: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
representative.author: American Museum of Natural History

snapshot.title: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
snapshot.evidenceText: A famous Scottish fossil is forcing scientists to rethink what claw-like feet really reveal about the move onto land. Pressed flat inside two slabs of Scottish rock, a 345-million-year-old skeleton seemed to carry some unmistakable signs of life on land. Its four limbs ended in five-digit feet, and the tips of its fingers and toes looked strikingly like claws. For decades, those features helped make Westlothiana lizziae , better known as “Lizzie,” a landmark in the story of how vertebrates moved away from water and gave rise to reptiles, birds, and mammals. Yet the fossil had been crushed so badly that much of its anatomy remained hidden inside the stone. Peering through that rock with X-rays has now exposed a very different animal. Researchers from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, reconstructed structures that could not be seen from the fossil’s surface. Their results, published in Nature , revealed a primitive skull, ossified internal gills, and a fish-like mouth packed with thousands of tiny teeth. “Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades,” said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum’s Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. “But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected.” Discovered in Scotland in 1984 and formally described in 1990, Westlothiana had initially been interpreted largely from the anatomy exposed on the surfaces of its two slabs. Its nearly complete skeleton stood apart from many animals living around the same time because its limbs looked more suited to supporting a body than the more fin-like appendages seen in some early tetrapod relatives. Those visible feet helped secure Lizzie’s reputation as an early amniote, the branch of vertebrates that eventually produced reptiles, birds, and mammals. Researchers repeatedly used the fossil as an important reference point when estimating when animals with fully land-adapted lifestyles began appearing. Inside Lizzie’s skull, however, the synchrotron scans uncovered features that do not fit that interpretation. The internal gills and tooth-filled, fish-like mouth instead place the animal on a much older branch of the tetrapod family tree and indicate that it was aquatic or amphibious rather than a fully terrestrial reptile ancestor. “The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought,” said Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford. Keeping those reptile-like feet creates another surprise. Five toes, claw-like tips, and limb structures once treated as hallmarks of land-adapted amniotes were apparently already present in more ancient members of the stem lineage leading toward tetrapods. In other words, some pieces of the body plan associated with later land animals evolved before the animals carrying them had fully left the water behind. “This is a big surprise,” said study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum’s Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. “It shows that, although we think of amphibians as being more ‘primitive’ than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles.” Claw-shaped impressions preserved in still older fossil trackways may now need the same kind of caution. Some tracks dating to the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago, have been interpreted as evidence that amniotes had already evolved because they record four-limbed animals walking on claw-like digits. If creatures as primitive as Westlothiana could also possess claw-like structures, those tracks no longer provide a simple fingerprint of an amniote. Some may instead have been left by amphibious tetrapod relatives that carried land-like anatomical features while still dividing their lives between water and shore. “The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water,” Jenkins said. Reference: “Evolution of terrestrial anatomy revealed by a derived stem tetrapod” by Ben Igielman, Xavier Jenkins, Jason Head, Vincent Fernandez, Lucy Roberts, Timothy Smithson and Roger Benson, 30 September 2026, Nature . representative.title: China shock: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports | Fortune
representative.author: Sam McNeil, Kanis Leung, Elaine Kurtenbach, The Associated Press

snapshot.title: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports and lower tariffs for some European exports to China | Fortune
snapshot.evidenceText: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said. Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains. The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation. The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU. He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.” The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year. China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures. He said that China is not the root of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them. The head of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Sigrid de Vries, said that the deal appears to avert further instability in the EU and “can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties.” Sefcovic said he will brief EU leaders meeting in Brussels next week and seek their approval. “They would have to see that this is convincing enough to take the other steps,” he said. “We are in a situation that they (China) could put under the threat whole sectors in the European industry, literally thousands of jobs and the public opinion and the leaders clearly expect very fast action from our side.” Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value. The two sides will meet next by video in January and then in person in March. China has been pushing for the EU to stop blocking Chinese imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington’s behest. Earlier, Sefcovic had said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing. Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire. Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China’s global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics. And on Wednesday, Germany blocked the sale of a major logistics firm in the port of Hamburg to the state-owned Chinese shipping behemoth Cosco over security concerns. “As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement. “The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.”
snapshot.imageAlt: Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, meets with European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 9, 2026.

Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China’s global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics. And on Wednesday, Germany blocked the sale of a major logistics firm in the port of Hamburg to the state-owned Chinese shipping behemoth Cosco over security concerns. “As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement. “The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.”

representative.title: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants

snapshot.title: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants
snapshot.evidenceText: Syria's Permanent Representative to the OPCW, Mohammad Katoub, announced that operations to destroy remnants of the Assad-era chemical program have begun, while warning that Israeli attacks hinder the process and that a timeframe for completion has not yet been set. Syria's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Mohammad Katoub, stated that his country continues full cooperation with the organisation's Technical Secretariat to completely eliminate remnants of the chemical weapons program from the Assad era. He confirmed that destruction operations have already begun, describing this as tangible progress in the capabilities of Syria's national teams working on this sensitive file. The announcement falls within an internationally monitored process overseen by the OPCW, the body responsible for verifying the elimination of banned weapons programs. Ongoing work includes verification, inspection, and destruction of remaining materials and facilities linked to the former program. Katoub pointed out that Israeli attacks constitute a real obstacle to the removal of the chemical program's remnants, imposing security challenges and operational complications on field teams. In practical terms, these obstacles tie the pace of work to security conditions at the affected sites, making movement, equipment handling, and field coordination more difficult. He explained that Syria is working with OPCW teams to develop a realistic timeframe for completing verification, inspection, and destruction operations, but this framework has not yet been announced, as work continues on shaping it in light of field and security conditions. The Syrian envoy stressed that pursuing and holding accountable those involved in developing and using chemical weapons is among Syria's top priorities at this stage. This judicial track runs parallel to the technical work of destroying the remnants, as part of an effort to close the file of the former chemical program from both ends: materially through destruction, and legally through accountability. The step marks a shift of the chemical file from declarations to actual destruction on the ground — a significant development for Syria's international standing and its relations with international organisations, which could gradually reflect in reduced pressures and isolation on the country. However, the absence of an announced timeframe means Syrians will not see a defined end to this file any time soon. The continued Israeli attacks as a disrupting factor also serve as a reminder that security conditions remain the key variable determining the pace of sensitive files like this one, directly affecting civilians in the affected areas. representative.title: Ramaphosa presses South Sudan to implement peace agreement before December elections - Ubuntu Times South Africa
representative.author: Megan

snapshot.title: Ramaphosa presses South Sudan to implement peace agreement before December elections - Ubuntu Times South Africa
snapshot.evidenceText: South African Fashion Week 2026 to Unite Fashion, Ballet and Sport in a Landmark Johannesburg Showcase Twyg Sustainable Fashion Awards 2026 spotlight circular and responsible African fashion South African Beauty Trends Embrace Bold Makeup, 1990s Nostalgia and Metallic Gold for the New Season South African Design Week Puts Personal Style and Meaningful Accessories in the Spotlight “South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has urged South Sudanese President Salva Kiir Mayardit to fully implement the country’s revitalised peace agreement and ensure an inclusive electoral process ahead of the planned December 2026 elections. The discussions in Pretoria underscore South Africa’s continuing diplomatic role in African peacebuilding, while highlighting concerns about unresolved political challenges, trust between South Sudanese stakeholders and the practical preparations required for credible elections.” South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has intensified diplomatic engagement with South Sudan, urging President Salva Kiir Mayardit to implement the country’s peace agreement fully as the world’s youngest nation prepares for planned general elections in December 2026. The discussions, held in Pretoria during Kiir’s working visit to South Africa, highlight Pretoria’s continuing commitment to regional stability, democratic governance and peaceful political transitions across the African continent. According to a statement issued by the South African Presidency on 7 October, Ramaphosa emphasised that full adherence to the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (R-ARCSS) is essential for advancing the peace process and establishing lasting stability. He also stressed the importance of an inclusive electoral process founded on mutual trust and cooperation among South Sudanese political stakeholders. The engagement comes at a crucial moment for South Sudan, where delays in implementing political and security reforms have complicated preparations for elections. South Africa’s diplomatic intervention therefore reflects broader African efforts to prevent renewed conflict and support a credible transition towards representative government. South Africa has maintained an active role in African diplomacy, particularly in initiatives addressing political instability, conflict resolution and institutional development. Its engagement with South Sudan forms part of wider regional cooperation involving the African Union and neighbouring countries. During the Pretoria meeting, Ramaphosa and Kiir discussed bilateral relations, economic cooperation, institutional development and implementation of the peace agreement. The South African Presidency said the meeting reaffirmed the importance of sustained regional engagement and collaboration in support of peace, stability and political progress in South Sudan. Ramaphosa’s position is significant because South Africa chairs the African Union High-Level Ad Hoc Committee on South Sudan, commonly known as the C5. This mechanism brings together regional leaders to support the implementation of the peace agreement and encourage progress towards an inclusive political settlement. The committee’s work provides South Africa with a diplomatic platform to encourage dialogue between South Sudanese leaders while coordinating support from African partners. However, lasting progress depends on cooperation among the country’s political factions, institutions and communities rather than diplomatic pressure alone. The Pretoria discussions consequently represent part of a wider regional effort to translate commitments into measurable progress before the election deadline. The R-ARCSS was signed in September 2018 following years of devastating conflict. It established a framework for power-sharing, security arrangements, institutional reforms and preparations for elections. The agreement was intended to help South Sudan move away from armed confrontation towards a more stable political system. Nevertheless, implementation has faced persistent obstacles, including disagreements between political leaders, delays in security sector reforms and difficulties completing institutional preparations. The agreement remains central to international and regional efforts to support peace in South Sudan. Its implementation is also important for restoring public confidence in political institutions and creating conditions in which citizens can participate peacefully in national decision-making. For Ramaphosa, the challenge is to encourage the South Sudanese leadership to treat the agreement as a practical roadmap rather than simply a diplomatic commitment. The distinction matters because signing a peace agreement does not automatically resolve political disputes or guarantee that institutions will function effectively. Implementation requires cooperation, sustained funding, administrative capacity and willingness among competing political actors to honour their obligations. The coming weeks will therefore be important in determining whether South Sudan can demonstrate sufficient progress to strengthen confidence in its political transition. The planned December 2026 elections represent a significant milestone in South Sudan’s political development. However, their credibility will depend on more than the announcement of a voting date. An inclusive electoral process requires political parties to participate meaningfully, institutions to operate effectively and citizens to have confidence that their votes will be respected. It also requires adequate preparations, clear procedures and a political environment in which disagreements can be addressed without violence. Ramaphosa’s emphasis on mutual trust and cooperation reflects these requirements. The South African President urged South Sudanese stakeholders to address outstanding challenges and create an enabling environment for implementation of the peace agreement ahead of the elections. South Sudan’s electoral preparations have previously encountered delays. The authorities have postponed elections that were initially expected earlier, citing the need to complete important elements of the transition. The December timetable therefore carries considerable political significance. If preparations advance successfully, the elections could provide an opportunity to strengthen public participation and move the country towards more representative governance. Conversely, unresolved disagreements or inadequate preparations could undermine confidence in the process and intensify political tensions. South Africa’s diplomatic message is consequently focused on ensuring that electoral preparations remain connected to the wider peace agreement. South Africa’s involvement is part of a collective African diplomatic approach. The African Union and regional partners have repeatedly emphasised the importance of implementing the peace agreement and supporting peaceful, credible, inclusive and transparent elections. A declaration adopted by the C5 Plus at a virtual summit on 29 September 2026 reaffirmed the African Union’s commitment to supporting South Sudan’s political transition. It identified 22 December 2026 as the scheduled date for general elections and called for coordinated support towards completing the transition and conducting the vote. The declaration also acknowledged renewed hostilities and reported ceasefire violations, underlining the fragility of the political and security environment. These concerns demonstrate why regional coordination remains important. South Sudan’s challenges cannot be addressed through bilateral diplomacy alone. The African Union, regional governments and international partners have roles in encouraging dialogue, supporting institutional development and coordinating assistance. South Africa’s position as chair of the C5 provides an opportunity to help align these efforts. Nevertheless, diplomatic statements must be followed by practical cooperation, including support for electoral preparations and the implementation of agreed reforms. The effectiveness of this approach will ultimately depend on whether the different partners can maintain a consistent message while respecting South Sudanese ownership of the political process. Political stability remains closely connected to security conditions across South Sudan. Renewed fighting and political tensions have raised concerns about the durability of the peace process. Recent reporting by The Guardian on 8 October described heavily strained trauma services in South Sudan amid renewed fighting between government forces and opposition-aligned groups. The report highlighted the humanitarian consequences of insecurity and the risks associated with the country’s unresolved political crisis. Such conditions complicate electoral preparations. Insecurity can restrict movement, disrupt public services and make it harder for communities to participate in political activities. It can also divert government resources away from institutional development and essential services. A sustainable peace process therefore requires progress beyond formal political negotiations. Security arrangements must be implemented, disputes must be managed peacefully and public institutions must be able to operate without intimidation or disruption. South Africa’s emphasis on implementing the peace agreement is relevant to these interconnected challenges. A credible political transition could help strengthen confidence in institutions, although elections alone cannot resolve every underlying cause of instability. For regional partners, the priority is to encourage political progress while recognising that peacebuilding also requires long-term investment in security, governance and community reconciliation. The Pretoria meeting also addressed bilateral relations, economic cooperation and institutional development, illustrating the broader scope of South Africa’s engagement with South Sudan. Peace and economic development are closely linked. Political uncertainty can discourage investment, disrupt trade and weaken the ability of governments to plan and deliver public services. More predictable institutions, by contrast, can create better conditions for economic cooperation. South Africa’s engagement could provide opportunities for exchanging institutional experience and exploring practical areas of cooperation. However, the official statement did not announce a specific new economic agreement or financial commitment arising from the meeting. The distinction is important because diplomatic discussions establish priorities but do not automatically produce completed projects or measurable economic outcomes. For South Sudan, progress towards a stable political settlement could support longer-term efforts to strengthen public administration and improve economic prospects. For South Africa, regional stability contributes to broader continental interests, including peaceful cooperation, trade and development. These potential benefits depend on sustained implementation rather than diplomatic announcements alone. South Africa’s approach faces several challenges. The first is the gap between political commitments and implementation. Leaders may publicly endorse a peace agreement while disagreements over power-sharing, security and institutional arrangements continue to delay progress. The second challenge is maintaining coordination among regional partners. The African Union and participating governments must sustain engagement, communicate consistent expectations and provide support that responds to South Sudan’s actual needs. A third challenge is balancing diplomatic pressure with constructive dialogue. South Africa must encourage compliance with the peace agreement without undermining the cooperation necessary to move negotiations forward. The fourth concerns the timetable itself. As December approaches, authorities face pressure to demonstrate that electoral arrangements are sufficiently developed and that political participation can take place in a credible environment. These challenges mean that the success of Ramaphosa’s intervention should be assessed through observable developments. Relevant indicators include progress on outstanding provisions of the peace agreement, improvements in security, meaningful political dialogue and transparent electoral preparations. Without such progress, diplomatic engagement risks producing repeated declarations without sufficient change on the ground. The immediate priority is to translate the Pretoria discussions and wider C5 engagement into practical steps supporting South Sudan’s political transition. South Sudanese authorities and political stakeholders will need to address outstanding issues, strengthen cooperation and advance the preparations necessary for the planned December elections. Regional partners, meanwhile, will need to continue providing coordinated diplomatic and technical support. The African Union’s 29 September declaration offers an important framework for these efforts, while Ramaphosa’s meeting with Kiir reinforces South Africa’s commitment to the process. The coming weeks will be especially important because the credibility of the election timetable depends on implementation, not simply assurances from political leaders. Progress will require cooperation across political institutions and a sustained commitment to resolving disputes peacefully. For South Africa, continued engagement also presents an opportunity to demonstrate the value of African-led diplomacy in addressing regional crises. However, Pretoria cannot determine South Sudan’s political future by itself. Ultimately, the responsibility for implementing the agreement rests with South Sudan’s leaders and institutions. President Cyril Ramaphosa’s call for the full implementation of South Sudan’s peace agreement underscores the urgency of preparing for credible elections in December 2026. His discussions with President Salva Kiir highlight the importance of political inclusion, mutual trust, regional cooperation and institutional development. The engagement also reinforces South Africa’s role in the African Union’s efforts to support peace and stability in South Sudan. Yet the effectiveness of this diplomacy will depend on whether political commitments lead to concrete progress on security, governance and electoral preparations. As the election deadline approaches, South Sudan faces a consequential test of its transition from conflict towards representative government. South Africa and its regional partners can provide diplomatic encouragement and coordinated assistance, but lasting progress will require South Sudanese stakeholders to implement the agreement and resolve their differences peacefully. The central question is therefore whether the renewed diplomatic engagement will produce sufficient practical progress to support an inclusive and credible electoral process. The answer will have implications not only for South Sudan but also for wider African efforts to prevent conflict and strengthen democratic governance.
