snapshot.title: Canada Gazette, Part 1, Volume 160, Number 41: ORDERS IN COUNCIL
snapshot.evidenceText: Whereas the West Coast Oil Pipeline project (the Project) is an interprovincial pipeline being advanced by Trans Mountain Corporation, Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission and Pembina Pipeline Corporation; Whereas, on July 2, 2026, the Government of Canada announced that it was launching a process to consider listing the Project as a national interest project under the Building Canada Act (the Act); Whereas, on August 1, 2026, in accordance with subsection 5(1.1) of the Act, a notice of more than 30 days, which included the name and description of the Project, was caused to be published in the Canada Gazette , Part I, advising that the Governor in Council may amend Schedule 1 of the Act to list the Project as a project of national interest; Whereas the President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada, being satisfied that the conditions set out in subsection 5(6.1) of the Act have been met, recommends that the annexed Order under subsection 5(1) of the Act be made; Whereas, in accordance with subsection 5(7) of the Act, the President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada, before recommending that the annexed Order be made under subsection 5(1) of the Act, consulted with other federal ministers that the Minister considered appropriate, with the governments of Alberta and British Columbia and with Indigenous peoples whose rights recognized and affirmed by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 may be adversely affected by the carrying out of the Project; Whereas the Governor in Council, in deciding whether to make an order under subsection 5(1) of the Act to add the name of the Project and a detailed description of it, including the location where it is to be carried out, to Schedule 1 of the Act, has considered the factors that the Governor in Council considers relevant, including those factors set out in subsection 5(6) of the Act, and has taken into account the concerns identified during consultations between the Crown and Indigenous peoples; Whereas the Governor in Council has considered the adverse impacts on marine and terrestrial environments that the Project may cause and the potential for those adverse impacts to be mitigated, and has determined that the potential benefits of the project outweigh its potential impacts, costs and limitations; Whereas the Governor in Council is satisfied that the consultation process between the Crown and Indigenous peoples provided meaningful dialogue, and that Canada has fulfilled the duty to consult, consistent with the honour of the Crown, in relation to the proposed amendment to add the Project to the list of national interest projects set out in Schedule 1 to the Act; And whereas the Governor in Council has determined that the Project would strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience and security while creating material economic benefits that will improve the nation’s prosperity, and that making an order under subsection 5(1) of the Act in respect of the Project at this time is warranted to build investor confidence and to ensure that Canada is acting swiftly to counteract the undervaluation of one of its most important exports and to unlock critical growth and revenue during a period of global economic instability and realignment; Therefore, Her Excellency the Governor General in Council, being of the opinion that the West Coast Oil Pipeline project is in the national interest, on the recommendation of the President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada, makes the annexed Order Amending Schedule 1 to the Building Canada Act under subsection 5(1) of the Building Canada Act . On July 2, 2026, the Government of Alberta submitted a proposal to the Major Projects Office (MPO), asking Canada to consider the proposed West Coast Oil Pipeline (the Project) for listing as a national interest project under the Building Canada Act (the Act, or the BCA). This proposal followed a November 27, 2025 Memorandum of Understanding and a May 15, 2026 Implementation Agreement completed between Canada and Alberta, in which both Canada and Alberta affirmed the importance of augmenting Canada’s export of domestic oil to foreign markets as one element in a national strategy to meet a pivotal global moment. The Project is a proposed interprovincial pipeline capable of transporting approximately 1 million barrels per day (MMb/d) of Canadian crude oil from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia (BC), where the oil would be transferred to vessels and shipped to global markets. The Governor in Council (GIC), pursuant to subsection 5(1) of the Act and on the recommendation of the Minister responsible under the Act, the President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada — the Honourable Dominic LeBlanc (the Minister) — amends Schedule 1 of the Act to add the Project as a national interest project, as specified in the Order in Council to which this Explanatory Note is appended. The objective of this Order is to enable the Project’s timely development by bringing it within the regulatory framework of the Act, based on the GIC’s determination that the Project is in Canada’s national interest and that the Act thus supplies an appropriate framework to structure applicable federal regulatory authorizations, ensure appropriate environmental safeguards, and meet Canada’s constitutional obligations to Indigenous peoples. The Act was enacted by Parliament on June 26, 2025, to provide a simplified, direct, timely and comprehensive process to secure federal regulatory authorization for projects determined to be of vital interest to Canada. The legislation provides Canada with a means to confront the reality that nation-building natural resource and infrastructure projects have long faced complicated, cumbersome and time-consuming federal regulatory processes. This has fostered uncertainty and deterred proponents from pursuing projects that could render vital social and economic benefits to Canada. The federal regulatory system for major projects has involved numerous authorizations and permitting decisions distributed among multiple federal agencies and departments, each requiring separate applications from project proponents, and entailing multiple, often disjointed processes of consultation with Indigenous communities. The duration and complexity of this system can delay federal authorization of worthy project proposals for years, and systemically limit the willingness of proponents to bring forward projects that complement Canada’s economic growth, security, and prosperity. Proponents are required to make large investments in project development, and to produce the detailed information required for project applications, without any certainty about whether the project would be approved until the end of these lengthy and complex processes. While this problem was already acute, it became pressing following the rupture of prior stable forms of international economic integration and trade brought about by the sudden change in policy orientation of the United States (US), Canada’s largest trading partner and the market for the majority of Canadian exports. Canada faces new geopolitical circumstances in which overreliance on trade and economic integration with a single dominant power threatens to undermine national sovereignty. Trade-exposed sectors and regions have already faced significant adverse impacts as a result of these changes, and the accompanying uncertainty has weighed on Canada’s economy, impacted Canadian workers, and placed livelihoods at risk. To preserve its sovereignty and quality of life, Canada must act ambitiously to grow domestic economic resources and strengthen access to more diverse trade and investment partners. Securing confidence in Canada’s ability to develop major natural resource and infrastructure projects is foundational. The Act provides a means to advance Canada’s ability to develop major natural resource and infrastructure projects. It enables the GIC to determine whether certain projects are of such importance to Canada that they warrant early confidence in the approval of applicable federal permits and authorizations, shifting Canada’s regulatory focus from “whether” a project should proceed to “how” it should proceed. This reorientation of federal decision-making occurs within the framework of Canada’s respect for Aboriginal and treaty rights as recognized and affirmed by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 ; its duty to consult with Indigenous peoples; its commitment to reconciliation; and its respect for the rights set out in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Crown-Indigenous consultation is explicitly required to inform key decisions taken under the Act, including decisions to list national interest projects. These decisions can be taken only after Canada has met its duty to consult and, where appropriate, accommodate Indigenous peoples whose Aboriginal and treaty rights may be adversely affected by the carrying out of the projects to which the decisions relate. The reorientation of federal decision-making itself is achieved in two steps. First, the GIC’s decision to list a national interest project under Schedule 1 of the Act (a listing decision) results in immediate, deemed fulfillment of substantive prerequisites to the release of federal permits and authorizations listed in Schedule 2 of the Act. Project proponents, investors, Indigenous communities, and Canadians thus receive the immediate confidence needed to marshal initiative and resources in support of the project. Consultation with Indigenous communities prior to a listing decision facilitates involvement early in project development. It allows for Indigenous perspectives on whether a project is in Canada’s national interest, and enables Indigenous communities to identify key issues and opportunities early to better inform subsequent project development and regulatory review. Second, the Act enables diffuse federal regulatory processes to be consolidated in support of a single, omnibus authorization from the Minister responsible under the Act. This omnibus authorization (the Conditions Document) defines the regulatory conditions under which project construction and operation can occur. These conditions are developed based on further assessment and consultation with Indigenous communities about the project’s impacts, following receipt of a regulatory application by the proponent. The consolidation of authorizations under a single framework streamlines the process for proponents, and provides a better coordinated process of consultation with Indigenous communities, building on the consultation undertaken prior to a listing decision. The Act also recognizes a commitment to working in partnership with Indigenous peoples and envisages opportunities for Indigenous peoples to participate in the advancement of major projects as proponents, stakeholders, and investors. The Act identifies the extent to which a project can advance the interests of Indigenous peoples as one of the key factors relevant to the GIC’s determination of whether a project is in the national interest. Finally, the Act reflects Canada’s commitment to safeguard the natural environment — including through the mitigation of potential effects of project development on critical species, habitats, and marine and terrestrial ecosystems — and to meet the challenges of climate change. MPO, as a Special Operating Agency within Canada’s Privy Council Office, supports the Minister in the administration of the Act. The Project is a proposed interprovincial pipeline to transport approximately 1 million barrels per day (MMb/d) of crude oil from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia. Key components of the Project include The Project corridor will begin at a receipt terminal in Bruderheim, Alberta, which will collect Canadian crude oil from various pipelines in Alberta, serving as a central hub where the product will be measured, stored, and then pumped into the pipeline. The pipeline and pump stations will transport the crude oil to a proposed marine terminal (Delivery Tank Terminal) near Delta, British Columbia, for loading onto marine vessels for export to global markets. The corridor for the pipeline largely aligns with disturbed land and existing infrastructure, including the existing Trans Mountain pipeline system (i.e. Line 2, the Trans Mountain Expansion Project [TMEP]). Two marine berths will be designed to support Very Large Crude Carriers; these vessels typically have a capacity of two million barrels. After loading, marine vessels would follow existing navigation lanes (i.e. International Maritime Organization-adopted traffic separation schemes) within the Delta area, British Columbia, and the 12-nautical-mile limit of Canada’s territorial sea at the western entrance to the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Trans Mountain Corporation (TMC), Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission (APMC), and Pembina Pipeline Corporation (Pembina) [together, the Ownership Group] will form and lead a new jointly owned company: In addition, a minimum of 10 percent ownership interest in the Project will be offered for purchase to Indigenous peoples. TMC will be responsible for the construction of the proposed Project, making regulatory submissions to receive permits to operate, and subsequent operation of the asset. TMC will be engaged by the new company to design, develop, permit, construct and operate the project. In this capacity, it is expected that TMC will represent the ownership group as “the Proponent” and is referred to as such for the purposes of this Note. Given that the Project would require dozens of federal permits and authorizations affecting its timely execution and economic viability, the Project would benefit from the streamlined regulatory framework, coordinated review, and consolidated authorization process enabled by the Act. While the list of required authorizations will be finalized as the project design is further developed, the Project is expected to require permits and authorizations under the Canadian Energy Regulator Act ; the Fisheries Act ; the Species at Risk Act ; the Canada Marine Act ; and the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 . Under the BCA framework, all of these authorizations can be issued through a Conditions Document. It is also informed by consultation with implicated provincial or territorial governments; by the Minister having consulted with other ministerial colleagues as he considers appropriate; and by the views of Canadians, including those who respond to the publication of the Notice of a potential listing decision in the Canada Gazette . The following reflects the GIC’s assessment of the merit in listing the Project. As elaborated in the sections below, the GIC is of the view that The GIC has concluded that the Project presents an exceptional opportunity to strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security. While Canada holds the world’s fourth-largest oil reserves (approximately 163 billion barrels), its oil exports are heavily concentrated in a single market. footnote 1 Over four fifths of Canada’s pipeline export capacity is oriented for U.S. export markets. In 2025, 90.1 percent of Canadian crude exports continued to be shipped to the United States, despite completion of the TMEP in 2024 and its resulting increase in Canada’s capacity to reach additional foreign markets. footnote 2 This creates structural vulnerabilities for the Canadian oil sector by contributing to wider price differentials between Canadian and U.S. crude, as well as price instability in the global trading system. Price differentials negatively impact producers by lowering the value realized from their production, as well as governments, by contributing to reduced tax revenues and royalties. Together, this weakens growth and prosperity. In 2024, the differential between West Texas Intermediate (WTI — crude benchmark for the United States) and Western Canadian Select (WCS — Canada’s heavy crude oil benchmark) was US$14.73/bbl. footnote 3 That differential reached as high as US$40–50/bbl at its peak in 2018, contributing to a mandatory production curtailment limiting Canada’s production and exports of oil. footnote 4 Studio.Energy estimates US$49 billion of foregone value from wide differentials between 2010 and 2025. footnote 5 While there are a range of factors that contribute to price differences for Canada’s WCS, the foregone value resulting from price differentials has severely hindered Canada’s ability to attain the full value and benefit of its natural resources. Growing geopolitical tensions and trade disruptions are increasing economic uncertainty and reinforcing the need for Canada to quickly pivot and diversify into new markets. Canada’s reliance on U.S.-directed export infrastructure is a structural vulnerability, given the limited ability to redirect barrels when trade, policy, or market conditions change. These risks have been further intensified within the current geopolitical context as the United States diversifies its crude imports by increasing imports from Venezuela. Notably, in 2025, Canada’s economic growth was slowed by weakness in exports linked to U.S. trade actions and uncertainty. footnote 6 This trade uncertainty has persisted and could continue for some time. For example, on July 20, 2026, the United States announced 50 percent tariffs on an additional C$27.6 billion of Canadian goods. The Bank of Canada’s most recent Monetary Policy Report (July 2026) noted that while Canada’s economy is showing signs of improvement, uncertainty still remains high. footnote 7 These uncertainties have negative impacts on Canadian jobs and growth. In real terms, Finance Canada noted in the 2026 Spring Economic Update that private sector forecasters expect Canada’s real GDP to remain about 1.6 percent below its pre-tariff path by 2029. footnote 8 These signs point not only to the need to pivot Canada’s export and trade strategies, but to develop supporting infrastructure urgently so that Canada is positioned to take advantage of new opportunities created by trade shifts. Market diversification is a key strategic benefit associated with the Project. In total, the Project would add an estimated one million barrels per day (MMb/d) of export capacity, providing additional large-scale sovereign access to global energy markets. The Project would significantly reduce Canada’s dependence on exports to the United States by enabling more exports to the Asia-Pacific region, including key markets such as South Korea, China, and Japan. Combined with optimization of the Trans Mountain system, the increase in export capacity contributed by the Project could reduce Canada’s overall structural fixed land-pipeline dependency on the United States from approximately 82–83 percent (2025) to the 65–70 percent range of capacity. Diversification would also benefit Canada by supporting greater economic resilience and providing additional options when trade disruptions occur, enabling more efficient pivots to different markets as global trading patterns shift. Expanding Canada’s crude oil export capacity to the Asia-Pacific region also aligns with the Government of Canada’s broader export diversification objectives, including Canada’s goal of doubling non-U.S. trade by 2035. The Government has established a target to generate an additional C$300 billion in trade and to reduce economic dependence on the United States as a trading partner. snapshot.title: Syrian army takes control of al-Shaddadi base after coordination with U.S.
snapshot.evidenceText: The Syrian Army has assumed control of the al-Shaddadi military base in northeastern Syria’s Hasakah province, following coordination with U.S. officials, according to the Syrian Defense Ministry’s media department. In a statement carried by Syrian Arab News Agency, the ministry said the base was formally handed over after arrangements were completed with U.S. authorities. Syrian army units have since moved to secure the facility and its surrounding perimeter. The transfer comes just days after Damascus announced it had taken control of the al-Tanf military base in southeastern Syria. On February 12, the Defense Ministry said the handover of al-Tanf followed direct coordination between Syrian and American officials, marking a significant shift in the military presence in the area. United States Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed its withdrawal from al-Tanf after nearly a decade of operations there. In a statement, CENTCOM said U.S. forces remain prepared to respond to any potential threats from ISIS and will continue supporting partner-led efforts aimed at preventing the group’s resurgence in the region. The twin handovers of al-Shaddadi and al-Tanf signal a broader reconfiguration of military deployments in Syria’s northeast and southeast, areas that have long been focal points in the fight against ISIS and in wider regional dynamics. Syrian officials described the developments as part of ongoing efforts to reassert state authority over strategic sites, while U.S. officials emphasized that counterterrorism operations against ISIS remain a priority despite the withdrawal from specific bases. snapshot.title: Syrian army takes control of al-Shaddadi base after coordination with U.S.
snapshot.evidenceText: The Syrian Army has assumed control of the al-Shaddadi military base in northeastern Syria’s Hasakah province, following coordination with U.S. officials, according to the Syrian Defense Ministry’s media department. In a statement carried by Syrian Arab News Agency, the ministry said the base was formally handed over after arrangements were completed with U.S. authorities. Syrian army units have since moved to secure the facility and its surrounding perimeter. The transfer comes just days after Damascus announced it had taken control of the al-Tanf military base in southeastern Syria. On February 12, the Defense Ministry said the handover of al-Tanf followed direct coordination between Syrian and American officials, marking a significant shift in the military presence in the area. United States Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed its withdrawal from al-Tanf after nearly a decade of operations there. In a statement, CENTCOM said U.S. forces remain prepared to respond to any potential threats from ISIS and will continue supporting partner-led efforts aimed at preventing the group’s resurgence in the region. The twin handovers of al-Shaddadi and al-Tanf signal a broader reconfiguration of military deployments in Syria’s northeast and southeast, areas that have long been focal points in the fight against ISIS and in wider regional dynamics. Syrian officials described the developments as part of ongoing efforts to reassert state authority over strategic sites, while U.S. officials emphasized that counterterrorism operations against ISIS remain a priority despite the withdrawal from specific bases. representative.title: Kauai’s Hawaiian salt makers seek help restoring harvest area | Hawaii News Now
representative.author: Dillon Ancheta

snapshot.title: Kauai’s Hawaiian salt makers seek help restoring harvest area
snapshot.evidenceText: HANAPEPE (HawaiiNewsNow) - The 22 Kauai families keeping traditional Hawaiian salt making alive in Hanapepe are seeking the community’s help to restore their harvest site. Storm surge from Hurricane Lowell drastically changed the area. “The sand dunes were depleted. It was gone. It was a new landscape. I didn’t recognize it,” said Malia Nobrega-Olivera. Nobrega-Olivera and her ‘ohana have been Hawaiian salt makers for decades. She said the storm damage was the worst she’s seen. “It is different from all of my 55 years growing up in Hanapepe. It was a new space,” she said. Lowell pushed incredible amounts of sand into the beach park and salt beds, changing the composition of the land, making the clay more porous. “We are using this clay to seal the aina so that it can evaporate over time. But with the mixture of the sand, the practice doesn’t exist,” she said. Nobrega-Olivera is also the president of Hui Hana Pa’akai O Hanapepe, the group established for the salt makers. Together, they’re hosting a community work day on Saturday to restore the area. “Bring your tools. If you don’t have, just show up and your hands will be a good enough tools to be with us,” she said. They’ve also been getting assistance from the county and other partners to move sand as they prepare for the work day. There have been floods in recent years, and the group was already working on a dune restoration project. “Our practice is dictated by the weather, so you know, we wait until everything dries up and then we’re ready to go back in,” Nobrega-Olivera said. “And once the place is flooded, our salt-making time gets shorter and shorter.” She added the best harvest she’s had yielded 55 large buckets worth of salt. But if conditions aren’t right, that number is drastically less. Steeped in tradition, Hawaiian Salt is crucial to the culture. “Salt is not only used for our food, salt is used for medicinal purposes, for healing in all different ways,” she said. The workday runs from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., and more will be scheduled in the future. To stay connected with the group, contact them online at ProtectPaakai.org .

representative.title: In a surprise appearance, Bassem Yakhour teases the audience about the fourth season of "Ma Ekhtalefna" - Roya News
representative.author: غرفة أخبار رؤيا نيوز

snapshot.title: In a surprise appearance, Bassem Yakhour teases the audience about the fourth season of "Ma Ekhtalefna" - Video
snapshot.evidenceText: Syrian artist Bassam Yakhour sparked widespread reaction among his followers after he appeared with an unusual look, sporting a huge mustache and a thick beard, during the filming of scenes for the fourth part of the comedy series “Ma Ekhtalafna”, which is scheduled to be shown during the Ramadan 2027 drama season. Yakhour shared a video on his official Instagram account from behind the scenes of the work in the Izraa area in the countryside of Daraa Governorate in southern Syria, during which he revealed a part of the atmosphere of filming and the preparations underway for the new season. The Syrian artist appeared amidst a number of crew members and local residents, wearing a red and white shirt and a black hat. His new features attracted attention and raised questions among followers about the nature of the character he will portray in the series. Yakhour attached the video with a comment saying: “Live from the east of Izraa… Behind the scenes of filming Ma Ikhtalafna Part 4. All my love.” The clip received a positive response from the audience, who expressed their enthusiasm to follow the new season, praising the spontaneous atmosphere that appeared in the recording. The fourth part of “Ma Ikhtalafna” witnesses a remarkable change in the filming locations, as the crew moved to Syria to film all the scenes of the new season between the capital Damascus and a number of governorates, after the previous three parts were filmed in Lebanon. This change comes as part of preparations for a new season of the show, which in its previous seasons has attracted a wide audience of fans of social comedy. The series “We Didn’t Disagree” belongs to the genre of dark comedy, which relies on satire of social paradoxes and daily contradictions, through situations that combine humor and social criticism.

representative.title: IAEA Closes Syria Nuclear Investigation | Arms Control Association

snapshot.title: IAEA Closes Syria Nuclear Investigation | Arms Control Association
snapshot.evidenceText: “We continue to count on the valuable contributions of the Arms Control Association.” The International Atomic Energy Agency Board of Governors voted to close the investigation into Syria’s nuclear program after the agency reported that the new Syrian government provided the necessary cooperation to resolve long-standing questions about the illicit nuclear activities of the deposed Assad regime. The Sept. 9 resolution, which passed unanimously, welcomed Syria’s cooperation. It noted that Syria has “taken the measures required to remedy the non-compliance found by the Board” in 2011 and closed the investigation. IAEA Director-General Rafael Mariano Grossi hailed Syria’s cooperation with the agency as a “breakthrough” in a Sept. 7 statement to the board. The government’s transparency and cooperation facilitate “resolution of the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria’s past nuclear activities,” he said. In a Sept. 14 video statement to the IAEA General Conference, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani expressed gratitude to the IAEA and board for closing the noncompliance case “inherited from the previous regime.” He reaffirmed Syria’s commitment to transparency and IAEA safeguards going forward. Shibani said that Syria offers a “model” for resolving nonproliferation threats in the region and called on all nuclear facilities “without any exception, to be placed under safeguards.” The IAEA was able to resolve its concerns about Syria’s past nuclear activities after the new Syrian government negotiated an access agreement with the IAEA July 29. Before that agreement, Syria notified the agency in a July 17 letter about the discovery of a cache of undeclared nuclear materials dating from when President Bashar al-Assad ruled the country. He was ousted in 2024 by opposition forces. As a result of the information and access provided under the July 29 agreement, the IAEA assessed in a Sept. 1 report that it was able to “establish that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities as required” under the nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT) safeguards agreement. The report affirmed previous IAEA assessments, which led the Board of Governors to pass a resolution in 2011 that declared Syria in violation of its NPT-required safeguards agreement for constructing a nuclear reactor at Deir el-Zour without informing the agency. The IAEA requested access to the site after Israel bombed it in 2007, but the Assad regime refused to cooperate with the agency, leading to the board’s decision to declare Syria in noncompliance. The Sept. 1 report concluded that Syria took “measures to remedy the situation by providing to the Agency the required nuclear material accounting reports and design information for the above-mentioned facilities in accordance with its NPT Safeguards Agreement.” The IAEA noted 73 tons of natural uranium metal, 55 tons of which are in the form of fuel rods and 18 of which are uranium waste and scrap, when it inspected the newly discovered site. Syria declared the nuclear material to the agency and provided an accountancy report Aug. 27, according to the IAEA report. That material is now under IAEA safeguards in Syria. The agency’s excavations at the Deir el-Zour site confirmed previous assessments that Syria was building an undeclared nuclear reactor at the site. According to the report, the IAEA uncovered “cooling infrastructure” that is “consistent with that of a nuclear reactor.” The Sept. 1 report also noted that agency inspectors visited three locations connected to Deir el-Zour, including a facility intended for fabricating fuel for the reactor. The IAEA visited those sites in 2024 to take environmental samples, which tested positive for uranium. Despite the closure of the investigation, the Sept. 9 resolution requested that the IAEA director-general provide an update about the agency’s ongoing activities in Syria “upon their completion.” In a Sept. 10 speech, the U.S. ambassador to the IAEA, Wells Griffith III, called the adoption of the resolution a “historic milestone” but noted that the “work of Syria and the IAEA is not yet complete.” He said that “many questions related to Assad’s program remain unanswered” and requested a “detailed assessment of Syria’s previously undeclared nuclear program” from Grossi. Griffith called on Syria to sign an additional protocol—giving the IAEA expanded access to sites and more tools to verify that a state’s nuclear program is entirely peaceful—to its safeguards agreement “as early as possible.” Adopting an additional protocol “would be an important demonstration of the Syrian government’s enduring commitment to transparency and to fostering international trust,” he said.— The Arms Control Association depends on the generous contributions of individuals who share our goal of promoting public understanding of and support for effective arms control policies. representative.title: L.A. homeless agency meeting canceled after voter turnout surge - Los Angeles Times
representative.author: Doug Smith

snapshot.title: Bass-led turnout surge crashes meeting to replace L.A. homeless outreach agency
snapshot.evidenceText: It's not unusual for a public meeting to be canceled for lack of a quorum. But there isn't even a word for what happened Friday when a once-obscure board canceled a meeting to decide the future of homeless services in Los Angeles because too many people came to vote. More than 1,500 potential voters signed up for a meeting of the Los Angeles Continuum of Care board to pick a replacement for the core duties of the beleaguered Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority. Under the board's unusual charter, they all were eligible to vote merely because of their interest in homelessness. The onslaught was organized by Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who sent out a blast message through her communications networks urging people to join the meeting via Zoom to vote down the board's recommendation that Los Angeles County assume those duties. The response was overwhelming, but it didn't work. Over cries of foul from those who came in person, the board's attorney Shayla Myers announced the meeting was canceled because the Zoom channel had a capacity of only 1,000. Later, the board issued a formal statement saying, "The vote had to be continued today to ensure that all LA CoC members would be able to participate, given an unexpectedly high number of individuals who joined the online meeting." Bass and four City Council members then put out a statement lambasting the board for a failure that disenfranchised members. "Without collaboration and transparency, management of this complex issue will continue to falter, and worse, our unhoused neighbors will continue to suffer," the statement said. The cancellation deepens a crisis over the region's federally mandated homelessness functions. At stake is control over the annual homelessness count, the database that tracks every interaction with homeless people, the matching system that determines who receives housing and the responsibility for submitting applications for federal funding on behalf of dozens of local agencies. The Trump administration touched off the crisis in June when it suspended LAHSA as the agency performing those functions, citing a history of mismanagement and possible fraud. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development said local homeless service providers would have to apply directly to it for funding. LAHSA contested the move in federal court. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter temporarily stayed the suspension, keeping LAHSA in place for now but allowing 60 days to choose a replacement to assume its duties. That decision, upheld on appeal, put the onus on the Continuum of Care, an amorphous entity with a board and open membership that had long functioned as an appendage of LAHSA but actually had the statutory power to hire or fire the agency. Carter ordered the CoC, as it is commonly called, to report on its recommendations Tuesday and set Oct. 27 as the date to name the new agency. The CoC board, which includes representatives of homeless services contractors, hired outside consultants to set up an emergency bidding process and score the applicants. The City of Los Angeles applied for two of LAHSA's functions, the homeless database and the matching system, but scored below Los Angeles County in both. The county applied for all four functions and won the recommendation. The final step was a vote of the membership on Friday. The meltdown was foreseeable. A member of LAHSA's governing commission predicted it in an August LinkedIn post. Noting that membership “consists of persons and entities interested in collaborative, solution-oriented planning to address homelessness in LA County,” Justin Szlasa concluded, "that could arguably include tens or even hundreds of thousands of people. No comprehensive list of general members currently exists," and it would be almost impossible to compile one. "As the LA CoC takes on more authority and moves out of the orbit of LAHSA, effort should be made to broaden and deepen engagement with stakeholders in our homeless response system ... who are all, by definition, members of the LA CoC," Szlasa wrote. Bass turned that advice into a crash course. As enrollment in Friday's Zoom passed the 1,000 mark, Myers, the CoC attorney, told those present in the downtown meeting room that "because we have reached capacity on Zoom and CoC members are not able to participate, we have to continue this." The board is now working to upgrade its Zoom account and has yet to set a new date. Bass and the council members blamed the CoC for not planning adequately for a large audience. "Angelenos want a voice in the future of homelessness services, and they were silenced today. The current proposal for County-only administration, recommended by the LA CoC Board, leaves no room for those voices to be heard," the statement said. Ben Kay, chair of the CoC board, countered that it could not have anticipated the mayor and City Council using their "immense communications infrastructure to push public turnout" to defeat the recommendation. "Suggesting the board was unprepared for the city's unprecedented actions plays directly into the hands of HUD, which started all of this by saying the L.A. region shouldn't be allowed to make its own decisions about homeless services," Kay said. In a statement Saturday, Supervisor Lindsey Horvath said that, "failing to hold yesterday’s meeting is unacceptable and erodes public trust." Horvath said the county is prepared to partner with every city in the county to "listen to their concerns, and work toward solutions that address them." The county has committed that the City of Los Angeles would "at a minimum" maintain its access to the database and matching system, Horvath said. Times staff writer David Zahniser contributed to this report.

representative.title: L.A. homeless agency meeting canceled after voter turnout surge - Los Angeles Times
representative.author: Doug Smith

snapshot.title: Bass-led turnout surge crashes meeting to replace L.A. homeless outreach agency
snapshot.evidenceText: It's not unusual for a public meeting to be canceled for lack of a quorum. But there isn't even a word for what happened Friday when a once-obscure board canceled a meeting to decide the future of homeless services in Los Angeles because too many people came to vote. More than 1,500 potential voters signed up for a meeting of the Los Angeles Continuum of Care board to pick a replacement for the core duties of the beleaguered Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority. Under the board's unusual charter, they all were eligible to vote merely because of their interest in homelessness. The onslaught was organized by Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who sent out a blast message through her communications networks urging people to join the meeting via Zoom to vote down the board's recommendation that Los Angeles County assume those duties. The response was overwhelming, but it didn't work. Over cries of foul from those who came in person, the board's attorney Shayla Myers announced the meeting was canceled because the Zoom channel had a capacity of only 1,000. Later, the board issued a formal statement saying, "The vote had to be continued today to ensure that all LA CoC members would be able to participate, given an unexpectedly high number of individuals who joined the online meeting." Bass and four City Council members then put out a statement lambasting the board for a failure that disenfranchised members. "Without collaboration and transparency, management of this complex issue will continue to falter, and worse, our unhoused neighbors will continue to suffer," the statement said. The cancellation deepens a crisis over the region's federally mandated homelessness functions. At stake is control over the annual homelessness count, the database that tracks every interaction with homeless people, the matching system that determines who receives housing and the responsibility for submitting applications for federal funding on behalf of dozens of local agencies. The Trump administration touched off the crisis in June when it suspended LAHSA as the agency performing those functions, citing a history of mismanagement and possible fraud. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development said local homeless service providers would have to apply directly to it for funding. LAHSA contested the move in federal court. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter temporarily stayed the suspension, keeping LAHSA in place for now but allowing 60 days to choose a replacement to assume its duties. That decision, upheld on appeal, put the onus on the Continuum of Care, an amorphous entity with a board and open membership that had long functioned as an appendage of LAHSA but actually had the statutory power to hire or fire the agency. Carter ordered the CoC, as it is commonly called, to report on its recommendations Tuesday and set Oct. 27 as the date to name the new agency. The CoC board, which includes representatives of homeless services contractors, hired outside consultants to set up an emergency bidding process and score the applicants. The City of Los Angeles applied for two of LAHSA's functions, the homeless database and the matching system, but scored below Los Angeles County in both. The county applied for all four functions and won the recommendation. The final step was a vote of the membership on Friday. The meltdown was foreseeable. A member of LAHSA's governing commission predicted it in an August LinkedIn post. Noting that membership “consists of persons and entities interested in collaborative, solution-oriented planning to address homelessness in LA County,” Justin Szlasa concluded, "that could arguably include tens or even hundreds of thousands of people. No comprehensive list of general members currently exists," and it would be almost impossible to compile one. "As the LA CoC takes on more authority and moves out of the orbit of LAHSA, effort should be made to broaden and deepen engagement with stakeholders in our homeless response system ... who are all, by definition, members of the LA CoC," Szlasa wrote. Bass turned that advice into a crash course. As enrollment in Friday's Zoom passed the 1,000 mark, Myers, the CoC attorney, told those present in the downtown meeting room that "because we have reached capacity on Zoom and CoC members are not able to participate, we have to continue this." The board is now working to upgrade its Zoom account and has yet to set a new date. Bass and the council members blamed the CoC for not planning adequately for a large audience. "Angelenos want a voice in the future of homelessness services, and they were silenced today. The current proposal for County-only administration, recommended by the LA CoC Board, leaves no room for those voices to be heard," the statement said. Ben Kay, chair of the CoC board, countered that it could not have anticipated the mayor and City Council using their "immense communications infrastructure to push public turnout" to defeat the recommendation. "Suggesting the board was unprepared for the city's unprecedented actions plays directly into the hands of HUD, which started all of this by saying the L.A. region shouldn't be allowed to make its own decisions about homeless services," Kay said. In a statement Saturday, Supervisor Lindsey Horvath said that, "failing to hold yesterday’s meeting is unacceptable and erodes public trust." Horvath said the county is prepared to partner with every city in the county to "listen to their concerns, and work toward solutions that address them." The county has committed that the City of Los Angeles would "at a minimum" maintain its access to the database and matching system, Horvath said. Times staff writer David Zahniser contributed to this report.

The Hindu On Books Books of the week, reviews, excerpts, new titles and features. Updated - October 11, 2026 11:37 am IST - PALAKKAD Retirement has yet to find a place in P.B. Menon’s vocabulary. At 100, the Palakkad lawyer continues to walk into court with a brief in hand, nearly eight decades after he first donned the black coat. For him, the practice of law is not a career that has run its course, but a calling that continues to give his life purpose. Mr. Menon, who turned 100 on Saturday (October 10, 2026), holds the Guinness World Record for the longest career as a practising lawyer. Three years ago, he completed 73 years and 60 days in practice, surpassing the record of Gibraltar lawyer Louis Triay, whose career spanned 70 years and 311 days. Mr. Menon has continued practising since then, extending a record built on an extraordinary commitment to the profession. He celebrated his centenary with family and friends on Saturday (October 10, 2026). Prime Minister Narendra Modi was among those who greeted him, commending his contribution to the legal profession and his service to people over several decades. “A century is a remarkable milestone. To dedicate one’s time and energy over such a long period in the service of people is even more inspiring,” Mr. Modi said in his message. He pointed out that Mr. Menon had helped hundreds of people in their quest for justice and expressed confidence that his achievements and experience would inspire generations of lawyers. A group of lawyers felicitate P. B. Menon on the eve of his turning 100 years old. Photo: SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT For Mr. Menon, however, a lawyer’s worth has never been determined by the number of years spent in court or the number of cases handled. What matters is the trust clients place in him and the responsibility that comes with representing them. A graduate of Government Victoria College, Palakkad, in 1947, he went on to study law at Madras Law College (now Dr. Ambedkar Government Law College), Chennai. He began his career at the Madras High Court, where he practised for two years, before returning to Palakkad to establish his practice. An encounter with a senior judge at a sub-court in Kochi proved to be a turning point. After Mr. Menon won a criminal case as a junior lawyer, the judge advised him to concentrate on civil law. “That was a turning point in my career and life. I begin my days by remembering that senior judge,” he recalled. Also Read : ‘Being Sheela: The Life Journey of an Immigration Lawyer’ review: At the forefront of the good fight for immigrants Civil law subsequently became his life’s work. Over the decades, he earned a reputation for meticulous preparation, concise arguments and an honest assessment of cases. He believes that a strong case does not necessarily require lengthy arguments; a thorough understanding of the matter and the ability to anticipate the opposing side’s arguments are far more important. P. B. Menon (right) with former Deputy Director of Prosecution P. Premnath. Photo: SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT P. Premnath, former deputy director of prosecution, sees Mr. Menon as much more than a lawyer with an extraordinary record. “He is a phenomenon, a legal institution from which today’s practitioners have many lessons to learn,” Mr. Premnath said. E. Krishnadas, lawyer and BJP State treasurer, describes him as a legend in his own right. “His nearly eight decades in legal practice are a testament to his dedication, perseverance and extraordinary lifelong commitment to the profession,” he said. Mr. Menon has never considered a case too small to merit his full attention. His daughter, Subhadra Muraleedharan, says that he approaches every brief with seriousness, keeping the pursuit of justice for his client at the forefront. His home, Rose Land at Puthur in Palakkad town, has long been a meeting place for lawyers and clients. Younger practitioners have found in him a mentor willing to share the lessons of a lifetime at the Bar. While many of his contemporaries went on to become judges, Mr. Menon chose to remain a practising lawyer. The greatest reward, he believes, is the confidence of a client who considers him dependable and values his honest opinion. At 100, with no plans to retire, Mr. Menon continues to find purpose in the work he has pursued for nearly eight decades. His record may be measured in years, but his legacy rests on something less easily quantified: the trust he has earned, one client at a time. representative.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
representative.author: Tom Ayers

snapshot.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: A Mi'kmaw community in Cape Breton is placing a big bet on new technology that it says can turn seawater into environmentally friendly jet fuel. Eskasoni First Nation has invested $1.5 million and is the majority owner in a joint venture called eFuels Mi'kmaq Limited that plans to build a pilot project on band-owned land in Cape Breton Regional Municipality's industrial park in Sydney harbour. Bertram Bernard, a band councillor and chair of Eskasoni Corporate Services, said the investment will create local jobs for band members and is an important step in taking a meaningful role in a growing industry. "For us, this is about creating long-term economic opportunities, while continuing to be responsible stewards of our land and waters," he said during an announcement Thursday at the Sarah Denny Cultural Centre in Eskasoni. The newly formed eFuels Mi'kmaq plans to extract hydrogen from seawater and draw carbon dioxide from the air to create what is known as drop-in fuel, meaning it can be burned like any other fuel without any engine modifications. The process is expected to be powered by wind energy from onshore and offshore sources as they become available. Eskasoni band councillor Bertram Bernard says the joint venture will create lasting economic benefits while ensuring stewardship of resources. (Tom Ayers/CBC) The joint venture is with Aeon Blue, a company that started in the United States but moved to Sydney to take advantage of federal government incentives and the research facilities at the Verschuren Centre on Cape Breton University's campus. Lark Meadow, a co-founder and CEO of Aeon Blue, said it was important to her and her brother, co-founder Deois Ua Cearnaigh, to have Indigenous participation. "We are partnering all the way from piloting to commercialization, so we are going to grow our partnership and the facilities together," she said. Ua Cearnaigh, who is an electrochemist, said the technology to separate hydrogen from seawater and combine it with carbon dioxide to make all kinds of fuels has been around for decades. Aeon Blue CEO Lark Meadow says although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, jet fuel was chosen because of growing demand. (Tom Ayers/CBC) But he said his patented process improves on the technology and makes it economical on a commercial scale. "It's kind of like saying the cart, four-wheeled vehicles, are thousands of years old, but the car only came around in the 1910s," he said. It also draws more carbon from the air than it uses, with the excess carbon dioxide being sequestered. Meadow said that may be in the ground or in other ways that have yet to be decided. Although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, Meadow said jet fuel was chosen because there's a growing demand for green fuel in air travel. Officials say the joint venture is expected to produce 12 jobs next year and up to 80 when the efuel process reaches full commercialization. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Ua Cearnaigh said the move from their home in Texas not only made sense because of the government's financial incentives, but he said the Verschuren Centre's laboratories are superior to others and the geography means all of the components needed for the process are readily available. "Cape Breton has sort of this magical location where it is as close to the southern extent of winter sea ice as you can go and still have ice-free ports in the winter, and yet also the wind howls like nobody's business," he said. "It really is an X marks the spot. If you were going to do an efuels project, doesn't matter who you are, you would pick this island." Meadow said a pilot project will be located on Eskasoni's land in Sydport and is expected to start making fuel next year. It is expected to scale up the following year, with full commercialization to follow by 2030. eFuels Mi'kmaq Ltd. plans to build a pilot project on Eskasoni land in Sydport industrial park to make jet fuel from seawater. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Meadow said large-scale commercialization will require more land, but the manufacturing site will still be located along the coast of Cape Breton. The joint venture is expected to start training up to 12 Eskasoni band members in engineering, operations and management next year, and could create up to 80 full-time jobs when full commercialization is achieved. Steve Parsons, CEO of Eskasoni's corporate division, said the deal has been in the works for about 18 months. "We're very excited," he said. "This is a great opportunity for the community." representative.title: River swallows char beside Padma Bridge, 4 villages under water | The Daily Star
representative.author: Jahid Hasan

snapshot.title: River swallows char beside Padma Bridge, 4 villages under water
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The clang of hammers and crowbars echoed across Alam-Khankandi village yesterday morning as families dismantled their own homes, racing against a river that has already devoured four char villages and is eating into a fifth. In two years, 1,803 families in five villages have lost their homes to erosion of char land beside the Padma Bridge. Of them, 303 families in Alam-Khankandi have been displaced since August, according to the Shariatpur Water Development Board (WDB) and Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. About 150 families still living in the village are at imminent risk. The char emerged about three decades ago in Painpara mouza on the northern bank of the Padma. According to WDB sources, the char formed Naodoba Union Parishad, which includes six villages and constitutes wards 2 and 3. During a visit yesterday, this correspondent found families preparing to leave. Those already homeless lived beside roads or in tin-sheet shelters on rented land, while others planned to cross the Padma by engine-run trawlers to rent land in Zajira or Munshiganj. Duluna Begum, 60, travelled from Digholi in Bikrampur, Munshiganj, after her daughter called her at night on her phone to tell her that her in-laws’ house was being devoured by the river. “I came here early in the morning with other people to help them dismantle the house before the river swallowed it whole,” she told The Daily Star. “Five days ago, nine bighas of cultivated land were lost in river erosion. Now where will my daughter go with her four children?” Maksuda Begum, 55, of Farazi Kandi in Zajira also came with helpers to dismantle her daughter’s in-laws’ house. For Md Shahid Fakir, 38, erosion destroyed both his livelihood and his house. He once owned 25 bighas, where he grew ginger, garlic, and vegetables, and a trawler to carry the produce across the river. “Having lost everything to river erosion, I am now destitute. I have no place to call my own anymore,” he said. He is now building a shack on land lent to him by someone. “If the government gave a little space to live on khas (government) land, then I could somehow spend my life raising a house there,” he said. Last year, erosion destroyed four villages in ward 2 of the union. They are Ahammad Majhikandi, Mongol Majhikandi, Alim Uddin Beparikandi, and Majhikandi, leaving around 1,500 families homeless. Painpara Government Primary School No 52 was washed away in August 2024, and about a year later Rezia Amin Government Primary School and a community clinic followed, said Altaf Hossain Khan, chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. At least 5,000 acres of cropland in Painpara mouza have been lost over the past year, and No 122 Altaf Khan Government Primary School is now under threat, he added. A 4.5-kilometre paved road built in 2021 has lost four kilometres to the river. Electricity reached 1,200 consumers across the six villages through a 30-kilometre transmission line, including submarine cables along the riverbed, at a cost of Tk 4.5 crore. Nazmul Hasan, deputy general manager (technical) of Shariatpur Palli Bidyut Samity, said 22 kilometres of the line had been dismantled as villages disappeared. Another 3.5 kilometres were removed from the Alam-Khankandi area in the past three months to keep the line from falling into the river, though supply continued. Residents now living in the open without power can apply for reconnection under existing rules if they relocate near electricity poles, he said. The chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad said residents had informed the WDB repeatedly about the erosion for the last 3-4 years, but saw no effective action from their part. He said some displaced families had moved to Louhajang in Munshiganj, while others rented homes or leased land in Shariatpur. At least 250 families who cannot afford either have taken shelter at a construction yard near the Padma Bridge’s southern end, living in fear as the Bangladesh Bridge Authority occasionally serves eviction notices. Appeals to the UNO and DC have yielded little, he said. With few jobs remaining nearby, many families struggle to eat adequately, he added. “The way the WDB treats us makes us feel like as though we are criminals. They do not answer our calls, nor do they want to speak to us even when they visit,” he said. MP Sayeed Ahmed distributed rice, lentils and dry food among 273 affected families about a month ago, the chairman said. WDB Executive Engineer Md Milton Hossain said the board was aware of the erosion and had informed higher authorities. “Protecting the mainland is our priority in cases of river erosion. That is why it is often not possible to take measures in char areas,” he said, adding that the Ministry of Water Resources was not currently taking emergency measures there. He said he would inspect the area and take necessary steps, subject to approval from higher authorities. representative.title: River swallows char beside Padma Bridge, 4 villages under water | The Daily Star
representative.author: Jahid Hasan

snapshot.title: River swallows char beside Padma Bridge, 4 villages under water
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The clang of hammers and crowbars echoed across Alam-Khankandi village yesterday morning as families dismantled their own homes, racing against a river that has already devoured four char villages and is eating into a fifth. In two years, 1,803 families in five villages have lost their homes to erosion of char land beside the Padma Bridge. Of them, 303 families in Alam-Khankandi have been displaced since August, according to the Shariatpur Water Development Board (WDB) and Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. About 150 families still living in the village are at imminent risk. The char emerged about three decades ago in Painpara mouza on the northern bank of the Padma. According to WDB sources, the char formed Naodoba Union Parishad, which includes six villages and constitutes wards 2 and 3. During a visit yesterday, this correspondent found families preparing to leave. Those already homeless lived beside roads or in tin-sheet shelters on rented land, while others planned to cross the Padma by engine-run trawlers to rent land in Zajira or Munshiganj. Duluna Begum, 60, travelled from Digholi in Bikrampur, Munshiganj, after her daughter called her at night on her phone to tell her that her in-laws’ house was being devoured by the river. “I came here early in the morning with other people to help them dismantle the house before the river swallowed it whole,” she told The Daily Star. “Five days ago, nine bighas of cultivated land were lost in river erosion. Now where will my daughter go with her four children?” Maksuda Begum, 55, of Farazi Kandi in Zajira also came with helpers to dismantle her daughter’s in-laws’ house. For Md Shahid Fakir, 38, erosion destroyed both his livelihood and his house. He once owned 25 bighas, where he grew ginger, garlic, and vegetables, and a trawler to carry the produce across the river. “Having lost everything to river erosion, I am now destitute. I have no place to call my own anymore,” he said. He is now building a shack on land lent to him by someone. “If the government gave a little space to live on khas (government) land, then I could somehow spend my life raising a house there,” he said. Last year, erosion destroyed four villages in ward 2 of the union. They are Ahammad Majhikandi, Mongol Majhikandi, Alim Uddin Beparikandi, and Majhikandi, leaving around 1,500 families homeless. Painpara Government Primary School No 52 was washed away in August 2024, and about a year later Rezia Amin Government Primary School and a community clinic followed, said Altaf Hossain Khan, chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. At least 5,000 acres of cropland in Painpara mouza have been lost over the past year, and No 122 Altaf Khan Government Primary School is now under threat, he added. A 4.5-kilometre paved road built in 2021 has lost four kilometres to the river. Electricity reached 1,200 consumers across the six villages through a 30-kilometre transmission line, including submarine cables along the riverbed, at a cost of Tk 4.5 crore. Nazmul Hasan, deputy general manager (technical) of Shariatpur Palli Bidyut Samity, said 22 kilometres of the line had been dismantled as villages disappeared. Another 3.5 kilometres were removed from the Alam-Khankandi area in the past three months to keep the line from falling into the river, though supply continued. Residents now living in the open without power can apply for reconnection under existing rules if they relocate near electricity poles, he said. The chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad said residents had informed the WDB repeatedly about the erosion for the last 3-4 years, but saw no effective action from their part. He said some displaced families had moved to Louhajang in Munshiganj, while others rented homes or leased land in Shariatpur. At least 250 families who cannot afford either have taken shelter at a construction yard near the Padma Bridge’s southern end, living in fear as the Bangladesh Bridge Authority occasionally serves eviction notices. Appeals to the UNO and DC have yielded little, he said. With few jobs remaining nearby, many families struggle to eat adequately, he added. “The way the WDB treats us makes us feel like as though we are criminals. They do not answer our calls, nor do they want to speak to us even when they visit,” he said. MP Sayeed Ahmed distributed rice, lentils and dry food among 273 affected families about a month ago, the chairman said. WDB Executive Engineer Md Milton Hossain said the board was aware of the erosion and had informed higher authorities. “Protecting the mainland is our priority in cases of river erosion. That is why it is often not possible to take measures in char areas,” he said, adding that the Ministry of Water Resources was not currently taking emergency measures there. He said he would inspect the area and take necessary steps, subject to approval from higher authorities. representative.title: FoN Campaign Defends Ghana's Expanded Fishing Zone
representative.author: Kwame Darko

snapshot.title: FoN Campaign Defends Ghana's Expanded Fishing Zone
snapshot.evidenceText: Government has doubled Ghana's Inshore Exclusive Zone from six to 12 nautical miles for artisanal fishers — now Friends of the Nation is training coastal communities in Ahanta West to stop trawlers from crossing the new line. Barely days after a canoe fisherman in Butre spoke of his fears that marine protection rules could push small-scale operators further out to sea, an environmental NGO has launched a campaign aimed at making sure the opposite happens — that industrial trawlers, not artisanal canoes, are kept out of protected waters. Friends of the Nation (FoN) launched its "Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future" campaign at a day-long workshop held in Upper and Lower Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region on 11 October 2026, according to the Ghana News Agency (GNA). The workshop brought together fishers, fishmongers and other industry stakeholders to explain recent regulatory changes and the boundaries of Ghana's newly expanded Inshore Exclusive Zone (IEZ). The IEZ is a stretch of sea reserved exclusively for canoe fishers and other small-scale, artisanal operators, where larger industrial vessels are barred from casting nets. According to FoN, government has extended this protected zone from six nautical miles to 12 nautical miles offshore, effectively doubling the area set aside for Ghana's coastal fishing communities. Mevuta Donkris, FoN's Executive Director, thanked government for the extension but cautioned that the new boundary would only mean something if fishers themselves remained alert, GNA reports. He warned that pair trawlers — heavy industrial vessels that fish in coordinated pairs — could still attempt to encroach on the IEZ and deplete stocks of small pelagic fish, the smaller species such as sardinella that artisanal fishers depend on for their livelihoods. Kenneth Arthur, Secretary-General of the Canoe and Fishing Gear Owners Association of Ghana (CaFGOAG), welcomed the extension and said any Chinese-owned pair trawlers fishing within the IEZ would be committing an unlawful by-catch. He noted that such encroachment had already been a problem when the protected zone was only six nautical miles, and urged fishers to stay united and vigilant now that the boundary has been pushed further out, according to GNA. Frank Eshun, an official of the Fisheries Commission in Takoradi representing the Western Regional Director, told the workshop that heavy vessels are permitted to pass through the 12-nautical-mile zone but are prohibited from fishing within it. He compared pair trawling to galamsey, describing both as ecologically destructive practices that disrupt natural ecosystems — in this case, marine life. Eshun said the Commission would continue sensitising artisanal fishers to protect their boundaries and to report any trawlers caught fishing inside the IEZ to the authorities for action, GNA reports. The campaign comes amid an ongoing crisis around declining fish catches along Ghana's coast, which has repeatedly strained the incomes of canoe fishers and fishmongers in towns like Dixcove and Butre. As Chale News reported earlier this month , some fishers worry that new marine protection measures could complicate their own access to fishing grounds even as the rules are meant to shield them from industrial competition. FoN's campaign appears designed to address that tension by ensuring the expanded zone works in fishers' favour rather than becoming another source of confusion or conflict at sea. None of the sources indicate a specific timeline for further workshops or enforcement actions beyond the Fisheries Commission's stated intention to continue sensitisation efforts and to act on reports of encroachment. It also remains unclear from available information how boundary violations will be monitored or policed in practice along the 12-nautical-mile line. representative.title: Greenpeace calls for ban on “dead waste” textile imports into Ghana  | Ghana News Agency
representative.author: GNA

snapshot.title: Greenpeace calls for ban on “dead waste” textile imports into Ghana | Ghana News Agency
snapshot.evidenceText: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Accra, Oct. 8, GNA – Greenpeace Africa, an independent environmental campaigning organisation, has called on the Government to ban the importation of what it calls “dead waste” textiles into the country, describing them as clothing that cannot be reused, repurposed or resold. The call follows a brand audit of some 201 discarded garments collected from James Town Beach, Kantamanto Market and Agbogbloshie in Accra, which identified labels of global fashion brands including H&M, Primark, Marks & Spencer (M&S) and Next, as major contributors to Ghana’s textile waste. The organisation said the growing volume of discarded clothing in Accra highlighted the need for action both at the source of production and at Ghana’s borders. Presenting the audit findings on Wednesday in Accra, as part of its campaign on “waste colonialism” and the environmental and economic effects of the global fast-fashion industry, Ms Hellen Kahaso Dena, Project Lead for the Plastics Project and Fast Fashion at Greenpeace Africa, said the organisation’s investigations across Accra showed that textile waste was accumulating at several locations, including Kantamanto Market, James Town Beach and Agbogbloshie. She said the problem needed to be addressed by reducing excessive production by global fashion companies and ensuring that only clothing capable of being reused entered Ghana. “We want to tackle this problem at the source, and the source of this problem is the overproduction,” Ms Dena said. She said traders at Kantamanto estimated that about 40 per cent of clothing entering the market was waste, meaning it could not be effectively reused or resold. Ms Dena explained that while Greenpeace was not calling for a complete ban on second-hand clothing imports as the trade provided livelihoods for many Ghanaians, it could also not be left unchecked. “What we do not want is for fashion brands in the global North to actually use that loophole to continue dumping,” she said. She urged the Government to establish standards to ensure that imported second-hand clothing was of sufficient quality for reuse, while supporting Ghana’s local textile and fashion industries, artisans and other workers in the sector. Mr Sam Quashie-Idun, Head of Investigations at Greenpeace Africa, said the audit formed part of wider investigations into the environmental effects of discarded clothing in Ghana. He said the team collected garments and engaged traders and other stakeholders involved in the second-hand clothing trade at the three locations. He explained that the presence of labels from H&M, Primark, M&S and Next demonstrated the international nature of the clothing waste entering Ghana. He also expressed concern about plastic and microplastic pollution arising from synthetic fibres used in many garments. Mr Quashie-Idun cited Greenpeace’s 2024 report, “Fast Fashion, Slow Poison”, which found that 89 per cent of 164 discarded garments tested at three dumpsites in the Greater Accra Region contained synthetic fibres. He said an earlier investigation into the burning of textile waste as fuel at three public washhouses in Old Fadama also detected benzene, a known carcinogen, in samples collected in 2023. Greenpeace also unveiled a six-metre installation, “Fast Fashion, Lasting Damage”, created from discarded garments by The Revival, an upcycling collective based at Kantamanto Market. The installation depicts a model wearing a dress whose large skirt extends onto the ground and merges with hundreds of discarded garments. As part of the campaign, Greenpeace and its partners presented a petition signed by more than 25,000 people to the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry. The petition called for a ban on unusable textile waste, transparent grading and trading practices, stronger producer responsibility mechanisms, investment in Ghana’s textile industry and support for traditional craftsmanship, repair and reuse. It also called for stronger Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regulations requiring fashion companies to contribute to managing the environmental impact of their products throughout their life cycle. Isabelle McAllister, a Greenpeace spokesperson from Sweden, called on fashion companies to remain responsible for their products even after they left their original markets. “We don’t want to see a total ban on import here. The quality needs to be better and we have to stop the overproduction,” she said. Head Office Location Opp. Registrar General's Department Dodoo Lane, Ministries, Accra Digital Address: GA–144–5449

representative.author: GNA

snapshot.title: Volta House of Chiefs makes giant strides in wooing partnerships and investments from China | Ghana News Agency
snapshot.evidenceText: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Ho, Oct 9, GNA-A delegation of chiefs from the Volta Regional House of Chiefs have returned from China, beaming with development prospects as they notched some bilateral partnerships and strategic investment opportunities with some Chinese companies. Togbe Tepre Hodo IV, President of the House, in a debriefing exclusive interview with the Ghana News Agency, described the business trip as “strategic, enormous, insightful and timely.” The visit, at the invitation of Ghana’s Ambassador to the People’s Republic of China, Mr Kojo Bonsu, is aimed at exploring concrete investment partnerships to support development initiatives and address key challenges facing the Volta Region. The delegation, coordinated by Mr Peter Ahiakpor, a Volta native and businessman, includes Togbe Gabusu VII of Hohoe, Togbe Atikpladza Agbi Yao VIII of Kpalime, Togbe Sei II of Botoku, Togbe Dagadu IX of Kpando, Togbe Tenge Dzokoto Gligui VII of Anyako, and Togbe Adama III of Some’. The Chiefs were received at the Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport by Ambassador Bonsu, a team of Chinese business executives, Mr Jiang Jia Hua and Mr Blaze Li of Sinohui Investment Corporation, and Madam Aku-Sika Kpene, a daughter of the Volta Region and Board Member of the Produce Buying Company (Shea). The investment mission focused on opportunities in Information and Communication Technology, technology transfer, education and skills development, agriculture and agribusiness, sanitation and waste management, as well as tourism and heritage development. During the 10-day business trip, four strategic agreements were signed with Chinese companies to promote international partnerships and investment, technology and skill transfer, infrastructure development and aquaculture in the Volta Region, to support sustainable development in the region. The first Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed with Guangdong Welleap Information Technology Company, a Chinese technology firm, to promote digital transformation and facilitate technology transfer to the Volta Region. The second agreement, with Foshan Jinting Construction Engineering Company Limited, a construction and engineering firm based in Foshan, focuses on infrastructure and industrial development. A third comprehensive investment agreement was signed with SINOHUI Investment Ghana Limited, which specialises in urban road construction and urban sewerage systems is meant to explore opportunities for cooperation in infrastructure development and engineering services, would provide a platform for channelling Chinese direct investment into Ghana. Togbe President indicated particularly that the ICT school, to be equipped with practical training facilities and laboratories would provide hands-on technical training and to potentially attract students from neighbouring countries, including Togo, Benin, and Nigeria. He said a collaboration with existing Ho Technical University in the region is also being considered. The fourth agreement, signed with Moaming Yuantian Food Co., Ltd., a major Chinese aquaculture company, focuses on investment in commercial fish farming in the Volta Basin. Togbe Tepre Hodo said the Moaming Yuantian Food Co., Ltd. is reported to have a daily tilapia processing capacity of 150,000 kilogrammes across nine production lines and exports fish products to about 70 countries. He said the aquaculture partnership is expected to support increased fish production, create employment opportunities and promote the development of commercial fish farming in the Volta Basin. Again, Togbe Tepre Hodo disclosed that waste treatment and management featured strongly in the bilateral partnerships to introduce another important component of waste treatment equipment and operation services to the region. He said his development was underpinned to sustain the ‘Oxygen City’ accolade of the regional capital, Ho, for Chinese company to deploy own equipment to collect waste, sort waste into plastic, glass, paper, and organic waste to facilitate recycling measures. He said the long-term benefits would be to turn waste to energy. “Can you imagine the employment potentials of these projects, off-the-chest of the government, the economic fallouts to the regional space and beyond is enormous,” Togbe postulated? Togbe Tepre Hodo said the House had swiftly swung into preparatory works fashioning out details of incorporation of companies, apply for the necessary permits, licenses, and other regulatory regimes to pave the way for implementation of these projects with dispatch. Overall, Togbe President said the visit established potential partnerships in technology, skills development, waste management, and infrastructure. The next priority is to translate the agreements and investment proposals into concrete projects that can create jobs, build local technical capacity, attract further investment, and contribute to the Volta Region’s economic development.
