representative.title: Pamela Atkinson dies at 94; tireless advocate for people in need in Utah
representative.author: Sean P. Means

snapshot.title: Pamela Atkinson, who spoke out for Utah children and people in poverty, dies
snapshot.evidenceText: (Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson waves while providing homelessness services to people in Salt Lake City in 2005. Pamela Atkinson, a tireless advocate and organizer for Utahns who needed help — children, the elderly and people dealing with poverty — has died. Atkinson died Saturday, according to Fox 13 News . She was 93. Over her long career speaking out for people in need, Atkinson was often called — by former Gov. Gary Herbert, among others — “Utah’s Mother Teresa,” referring to the Catholic nun who ministered to the poor in Kolkata, India. It’s a comparison Atkinson once said embarrassed her. “I don’t feel like a Mother Teresa,” Atkinson told a Salt Lake Tribune reporter in 2001. “I feel like I’m just an ordinary person who’s gotten some things done.” (Ryan Galbraith | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson loads groceries for preparing Thanksgiving meals to the homeless in 1999. (Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson makes her way to a lecture at Judge High School in 2001. (Ryan Galbraith | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson plays games with her grandchildren Nate, Will, and Chase in 2001. (Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson talks with a member of the unsheltered community in 2005. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson joins others at Pioneer Park in 2005 for a candlelight vigil in honor of those Salt Lake residents who died while homeless over the last year. (Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson waves while providing homelessness services to people in Salt Lake City in 2005. (Trent Nelson | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson speaks at the annual candlelight vigil for homeless Utahns who died in 2011. (Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson delivers a hot meal, boots and a warm coat to a homeless man who lives in a camp along the Jordan River in 2012. (Chris Detrick | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson greets the Dalai Lama at the Huntsman Center at the University of Utah, Tuesday June 21, 2016. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson, right, attends a news conference in Salt Lake City regarding homeless resource centers on Friday, Feb. 24, 2017. (Leah Hogsten | The Salt Lake Tribune) Sharonne Zippel talks with Pamela Atkinson prior to a Shabbat candle lighting at the Chabad Lubavitch of Utah in 2019. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Eva May Densley, carried by her mother Michelle, calls out for "grandma" after catching a glimpse of Pamela Atkinson while touring the YWCA Center for Women & Families in Salt Lake on Tuesday, March 20, 2018. (Trent Nelson | The Salt Lake Tribune) Gov. Gary Herbert and Pamela Atkinson at the groundbreaking ceremony for Pamela's Place Apartments in Salt Lake City on Wednesday April 17, 2019. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson at a temporary shelter as it gets ready to open for the night in Sugar House, Thursday, Jan. 23, 2020. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson helps hand out warm meals as The Rescue Mission of Salt Lake serves their annual Thanksgiving Banquet as part of their ongoing outreach to help the homeless on Monday, Nov. 22, 2021. (Rachel Rydalch | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson and Gov. Spencer Cox take a tour of Pamela’s Place Apartments located in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Feb. 15, 2022. Atkinson — who in her career advised governors and mayors, and consulted with clergy across faiths — had three passions, she said: children, or “little ones,” as she called them; education; and helping people experiencing homelessness and poverty. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson posted a remembrance on X Saturday, saying that “Pamela has been an example to me of loving your neighbor unconditionally. Our state is in a better place because of her influence for good.” This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Gov. Spencer Cox followed Sunday on X with a statement that read in part: “There are angels on this earth — and yesterday, one of them went home. It is possible to make the case that Pamela Atkinson has had a bigger impact and done more good than anyone in Utah over the past 30 years. She was more than an advisor and confidant, she was a friend. She treated me the exact same way she treated her homeless friends — with love and respect.” In 2001, just before she retired from her position as vice president of mission services for Intermountain Healthcare, Atkinson said that when she was in her 20s, a group of her school friends were talking about their various talents, from singing to crochet. When it was her turn to speak, Atkinson said she stayed silent — and another young woman said, “Pamela doesn’t have any talents.” The comment stayed with her many decades, and many accolades, later. (Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson delivers a hot meal, boots and a warm coat to a homeless man who lives in a camp along the Jordan River in 2012. When author Sue Bender met Atkinson at a dinner party and was told of her work for people living in poverty, Bender blurted out, “Pamela, you are an artist!” Bender recounted this moment in her 2001 book, “Stretching Lessons,” which Bender, who died in 2025, said Atkinson inspired. “I realized that Pamela sees the dignity in her homeless friends,” Bender told The Tribune shortly after the book was published. “Her art is her caring.” One of her motivators, Atkinson said, was anger. What made her angry? “Injustice. When people are not treated fairly. Abuse,” she said. “If I’m angry about something, I darn well better do something about it.” (Trent Nelson | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson speaks at the annual candlelight vigil for homeless Utahns who died in 2011. Atkinson was born Pamela Collin in the London borough of Bromley, the third of five children. She knew poverty firsthand in her youth. Her father was a gambler who owned greyhounds for racing. He once sold the dogs and lost the family’s money, then left for good. Her mother held menial jobs, but had no career skills, she said. She and her siblings survived on bread and potatoes, using newspapers as toilet paper. The kids slept three to a bed, with mice running around the house. “It’s very hard going to school with people knowing you’re so poor,” she said in 2001, adding that she never invited friends home because “our house was horrible.” After finishing high school — she was the only one of her siblings to do so — she traveled the globe, and spent a year as an exchange student in New York. She landed in the Bay Area, attending night classes at the University of California at Berkeley and San Francisco in the 1960s. She worked as a nurse to support herself, using credentials she earned at a London hospital. She married and raised three children. She divorced, but remained on good terms with her ex-husband, she said. As an administrator at Salt Lake City’s LDS Hospital in the 1980s, one of Atkinson’s initiatives was holding a “teddy bear clinic,” to help children overcome their fear of seeing the doctor. She also helped organize mock disaster drills for doctors and paramedics. Atkinson took on several positions at LDS Hospital’s parent company, Intermountain Healthcare, including director of its senior services, rehabilitation services and medically needy services. In 1990, she was promoted to vice president of mission services — a job created specifically for her. The job, Intermountain’s senior vice president, Steven D. Kohlert, said at the time, was designed “to coordinate more effectively all of [Intermountain’s] charitable programs for the needy, the aging and the homeless.” Atkinson was “the ideal person” for the job, Kohlert said, “because of her long and active involvement with such programs.” Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune Pamela Atkinson, right, stands with political leaders in 2017 — from left, House Speaker Greg Hughes, Salt Lake County Mayor Ben McAdams, Salt Lake City Mayor Jackie Biskupski and Lt. Gov. Spencer Cox — during an announcement that Salt Lake City was dropping two of four planned homeless resource centers. During her time at Intermountain Healthcare, Atkinson also was the only person to serve simultaneously on Utah’s three educational boards: the state school board, the higher education Board of Regents and the board of the Utah College of Applied Technology. In 2001, in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Atkinson was one of the Utah civic leaders to take part in the “Alliance for Unity,” formed by billionaire Jon Huntsman Sr. and then-Salt Lake City Mayor Rocky Anderson. The group, in its formation statement, set a goal “to help people cross boundaries of culture, religion and ethnicity to better understand and befriend one another.” (Trent Nelson | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson speaks at the groundbreaking ceremony for Pamela's Place Apartments in Salt Lake City on Wednesday April 17, 2019. The Salt Lake Tribune named Atkinson “Utahn of the Year” in 2005. In 2019 , Salt Lake City’s Housing Authority broke ground on Pamela’s Place Apartments, a 100-bed facility on the western edge of downtown, devoted to permanent supportive housing for people experiencing homelessness. Three years later , a homeless resource center in South Salt Lake was named for Atkinson. The Fourth Street Clinic near Pioneer Park also bears her name. Her name also appears on the Pamela Atkinson Trust Fund , a state fund that pays for emergency services, housing and other support for people in need. Utah residents are given the opportunity to contribute to the fund on their state income tax returns, or when rounding up their purchases at state liquor stores. When such honors were given to her, Atkinson often deflected the praise. At the groundbreaking for Pamela’s Place, she said, “Today belongs to the building, and what it is going to do for a hundred of our homeless friends who are going to take those steps out of homelessness right here.” Information on Atkinson’s survivors was not immediately available. snapshot.title: Child marriage in Gaza:
snapshot.evidenceText: Sign in. It’s quick, free and it’s up to you. An account is an optional way to support the work we do. Find out more. SHE WAS 15 when she became a wife. Four months later, she was pregnant. The teenager married her 23-year-old cousin after both families were displaced to Rafah, at a time when hunger was tightening its grip on Gaza. Her family had lost their home and had little income. Her father was not working, and they were surviving largely on aid. Then her brother, who had helped support the family, was killed while going to collect aid. Soon afterwards, the family married off two of his sisters. One was 19. The other was 15. There was no wedding hall for the younger bride, no new bedroom furniture and no home for the couple to move into. The family held a small celebration in their displacement tent. Her dowry was around 2,000 Jordanian dinars — far below what relatives say would have been expected before the war. Stock image, Gaza. Alamy Stock Photo Alamy Stock Photo Dina (29) lives in the same household. She watched what came next at close range. During the first months of marriage, she remembers the teenager frequently complaining of abdominal pain and exhaustion. Then she became pregnant, amid severe food shortages and limited access to vitamins and medical care. The pregnancy was difficult, and so was the birth. Dina said the teenager spent four days in hospital and struggled during labour before her daughter was delivered with the help of suction. Today, mother and baby are doing well, but the young family survives on very little. Her husband sells cigarettes for an income. Some relatives had opposed the marriage from the beginning. Dina remembers her mother telling the groom: “It is wrong. She is still young.” His response, she said, was: “We will raise her with us.” A Palestinian family displaced from Gaza City spreads out on the road due to the lack of a tent or any other. Alamy Stock Photo Alamy Stock Photo For Dina, that sentence captures a contradiction she now sees around her: girls young enough to still need raising are becoming mothers themselves. “There is hardly a young girl left in the family who has not married,” she said. Before the war, Dina said, families around her wanted their daughters to finish school and often university before marrying. But displacement, hunger, lost incomes and the collapse of education have changed those calculations. The teenager’s story reflects a broader shift that aid workers say is unfolding across Gaza, as war dismantles many of the safeguards that once helped delay marriage — from education and household income to functioning health and protection systems. The pressure has intensified as hunger has deepened. UNFPA recorded a 123% increase in reported forced and child marriages between January and June 2026, amid severe hunger, poverty, lost incomes and prolonged disruption to education. Research among 230 displaced women in Gaza City and Khan Younis offers a glimpse into what those pressures can mean inside families. Women described severe shortages of food, shelter and other necessities creating new forms of exploitation, while UNFPA identified resource scarcity as one of five major factors increasing risks for women and girls. The agency warned that families facing acute food insecurity may resort to child marriage as a way of coping with survival. The loss of parents and breadwinners can narrow girls’ choices further. One woman in Gaza City told researchers she had attended the weddings of two girls in her extended family, aged 14 and 15, after both their parents were killed. Their uncles, who had become responsible for them, married them off because they wanted to be relieved of the responsibility and expense, she said. “They don’t understand what marriage or life is,” the woman said. “If their parents were alive, they might not have married them off so young.” Emergency court records provide one indication: at least 400 girls aged 14 to 16 were granted permission to marry in just four months of 2025, according to records reviewed by UNFPA partner organisations. The true scale is difficult to establish because some wartime marriages are not formally registered until services resume, a girl reaches legal age or becomes pregnant. War has not only made families poorer; Dina believes it has also made marriage cheaper. Before the war, a groom was expected to shoulder the costs of a wedding celebration, furniture and setting up a home. Displacement has stripped many of those expectations away. Couples can marry in a tent, without a hall or a furnished home, lowering the financial threshold for young men who might previously have postponed marriage. “There is no bedroom set, no house and no wedding hall, it is just a tent,” Dina said. For her, reopening Gaza’s schools and universities would therefore mean more than restoring education. It could restore an alternative to marriage. “If schools and universities return, minds will open again,” she said. “Before the war, families wanted their daughters to study. The war forced them to change.” For some families, marriage has come to represent something else: a possible way out of Gaza. Mona (54) lives with her children in a tent west of Gaza City after her husband was killed in the war. Recently, a relative who moved to Belgium years ago proposed marrying her eldest daughter, 21. Under different circumstances, Mona said, she would not have considered the match. But she saw in it a rare chance for her daughter to leave Gaza — and hoped that, eventually, it might open a path for the rest of the family to follow. She was torn between the age gap and what she saw around her: displacement, poverty and life in a tent. She wanted, she said, to preserve what remained of her daughters’ dignity. The disagreement divided the family until relatives intervened. Mona ultimately accepted that she could not force her daughter to marry. Her daughter told her she would rather try to find work — or wait for a husband closer to her own age. Related Reads ‘We are next’: Gaza families living in homes they know could collapse Opinion: Ed Sheeran says he’s apolitical. His Macklemore decision tells a different story Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour after backlash over pro-Palestine chant For Mona, it was a marriage she would once have rejected. War had made it look like an opportunity. For families displaced into tents, early marriage is not driven by poverty alone, said Walaa Hijazi, a psychologist with Dar Al-Rahma , which supports orphaned children and those who have lost family care in Gaza. With privacy and family protection eroded by displacement, some parents increasingly see a husband as a form of protection — particularly for girls who have lost a father or both parents. “She needs someone to be responsible for her, and suddenly, she is expected to become responsible for a family,” Hijazi said. That pressure is unfolding as Gaza’s wider protection system has been severely disrupted. Unicef says destruction of civilian infrastructure and movement restrictions continue to limit access to protection services, while routine monitoring systems have also been disrupted. UNFPA says organisations are still providing case management, shelters and safe spaces, but under immense operational constraints. War has also made marriage cheaper, Hijazi said. Weddings are simpler, expectations have fallen and couples may marry without the home, furniture and celebrations once expected — even when young husbands themselves have little means to support a family. Hijazi fears the consequences will outlast the war. Girls are entering marriage with little preparation for their rights, pregnancy or parenthood after years of disrupted education, hunger and psychological strain. “The caregivers themselves need care,” she said. The legality of a marriage should not be confused with whether a girl is still a child, said Hanadi Salah, a human rights lawyer and legal officer at Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children in Gaza, who has worked on women’s and children’s rights. Palestinian child law generally defines anyone under 18 as a child, Salah said, in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Internationally, a marriage involving anyone under 18 is considered child marriage. “A marriage contract does not erase the fact of her age or the protection she is entitled to as a child,” Salah said. For Salah, that distinction is even more important in wartime. A girl who is 16 today was around 13 when the war began, meaning some of the most formative years of her adolescence have been spent amid displacement, disrupted education, insecurity and the breakdown of ordinary protection systems. “The difference is significant between reaching the age of 16 and having the maturity, independence and capacity that society may assume when it pushes a girl at that age into marriage, and then pregnancy and motherhood,” she said. Physical maturity, Salah added, is not the same as psychological readiness or free consent — particularly when poverty, displacement and the loss of a breadwinner leave girls with fewer meaningful alternatives. “She may move within months from being a child who needs protection to a wife and mother responsible for another child,” she said. Gaza’s devastated education system has meanwhile left around 700,000 school-aged children without normal schooling, removing what Dina sees as one of the strongest alternatives to early marriage. Before the war, she said, families around her wanted their daughters to finish school and often university before considering marriage. Reopening classrooms, for her, would therefore mean more than restoring education. It could restore another future for girls. “If schools and universities return, minds will open again,” Dina said. “Before the war, families wanted their daughters to study. snapshot.title: In backroom ‘sewing’ classes, Afghan women stitch together an education in secret
snapshot.evidenceText: Our name is about honesty. The Monitor is owned by The First Church of Christ, Scientist, and we’ve always been transparent about that. The church publishes the Monitor because it sees good journalism as vital to progress in the world. Since 1908, we’ve aimed “to injure no man, but to bless all mankind,” as our founder, Mary Baker Eddy, put it. Here, you’ll find award-winning journalism not driven by commercial influences – a news organization that takes seriously its mission to uplift the world by seeking solutions and finding reasons for credible hope. Get unlimited access to global news that cuts through the noise and brings perspectives you won’t get anywhere else. It has been five years since the Taliban outlawed women’s education beyond sixth grade, forcing English and math lessons underground. Across Afghanistan, in basements and storefronts promising sewing classes, a hidden rebellion is taking place. Five years after the Taliban swept back into power, the ban on girls’ education past sixth grade remains perhaps the movement’s most visible act of repression. Afghanistan is the only country in the world where girls are legally prohibited from continuing their education beyond primary school. Yet in secret, women are educating themselves, their schoolbooks hidden inside sewing bags as they listen closely for an unexpected knock at the door. The backroom courses in English, math, or nursing are no substitute for those shut down by the government. Women remember with heartache the day those closures took effect, but they have not yielded. In Afghanistan, courageous teachers and students are finding ways to educate girls right under the Taliban’s nose. These underground networks reflect Afghans’ hopes for a better future. Some 40% of Afghan women “still imagine a future where change and equality are possible,” according to a 2025 survey by UN Women . The underground education networks across the country are a testament to that hope. At 23 years old, Arghawan says she should be finishing medical school right now. (As with all women interviewed for this article, her name has been changed and her location withheld to protect her from retaliation.) Instead, she’s taking clandestine classes in the basement of a vocational center. It’s a dark, sparse, and bitterly cold space once winter sets in, lit by weak solar lamps whenever the power cuts out. If someone spots the morality police approaching, English lessons are wiped from the whiteboard in seconds, and notebooks are replaced with needlework. But when she’s there, the memory of the life she once had – and she hopes to have once again – flickers into view. “I feel as though I am back in my school classroom,” she says. “I feel as though I am alive again.” Polls are clear. Afghans overwhelmingly want to educate their girls and young women. The UN Women report found that 92% of respondents in a national door-to-door survey said it was “‘important’ for girls to continue their schooling.” Support was no lower than 87% among both men and women, in both rural and urban areas. The Taliban banned women from secondary education in 2021 and college education in 2022. Those moments remain seared into the collective consciousness of women nationwide. Arghawan was 17 then, in the 11th grade, with plans to become a doctor or a prosecutor. She remembers the morning being sunny and the market a little quieter than normal. She had no idea the walk to school that day would be her last. Taliban vehicles were already blocking the gate when she arrived. When she asked why, a man who called himself a qari – a Quran reciter – told her and her classmates they were “stupid and irrational,” and asked whether girls like them were supposed to be the ones who built the nation. Once through the door, she says, she found her classmates and gripped their hands tightly. It felt as if letting go might mean losing each other forever. “Unfortunately, our school has been closed,” a teacher said, turning to the blackboard so the girls wouldn’t see her wipe her face. “It was truly like a funeral,” says Arghawan. The Taliban ordered everyone out. Students who resisted were beaten back with sticks. At another school nearby, girls were lined up in the schoolyard and told that anyone above sixth grade could no longer come to class. Some teachers tried to record the moment on their cellphones, but within the hour, the Ministry of Education called the principal and warned that anyone caught filming would be detained. The teachers deleted their videos in front of their students and the Taliban fighters standing at the gate. “We kissed the girls on their faces and sent them home,” says Fazilah, a former math teacher and administrator at the school, “all of them in tears.” Five years later, however, Fazilah is still teaching as best she can. Eleven girls, all former students, now come to her basement to learn English, math, chemistry, and physics. If anyone asks, they are there to learn sewing. Fazilah charges next to nothing, just enough to cover supplies. “I love teaching,” she says. “I believe teaching girls is my right.” She knows the risks. An earlier class she ran – better equipped and teaching English and computer skills more openly – lasted four months before the Taliban found it. She was interrogated and warned that a second offense meant prison. She also knows the threat is real. A colleague was once arrested and released only after community elders intervened, forced to sign a pledge never to teach again. Rana had a year of engineering left when the Taliban closed her college. By the end, there were signs of what was coming. One professor routinely exhorted the class to give up and get married, saying none of them would ever be permitted to work in their chosen field anyway. Today, she teaches at a vocational center where the front door advertises sewing. In the back rooms, Rana teaches mathematics for free, alongside women running secret lessons in English and computer skills under cover of sewing and beadwork. The center has already been raided once, on a tip, Rana says. Staff hid the books and the handful of computers, leaving only sewing patterns chalked on the board. She suspects some of the center’s staff might be informants. She also knows girls whose relatives work for the government, quietly attending the secret classes without disclosing it, and has learned not to say an ill word about the Taliban. But not all encounters with Taliban officials have been catastrophic. Arghawan recalls the time officers walked straight into her classroom without warning. “It was one of the most frightening moments of my life,” she says. “I thought they were going to take us to prison.” They said that they had only come “to advise these women,” she recounts, then delivered a lecture on hijab, prayer, never leaving home without a male guardian, obeying husbands and in-laws, and marrying because it was “God’s command.” Then, they thanked the women in the room for their time and left. Arghawan had tried to stay at home in the years after her high school was closed, but she says she felt “like a prisoner,” unable to move freely even to go to the market. Research by UN Women suggests that fewer than half of Afghan women (41%) leave their homes at least once a day, compared with 88% of men. Some 14% of women leave their homes only once a week. Arghawan waited a year for the closure to lift. It didn’t. An online English class filled seven months until it, too, fell apart. Arghawan says she slid into a depression severe enough that she eventually saw a mental health professional, who told her to hold onto small routines: study, family time, a walk outside when she could manage it. Today, when she leaves for her classes, Arghawan tells her family she’s going to study the Quran. She must wear a black hijab, gloves, and a niqab, leaving only her eyes showing. On one scorching afternoon, she began to collapse from heat exhaustion and was rushed to a hospital. Rana, the former engineering student, carries nothing but a pen and a scrap of paper to her lessons. She has heard what happens to women caught by the morality police on similar pretexts: arrests, days in custody, mistreatment, and in some cases, assault. “I keep my eyes on the road, so that no one pays attention to me.” she says. “But inside, I am afraid.” Afghanistan has been here before. When the Taliban first took Kabul in the mid-1990s, they enacted a similar ban on women’s education, which has since been blamed for many of the country’s problems, including its high maternal mortality rates. Back then, Fazilah’s family fled to neighboring Pakistan, returning only after the Taliban were ousted in 2001. Now she’s thinking ahead to a future where Afghanistan realizes, once again, that it needs female doctors, judges, and engineers. And as a former administrator, she has a clear sense of what young women need to prepare for these roles. They need money for informal schooling, sent through channels that won’t let it be skimmed off along the way. They also need curriculums for compressed, internationally recognized degrees, to make up the time they have lost. And they need scholarships abroad, on the condition that they return home once they’re qualified. Deepen your worldview with Monitor Highlights. representative.title: A Laboratory Made of Bottles - shikshalokam.org

snapshot.title: A Laboratory Made of Bottles - shikshalokam.org
snapshot.evidenceText: A plastic bottle, a balloon, a pinch of turmeric, half a lemon. In most schools, these would be rubbish or kitchen scraps. In Shobha Singh’s classroom in Jamui, they are laboratory equipment. The school had no laboratory, and before Shobha arrived, it had never had a science teacher. The bottles were the answer to a simple refusal: the missing laboratory would not be allowed to mean missing science. Shobha grew up in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, in a home shaped by a father in the Police Department and by discipline, responsibility and service. The love of science came from a science teacher at school, who taught not just the subject but how to observe, and how to ask why things happen. That teacher is the reason Shobha chose science, and then chose to teach it. On 3 June 2013, Shobha joined the government middle school at Malaypur, in the Barhat block of Jamui district, Bihar. It is an area long affected by Naxal violence, and few people there expected much from school. Not many children were interested in studying. The school had very little to teach science with. There was no laboratory and no science teacher had ever worked there. For most children, science was something to read and memorise from a textbook, a list of answers with no questions behind them. They had almost no chance to watch something happen, to try something out, to ask why and find out for themselves. Shobha could have waited for equipment to arrive. Instead, the work started with what was already lying around. Used bottles, balloons, tetra packs, paper, straws, lemons, turmeric, vinegar, salt, sugar and matchsticks became the tools of the science class. Over the years, Shobha built more than forty hands-on activities out of materials like these, all without a conventional laboratory. With them, children explored light and reflection, air and water pressure, how heat travels, electricity, photosynthesis, osmosis and chromatography. They tested food for adulteration and watched seeds germinate. They took a science class to the river to study its ecosystem. In one photograph from Shobha’s classroom, a red laser beam zigzags between mirrors across a darkened room. The point was never to hand children the answer. In Shobha’s class, they were asked to look first, then guess what would happen, then test it, argue about it, and reach their own conclusion. When there was no microscope, Foldscopes, folding paper microscopes that cost very little, let children look at the microscopic world for the first time. When the children first saw the stomata on a leaf, one of them said, “Wow! Leaves also have mouths like us!” Another, looking at a single drop of pond water crowded with living things, asked, “Aree, koi jeev itna chhota bhi ho sakta hai?” Can anything alive really be that small? Shobha also designed a Low-Cost Science Kit so that several concepts could be taught with simple materials, in any classroom. Shobha wanted learning to leave the classroom, too. So the school started a Learning Farm, and it became a living laboratory. Children grew crops side by side with organic and chemical methods, made compost and vermicompost, and watched what each choice did to the soil, the plants and the environment around them. They observed, compared, looked things up and argued over what they saw. More than 250 students have learned this way. Slowly, the habit of asking questions turned into a habit of solving problems. That habit shows up in what the children now build. Priyanshu Kumar, a Class 8 student, knew someone who died when a bike crashed into a roadside tree at night. Priyanshu’s answer was a Green Tree Safety Reflector: reflective strips fixed to tree trunks so that headlights pick them up from a distance. Another student, Sanskar, was tired of watching the family unclog the sink at home, and designed a removable mesh drain guard to stop it from happening. Every year, students from the school are selected for the INSPIRE Award MANAK, a national programme for school students’ innovations, and for the Medha Scholarship. One of them, Ayush Kumar Singh, reached the national level of INSPIRE MANAK with a Bike Towing Tool of Ayush’s own invention. Her students from the school have also represented Bihar at the Eastern India Science Fair. More than 80% of students consistently pass in the first division. Parents noticed. Their children were more curious, more confident, and more willing to ask questions and try new things. More than 50 children have moved from private schools to this government school. The laboratory at Malaypur is still not a room. It is a shelf of bottles and balloons, a farm behind the school, a river bank, but a class full of children who have learned to ask why before they are told. After thirteen years in the classroom, Shobha teaches science and mathematics and works as a master trainer for other teachers at the district and state levels. In 2025, Bihar’s SCERT selected Shobha to represent Jamui district at a state science seminar in Patna. A dreamer at heart, Sonal finds solace in the fictional realms of a book, often preferring them over the real world. A designer and illustrator by instinct, she is driven by the desire to make the world more aesthetic, vibrant, and meaningful than she found it. Currently, managing communications at ShikshaLokam, she is on a journey to become a storyteller- one who bridges emotion, purpose, and design to inspire change. With over 12 years of experience in teaching, she brings the depth of an education enthusiast who believes deeply in the transformative power of knowledge, the right opportunities, and the quiet magic of hard work. representative.title: Gujarat Solar Village: India's First Solar-Powered Village Embraces Electric Mobility for a Sustainable Future, ETEnergyworld

snapshot.title: Gujarat
snapshot.evidenceText: Gujarat’s Modhera expands solar-powered living to green mobilityModhera, known as India's first 24x7 solar-powered village, is extending its clean-energy initiative towards green mobility, with residents adopting electric vehicles and solar-powered charging infrastructure supporting the transition.Under Solar Village Modhera 2.0, the village is integrating renewable energy with everyday transportation. The broader project includes a 6 MW solar power plant and a 15 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), supporting the use of clean energy beyond household electricity consumption.An electric vehicle charging station has also been established near the Sun Temple, allowing residents to charge their vehicles using solar-generated electricity."An electric vehicle charging station has also been set up near the Solar Temple, with its power supply coming from the solar ground-mounted power plant. People can use it to charge their vehicles, helping them save on petrol and diesel and reduce carbon emissions. This charging station provides an additional benefit to the community," said Dilip Kumar, Deputy Engineer at Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited (GUVNL).The shift towards electric mobility is also gaining relevance for residents who depend on two-wheelers for daily commuting and small business activities. With electric bikes and scooters becoming part of local travel, residents see an opportunity to reduce their dependence on conventional fuels."This will help us save a significant amount of petrol and diesel. With solarisation, we are able to travel several kilometres and carry out various small businesses and daily activities at a lower cost," said Bharatbhai Suthar, a resident of Modhera village.Solar energy is also contributing to household electricity needs, with residents using it to operate appliances ranging from televisions and refrigerators to air conditioners and washing machines."With the solar system, we are able to run many household appliances such as the refrigerator, TV, AC, household flour mill and washing machine. We benefit greatly from using solar energy for these appliances," said Khushi Bharatbhai Patel, another resident of the village.Modhera's clean-energy initiative builds on its solar-powered infrastructure by linking electricity generation, battery storage and electric vehicle charging. The approach highlights how renewable energy can support both household needs and local transportation, while helping residents reduce fuel expenses and carbon emissions.As the village expands its use of solar energy, the integration of green mobility offers a model for exploring sustainable transportation in rural areas.

representative.title: Guano mining left Lady Elliot Island a barren wasteland. Now it's a tropical oasis - ABC News
representative.author: Grace Whiteside, Johanna Marie, Rachel Kelly

snapshot.title: Family turns bare island into reef oasis after guano mining destroys it
snapshot.evidenceText: For thousands of years the tiny island at the southernmost tip of the Great Barrier Reef was alive with cacophonous birdsong. But within a decade of guano miners arriving in force with their picks and shovels in the 1860s, Lady Elliot Island was silent, denuded of all foliage and bereft of the seabirds that once lived there. It remained a barren wasteland for more than 100 years before one family decided to revive it and started planting trees. The cotton-wool clouds separate to reveal the first glimpse of Lady Elliot Island. A ring of waves crashes on the outer edge of the reef, and the island's airstrip is a prominent ribbon of jade encased in forest green. From the sky, the coral cay 80 kilometres off the coast of Bundaberg is a picture of pristine natural beauty. Humans now have a permanent presence here, but for millennia, this island belonged solely to seabirds. That's what made it such a prize to guano miners in the mid-19th century. "The thing that seabirds do really well is poo," says Christine Dudgeon, who manages the island's research and rehabilitation program, Leaf to Reef. Guano, the accumulated waste from birds or bats, is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium. This nutrient powerhouse fuelled the new world of modern, input-intensive farming that emerged in the early 1800s. After German explorer Alexander von Humboldt took samples of guano back to Europe, farmers' demands for the fertiliser soared. Commercial guano mining started in Peru in 1840, but the profitable global trade quickly expanded to hundreds of Pacific and Caribbean islands that were uninhabited by humans. Seabird colonies along Australia's east and west coasts were displaced as miners moved in, destroying entire island ecosystems to meet agriculture's insatiable demand for fertiliser. With hundreds of thousands of seabirds nesting, feeding and pooing on the 45-hectare Lady Elliot Island, settlers quickly identified the coral cay as a guano goldmine. However, initial attempts to remove guano from Lady Elliot Island in the early 1850s were thwarted when two ships, the Bolton Abbey and The Countess of Minto, came to grief. One was wrecked on the reef encircling the island and the other was driven out to sea. Ten years later, in 1863, the Queensland government granted Jack Askunas the first official mining lease for the island for £300 a year. He cleared trees, shrubs and grasses to reach the guano, destroying habitat that had supported birdlife for thousands of years. An estimated 20,000 tonnes of guano, with a raw market value equating to about $30 million today, was removed from the island over the next decade. In his wake, Askunas left a demolition site, uninhabitable even by the seabirds that used to nest there. "This became like a moonscape, absolutely barren," Dr Dudgeon says. "Then after that, they [the miners] put some goats onto it just in case there were shipwrecks, so that there was some food [for survivors]." Any plants that sprouted were eaten by the goats. Then came the lighthouse keepers, who arrived with very pretty but very invasive plants, which the island's environmental staff are still trying to eradicate. It took the bird's eye view of an entrepreneurial aviator to change the island's fortunes. Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Aviator Don Adams saw the potential for tourism opportunities when he flew over Lady Elliot Island in the 1960s and was immediately attracted to its coral reef. But with almost no vegetation, he knew substantial rehabilitation of the island would be essential. All that remained were eight Pisonia trees that the miners had left behind. Those trees still stand today, making them at least 160 years old. Mr Adams and his wife Moya reached an arrangement with the Commonwealth Department of Transport to build an airstrip on the island in return for a lease on a portion of land for recreational purposes. Their son, Peter Adams, remembers many weekends and holidays sharing the island with daytrippers, who his father would take snorkelling and scuba diving on the reef. At that time, it was far from a luxurious resort. "The accommodation was pretty basic. We had an A-frame house, we had kerosene fridges and gas lights. We only had tank water," Mr Adams recalls now. "Before the airstrip, the lighthouse keepers used to refer to it as the Alcatraz of the Barrier Reef because … you got sent there and that was it. "But [with] the aeroplanes, you could be in Bundaberg within half an hour." Mr Adams spent the last half of his childhood, from ages nine to 18, on the island and recalls flying model aeroplanes, go-karting and riding motorbikes around its two-kilometre circumference. He distinctly remembers that the vegetation was so sparse at the time that you could see from one side of the island to the other. Wanting to rehabilitate the coral cay correctly, Don and Moya started by surveying native species growing on similar islands in the Great Barrier Reef. Coconuts collected from Dunk Island were used to grow coconut palms on Lady Elliot that are still standing. But the real engine room of the revegetation project was a nursery created in the backyard of the Adams family home in Hervey Bay, where Moya propagated casuarina, pandanus and umbrella trees. The family flew hundreds of saplings to the island. Then the hardest part started; planting and watering by hand. "I distinctly remember digging holes in the coral with a crowbar," Mr Adams says. "I remember … walking around with a bucket of water trying to keep these things alive for a long time." He says "it was a start" to the rehabilitation program that won Don and Moya a conservation award from the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland in 1974. "I remember somebody saying, 'Why did you cut down the trees to make the airstrip?' And, well, the airstrip was there before the trees grew," Mr Adams says. "It was a bit of a sanctuary for Dad out there," he says. "Out of all the things Dad did in his life, I remember him once saying his small involvement with Lady Elliot was the thing he was most proud of." Now known as the Home of the Manta Ray, Lady Elliot Island's menagerie of marine creatures and its spectacular coral reefs are marketed as its main tourism drawcards. But it is the ubiquitous birdlife, which has triumphantly reclaimed this island in recent decades, that provides the holiday soundtrack for visitors to its eco-resort. The view of the Sun setting over the horizon is crisscrossed by thousands of dark streaks as white-capped black noddies return to nest after a day of fishing, swooping between guests on their way to dinner. They are among a diverse range of seabirds now nesting and roosting on the coral cay once again. By day, wedge-tailed shearwaters, or mutton birds, along with brown boobies and crested terns soar over the breaking waves, looking for their next meal. On land, red-tailed tropicbirds can be found hunkering under shrubbery as they keep their newly hatched chicks warm. It is perhaps not so surprising then to find that earplugs are supplied in the resort's rooms to help guests block out the birds' night-time calls. It's a professional hazard that brings much joy to University of the Sunshine Coast seabird researcher Zerra Egerton. "We are in their territory. I always think of us as guests here," she says. "So when I hear the babies crying all night long, I am just stoked. They can wake me up as much as they like. "It's true that maybe not a lot of people necessarily come here to experience the bird life. But once they're here, and especially in summer, you cannot avoid the birds. "They will be seen. They will be heard. They will be felt, occasionally." The birds have an intricate and symbiotic relationship with the island's vegetation. The trees and foliage once again provide protection and nesting materials, while the birds bring nutrients from the sea to the land, which supports vegetation growth. "There was no-one here [in the 1800s] except the birds," Ms Egerton said. "To [the miners], it just looked like a resource that they could take without any moral implications … it was just an opportunity. The care and preservation baton has been passed on to the Gash family. Husband and wife duo Peter and Julie first visited the island in the 1980s and became involved in its tourism activities in 1997 when their company, Seair Pacific, began flights to and from the island. Once their daughters Amy and Chloe arrived, the family's attachment to Lady Elliot's unique beauty deepened, and the Gashes became the island's custodians (leaseholders) in 2005. Determined to continue the rehabilitation work started by the Adams family, and maintained by the intervening leaseholders, the Gashes investigated ways to create an even more eco-friendly resort. Two decades on, 33-year-old Amy Gash is now the resort's executive general manager, and often scoots around the island on a battery-powered buggy. "We believe it's our responsibility to keep this place as pristine and as beautiful as it is for today, and also [for] the future," she says. "We really wanted to … minimise our footprint and basically transition from that traditional reliance on fossil fuels." In 2008, the family built a "first-of-its-kind hybrid solar power station", and has now installed more than 1,000 solar panels and 250 batteries on the island. "We can almost confidently run 100 per cent of the time on solar power," Ms Gash says. Over the past two decades, more than 20,000 trees have been planted on the island. "We carry on that program that was started in the 70s by Don Adams," Ms Gash says. "We're really proud to have partnered with the Great Barrier Reef Foundation in about 2017, which really helped us accelerate the planting of trees here at Lady Elliot. Liam Turner, the ecosystem manager of the revegetation program, said that in the 10 years since the island's nursery was established, staff had propagated 22 species of native trees, shrubs and grasses. "The nursery is the beating heart of the whole program," he says, adding that revegetation has been completed across about 70 per cent of the island. However, taking care of the environment is a never-ending job, as 120 species of introduced weeds compete with native grasses and ground covers. "You can't just remove weeds and expect everything to return to some sort of semblance of what it was prior to guano mining," Mr Turner says. "In place of those weeds, we've got to put in all the native [plants] … And on top of that, we've got to continue doing maintenance in those areas to keep the weeds away and allow that native vegetation to establish. "They do suppress and naturally compete with the weeds once they start getting established, but you've got to get them to that point." This is where the eco-resort plays a role, with all food scraps providing an essential ingredient for the nursery's potting mix. "It gets mixed in with cardboard and woodchips, goes through a big auger and then that gets turned into a pretty nasty putrefied substance [that comes] out … after about two weeks," Mr Turner explains. The substance is then mixed with green waste and isolated for two years. "We get this beautiful black soil at the other side of it, which we use for all our potting mixes that we have in the nursery," he says. "It's good that we can produce it here so we're not importing soil to the island and … [potentially] introducing all sorts of pests and diseases. "My big dream is that eventually we'll get to a point where none of that's necessary and the ecosystem's kind of self-sustaining and can sort itself out, which we are seeing signs of, which is fantastic." The thriving seabird population on Lady Elliot Island is testament to the success of Don Adams's vision to rehabilitate the barren wasteland left by guano miners in the mid-1800s. Dr Dudgeon says the birdlife has made "an extraordinary recovery". The primary species responsible for the nutrient flow is the black noddy, about 100,000 of which nest on the island each year, up from just a few thousand in the 1960s. Another of the island's notable species is the red-tailed tropicbird, which is only found in two locations in Queensland. "Tropicbirds started nesting here in the 1980s and it certainly seems that their nests are increasing over time, which is parallel with increasing vegetation that's available for them," Dr Dudgeon says. She says seeing the changes to the island's ecosystem is encouraging. "A lot of us work in places where you're seeing the more negative impacts all the time," she says. Like Dr Dudgeon, Ms Egerton is astounded by the transformation from desolate island to subtropical paradise. "It was quite bleak, just a bare white rock and quite a gruelling place to exist on for months on end," she says. "It's incredible what's been achieved in such a short period of time in terms of the seabirds returning and the vegetation." While the birdlife can be noisy, sleep-disruptive and a tad smelly, Ms Egerton wouldn't have it any other way. "It's very, very special to have seabirds that breed [here] because that means that this island is literally sustaining their populations," she says. representative.title: A Body Encased in Salt: Forensic Scientists Report First Modern Case of
representative.author: Ophelia Keating

snapshot.title: A Body Encased in Salt: Forensic Scientists Report First Modern Case of
snapshot.evidenceText: When forensic pathologists in southern France were called to examine a male body discovered encrusted in a thick, crystalline crust of salt, they knew they were looking at something extraordinary. The body was not wrapped, treated, or deliberately preserved. Instead, the environment itself had done the work of an embalmer, coating the remains in a layer of halite roughly four centimeters thick and transforming the tissue into a dry, leathery shell. According to a case report published in the International Journal of Legal Medicine by Clémence Delteil of Marseille University Hospital and her colleagues, this is the first modern forensic case of natural salt mummification ever described, and it offers a rare glimpse into how extreme chemistry can rewrite the rules of human decomposition. Mummification is usually associated with deliberate ritual practice, from the embalmers of ancient Egypt to the salt-packing techniques documented in historical funerary customs. But nature occasionally produces the same result on its own. Salt works as a preservative through two complementary mechanisms. First, it is strongly hygroscopic, drawing water out of tissue by osmosis and creating a desiccated state in which the chemical reactions of decay slow dramatically. Second, high salinity is antimicrobial: most of the bacteria that drive putrefaction cannot tolerate concentrated brine, so the microbial ecosystem that normally dismantles a corpse simply collapses. Deprived of both moisture and microbes, soft tissue can survive for months, years, or even millennia. The archaeological record is full of proof. The most famous examples are the salt men of Chehrābād in northwestern Iran, miners who perished in collapses at the Douzlākh salt mine as early as the fourth century BC and were preserved so completely that ancient DNA, isotopic signatures of their diet, and even the fibers of their clothing have been recovered. Previous laboratory work, including experiments in which human tissue was deliberately mummified in salt, has confirmed how rapidly salt halts both microbial growth and DNA degradation. Yet despite this rich archaeological literature, no forensic scientist had ever documented a naturally salt-mummified body in a contemporary medico-legal context, until now. The French case is unusual not only because it happened at all, but because of where it happened. Unlike the Iranian salt men, who were entombed in a dry, cool salt mine, this body was found in a warm, humid, anthropogenic saline environment, a human-made salt production setting in the Mediterranean south of France. The region has a seventy-year history of managed coastal salinas, shallow basins where seawater is evaporated to harvest salt, and abandoned sites where hypersaline water pools and crystallizes under the intense Provençal sun. Local geochemical studies of nearby lagoons such as Lavalduc have documented active precipitation of halite, the mineral form of sodium chloride, in and around these basins. It was in this evaporative, salt-saturated setting that the body lay undisturbed long enough for a crystalline shell to grow around it. External examination revealed a completely desiccated body, brown and leathery in appearance, with the facial features and the morphology of the limbs and extremities remarkably preserved. That degree of anatomical integrity is forensically valuable: it allowed the team to attempt a biological profile of the deceased, the standard assessment of sex, age, and body characteristics that forms the first step toward identification. In many decomposed or skeletonized bodies, such profiling is severely compromised by tissue loss. Here, the salt had effectively frozen the external anatomy in place, demonstrating that natural mummification can paradoxically make a body more identifiable, not less. Autopsy, however, told a more complicated story. Inside the leathery exterior, the researchers found extensive tissue desiccation consistent with prolonged exposure to a highly saline environment, but the preservation was strikingly uneven. Some regions showed classic mummified changes, while others displayed focal putrefactive alteration, including complete liquefaction of the brain. This hybrid pattern, in which desiccation and decay coexist in the same body, had not previously been described in the modern forensic literature. The authors attribute it to the specific dynamics of the anthropogenic saline setting: fluctuations in salinity, intermittent moisture, and ambient heat likely allowed pockets of decomposition to proceed before full desiccation took hold, producing a mosaic of preservation that contrasts with the uniform mummification seen in mine contexts. The case also illustrates the hard limits of forensic science when preservation is this unusual. Toxicological analyses of visceral samples came back negative for drugs and toxic substances, ruling out chemical causes of death detectable in the preserved tissue. DNA analysis and fingerprint examination were both performed, but neither produced an identification. The failure is instructive. Even when tissue appears well preserved, the same osmotic and chemical stresses that stop decay can fragment genetic material in ways that defeat standard amplification, and desiccated skin often cannot yield usable friction ridge prints. For the identification effort, the team had to fall back on contextual and morphological evidence rather than laboratory confirmation. Perhaps the most innovative part of the investigation was environmental. Rather than relying solely on the body itself, the researchers reconstructed the salinity dynamics, evaporation rates, and local climate conditions of the site, and used that reconstruction to support a tentative hypothesis about the post-mortem interval, the elapsed time since death. The logic is analogous to entomological dating, where insect development stages clock the interval, but here the clock is geochemical: the thickness of the salt crust, the rate at which brine evaporates under the regional climate, and the seasonal behavior of the saline basin together constrain how long the body must have lain there. The authors emphasize that this estimate is tentative, but the approach itself is a proof of concept for reading time from the environment in cases where conventional markers are absent. The report arrives amid growing attention to what forensic scientists call complex bodies, remains whose preservation state falls outside the familiar categories of fresh, decomposed, skeletonized, burned, or water-immersed. Recent systematic reviews and procedural proposals have argued that such cases demand a multidisciplinary response, combining pathology, anthropology, radiology, genetics, toxicology, entomology, botany, and environmental science, guided by standardized on-site inspection protocols such as those developed by the European Council of Legal Medicine. The salt mummy of southern France is a textbook argument for that approach: no single discipline could have interpreted the body, but the combined evidence of morphology, chemistry, and environmental reconstruction extracted real forensic information from an apparently intractable case. For the wider forensic community, the implications are twofold. First, investigators encountering desiccated remains in or near saline environments, from abandoned salinas to industrial brine facilities, should now consider natural salt mummification as a genuine possibility rather than a curiosity confined to archaeology. Second, the case expands the known range of environments capable of natural preservation into warm, humid, human-modified settings, which means the global geography of potential salt mummies is far larger than the arid mines and deserts of the archaeological record. As the authors conclude, environmental analysis and multidisciplinary investigation are essential tools for identification and post-mortem interval estimation in complex bodies, and this unique case, a man sealed in salt under the Mediterranean sun, may be only the first of its kind to surface. snapshot.title: حرف حلب التراثية تقاوم الاندثار وتستعيد بريقها بلمسات معاصرة
snapshot.evidenceText: اختتم في مدينة حلب السورية معرض المهن الحرفية والتراثية القديمة، الذي أُقيم تحت شعار "لكل حرفة تاريخ يُروى"، بمشاركة حرفيين وفنانين وأصحاب مشروعات سعوا إلى إحياء الحرف المهددة بالاندثار، وتطوير منتجاتها بما يجمع بين الأصالة والحداثة، ونقل خبراتها إلى الأجيال الجديدة. وجاء المعرض في إطار مشروع "صون"، الذي ركز على المهن التراثية الحلبية، بهدف الحفاظ على هذا الإرث الثقافي غير المادي، وتعريف الأجيال الجديدة بالحرف القديمة التي ارتبطت بتاريخ المدينة وحياة سكانها، فضلا عن مساعدة العاملين فيها على تطوير مشروعاتهم وتحويل مهاراتهم التقليدية إلى فرص عمل مستدامة. وقالت مديرة المشروع روميسة شيخ، إن العمل بدأ باستقطاب المستفيدين وفق معايير محددة، مع تخصيص النسبة الكبرى من المشاركين للنساء، مقابل 20% للرجال، بهدف مساعدة النساء اللواتي يمارسن الحرف التراثية في المنازل على الانتقال إلى ريادة الأعمال، وتوسيع نطاق أعمالهن لتصل إلى الأسواق. وأوضحت أن المشاركات خضعن لدورات تدريبية تناولت التسويق والتسعير الرقمي، وآليات ترخيص المشروعات، وبناء هوية بصرية مميزة لكل مشروع، بما يساعد صاحبات الحرف على تقديم منتجاتهن بصورة أكثر احترافية والوصول إلى شرائح أوسع من الزبائن. وأضافت شيخ أن المشروع نظم جولات في أسواق حلب القديمة للتعرف إلى تاريخ الحرف وطبيعة ممارستها، قبل إقامة المعرض الختامي على مدى 3 ليال، في موقع اُختير بمحيط قلعة حلب ، بما يتناسب مع الهوية التاريخية للمكان وطبيعة المبادرة التي تمحورت حول التراث وسبل الحفاظ عليه. وتراوحت أعمار المشاركين بين 17 و60 عاما، في دلالة على اهتمام فئات عمرية مختلفة بالحرف التقليدية، ورغبة أجيال جديدة في تعلمها وتطويرها. ومن بين المشاركين في المعرض الفنان التشكيلي والنحات على الخشب أحمد هنداوي الذي عمل على إحياء هذه الحرفة التي باتت مهددة بالاندثار، من خلال إدخالها إلى مجالي الديكور والخط العربي، وتقديم أعمال جمعت بين التقنيات التقليدية واللمسات الفنية الحديثة. وأوضح هنداوي أنه سعى إلى نقل النحت على الخشب من الاستخدامات التقليدية المرتبطة بالأثاث إلى إنتاج قطع فنية يمكن اقتناؤها بوصفها لوحات تزين المنازل، بما يمنح الحرفة أبعادا جمالية جديدة ويسهم في الحفاظ على جانب من تراث حلب الصناعي والفني. وأشار إلى أن المدينة كانت رائدة في مجال النحت على الخشب خلال الفترة الممتدة من سبعينيات القرن الماضي إلى تسعينياته، معربا عن أمله في استعادة هذه المكانة، ليس من خلال إقامة المعارض فحسب، بل عبر إنشاء أماكن متخصصة لتعليم الحرفة وتحويلها إلى مادة دراسية أو منهج تدريبي يتيح للشباب تعلمها وتطويرها وإضافة أفكار جديدة إليها. بدورها، عرضت الحرفية المتخصصة في المكرمية رغد وزان تجربتها في تطوير هذه الحرفة التراثية وتوسيع استخداماتها. وأوضحت أن المكرمية ارتبطت تاريخيا بصناعة شبكات الصيد لدى البحارة، الذين كانوا يستغلون رحلاتهم الطويلة في إنجاز قطع يدوية، فيما اشتهرت في حلب باستخدامها في صناعة حاملات النباتات. وقالت رغد إنها عملت على تطوير منتجات المكرمية لتشمل الديكورات والمستلزمات المنزلية المتنوعة، وإعادة إدخالها إلى البيوت الحلبية، لما تمنحه من إحساس بالدفء والنعومة، فضلا عن تعريف الشباب والأطفال بتاريخ الحرفة وتشجيعهم على ابتكار تصاميم جديدة مستوحاة منها. وأبدت إحدى زائرات المعرض اعتزازها باستمرار الحرف اليدوية في المدينة، بعدما اعتقد كثيرون أنها مهددة بالاختفاء، مشيدة بالدعم الذي يحظى به الحرفيون وبالدقة الفنية التي ظهرت في المنتجات المعروضة. وقالت إن النحت على الخشب كان من أبرز الأعمال التي لفتت انتباهها، لما يتسم به من دقة وتفاصيل فنية تعكس روح الحرفي الذي أنجز القطعة، معربة عن أملها أن تصل المنتجات التراثية الحلبية إلى الأسواق الخارجية، بما يعزز حضور المدينة بوصفها مركزا عريقا للحرف والأصالة. وشكل المعرض مساحة لعرض المهارات التقليدية أمام الجمهور، وفرصة لربط الحرفيين بالأسواق الحديثة، في محاولة للحفاظ على الموروث الحرفي الحلبي وضمان استمراره عبر الأجيال، مع تطويره بما يتناسب مع متطلبات الحياة المعاصرة.

representative.title: ‘Citizen Osama’ turns life under bombardment into urgent, intimate cinema – Mondoweiss
representative.author: Davide Abbatescianni

snapshot.title: ‘Citizen Osama’ turns life under bombardment into urgent, intimate cinema
snapshot.evidenceText: At barely 70 minutes, Ahmed Hassouna’s Citizen Osama feels much larger than its running time. Not because it drags, but because of how much life, death and uncertainty it compresses into a short span. Events arrive with the relentlessness of a permanent emergency. Buildings are bombed, people are pulled from rubble, colleagues are killed, food becomes harder to find, and humanitarian aid appears only to prove painfully insufficient. Between these episodes, Osama Al-Ashi goes home to his wife, his young child and his anxious parents. The result is a film in which public catastrophe and private life can no longer be separated. That perspective gives Citizen Osama a striking place beside NAZA , Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary, which has recently drawn significant international attention. Where NAZA examines Israeli military systems through testimony from Israeli personnel, Hassouna remains on the ground with those living beneath their consequences. The films approach the same historical moment from radically different positions. Premiering in Venice Open at this year’s Venice Film Festival, Citizen Osama follows Al-Ashi, once an artistic photographer and now a war documentarian living in northern Gaza. Hassouna shot the film himself; Denis Le Paven edited it, while Rasmus Steen composed its restrained score. The documentary has also been selected as Palestine’s submission for the 2027 Academy Awards. There is little distance here between journalism and filmmaking. Osama’s camera exists first because there is something that urgently needs to be documented. Yet the accumulation of those images, and Hassouna’s shaping of them, gradually transforms reporting into cinema. The distinction becomes almost irrelevant. Recording events is at once a professional duty, a means of producing evidence, an act of memory and, eventually, storytelling. Some of the film’s most difficult passages show people trapped beneath destroyed buildings and the desperate collective effort to reach them. Elsewhere, the deaths of journalists puncture any illusion that the word “PRESS” printed across a protective vest can offer real security. The killing of Al Jazeera journalist Ismail al-Ghoul, one of the colleagues mourned in the film, becomes another reminder that Osama can leave home to work and simply not return. Al-Ghoul and cameraman Ramy El Rify were killed in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City in July 2024. But Citizen Osama understands that catastrophe is experienced not only through explosions and death. Sometimes it is measured in flour. Osama searches for basic food for his family and finds flour contaminated with mold and worms: technically available, but barely fit for consumption. Diesel is another constant problem. These details are small compared with the scale of the destruction, and that is precisely why they matter. Hassouna shows what happens when the tasks that ordinarily structure everyday life — buying food, moving around, caring for a child — become precarious logistical operations. A similarly memorable sequence observes humanitarian aid falling from airplanes. Some packages appear to land in the sea, prompting people to enter the water to retrieve them; those that reach land are immediately surrounded by crowds. Hassouna does not need to stop and explain the absurdity of these images. The aid is visible, desperately needed, and, at the same time, clearly inadequate to the need around it. The film’s tight editing is crucial. Citizen Osama could easily have become a succession of horrors, each image attempting to overwhelm the previous one. Instead, Le Paven repeatedly returns the film to Osama’s family and colleagues. His parents worry about both Gaza’s future and the immediate possibility that their son might not come home. His wife and child embody another responsibility, one that exists uneasily beside his determination to continue working. In one deceptively minor scene, Osama and other journalists trade terrible jokes. They are not especially funny, which is part of what makes the moment so affecting. Humor becomes less an escape from reality than another way of continuing to exist inside it. Citizen Osama repeatedly notices these fragments of ordinary behavior without sentimentalizing them. “Resilience” is a word so often applied to Palestinians that it risks becoming an abstraction. Hassouna makes it physical. It means digging through ruins to help another person. It means finding something to eat. It means going back to work. It can also mean telling a bad joke when almost nothing around you provides a reason to laugh. This creates the film’s central tension: between agency and inevitability. Osama is constantly acting — filming, moving, providing, helping, protecting — within circumstances over which he possesses almost no control. Hope therefore does not emerge from any suggestion that conditions are about to improve. Citizen Osama offers little basis for that kind of optimism. What survives instead is the refusal to surrender every remaining form of agency. Hassouna largely avoids turning the documentary into an exercise in political exposition. There are no lengthy explanatory passages instructing viewers how to process what they are seeing. The images and Osama’s circumstances carry the argument. Its graphic moments can be extremely difficult to watch, but sanitizing them would produce a different and considerably less truthful film. The spare use of music works for the same reason: the film rarely needs to tell us when an image is devastating. In the film’s press notes, Hassouna describes Osama as more than an individual protagonist, someone through whom he could express something of his own experience and that of others who have lived through the war. He calls the film an attempt to preserve what they have lived through and to safeguard their humanity. In the same notes, he describes Venice as an opportunity to tell their story in their “own voice and through our own images.” That phrase may provide the clearest key to Citizen Osama . The camera cannot stop the destruction surrounding Osama. It cannot guarantee his safety, find food for his family, or bring his colleagues back. What it can do is preserve evidence that these lives existed in all their fear, exhaustion, affection, absurdity, and stubborn humanity. That is also why the comparison with NAZA matters. One film interrogates military systems from within Israeli society; the other records what life looks like underneath their consequences. Citizen Osama may not yet have received comparable attention, but it belongs fully to the same cinematic reckoning — not as an accompanying document, but as a work in its own right. For its rather brief duration, it turns the act of looking into an act of survival. Since we’re talking about documentaries, recently I saw Tantura , a film about events that transpired in the Palestinian village of Tantura in 1948. On the surface it’s about what happened, but on a deeper level it’s about a society that can’t come to grips with its own history. It’s also the story of Teddy Katz, a graduate student in history. When he did his maste’rs thesis on Tantura…..well, not to spoil it, you can read his story here: The Tantura Case in Israel: The Katz Research and Trial | Institute for Palestine Studies ‘Tantura’ director: Israelis have been lied to for years about alleged 1948 massacre | The Times of Israel George Washington owned slaves, and David Ben-Gurion ( from ChatGPT): David Ben-Gurion directed a group of scholars and researchers between 1960 and 1964 to compile historical materials supporting the claim that Palestinian refugees left of their own volition in 1948 rather than being expelled . [ 1 ] And since we’re talking about journalists in Gaza, recently the IDF claimed that 170 members of the press in Gaza were really Hamas military operatives: EXPOSED: HAMAS AND PIJ MILITARY OPERATIVES POSED AS JOURNALISTS Debunking Israel’s latest list of ‘terrorist’ journalists in Gaza The evidence against the 170 media workers named in ‘The Press Files’ includes empty pages, clearly edited documents, and unverifiable snippets… Mohammed is one of 59 journalists included in “The Press Files” whose pages are devoid of any evidence or documentation whatsoever. Naturally, these names are all buried at the bottom of the list. In the cases of Al Jazeera’s Ahmed Al-Louh and Sawt Al-Aqsa’s Hassan Sammour , their pages don’t even contain the claim “based on multiple intelligence sources.”…. My quote doesn’t do justice to the 972 piece, I recommend reading the article in its entirety. Davide Abbatescianni is a Rome-based film critic and journalist covering international cinema, film festivals and the European and MENA audiovisual industries. His work has appeared across several international film and culture publications, and he regularly reports from major festivals including Venice, Cannes, Berlin, Toronto and Locarno. representative.title: The loss no damage report will ever price
representative.author: Md. Ashequl Morsalin Ibne Kamal(Team Lead, Niloy Saha(Sr. Software Engineer, Jobayer Hossain(Software Engineer

snapshot.title: The loss no damage report will ever price
snapshot.evidenceText: At 71, Kurigram's Rahima Begum knows how to begin again. She has done it 17 times. Each time, the river took her home, washing away the walls, roofs and floors of the home she built. Each time, she gathered what could be salvaged and started over. Today, Rahima stitches kantha quilts to survive. Her grandson lives with her; not her own children. In that simple arrangement lies a story rarely captured by conventional accounts of climate damage: a grandmother raising a grandson because the generation between them has stepped away. Rahima's story emerged from fieldwork under EBAAN, or Evidence-Based Approach to Address Non-Economic Loss and Damage, a project of the International Centre for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD). EBAAN looks beyond houses destroyed, land submerged and crops ruined, to understand losses that cannot easily be converted into money. This is where Non-Economic Loss and Damage, or NELD, becomes important. It includes losses of home, identity, social ties, dignity and ways of life. For Rahima, those losses have accumulated over the decades. Her story begins long before the river. Rahima was married at nine, an age when a child might ordinarily be learning, playing or discovering the world. Instead, she was given into marriage without the age or agency to understand what it meant. At 20, she had her first child, and she would eventually have three. Somewhere between those ages, a girl became a wife and then a mother without the years most people associate with growing up. There is no compensation scheme for a childhood that never happened, or an easy calculation for the loss of agency that comes with child marriage. For much of her adult life, Rahima worked in other people's homes. She cooked, cleaned and did whatever work was required, but she was not paid a wage. Instead, she was fed. Her labour was exchanged for survival, leaving her without the financial security that comes from being paid for one's work. She spent years giving her labour to households that were not hers without building savings or property. It was work, but it did not create independence. Each time the river took her home, Rahima had to start again without resources of her own. It was much later that Rahima began stitching kantha quilts. Kantha is often romanticised as heritage, with old sarees transformed into blankets through the running stitch. For Rahima, however, it became a way for her labour to finally put money directly into her own hands rather than being exchanged for food. The quilts carry cultural value, but also represent a late form of economic agency. At 71, the needle in her hand is not simply a symbol of tradition. It is one of the few tools through which she can still exercise a measure of independence. Then there is the river. Seventeen times, it took her home. Climate change is often narrated through numbers: hectares of land lost, households displaced, crops destroyed and homes damaged. Those numbers matter, but they do not tell us what repeated displacement does to a person. Every destroyed home carries other losses. Someone has to gather what remains, find somewhere to go and rebuild. Much of that invisible work falls on women, who may also lose land, savings, social relationships or bargaining power within a household. Rahima rebuilt 16 times. Then came the 17th loss, and she says she does not have another rebuilding left in her. The sentence is striking because of how easily the language of climate adaptation celebrates resilience. People affected by displacement are expected to endure, recover and begin again. But resilience becomes an uncomfortable word when it is repeatedly demanded from people who have already endured more than they should have had to. At some point, resilience stops being a compliment and starts becoming an expectation. Old age has brought no clean end to that struggle. Rahima's children do not care for her, and her grandson lives with her. A lifetime of work has not given her security in old age. What remains is a grandson, a needle and whatever a finished quilt can bring. This too is a form of loss, not simply the absence of money, but the loss of security after decades of work and displacement. This is what a NELD lens makes visible. It asks not only how much land was lost, how much a house cost or how many families were displaced, but what happened to the person who lived there. What did repeated displacement take from Rahima? What did early marriage take? What did decades of unpaid labour take? These questions resist measurement. A house can be valued and rebuilt. Land can be assessed. But there is no straightforward formula for the cost of losing a childhood, a home 17 times, a sense of belonging or the dignity of growing old with security. Rahima cannot recover the years she lost, nor can she rebuild the homes the river took from her. What remains is more basic: the possibility of living out the rest of her life with dignity. That may sound small beside 17 lost homes, but it is not. It is precisely the kind of loss conventional damage reports struggle to see, and the kind climate accounting will underestimate until it counts what remains inside the lives of survivors. For Rahima, the river has already taken enough. Jarin Tasnim Mim is an independent researcher with ICCCAD's Evidence-Based Approach to Address Non-Economic Loss and Damage project.
