representative.title: How Effia-Kwesimintsim Health Directorate uses indigenous languages to counter misinformation on health | 3News
representative.author: Portia Cudjoe

snapshot.title: How Effia-Kwesimintsim Health Directorate uses indigenous languages to counter misinformation on health
snapshot.evidenceText: Health authorities are now relying on indigenous languages after using English as their primary means of communication failed to achieve the desired results. One challenge the Effia-Kwesimintsim Municipal Health Directorate identified in promoting the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine was not the virus itself, but rumours spreading on social media and in neighbourhood conversations. Though seemingly simple, the health directorate found an effective response after a series of failed attempts to counter the misinformation surrounding the vaccine. Health authorities are now relying on indigenous languages after using English as their primary means of communication failed to achieve the desired results. This approach has increased HPV vaccine uptake, but the proportion of people who have received it remains well below the number health authorities want to reach. Although this approach has not yet brought vaccination coverage up to the health directorate's target, officials consider the increase in uptake a positive development. When rumours about the HPV vaccine began circulating in Effia-Kwesimintsim in the Western Region — including claims that the injection could cause infertility, miscarriages, or leave children unable to walk — health workers found that simply correcting the claims from behind a facility desk was not working. Human papillomavirus is a common infection spread mainly through sexual contact. In most people, the body clears it. Persistent infection with certain high-risk types can change cervical cells and, over years, lead to cervical cancer. HPV is also linked to some other anogenital, oral, and throat cancers. Because progression takes years, cancers diagnosed today reflect infections acquired long ago, so prevention must start before exposure. Ghana is estimated to see about 3,000 new cervical cancer cases and 1,800 deaths each year. Older figures still in circulation — such as 2,797 cases and 1,699 deaths — come from a 2021 ICO/IARC fact sheet. These are modelled estimates, not counts of recorded cases. HPV genotype surveillance data is limited and old. A study of 256 cervical cancers diagnosed at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, covering January 2004 to December 2006, found HPV DNA in 230 (89.8%). HPV 18 (47.4%), HPV 59 (42.2%), HPV 45 (37.4%), and HPV 16 (9.0%) were the most common types, and 52.2% of positive samples carried more than one type. The percentages overlap and are not additive. The study covered one hospital and was conducted over a specific period. The most recent data come from samples submitted for testing between July 2022 and March 2025. HPV positivity in the Ghana screening group was 34.9%, and 39.2% of positive cases carried multiple genotypes. HPV-39 was the leading genotype in that group, especially among women under 30, followed by HPV-53 and HPV-68. In clinician-collected samples, HPV-16 was the most common. Screening is the second line of defence, though it remains underexplored. Ghana's 2023 STEPS survey found that only 3.6% of women had ever been screened for cervical cancer. Vaccination reduces infection risk but does not replace screening. Ghana's first nationwide HPV campaign began on Oct. 8, 2025, aiming to reach 2.4 million girls aged 9 to 14 years, in and out of school. WHO reports 1,825,425 girls vaccinated, or 82% of those eligible. The vaccine is now part of routine immunisation, and the schedule has moved to a single-dose regimen. Nationally, then, the campaign reached most eligible girls, but in Effia-Kwesimintsim it reached far fewer. Mamuna Garriba, a senior community health nurse at the directorate, said parents raised a consistent set of concerns during the HPV vaccination exercise. Some compared the HPV vaccine to the COVID-19 vaccine and cited side effects associated with COVID-19 vaccination. Others asked why children aged 9 to 14, who were not sexually active, needed a vaccine against cervical cancer. Many wanted to know whether the vaccine would affect their children's fertility later in life. Garriba said claims circulating in the communities linked vaccination to menstrual problems, infertility, and miscarriage. She said parents encountered those claims through social media and conversations with neighbours. “Sometimes when one person hears something and tells another person, it creates fear,” Garriba said. “The other parent may also begin to think that the same thing can happen to her child.” The consequences, she said, are far-reaching. Health teams sometimes travel to communities with vaccines and medicines, only to be turned away by parents who have heard negative claims about them. Some ask the health workers to return later, while others decline without explanation. “Sometimes you go with the vaccines to the community, but because of what somebody has heard, the parent will not allow the child to take it,” she said. Garriba said doses that go unused in this way risk being wasted if they expire before they can be administered. The directorate had targeted 6,955 children aged 9 to 14. For several weeks, rumours kept uptake low. The first approach — using English and correcting claims at health facilities — did not shift parents' minds. The team then changed who spoke and how they delivered the message. Emelia Kpodo, a senior health promotion officer, said staff are matched to communities by language. In Apremdo, Whindo, Kwesimintsim, Apollo, Anaji Fie, Adientem, and Assakae communities, where Ahanta is widely spoken, Ahanta-speaking health officers run the sensitisation. Nzema and Fante speakers are deployed elsewhere. "When you have somebody who speaks the language of the community, it makes communication easier because the people feel that one of their own is part of the team," Kpodo said. _Education on routine vaccination and HPV at Assakae Community Information Centre. Source: Effia-Kwesimintsim Health Directorate._ The work runs through four channels: community education, face-to-face discussions, community information centers, and school engagements such as PTA meetings where parents ask questions directly. The method matters as much as the language. Health workers do not start by telling parents a rumour is false. They explain what HPV is and what the vaccine does, then invite parents to say what they have heard in their own words. Afterwards, staff answer using familiar expressions and examples. Kpodo describes the sequence as listening to the concern, finding where it came from, and then responding with accurate information. _Emelia Kpodo, Senior Health Promotion Officer at Effia-Kwesimintsim Health Directorate. Source: DUBAWA_ After sustained education in local languages, 2,372 (34%) of the 6,955 target children had been vaccinated. Kpodo described this as a significant improvement on where the exercise stood before the language-led engagement. By the directorate's own numbers, about two-thirds of the target group — 4,583 children — had still not been vaccinated at that point. The result is real progress, not target coverage. _Parents being educated in their local dialect at a school PTA meeting. Source: Effia-Kwesimintsim Health Directorate._ Kpodo acknowledged that some parents remained hesitant after the engagements. Whether the model can be sustained is a separate question. It depends on having staff who speak the relevant language in each community, a constraint the directorate has not quantified. _Community engagement at Anaji Fie. Source: Effia-Kwesimintsim Health Directorate._ _A student receiving the vaccination. Source: Effia-Kwesimintsim Health Directorate._ The Effia-Kwesimintsim experience points to a simple mismatch that health communicators across Ghana face: a rumour that reaches a parent in Ahanta from a neighbour is rarely undone by a correction delivered in technical English at a health facility. For Kpodo, the sequence is what matters: listen to the concern, find out where it came from, then respond with accurate information. When misinformation spreads in the language of the community, the correction may have to speak that language too. representative.title: A last-ditch effort to revive salmon stocks takes shape on BC’s central coast - MBC Radio
representative.author: MBC News

snapshot.title: A last-ditch effort to revive salmon stocks takes shape on BC’s central coast - MBC Radio
snapshot.evidenceText: Photo: Wuikinuxv Creek walkers navigate fallen logs and moss-covered rocks while making their way along the creek. Every summer, Wuikinuxv Nation crews walk the streams of Rivers Inlet on BC’s remote central coast, counting how many salmon have returned from the ocean to spawn. This year, for the first time, the creek walkers — local members who monitor salmon and stream conditions — are working with a restoration expert to assess habitat and develop plans for larger-scale restoration efforts, building on observations from this year and previous years. The Wannock River system, which flows from Owikeno Lake into Rivers Inlet, once supported one of BC’s largest sockeye runs and remains home to all five salmon species. But historic logging and increasingly unpredictable water levels have damaged the streams the fish depend on, said Raven Walkus, the nation’s salmon restoration co-ordinator. She said crews had already noticed “a big drop” in returning salmon compared with last year, while lower water levels in many creeks were making it harder for fish to reach their spawning grounds. They had also seen flooding that can wash out stream channels and salmon eggs. “We can already tell it’s going to be a tough year,” she said. Local salmon stocks are struggling, with Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) expecting fewer sockeye to return to Owikeno Lake and Chinook numbers in the Wannock River system remaining uncertain. Those warning signs have led Wuikinuxv to expand its seasonal monitoring into a broader restoration effort. The nation’s roughly 11-week creek-walking season runs until late October. This year, crews are using it to map where water is disappearing, banks are washing away and salmon habitat has been lost — information that will help Wuikinuxv decide where future restoration money should go. Earlier this summer, Tom Balfour, a biologist and field operations manager with the Redd Fish Restoration Society, joined the Wuikinuxv crews. They walked the streams together, reviewed sites the creek walkers had identified and used a drone to survey the river systems. Balfour said two major river systems in the territory will require significant work. Logging removed the large trees that once slowed rainfall, stabilized riverbanks and supplied the logs that create pools and shelter for salmon. “Big trees are essential to the function of the river,” Balfour said. Future restoration could include planting trees, stabilizing slopes and placing large logs in river channels. But the work will be difficult in Wuikinuxv’s remote watershed, where the roads, barges, trucks and heavy equipment once used by logging companies are no longer available. Moving machinery or large logs by helicopter could cost $20,000 to $30,000 a day, Walkus said. For now, Wuikinuxv is piecing together government and other funding to keep creek walkers in the field and the Redfish Restoration assessment is expected to help the Nation find future funding. Until that money is secured, creek walkers are taking on smaller fixes they can safely carry out themselves, such as opening drying pools, guiding salmon away from shrinking channels and clearing debris that blocks their passage. The nation is making the most of its short field season at a time when funding for salmon monitoring is becoming increasingly uncertain across coastal BC. DFO provides support one year at a time and many neighbouring communities have lost funding or seen their seasonal creek-walking programs reduced. “We are super fortunate that we are getting any funding at all from DFO,” Walkus said. Wuikinuxv also has a much smaller stewardship department than some coastal nations, but Walkus said its crew has still managed to take on monitoring and early restoration work. Ted Walkus, a hereditary chief of the Wuikinuxv Nation, said creek walking is also a responsibility passed through his family. His nephew is the fourth generation of their family to monitor the streams. For decades, Wuikinuxv members were mainly hired as trail guides or field workers while outside officials directed the monitoring program and controlled the information gathered from the rivers. Now, in the third year of running the work themselves, nation members are deciding where to send crews, what changes to record and how those observations can guide restoration. The program is also bringing younger people onto the land to learn how the territory is changing. They see where water levels are dropping, where salmon are spawning and where logging damage continues to affect the rivers. Raven Walkus said that knowledge stays in the community instead of leaving with outside agencies or disappearing when a seasonal contract ends. “It’s not just a job,” Ted Walkus said. “It’s a way of life and it’s a way of sustaining ourselves.” Sonal Gupta / Local Journalism Initiative / Canada’s National Observer.

representative.author: Kenn Oliver

snapshot.title: Ontario police warn public as repeat sex offender release again | National Post
snapshot.evidenceText: For the third straight year, an Ontario police force is warning about the release of the same high-risk sex offender with several past convictions for sexual assaults against a child and women dating back almost 20 years. Enjoy the latest local, national and international news. Enjoy the latest local, national and international news. Create an account or sign in to continue with your reading experience. Create an account or sign in to continue with your reading experience. The Durham Regional Police Service (DRPS) has issued a safety alert that 48-year-old Keith Theodore Constantin, “who poses a significant risk to the community, especially children,” will be living at an undisclosed location in the region effective Sunday. Constantin is “subject to electronic monitoring” 24-hours daily, but DRPS said in a Saturday news release that its offender management unit will also keep tabs on his “whereabouts and activities.” Get a dash of perspective along with the trending news of the day in a very readable format. A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder. The next issue of NP Posted will soon be in your inbox. We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again The Hamilton native was in custody after being arrested last March for breaching the conditions of his release in the Oshawa area after just two days of freedom, according to DRPS . The police service also warned of his release in May of 2024, as reported by the Toronto Sun . It’s not immediately clear what Constantin had been imprisoned for at the time. National Post has contacted the Parole Board of Canada for more information about his release. DRPS warned that Constantin has a history of sexual assault with a weapon, robbery, possession of explosives and uttering threats, among other crimes. His first serious convictions came in 2000 when he was sentenced for two armed robberies and two sexual assaults — one against a seven-year-old boy he’d lured to a park and another on a 45-year-old blind woman who lived in the same building as him. It’s not clear how much time he served, but he was free in fall 2007, as he was later convicted of sexually assaulting an epileptic woman in the basement apartment of his parents’ home as she was recovering from a seizure that September, according to a 2014 story in The Hamilton Spectator . He said “Shut up, or I will kill you,” when she screamed for help, CBC reported. He never went to trial because the stress induced seizures and fears of suicide in his 27-year-old victim. Instead, he made a plea deal in 2009, was sentenced to eight years and received four years’ credit for time served. It also earned him a spot on the national sex-offender registry for life. His 2014 release was met with considerable pushback in the Hamilton neighbourhoods where he was set to reside when York Regional Police (YRP) warned of it, National Post reported , leading him to break curfew and ask to be imprisoned again. YRP issued another warning in December 2015 when he was released again after serving 18 months for the curfew breach. During a 2014 court hearing, Constantin said he’d begun taking a chemical castration drug, The Spectator reported, and that he is no longer a serious risk to the community. “When I was younger I did mess up a lot, I did screw up, and I think I paid the price for it. But I do understand the seriousness of it, I do understand what I’ve done,” he said, adding that he would have his genitalia “surgically removed” to prove it if he could afford to do so. “I know in my heart and my mind that I’d never do it again,” he said. The Parole Board of Canada felt different at the time, according to a decision obtained by The Spectator, which highlighted Constantin’s own “urges of reoffending against children and young women and that (he) has thoughts of killing.” The documents indicate diagnoses of alcohol and drug addiction, paranoid schizophrenia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression, an “extremely low range of intellectual ability,” and “character features associated with psychopathy.” He was also a problematic inmate who threw urine and feces at correctional officers, threatened suicide with a razor blade and ignored personal hygiene. His behaviour led him to spend time in maximum security facilities and in segregation, led to the suspension of mental health supports, and got him kicked out of prison programs. Oshawa Mayor Dan Carter issued a press release thanking the DRPS for “proactively informing the public and for its continued efforts to monitor high-risk offenders.” Carter said residents are right to be concerned and that he supports provincial and federal work “to strengthen bail and sentencing laws, particularly for repeat and violent offenders and those convicted of serious crimes. “These reforms are vital to enhancing public safety and ensuring that justice is served fairly and effectively. DRPS said Constantin is bound by multiple conditions as part of his high-risk release peace bond under the Criminal Code of Canada. He must report to them weekly and abide by a 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. curfew, less lenient than the 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. curfew applied when added to the RCMP’s high-risk child sex offender database at age 45. He’s not allowed to “associate or communicate” with kids under 16, nor “engage in any activities that involve contact with anyone under” that age. He’s also forbidden from being near daycares, swimming areas, school grounds, playgrounds or any community centre where children under 16 are present. He can go to public places where children under 16 may be, but only when accompanied by someone 21 or older. He’s not allowed to possess, purchase or consume any alcohol, drugs, narcotics or controlled substances. Nor can he use “the internet or other digital networks” or possess a device that can go online. He’s prohibited from associating with criminals or people with a record, can’t own or possess weapons and cannot be in a relationship with a parent of a child under 16. “Police are asking the public to stay vigilant and remain aware of their surroundings,” DRPS wrote. “Any suspicious or dangerous behaviour should be reported directly to the police.” Postmedia is committed to maintaining a lively but civil forum for discussion. representative.title: More newcomers on the ballot in the GTA but winning is another story | The Pointer
representative.author: Shawgi Mustafa

snapshot.title: More newcomers on the ballot in the GTA but winning is another story
snapshot.evidenceText: Ontario's 2026 municipal election has seen a record number of first-time candidates. But immigrant and racialized residents — especially women — say the playing field remains uneven. They point to problems such as raising money, getting media coverage, facing online harassment and the advantage that incumbents already have in election campaigns. The Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) reports that 4,502 people — 68 percent of all municipal candidates — have never held office before, up from 66 percent in 2022. "One of the notable things about the 2026 municipal election is the number of people stepping forward for the first time," AMO executive director Lindsay Jones said. "That is encouraging for the future of local democracy, but getting on the ballot is only one part of participating meaningfully." On paper, this looks like progress. But AMO's research, together with interviews with four diverse candidates in the GTA, reveals that deep-rooted barriers still prevent many qualified newcomers from entering the race and competing against candidates with stronger financial and political networks. "There isn't a single explanation, and election outcomes are shaped by many factors," Jones said. "What AMO’s research does show is that candidates from diverse and under-represented communities can encounter a combination of barriers throughout the campaign process." These barriers include access to campaign donations, volunteers, mentors and established networks, as well as concerns about discrimination, harassment and exclusion. Data from the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) shows 68 percent of the 6,663 candidates in Ontario’s 2026 municipal elections are running for office for the first time. (AMO) For more than 20 years, Jagruti Bhatt has called Canada home. Now the South Asian woman is running for mayor of Brampton on a platform built around accountability, healthcare expansion and housing that accommodates multi-generational families. She made the move to politics after watching problems pile up while City Hall seemed focused on "everything except what affects our actual lives”. But getting her message out has been an uphill battle. As a first-time candidate, she’s had to build her campaign from the ground up. "Fundraising and securing community support have definitely been uphill battles," Bhatt said. Many groups now think twice before hosting open discussions or backing challengers. She pointed to a chilling effect created by how the City hands out grants. "Many groups that should feel free to host discussions or engage openly now feel they have to stay silent, or quietly back incumbents out of fear that welcoming challengers could cost them their funding next year." Jagruti Bhatt is a realtor and a business owner who has put her name in the bid for Brampton’s next mayor. (Alexis Wright/The Pointer) Bhatt also described personal attacks online targeting her English language skills, despite more than 15 years of grassroots work and a career in real estate built on trust with local families. "Being able to connect with people and advocate for them doesn't come from smooth, rehearsed political speeches; it comes from showing up and doing honest work," she said. "Treating accents or language skills as a barrier is something far too many immigrant candidates run into, and it sends a harmful message that no matter how long you've contributed to your community, you're still treated as an outsider." Her prescription is concrete: Match small donations for first-time candidates; offer real mentorship and pre-season training; firewall community grant decisions from electoral politics; and review city rules that favour incumbents. East of Brampton, in Toronto's Ward 20 — Scarborough Southwest —Sharmina Nasrin, a former public servant who immigrated from Bangladesh in 2018, said she is running because she has practical ideas for her riding: Safer neighbourhoods, better parks, reliable transit services, tenant protections and stronger communication between residents and City Hall. But as a first-time candidate without a large political organization, Nasrin has had to build everything from the ground up. "Fundraising has been particularly challenging because I am running a grassroots campaign," she said. “I wasn’t born in Scarborough. Scarborough is where I became who I am,” Sharmina Nasrin said. (Sharmina Nasrin/ Campaign Website) Reaching voters across a large, diverse ward has meant long hours of knocking on doors. But those challenges have also become one of the most meaningful parts of this campaign. "Every door I knock on, every conversation I have and every volunteer who joins me is helping me build something," she said. "I may not have the biggest campaign machine, but I am building a campaign based on relationships, hard work and trust." Nasrin says there are more immigrant women who have the education and experience to serve but lack networks and confidence. She believes more support and visible role models would help close that gap. "We need more mentorship, community-based political leadership programs and opportunities for women to build networks before they decide to run," she said. "Most importantly, immigrant women need to see other women like themselves participating. Representation can change what people believe is possible." Bahira Abdulsalam, an engineer and independent candidate for mayor of Toronto, believes the biggest barrier she faces is not that she's an immigrant — it’s that she’s running without a party machine or significant funding. "Many people don't even realize a candidate can run for mayor without a party; the model itself is unfamiliar." Bahira Abdulsalam aims to “bring an engineer’s discipline to City Hall, fix what we have, spend honestly, and put people first”. (Bahira Abdulsalam/Campaign Website) Abdulsalam, who came to Canada from Egypt two decades ago, says she is running without funding and with minimal contributions because her campaign is focused on people already struggling financially. "What I have instead is a wealth of experience and an extraordinary team of volunteers who give their time because they believe in the cause, but money is still a wall," she said. On visibility, Abdulsalam said the pattern is telling. "In 2023, I was covered by mainstream Canadian outlets. In 2026 so far, I haven't been (interviewed), even by the Toronto Star, CBC and Radio-Canada, even as international media have taken an interest." She said that she has faced Islamophobia and xenophobia, and that her willingness to speak plainly on issues such as Palestinian and human rights and education reforms that others avoid has led some institutions to keep their distance. Abdulsalam said her name also does not appear in most polls. "Private polling firms charge thousands of dollars, so unfunded independents are simply left off the list and voters can't choose someone they're never shown," she said. Abdulsalam called for levelling the visibility playing field. "Access to debates, forums and official candidate information should follow from being a registered candidate — not from money or party." She also wants lower costs of entry and more value placed on lived experience. She said newcomers and people with international experience should have a stronger voice in how the city makes decisions. "This city needs international experience and geopolitical knowledge to make room for them on city boards, in genuine consultation before decisions are made, and in the rooms where power actually sits," Abdulsalam said. To better understand who is running and who is not, Ontario’s municipalities association asked the province to change its rules to allow municipalities to collect voluntary demographic information from candidates and elected officials. "Having better information about who is running, who is elected and who is not successful would help municipalities, the province and organizations like AMO better understand where barriers may exist and where additional supports are needed," said the organization's executive director. Until that data is widely available, stories like those of Bhatt, Nasrin and Abdulsalam offer a window into the gap between the surge of first-time candidates and the structural hurdles that keep many newcomer voices from breaking through. For Bhatt, the message to Brampton is simple: "You don't need to be a career politician to listen, care and get things done." "If more doors are opened, more immigrant women will walk through them," Nasrin said. Abdusalam agrees that the real litmus test of a democracy is “whether a woman without money or a party can still be heard”. At a time when vital public information is needed by everyone, The Pointer has taken down our paywall on all stories to ensure every resident of Brampton, Mississauga and Niagara has access to the facts. representative.title: A subway for Mississauga, lower taxes and fighting crime highlight tense mayoral race - Narcity
representative.author: The Canadian Press

snapshot.title: A subway for Mississauga, lower taxes and fighting crime highlight tense mayoral race
snapshot.evidenceText: Coming off the heels of an argumentative debate at Food Banks Mississauga on October 1 that left many residents walking away feeling perplexed, with more questions than answers after candidates repeatedly sparred with each other instead of directly addressing the main topic—affordability—they went head-to-head at a more civil mayoral debate on Monday. Incumbent Carolyn Parrish faced criticism from her three main opponents, even though she wasn’t there. “Carolyn, why do you think you don’t need to show up?” Alvin Tedjo asked. “Residents have been asking for the past two years, ‘Where are you?’ Now you’re reapplying for a job, and you don’t want to show up for the interview. Residents deserve better than a part-time mayor. Our voters deserve better than you hiding behind your desk and from your record of tax increases and rising crime. Mississauga deserves better.” Tedjo’s criticism of rising taxes came after he was one of only three Mississauga council members at the Region of Peel who approved a massive 23.3 percent, $144 million police budget increase for 2025 (a decision that was widely criticized and described as an “utter failure of governance” by Toronto’s former police board chair), the biggest driver of an overall 9.2 percent property tax hike that year. Tedjo also voted against a motion by fellow mayoral candidate Dipika Damerla earlier this year to appoint a permanent auditor general to keep City Hall spending in check and taxes down. Hosted at City Hall by POLICORNER on October 5, Parrish did not show up for Monday’s debate, leaving an empty podium on stage next to Bonnie Crombie, Dipika Damerla and Tedjo. Crombie also levelled criticism at Parrish and said her absence, though irresponsible, would at least help ensure a more constructive debate compared to what unfolded at the previous events. “We've demonstrated leadership in the past, and I know we will again,” Crombie said during her opening remarks. “I know it's going to be an amicable conversation, not like in the previous two debates.” Crombie later declared, “Mississauga, it's time to have a subway,” highlighting one of the key parts of her vision for the city, a new subway line extending from Toronto’s Bloor Line at Kipling Station into the heart of Mississauga. Crombie connected the subway extension to easing congestion across Mississauga, which has had a significant impact on productivity and quality of life in the city. “If it's cost-effective, people will leave their cars, and they will use more public transit. I like the idea of a subway. We've been floating it in every town hall we've been at, and everyone loves it. We have a premier who loves building subways, so I know that this will catch his attention, and we're already building the Ontario line. It's well in the works, and they're ahead of schedule, so I know that they will just love to have more work ahead of them, and this will be in the plan. We'll get that done first.” Damerla hammered home the point that nothing will get done inside City Hall if leadership is absent, which appeared to be a shot at Parrish who has been repeatedly criticized throughout her brief time as mayor since Crombie stepped down in 2024 to take over the Ontario Liberal Party, for being absent in the community, a characterization now dogging Parrish during the campaign after she did not show up for Monday’s debate. “It is true that the issues in front of us are about affordability, the fact that Mississauga doesn't feel as safe as it used to, and the fact that our quality of life is lower,” Damerla said Monday. “But the central question is, who do residents believe and trust to address these concerns?” Damerla highlighted her leadership when she introduced a motion this year to establish an auditor general for the City of Mississauga to get spending under control and lower taxes for residents, a move that was shot down by Parrish and Tedjo who voted against Damerla’s motion. She said she would reintroduce the motion for an auditor general if she wins, and Crombie said she would also bring in an independent auditor general for the City. “So I have the receipts, and that's why people will trust me,” Damerla said. “If there's anyone that this city trusts to establish an independent auditor general at the City of Mississauga, I believe it would be me.” Crombie said the move would help lower taxes. “The best way to make life more affordable is to reduce people's taxes. The tax rate over the past two years has been 15 percent, 10 percent last year and 5.5 percent this year, and only 5.5 percent because $33 million was taken out of a reserve [account] (which is meant for emergency needs) to (reduce) the taxes.” The most recent polls suggest a tight race, with Crombie pulling slightly ahead of Parrish, Tedjo not far behind and Damerla slipping. Crombie’s plan to get Mississauga’s first subway line built—a proposed extension of Toronto’s Bloor line that would continue on from Kipling Station into the heart of her city—is creating buzz, with residents reaching out to The Pointer expressing excitement over the vision. Damerla said, “the one thing the mayor really controls is property taxes, and my commitment is to freeze taxes in 2027. But everybody here is talking about freezing taxes at the City, but the elephant in the room is the Region of Peel, that's where our taxes are really going up, so my other commitment is to fix the policing formula.” Policing is a regional responsibility in Peel. All twelve Mississauga council members also sit on the 25-member Peel Region Council, joined by nine of Brampton’s council members, three from Caledon and a regional chair who only votes if there is a tie. Damerla said if the mayor is not committed to low taxes in Mississauga and at the Region, which accounts for a slightly larger portion of the annual combined property tax bill, “then there's just no way to fix the affordability crisis.” Monday’s debate, without Parrish, marked the first one where the issues received the lion’s share of attention, rather than personal attacks and candidates speaking over one another. Following a more subdued debate hosted by the Mississauga Board of Trade on September 25, the food banks event last week became more of a distraction as coverage ignored the pressing issues voters are facing in the high-growth municipality, instead highlighting the acrimony on stage.Crombie, the former mayor, who has a one-to-three percent lead over Parrish according to the latest polls (not accounting for the margin of error) joined Damerla and Tedjo in the more issues-based debate on stage Monday as rising property taxes, housing costs, crime, congestion and concerns about government accountability dominated the evening. Candidates were asked if they would use strong mayor powers to override a majority vote on council. Damerla and Tedjo opposed using the powers, which have often been criticized for undermining democratic governance, concentrating authority in the mayor’s hands and creating division on municipal councils. Crombie said “Maybe” and in the past has mentioned she only used the powers once as mayor, when she felt it was needed to support an affordable housing motion that also triggered tens of millions of dollars in federal funding. She said, at the time, the special powers were used after council made a bad decision to ignore affordable housing and the federal money. All three candidates said they do not want Mississauga to be part of the Region of Peel anymore, preferring the city be granted independent status like Toronto and others that stand on their own. Tedjo has faced criticism during the campaign over his pledge to freeze property taxes for the first two years in office. Damerla, during the Mississauga Food Banks debate last week, questioned him about why wealthier residents should be eligible and how criteria would be established for programs he suggested around property tax support. Tedjo was caught on his back foot and could not answer many of the questions. He has also been criticized for not explaining how millions of dollars in lost revenue would be made up, to ensure residents will not be crippled by even higher taxes and compounding costs in a few years. Tedjo has been widely panned for pandering to voters with a pledge to permanently freeze property taxes for some seniors by deferring them until their home is eventually sold, when the money would be recouped. His opponents have pointed out the move, which has been described on social media as a desperate play for votes, would never pass, even with strong mayor powers. His lack of experience, having served less than one full council term, has been questioned. His opponents have asked him how the city would run without tens of millions of dollars in lost revenue every year, while property taxes for most residents would skyrocket and force many out of their homes. Damerla has built a platform around accountability, transparency, reducing policing costs and ensuring residents receive better value for their tax dollars through the hiring of an independent auditor general for Mississauga after her motion earlier this year was voted down. On Monday, Tedjo said Parrish’s absence illustrated the type of leader she is and that residents deserve a mayor who is present and accountable to lead the city effectively. Parrish has said that after attending earlier debates she does not feel the need to participate in similar events when her platform has already been outlined. During the Food Banks Mississauga debate last week, Parrish emphasized what she said her administration had already accomplished during her two years as mayor. “The first thing I did after I was elected was put together 25 of our top developers to do a housing task force,” Parrish said. “Their first job was to tell our staff everything we were doing wrong that would take time and money to get their plans approved. It worked extremely well.” The remarks were not met well by residents who shouted from the crowd, “no more monopolies”. She said the fees developers pay to City Hall had been reduced, which has raised questions about how the lost revenue meant to pay for critical infrastructure to support growth will be covered. She said the fee cuts to builders will bring down the cost of new homes in the city, which is not supported by data that show incentives given to developers are often enjoyed as extra profits, not passed onto consumers. Parrish defended her record on policing last week, after massive increases to the Peel Police budget became a major point of debate. She approved the 23.3 percent, $144 million increase for 2025 while she sat on the police board, before quitting, claiming she could criticize the force more effectively if she was not part of its direct governance. “I jumped right off the police services board when the 23.3 [percent increase] came in,” Parrish said during the Food Banks debate, arguing she had continued fighting for Mississauga even after leaving the board. Parrish said that if re-elected she would not sit on the police board. Her remarks about challenging the police budget, even though she approved it at the board level, sparked immediate reaction from the crowd. One shouted, “You’re a lair,” before he was immediately told to sit back down. Parrish quickly snapped back: “And you’re my best friend.” Crombie, who sat on the Peel police board for nine years, levelled heavy criticism against Parrish for quitting the police board immediately after she joined it in 2024, when Crombie stepped down as mayor. “So I will say that people don't feel as safe as they once did,” Crombie said during Monday’s debate, which Parrish did not attend. “We've seen the rash of break-ins, home invasions, carjackings, car thefts. I get those videos in the morning…There was a rash of break-ins on one particular street near UTM, and the residents were scared… we had representatives from Peel Regional Police to give us advice on how to better protect ourselves; what could be done.” She said the board approved specific safety programs for particular neighbourhoods. “Carolyn Parrish has not been doing her job. She has not worked for the people of Mississauga. She went to a single meeting at the Peel Regional Police board, and then she quit. She quit the board. She quit on all of us. She left the board and said, ‘I don't want to bother negotiating. I'm not fighting for Mississauga. I'm not making sure that we have enough resources or police in boots on the streets’. And then when we were faced with the budget issue, that's when she walked away. She walked away. She quit. She abdicated the police board. I think it's the responsibility of the mayor to sit on the police board. That's where you learn about community safety. What are the hotspots in the city. What are the police doing about it. And that is where you initiate all kinds of programs, like we did the bodyworn cameras, CCTV cameras, the auto theft summit that we held to help bring down the rate of car thefts, et cetera. But the mayor abdicated, so she learned none of that. When it came time for the chief to present the budget to the board for approval, she didn't like it, so she quit.” Crombie argued that if Parrish thinks the funding formula for Peel police is broken she needs to be at the table to fix it. “She said the funding formula was unfair. We all agree that the funding formula is unfair, but until it's changed, it is the funding formula. And you sit there and you negotiate knowing that we are going to pick up 62 percent of the tab. It's not fair, but why quit? Why not sit there and get the best deal for the city and delay some of the increased costs into the future? I think we all support frontline policing. What we don't believe in is increasing our budget to the degree that it cripples our city.” Parrish also faced criticism from her opponents at last week’s event over her costly proposal to redevelop the area immediately surrounding City Hall, including the Living Arts Centre. Tedjo opposed demolishing the Living Arts Centre for the project, while Damerla questioned whether the City should be pursuing the proposal while residents were struggling with affordability. Crombie presented a different vision of how Mississauga would evolve under her leadership, with a focus on the subway, the coming Hurontario LRT which she helped approve and affordable housing to support these major transit investments along their key corridors. She repeatedly emphasized her experience running the city. At the Food Banks debate, Crombie introduced her Mississauga 2.0 plan, which draws on transit as the most ambitious part of her platform, including a new subway line to catalyze residential and commercial investment, job creation and significant tax revenue along the corridor to keep costs down for all residents. The same will be done along the Hurontario LRT corridor. Tedjo said that while he supports large transit proposals, he would take a different approach. “Let’s build the light rail. Let’s build the bus rapid transit. Let’s do the actual building that we can in the next four years to get people moving around this city.” To control City Hall spending, Crombie proposed a line-by-line examination of spending and said an auditor general should be used to identify where money is being wasted. But it’s Damerla who has owned the auditor general idea, and she has repeatedly reminded voters that she was the only council member earlier this year pushing for the oversight role. Tedjo highlighted his plan to create a Mississauga Housing Corporation that would use public land to form partnerships with non-profit and private-sector organizations to build affordable housing. Damerla and Crombie both said they would work with the federal government to develop co-ops on available land as it could provide deeply affordable homes while also creating stronger communities. Damerla emphasized over the past week that building the types of homes residents can realistically afford is a priority. She supports missing-middle housing, including six-plexes along certain arterial roads, and said the city needs more options for seniors looking to downsize. Damerla’s approach to transit is more focused on practical improvements. She proposes adding GO stops along the Lakeshore line and improving connectivity. She was also the only candidate during the POLICORNER who supported higher transit fares for better MiWay services. With advance voting open until October 11 and election day on October 26, Mississauga residents have less than three weeks to make a choice between the four clear frontrunners vying to lead one of Canada’s largest cities. representative.author: Olivia Gazis

snapshot.title: U.S. sanctions International Criminal Court, vowing to dismantle it
snapshot.evidenceText: The Trump administration imposed fresh sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court on Friday, taking action against the court itself after previously penalizing more than a dozen of its judges and prosecutors."Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the measures. The move came just hours after the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born human rights official who served as an ICC judge from 2003 to 2008. Pillay also led a U.N. inquiry that determined last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Israel strongly disputed the report's findings. Neither the United States nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute that established the ICC. Washington has long objected to the court's investigation of alleged war crimes by U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and its arrest warrants for Israeli leaders over alleged crimes in Gaza. The court maintains it can prosecute crimes committed on territory under its jurisdiction, even when the accused is a national of a country that has not joined. Rubio has previously described the ICC as a "fatally politicized supranational court" that has "maliciously abused its authority." He vowed Friday to dismantle it "brick by brick" if necessary. Under the designation, the court's assets under U.S. jurisdiction are blocked, and U.S. companies and individuals are generally barred from doing business with the court. For now, the Treasury Department is allowing some services to continue and giving the court 180 days to maintain certain operations while its member countries address Washington's objections. "We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns," Rubio said. "If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly." The ICC condemned the designation as an attempt to interfere with its work and intimidate those who cooperate with it, calling it "an assault on the rule of law." "The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality," ICC President Tomoko Akane said. The court also appealed to its 125 member states to help ensure it has adequate resources to continue operating, warning its future now depends in part on the governments that established it. The court's member states include most U.S. allies in Europe, including every NATO member besides Turkey, as well as Canada, Japan and Australia. The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. said in a statement later Friday that they "regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States.""[I]f put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families," the countries said. "They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims."Pillay, the Peace Prize recipient, left the court in 2008 to become the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, and currently serves on the International Court of Justice, which is separate from the ICC. She was also the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. In September 2025, the panel determined that there were "reasonable grounds" to conclude that "the Israeli authorities and Israeli security forces have committed and are continuing to commit" acts of genocide. Israel's foreign minister called the report "fake" and said it "relies entirely on Hamas falsehoods, laundered and repeated by others."Pillay referenced the U.S. campaign against the ICC in a video following news that she had won the Peace Prize."We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack," she said. "This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said the decision to award the Peace Prize to Pillay showed that the Nobel Committee "has lost its moral compass.""It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state," Netanyahu's office said in a post on X.The U.S. action against the ICC also follows a speech Rubio delivered Wednesday in Athens against the backdrop of the Acropolis, where he criticized Western governments for transferring national authority to international bureaucracies. "[W]ith every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control," he said.

representative.title: Govt bets on DP World | The Daily Star

snapshot.title: Govt bets on DP World
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The government yesterday signed a 15-year deal with DP World to operate the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT), banking on the Dubai-based logistics solutions provider’s pledged $150 million of investment to improve efficiency at the Chattogram port. The agreement signing ceremony took place amid protests outside the venue demanding the cancellation of the move to hand over the operation of the high-revenue-generating terminal to a foreign operator. DP World becomes the fourth foreign operator at Chattogram Port after RSGT International, AP Møller-Maersk and Medlog. “Our wider policy is to engage multiple international operators across terminals to improve service quality and reliability and strengthen supply chain resilience,” said Shipping Minister Sheikh Rabiul Alam at the agreement signing ceremony. The government will receive Tk 600 crore as signing money from DP World, with 25 percent paid at signing and the remaining 75 percent before the terminal is handed over to DP World. Bangladesh will receive 67 percent of the handling revenue per 20-foot container (TEU), while a minimum handling volume has also been set, Rabiul said. Based on current handling charges, the government’s share could average around $90-$100 per TEU, although the amount would vary. NCT, which began operations in 2007, currently handles around 1.23 million TEUs a year. The government expects the volume to rise to 1.6-1.8 million TEUs as efficiency improves. “The national interest will remain protected,” said Md Razib Ahsan, the state minister for shipping, adding that higher container volumes would increase government revenue from customs and other sources. DP World will invest to modernise NCT, including upgrading equipment and introducing greater automation to reduce container and ship stay time, which at 9.4 days and 2.53 days are well above those of India’s Jawaharlal Nehru Port and Vietnam’s Cai Mep. Modern equipment, digital systems, international operating standards and global logistics connections will make NCT more competitive, Rabiul said. Initial modernisation work is expected to be completed within six months, while the terminal is expected to operate at full capacity within about two years. Truck waiting time, currently around 24 hours, could fall to two hours in the first year and eventually to one hour, while vessel turnaround time is also expected to decline from about 2.5 days to between one and 1.5 days. The container dwell time at the port could fall to around three to four days after modernisation, he said. That could have a significant impact on trade. According to World Bank data cited at the event, cutting dwell time by one day could increase Bangladesh’s exports by about 7.4 percent. Faster cargo handling would shorten lead times for exporters and help make the garment and other export industries more competitive, Ahsan said. The government has also sought to allay concerns over job losses. The existing port employees would not lose their jobs under the agreement and their current gross salaries would remain unchanged, Rabiul said. “Modernisation could instead create demand for more skilled workers.” Rabiul acknowledged public concerns over the deal, saying some opposition was linked to fears over job security and loss of influence. “We respect their views,” he said, adding that the government would engage with stakeholders if they had specific concerns. DP World Executive Chairman Essa Kazim said the company would connect NCT with its global network of ports, logistics infrastructure and supply chain services. “Bangladesh is an increasingly important trading and manufacturing economy, and we are committed to supporting its continued development,” he said. After the signing ceremony, a DP World delegation led by Kazim met with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at his office in the secretariat and discussed various issues of mutual interest, including trade and investment between Bangladesh and the UAE, port management and development of the logistics sector. Tarique sought DP World’s investment in free trade zones and rail-based inland container depots in Bangladesh, reports UNB. The DP World representatives expressed interest in cooperation and investment in the areas. Over in the port city, leaders of protesting workers’ organisations at Chattogram have given the government a three-day ultimatum to open talks over the deal with DP World. They also announced a token hunger strike for Monday and warned that the movement would be intensified if the government failed to hold talks with protesting port workers and employees by October 11. The announcement came at a rally organised by Chattogram Bandar Rokkha Sangram Parishad, a platform of pro-BNP workers’ organisations active at the port, in front of the main gate of the port’s administrative building. Leaders and activists of several political and labour organisations, including Sramik Karmachari Oikkya Parishad, the Communist Party of Bangladesh, Bangladesher Samajtantrik Dal (Basad) and Basad (Marxist), also joined the programme under the banner of Chattogram Bandar Rokkha Committee. After the rally, participants brought out a procession through roads adjacent to the port area. Addressing the gathering, Parishad Coordinator Humayun Kabir said the protesters are still willing to engage in dialogue. They still believe the government is ready to discuss the issue and listen to the arguments of the port’s workers and employees. He criticised the government for signing the agreement without making its details public. Sheikh Nurullah Bahar, general secretary of the Chattogram divisional unit of Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal, accused the government of ignoring public opinion and the concerns of port workers and employees. He questioned what safeguards, if any, had been included in the agreement for workers. Bahar also accused Invest Bangladesh Chairman Ashik Chowdhury and the CPA chairman of influencing the government to hand over the NCT to DP World. No agreement would be accepted unless port workers and employees agree to it, said Parishad Co-Coordinator Ibrahim Khokan, who is also general secretary of Bandar Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal. representative.title: Federal government lists west coast pipeline as national interest - St. Albert News
representative.author: Tristan Oram

snapshot.title: Federal government lists west coast pipeline as national interest
snapshot.evidenceText: The oil pipeline heading to the west coast has been named a project of national interest. Announced at a news conference on Thursday, Oct. 1 by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Premier Danielle Smith, the Pacific Link pipeline will follow a route beginning in Bruderheim, Alta. and run north of Edmonton and St. Albert, and continue to a marine terminal near Delta, B.C. south of Vancouver. The project is now listed on Schedule 1 of the Building Canada Act , meaning it will be fast-tracked and the approval process, which includes environmental assessments, will be consolidated. "A pipeline to the west coast is part of our mission to transform our economy, to double our non-U.S. exports over the next decade," Carney said. He said the pipeline will allow Canada to export an additional one million barrels of oil per day to growing markets in Asia. The Government of Alberta and federally owned Trans Mountain Corporation will share equal ownership of Pacific Link at 45 per cent each, while Indigenous communities will be offered at least 10 per cent ownership interest with financing through the existing loan guarantee programs. Pembina Pipeline Corporation is also on board as a private sector investor and will own a 10 per cent stake for the construction portion. It is estimated that the pipeline will create 140,000 jobs across the country and generate more than $20 billion in GDP per year. Along with the pipeline, Carney announced that construction of a carbon capture and storage project to reduce 16 million tons of emissions every year, or the equivalent of taking 90 per cent of Alberta's cars off the roads, he said. That project is expected to create an additional 40,000 jobs. "Today marks a significant victory for Alberta’s and Canada’s energy future. The listing of Pacific Link as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act is an important step toward strengthening our economy, enhancing energy security and connecting Canadian energy to growing global markets," Smith said. "This listing sends a clear message: Canada is ready to build again. We are ready to harness our strengths, seize new opportunities and deliver the nation-building infrastructure our prosperity depends on." When reached by the Gazette , St. Albert MLA Marie Renaud pointed to a statement by Alberta NDP leader Naheed Nenshi, who said they were pleased that the southern route pipeline is moving forward. "We consulted extensively with industry to realize this route was the most feasible and most likely to get built, before actively advancing it with the most senior levels of the federal government and the public," Nenshi said. " It is worth noting, however, that this is not the pipeline Smith promised Albertans. She insisted on a route to Prince Rupert that no one proposed and everyone knew couldn’t be built and she said it would be a failure if it was a government-funded pipeline." The Major Projects Office will work with the Canada Energy Regulator through a streamlined review process to issue a conditions document for Pacific Link by Sept. 1, 2027, following which construction can begin. The pipeline is expected to be operational by 2032-33.

snapshot.evidenceText: Want to discuss? Please read our Commenting Policy first. What a surprise. Trudeau’s Bill C 69 the “no pipelines for you!” bill is found unconstitutional – again. My point is we all should admit we are not infallible. In any case, just get the pipeline done. Ben. The law is still on the books. Carney can rescind it at any time. But he chooses not to for cynical political purposes Big talking Carny does nothing to get rid of the red tape. It allows him to keep stalling because he has no intention of building a pipeline at all. This guy is a liar. Carny said he will build at speeds never seen before. Are you kidding me? Come election time we will still be talking about building pipelines and we will still have none. Let’s get on with building a pipeline. The Impact Assessment Act is not relevant any more. Danielle Smith cheering this ruling against federal overreach while simultaneously overreaching in municipal politics. And Elbows Up Carney continues to have this law in place. Hey Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin… you lost again! Take your ball and go home and stop wasting our taxpayer money on this TrudeauCarney unconstitutional fiasco!!! The LPC is incapable of getting out of its own way If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us . The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government’s Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional, following a second court challenge of the federal legislation. The act, otherwise known as Bill C-69 , was first passed by the Liberals under former prime minister Justin Trudeau to set out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines. In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction. “While Parliament may have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the (Impact Assessment Act) creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects,” the court wrote. “This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, on the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction.” The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren’t constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction. “The decision maker may regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project,” the court wrote. Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta’s legal challenge. The Impact Assessment Act has been staunchly opposed by oil and gas industry players and critics such as federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre. Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the “no more pipelines act.” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media Friday that the ruling was “yet another big win for Alberta.” “I’m calling on the federal government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean up this flawed Trudeau-era legislation once and for all so it no longer inhibits economic development in our country,” she said. The Alberta Court of Appeal just ruled that C-69 remains largely unconstitutional. I’m calling on the Federal Government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean… pic.twitter.com/aiyxRRAO3y — Danielle Smith (@ABDanielleSmith) October 9, 2026 Friday’s ruling comes as Ottawa and Alberta are partnering on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast. Earlier this month, the Pacific Link pipeline project became the first to receive a national interest designation under Ottawa’s new Building Canada Act. And while the Building Canada Act gives Ottawa the power to skirt a dozen federal laws to help move hand-picked projects forward, critics like Poilievre have long called for the Impact Assessment Act to be repealed. Through the newly tabled Bill C-39, Ottawa is trying to transfer the assessment process for pipeline and energy transmission projects from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator. The federal government has said it has been told by industry that the level of expertise on energy projects that existed at the Canada Energy Regulator couldn’t be found at the Impact Assessment Agency. Ottawa has said the Canada Energy Regulator will still be bound by the provisions of the Impact Assessment Act — which the Alberta Court of Appeal now says is unconstitutional — when carrying out its reviews. In a statement, the office of federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is reviewing the decision and considering next steps. ”To position Canada for long-term prosperity in a rapidly changing global economy, the Government of Canada is moving forward to build at a pace not seen in decades. The (Impact Assessment Act) is fundamental to the advancement of this work,” wrote press secretary Amy Falkner. ”The (Court of Appeal) opinion does not change our commitment to engage all provinces in the spirit of co-operative federalism.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026. snapshot.title: Ontario township of Centre Wellington grapples with controversial AI data centre proposal
snapshot.evidenceText:
How an Ontario township weighed the pros and cons of an AI complex in their backyard The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections. On a recent early fall evening, the mayor and six councillors of the southwestern Ontario township of Centre Wellington took their seats around a wooden horseshoe table in council chambers overlooking the picturesque village of Elora. The elected officials settled in for what was, in many ways, a typical small-town council meeting. They presented certificates to local teenage athletes and smiled for photos. They debated parking charges, approved a plan from the fire chief and passed a heritage designation for a 174-year-old limestone cottage. They also grappled with a big challenge: How should they handle a controversial proposal for an AI data centre in the neighbouring town of Fergus? A tech company proposes to build a data centre at this old copper tubing plant at 865 Gartshore St. in Fergus, Ont., about a two-hour drive from Toronto. Before them was a motion for a one-year moratorium on data centre projects in the area, which would allow staff to study possible issues with such facilities and develop guardrails. One councillor said a freeze was particularly important because of province-wide municipal elections later this month. “I really hope that this gives the new council the opportunity to understand what this is all about and make sure we’re doing the right thing for our community,” said Councillor Bronwynne Wilton, who proposed the motion. Policy-makers in towns and cities across the country are wrestling with complex and rapidly evolving technological challenges as an influx of AI data-centre proposals collide with residents’ concerns about energy demands, water use and noise. In the Greater Toronto Area, councillors in Mississauga and Oakville recently imposed one-year moratoriums on new data centre developments. Signs across from the proposed data centre promote candidates for Centre Wellington township. In Centre Wellington, a largely agricultural area of 35,000 people that includes the twin communities of Fergus and Elora about 100 kilometres northwest of Toronto, some residents are concerned about plans for an AI data centre. Spur Innovation, a Waterloo-based tech venture studio and AI infrastructure operator, is proposing to retrofit an old copper tubing plant into a data centre. The former Wolverine Tube site in Fergus currently stands vacant; Spur calls it a “contaminated brownfield.” Video surveillance and no trespassing signs hang on a chain-link fence around the 25-acre property as a flock of Canada geese wander in a grassy field. Across the street is a neighbourhood with tidy homes and a nearby elementary school. After reading local media coverage of Spur’s data centre plan in the summer, Carolyn Sharp, an artist who lives in Elora, started a petition calling for a moratorium. It received more than 2,300 signatures. “The community definitely does not want it,” she said. “It just feels like it’s being forced upon us, and I think there should be a lot more strict regulations in place.” In a presentation during the Sept. 28 council meeting, Ms. Sharp urged the township to “take a measured approach to a development that could fundamentally change the footprint of this community” by taking time to develop stronger standards for noise, energy, water, air quality and environmental protection. Sharif Virani, chief executive officer of Spur Innovation, also addressed councillors and argued that the project would support the area’s agricultural focus. Mr. Virani said the first phase of the plan is for an air-cooled data centre under 10 megawatts. The rest of the property would be “a test space for agricultural robotics, food innovation in a county where farming actually happens,” he said. “These computers are not the building; they are the utility in the corner,” he said. Spur hasn’t yet submitted an application to the municipality, however. Asked about timing, Mr. Virani said “it’s a longer-tailed question” involving financing and supply issues. He later said in an e-mail to The Globe that “we are still in consultation and planning.” The company has other AI data centres, including in the former BlackBerry RIM headquarters in Waterloo. Before council debated the motion, Brett Salmon, the township’s managing director of planning and development, told councillors they could prohibit data centre developments for a year and could later extend the freeze by an additional year under Ontario’s Planning Act. Councillor Jennifer Adams called on the Ontario government to provide “real legislation with real regulations” to help guide municipalities, noting that AI is advancing rapidly. “They definitely have more resources than we do,” she said. The data-centre proposal on Gartshore Street is one of many to crop up across Ontario as governments commit to expanding the technology. Other towns and cities have also urged Queen’s Park to act. In a submission last month, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario asked for “clear and consistent provincial guidance” for communities and a “collaborative process” for reviewing proposed facilities that involves the government, municipalities and Indigenous communities. The provincial government did not provide specific responses to questions from The Globe about Centre Wellington councillors’ call for stronger standards governing AI data centres. Premier Doug Ford has been critical of moratoriums. Evan Robinson, a spokesperson for Vic Fedeli, Minister of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade, said the province “will continue to work” with municipalities and companies on digital infrastructure projects. Mr. Robinson noted that the government launched its data centre “playbook” in the summer “to ensure Ontario is well positioned to benefit from the tremendous economic opportunities AI adoption will bring, while protecting critical data, safeguarding people’s information and ensuring Canadians’ data stays in Canada.” The framework requires data centres to pay their full electricity costs and invest in communities. In Centre Wellington’s council chambers, as the view through tall windows turned from daylight to sunset to inky black night, the mayor and councillors voted unanimously to pass a one-year moratorium on data centres.
