representative.title: Ice Age Arctic Ocean Was Cut Off From the Atlantic and Filled With
representative.author: Violet Maxwell

snapshot.title: Ice Age Arctic Ocean Was Cut Off From the Atlantic and Filled With
snapshot.evidenceText: One of the most contested ideas in polar science has just received a major boost from an unlikely corner of chemistry. For decades, scientists have debated whether the Arctic Ocean and the Nordic Seas—collectively known as the Arctic Mediterranean—were periodically sealed off from the North Atlantic during the deep freezes of the late Pleistocene, transforming into a vast, brackish lake beneath a kilometers-thick ice shelf. A new study published in Communications Earth & Environment now provides some of the strongest geochemical evidence yet that this dramatic scenario really happened, not once but repeatedly, during the glacial stages known as Marine Isotope Stages 6 and 4. The controversy began in 2021, when researchers reported widespread intervals in Arctic sediments that were barren of excess thorium-230, an isotope produced in seawater from the decay of dissolved uranium, alongside strikingly low concentrations of the cosmogenic isotope beryllium-10, which rains down from the atmosphere. The original team interpreted these signals as evidence of a freshwater-filled Arctic Ocean: without salty, uranium-bearing Atlantic water, little thorium-230 would be produced, and a permanent ice cover would starve the sea of atmospheric beryllium-10. Critics countered that sudden pulses of sediment could simply have diluted both isotopes, leaving the ocean connected after all. The debate has raged ever since, because the interpretation carries enormous implications for how the global climate system behaved during ice ages. The new research, led by Agathe Ollive of the Alfred Wegener Institute in Bremerhaven together with colleagues from Germany and Norway, sidesteps this dispute by turning to a cleverer tracer: the ratio of two beryllium isotopes, beryllium-10 and beryllium-9, measured in the reactive fraction of seafloor sediments. The beauty of this ratio lies in its resilience. While the concentrations of each isotope individually can be skewed by changing sedimentation rates and particle scavenging, normalizing beryllium-10 against beryllium-9 largely cancels out those effects. What remains is a fingerprint of the water masses themselves—essentially a chemical tag that records which waters bathed the seafloor when the sediments were deposited. The logic of the test is elegantly simple. Today, the Arctic Ocean is fed by two very different beryllium sources. Atlantic water carries a dissolved beryllium-10 to beryllium-9 ratio of roughly 5 to 7 times ten to the minus eight atoms per atom, while Arctic rivers deliver beryllium with ratios below 1.5 times ten to the minus eight. If North Atlantic inflow had continued during the glacial intervals in question, the sedimentary ratio should have stayed near Atlantic values. But if the Arctic Mediterranean was truly cut off and gradually freshened by river discharge, the ratio should have collapsed toward riverine signatures. The team measured 84 samples from sediment cores spanning the central Arctic Ocean, the Lomonosov Ridge, the Yermak Plateau, the Barents Sea slope, the Morris Jessup Rise, the Nordic Seas and the North Atlantic, at water depths from about 1,073 to 2,802 meters. The result was unambiguous. During the low-thorium glacial intervals, reactive beryllium-10 to beryllium-9 ratios fell to between 0.06 and 0.64 times ten to the minus eight—uniformly low values that are not merely riverine but even below the range of modern Arctic rivers. Remarkably, this signature appeared at every site, across all the major basins of the Arctic Mediterranean, despite huge differences in water depth, sedimentation rate and sediment source. Such basin-wide homogeneity is exactly what an isolated, freshened sea would produce, and it is utterly incompatible with an active Atlantic inflow, which would have delivered beryllium with ratios one to two orders of magnitude higher. During the warm interglacial of Marine Isotope Stage 5e, by contrast, the ratios rebounded to around 4 times ten to the minus eight in the Nordic Seas and about 1.4 times ten to the minus eight in the central Arctic, matching the signatures of Atlantic-influenced waters seen in modern deep Arctic sediments. The team then extended the story into the open Atlantic by analyzing core MD95-2016, a site today bathed in dense overflow waters spilling across the Greenland-Scotland Ridge. Because this core contains a continuous oxygen isotope record, it could be aligned precisely to global stratigraphy. Both the Atlantic core and the Nordic Seas core recorded nearly identical beryllium ratios of about 5 times ten to the minus eight during the interglacial, confirming an open connection. But during the MIS6 glaciation, both records plunged. The researchers interpret the low value in the North Atlantic core as marking the moment of reconnection, when water with an extremely low beryllium isotope ratio—stored up in the isolated Arctic during millennia of isolation—suddenly overflowed the Greenland-Scotland Ridge and flooded into the Atlantic. Crucially, the beryllium evidence converges with entirely independent tracers. In a central Arctic core, the glacial drop in beryllium-10 to beryllium-9 coincides with shifts in neodymium, hafnium and strontium isotopes away from North Atlantic endmember values and toward compositions characteristic of Siberian rivers draining the Putorana Basalts into the Kara Sea. The absence of dinocysts and planktic foraminifera in cores from the same intervals further points to a shutdown of Atlantic water and harsh surface conditions. When multiple unrelated proxy systems all swing in the same direction at the same time, the case for a genuine circulation reorganization becomes very difficult to dismiss. The authors also ran a steady-state mass balance model to test whether anything other than isolation could explain the numbers. Under modern conditions, the North Atlantic inflow supplies roughly 70 percent of the beryllium-10 entering the Arctic Ocean, and the model reproduces the observed water-column ratio of about 5.14 times ten to the minus eight. Reducing atmospheric deposition under permanent sea ice lowers the ratio by only about 20 percent—nowhere near enough. Closing the Bering Strait actually raises the modeled ratio slightly, because the Pacific inflow carries a relatively low signature. Even catastrophic meltwater outbursts from ice-dammed lakes such as Lake Komi and Lake Yamal, with combined volumes exceeding 30,000 cubic kilometers, could push the ratio down only to about 1.56 times ten to the minus eight. Only a complete shutdown of Atlantic inflow reproduces the measured glacial values of around 0.85 times ten to the minus eight. The team likewise ruled out hyperpycnal sediment flows, nepheloid plumes, brine rejection and benthic fluxes from seafloor diagenesis as primary drivers, each on quantitative grounds. The combined weight of the thorium and beryllium systems points to a single coherent picture: during parts of MIS6 and MIS4, the Arctic Mediterranean was largely cut off from the global ocean, its salts progressively replaced by river freshwater within perhaps less than 10,000 years, all sealed beneath a grounded ice shelf that blocked exchange across the shallow straits of the Greenland-Scotland Ridge. Such a state would have fundamentally altered deep-water renewal, strengthened stratification and limited oxygen penetration to the deep basins—conditions consistent with geochemical hints of past anoxia in both the Canadian and Eurasian Basins. It would also have meant that a key nursery of today's Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation simply switched off. Perhaps the most tantalizing implication lies at the end of each isolation episode. When the Arctic ice shelf collapsed and the straits reopened, the enormous reservoir of low-salinity water accumulated over millennia would have been released through Fram Strait in short order. Whether such pulses were powerful enough to disrupt North Atlantic thermohaline circulation and trigger the abrupt cooling events recorded in ice cores remains an open question, and one the authors flag as a priority for future work. What is already clear is that the Arctic Ocean of the ice ages was not simply a colder version of today's sea. It was, at times, a fundamentally different world—a giant, dark, freshwater basin sealed beneath ice, waiting for the lid to come off. representative.title: What's next for Issue 7A after unprecdented Colorado ballot error
representative.author: Katie Langford

snapshot.title: After unprecedented Colorado ballot error, what’s next for Front Range rail measure?
snapshot.evidenceText: Colorado election officials and Front Range Passenger Rail District leaders are in a bureaucratic quagmire after a communication failure caused four counties to send ballots that erroneously contained Issue 7A to roughly 800,000 voters starting late last week. State election officials sent guidance to the affected county clerks — Adams, Arapahoe, Douglas and Weld — late Wednesday on how to properly count the ballots, and election officials have pledged that only votes cast by those who are eligible to vote on Issue 7A will be counted. And while former election officials and law experts who spoke to The Denver Post on Thursday disagreed about the severity of the problem, all agreed the scale of the error is unheard of. “I am not aware of anything anywhere remotely near this magnitude occurring,” former Secretary of State Wayne Williams said. “You’re not talking about a few voters or a couple ballots that were in error, you’re talking about hundreds of thousands.” State and Front Range Passenger Rail District officials confirmed the error on Wednesday after learning that hundreds of thousands of ballots were printed to include Issue 7A, which asks voters to approve a sales tax increase to fund the expansion of the Colorado Connector, despite those voters not living within the district and not being eligible to vote on the measure. The error is connected to a 2026 law that changed the boundaries of the district to include only certain cities and towns along the proposed rail line. Updated information about the district boundaries never made its way to some county election officials, but accounts of how the communication breakdown happened vary. El Paso County Clerk and Recorder Steve Schleiker said he emailed the Front Range Passenger Rail District in July to request updated district boundaries ahead of the election and never heard back. The Denver Post reviewed a copy of the email Schleiker sent to the district’s general information inbox on July 23. Schleiker’s office eventually assigned boundaries to Issue 7A based on guidance from the 2026 legislation, Senate Bill 172, and used the municipal boundaries already in the county system, Schleiker said. Rail district general manager Sal Pace said the agency did not have a record of Schleiker’s email, but acknowledged not responding was an oversight. Front Range Passenger Rail District staff met with the Colorado County Clerk’s Association and “a number” of county clerks in March about the boundary changes and followed up in April, Pace said. The Colorado County Clerk’s Association did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday and Thursday. Doug Spencer, a law professor at the University of Colorado, said he can’t think of any similar ballot errors in Colorado. Usually county clerks know about changes to the ballot, like if a candidate withdraws at the last minute, he said. “This is just a disorganized miscommunication and a mess,” Spencer said. “But I don’t think it undermines democracy or calls into question how these systems run.” If anything, the mistake will add to rhetoric around election and ballot security, Spencer said. Federal officials in the Trump administration have repeatedly criticized and worked to limit mail-in voting . “This is really unfortunate because this isn’t actually a problem, it’s a bureaucratic snafu that won’t have an effect on the outcome but will give fuel to the argument that mail-in ballots are insecure,” he said. However, the system worked in finding the error before votes were counted, Spencer added. Williams — who lost reelection to current Secretary of State Jena Griswold in 2018 — said Griswold’s office bears some responsibility for the error and should have reached out to county clerks about the district boundary changes. “There’s a basic level of following the legal requirement and then there’s being proactive, addressing issues and being aware of things,” Williams said. “That’s the higher level we have the right to expect from people at the state.” A spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office did not respond to an email seeking an interview with Griswold. In response to a question about whether the secretary of state’s office communicated with county clerks about the rail district change, spokesperson Jack Todd on Friday morning said the Department of State is not responsible for notifying counties of the boundaries for special district elections. In a letter to the county clerks in Adams, Arapahoe, Douglas and Weld counties on Wednesday night, state election officials said most ballots will be processed normally because voting systems will be able to tell which ballots should be counted for Issue 7A and which should not. A small number of ballots in Bow Mar and Sterling Ranch may need to be counted by hand because of issues with different ballot styles. Those who voted on Issue 7A but were not eligible to do so will have their ballots duplicated onto the correct ballot style, state officials said. “We will support the counties to identify this group and make sure they follow the appropriate processes,” agency officials said. Pace on Thursday sought to redirect the conversation to what the district says passenger rail could correct, pointing to a Denver Regional Council of Governments estimate that increasing vehicle congestion in metro Denver will eventually cause rush hour to start at 2 p.m., rather than 5 p.m. “That’s why we have to do something about it,” he said. “That’s why we have to put our head down and focus on the mission at hand.”

snapshot.title: In 2006, Maryland couple bought a 116-acre farm. 20 years later, it
snapshot.evidenceText: When Louise and John Durocher from Maryland decided to buy a 116-acre farm in Kent County, they didn’t know that it would become a thriving wildlife haven, providing food and shelter to diverse wildlife. Initially, the Durochers bought the Tavern Creek Farm in 2006 for hunting, but 2 decades later they stopped growing crops and instead decided to give as much land as possible to nature. The gesture proved to be fruitful, as now the farm is bustling with animals and a wide range of plant species.Farm secured for conservation, native trees plantedThe Tavern Creek Farm has been permanently conserved through an easement with the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy (ESLC), as per a statement released by the organisation.134785711Louise and John Durocher planted shrubs, wildflowers, native grasses, as well as different varieties of trees, including white oaks, black walnuts, river birches, sycamores, pawpaws and tulip poplars, to name a few.Restored habitats support wildlife and protect waterwaysThe couple’s efforts finally paid off with open meadows connecting with forests through hedgerows. The space has become a haven for otters, beavers, opossums, muskrats and several other migratory birdsApart from that, the property also has about 26 acres of wetlands and 24 acres of woodland. With over 9,000 ft of the farm borders in Tavern Creek, trees and other vegetation help protect water quality in the Chesapeake Bay too.Preserving a family legacy for future generationsDurochers’ granddaughter, Sarah Starman, takes care of the Tavern Creek Farm. According to a report by People magazine, she has been watching the landscape grow and her grandparents nurturing it to usher change.134760089For Sarah, however, protecting the farm is not only about preserving the trees, wetlands, and wildlife. She is also keen on preserving the life her family has built around them over the years. In conclusion, Sarah hopes that the next generations will also kayak and fish in Tavern Creek, enjoying being one with nature.

representative.title: Who can hold al-Sharaa to account? Syria’s Constitutional Court and the president who appointed it – Who Rules Syria?

snapshot.title: Who can hold al-Sharaa to account? Syria’s Constitutional Court and the president who appointed it
snapshot.evidenceText: A constitutional court is meant to decide whether those in power have respected the constitution — including the head of state. In July 2026 Syria acquired a new Supreme Constitutional Court. This dossier sets out, from the official texts, who chose its judges, what it may and may not do, and whether it, or anyone else, can hold Ahmed al-Sharaa to account if he breaches the Constitutional Declaration he issued. Article 47 of the Constitutional Declaration of 13 March 2025 dissolved the existing court and provides: “The Supreme Constitutional Court consists of seven members named by the President of the Republic from among persons of integrity, competence and experience. The mechanism of its work and its competences are regulated by law.” 1 On 5 July 2026, sixteen months after the old court was dissolved, al-Sharaa signed Decree 149 of 2026, published on 7 July. It appoints Issam Khaled al-Khalif as president of the court and six members: judges Khairallah Nadim Ghannoum, Mohammed Mustafa Sbei’ and Iman Antoine Nouri, the academics Ismail Hamadi al-Khalfan and Ri’an Hassan Kuhailan, and the lawyer Aref Ahmad al-Shaal. 3 4 Under Article 3 of the decree, the judges swear their oath “before the President of the Republic”: “I swear by Almighty God to respect the Constitutional Declaration and to perform my duty with honesty and sincerity.” They did so on 11 July 2026 at the People’s Palace in Damascus, before al-Sharaa. 3 5 Until a law on the court is issued, Article 4 of the decree gives it four tasks: The decree does not say who may bring a challenge to a law, and gives no route for citizens, ordinary courts or a group of members of parliament to bring a case. It sets no term of office. As of its publication, the law that is meant to regulate the court had not been issued; at its first meeting on 19 July the court discussed a draft. 3 6 2 The presidency published the names and titles without explaining why each member was chosen. 6 We have no evidence of how any individual judge has ruled or will rule; what follows concerns the structure of the court, not the integrity of its members. The Constitutional Declaration contains no article on the president’s legal responsibility. It gives the People’s Assembly no power to charge, try or remove him, and gives the Constitutional Court no jurisdiction to try him. The only provision on the end of a presidency is Article 34: “in the event of a vacancy in the presidency, the First Vice President assumes the powers of the President of the Republic” — and the vice presidents are appointed and dismissed by the president. 1 Under the 2012 constitution, the president also named the members of the constitutional court (Article 141). But the text gave them a four-year term (Article 143) and stated that they could not be removed except in accordance with the law (Article 144). They swore their oath before the president “and in the presence of the speaker of the People’s Assembly”, promising to perform their duty “with impartiality and honesty” (Article 145). One fifth of the Assembly could challenge a law or a legislative decree before the court, and a party to a case could raise the unconstitutionality of a law before the courts (Article 147). Article 117 allowed the Assembly, by a two-thirds vote, to indict the president for high treason, and he was to be tried “before the Supreme Constitutional Court”. 8 These guarantees existed on paper only. In 2022 Syrians for Truth and Justice (STJ) concluded that presidential appointment had given Assad’s court merely “formal independence” and made it “a tool in the hands of the President of the Republic”. 9 The 2025 declaration and Decree 149 keep presidential appointment and leave out the term of office, the protection from removal, the parliamentary challenge and the treason procedure. 1 3 Human Rights Watch wrote in March 2025 that Article 47 “grants the president the authority to appoint all seven members of the Higher Constitutional Court without parliamentary or other oversight”, so that “the judiciary may have limited ability to hold the president accountable”, and that the declaration establishes “a rigid presidential model, with no parliamentary ability to impeach the president”. 10 In July 2025 STJ wrote that because the court is appointed “exclusively” by the president it becomes “an executive tool with a judicial cover”, and that the declaration deprives the People’s Assembly of the power to remove the president. 11 After Decree 149, Souria al-Ghad argued that appointing two drafters of the declaration to the court that interprets it “weakens the institutional distance required between drafting and oversight”. 6 According to the Kurdish news agency ANHA, the government argues that these powers reflect “the exceptional nature of the transitional phase”, and that full legal safeguards will come with the law regulating the court. 2 Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais said that with the formation of the court and the People’s Assembly “the constitutional pillars of the Syrian state are complete”. 12 The texts show that every member of Syria’s Supreme Constitutional Court was chosen by Ahmed al-Sharaa alone and swore its oath before him, that the court’s president came from the administration al-Sharaa’s movement ran in Idlib, that two members helped write the text they are to interpret, and that only al-Sharaa or the speaker can ask the court what that text means. They show no procedure — before the court, the Assembly or anyone else — by which the president can be charged or removed for breaching the Constitutional Declaration. 1 3 6 They do not show how the court will rule, whether its judges will act independently, or what the promised law on the court will contain. We have found no ruling or opinion issued by the court so far. We will update this page when the law is issued and when the court rules. Is Syria a democracy? Is al-Sharaa a dictator? representative.title: Silent killer in Sundarbans: Parasitic plants eating away at Sundari trees
representative.author: TIMES Report

snapshot.title: Silent killer in Sundarbans: Parasitic plants eating away at Sundari trees
snapshot.evidenceText: Sundari tree (Heritiera fomes), the principal flora and namesake of the world’s largest mangrove forest, is confronting a catastrophic new crisis in the Sundarbans: a widespread infestation of parasitic plants. Once restricted to branch tips, these parasites are now invading the main trunks of the trees, draining their essential sap and causing them to rapidly weaken, turn yellow, and die. Coming alongside the long-standing threat of salinity-induced top-dying disease, this escalating infestation has raised severe alarm across the Forest Department and scientific circles, with experts warning that the Sundari tree could face extinction within one to two decades if left unchecked. Spanning approximately 10,000 square kilometres across Bangladesh and India, the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Sundarbans mangrove forest covers 6,517 square kilometres within Bangladesh’s Khulna, Bagerhat, and Satkhira districts—representing 66 per cent of its total expanse. Home to 334 plant species, 453 wildlife species, and hundreds of criss-crossing waterways, the forest’s latest 2024 survey recorded 184 plant species, with Sundari, Gewa, and Goran collectively making up 70 per cent of the total canopy. The naturally sturdy Sundari tree plays a vital structural role by anchoring coastal soil against erosion and serving as a natural green wall against raging ocean waves, cyclones, storm surges, and saltwater intrusion from the Bay of Bengal. Moreover, its complex root systems and fallen leaves provide essential shelter and nursery grounds for numerous species of fish, prawns, and other wildlife, forming the bedrock of the Royal Bengal Tiger’s prey base and the entire mangrove ecosystem. Environmental pressures driven by climate change – including sea-level rise, frequent natural disasters, and extreme ocean salinity – are severely degrading the forest. Abnormal storm surges repeatedly submerge the forest floor with saline silt, creating an environment that fosters parasitic plants, creepers, and fungi. The crisis is particularly acute in the Eastern Sundarbans, where the once swift-flowing Bhola River has silted up into a narrow canal along a 16-kilometre stretch. Running between the forest and human habitations from the Daser Bharani Forest Patrol Post in Sharankhola Range to Joymoni, via the Nangli Patrol Post in Chandpai Range, Dhansagar station, Jiudhara station, and Kodalmateji Patrol Post, the choked waterway is now locally known as “Mora Bhola.” Related News Unplanned development destroying Cox’s Bazar nature: Anu Muhammad 146 elephants died in Bangladesh between 2016 and 2025: Minister Akash Neer: Dhaka’s new rooftop sanctuary for birds, biodiversity Scientists discover nine new deep sea sponge species The choking of the river has killed off internal forest canals and reduced freshwater inflows, accelerating top-dying disease and parasitic attacks on Sundari trees throughout the region. More than one million people directly depend on the Sundarbans for their survival, earning their living by catching fish and crabs, gathering honey and wax, cutting thatch grass, reeds, and golpatta (nipa palm), or working in tourism. Local forest workers report a dramatic decline in resources. Honey collectors Md Shahjahan Akon, aged 60, and Md Awal Khan, 55, from Khuriakhali village in Sharankhola upazila, who have harvested honey for 30 to 35 years, stated that former dense jungle zones have turned sparse as Sundari trees die off. Because honeybees do not build hives on dead trees, collectors now trek four to five kilometres without sighting a single honeycomb. Similarly, fishermen Md Ashraf Ali Faraji, 70, and Md Rustom Goldar, 60, from the same village noted that prized canal fish species such as Chitra, Shilon Tengra, and Dogri have virtually vanished due to silted waterways and lost tree canopy. The forest crisis also threatens thriving local e-commerce ventures. Online entrepreneurs such as Russel Ahmed from Sharankhola and Hafizur Rahman from Shyamnagar, Satkhira, who package and deliver forest fish, organic honey, golpatta molasses, and keora pickles across the country – generating Tk100,000 to Tk150,000 in monthly sales alongside running tour operations – expressed deep concern after observing vast stands of parasite-stricken, dead Sundari trees during their forest trips. They warn that the collapse of the Sundari tree will devastate the economy of the south-western region. Forest Department estimates indicate that 25 to 30 per cent of Sundari trees in the Sundarbans are currently infested by parasites. Highlighting the gravity of the situation, Prof Dr Wasiul Islam of the Forestry and Wood Technology Discipline at Khulna University noted that rising salinity from climate change is altering forest structure and accelerating die-offs. He warned that because artificial plantation is impossible inside the natural mangrove ecosystem, a failure to conduct comprehensive scientific research into controlling the parasite could lead to the complete collapse of the forest, its biodiversity, and coastal livelihoods. Concurrently, Dr Md Latiful Islam, Chief Scientific Officer at the Saltwater Station (Khulna) of the Bangladesh Fisheries Research Institute, explained that declining Sundari roots and leaf litter disrupt fish breeding grounds. He added that overall fish stocks are falling due to a combination of habitat loss, salinity, poison fishing, overfishing, and unplanned harvesting, placing the region’s large fishing community at risk of total economic ruin. Addressing these critical concerns, Md Rezaul Karim Chowdhury, divisional forest officer of the Sundarban East Forest Division in Bagerhat, confirmed that 25 to 30 per cent of Sundari trees across the Sharankhola and Chandpai ranges are infested with parasites, creating a major conservation crisis on top of existing top-dying disease. He pledged that the Forest Department will promptly initiate scientific research focused on the parasite. Regarding river restoration, DFO Chowdhury stated that out of the 16-kilometre silted section of the Bhola River, approximately one kilometre was excavated under the Sundarban Protection Project before work was suspended. Plans are now underway to resume and complete the remaining excavation, which he emphasised will restore vital freshwater flow and bring renewed vitality to a vast area of the Sundarbans. representative.author: "Norvan Acquah

snapshot.title: Dagbon Sets Jobs, Environmental Safeguards and Transparency Conditions for GNPC’s Voltaian Basin Drilling
snapshot.evidenceText:
" 
 	 Dagbon Sets Jobs, Environmental Safeguards and Transparency Conditions for GNPC’s Voltaian Basin Drilling 
 
Traditional authorities in Dagbon have set out a clear package of community expectations for the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation and its exploration subsidiary as preparations advance towards the first exploratory well in the Voltaian Basin.

The demands—local employment, skills development, environmental protection, community investment and transparent engagement—highlight the social and political tests that will accompany GNPC’s attempt to establish whether Ghana’s vast onshore basin contains commercially viable petroleum resources.

They also expose a lesson from Ghana’s offshore petroleum experience: finding hydrocarbons does not automatically translate into locally visible development, and community confidence must be built before drilling begins rather than after commercial expectations have hardened.

The issues emerged during a condolence visit by a joint delegation from GNPC and GNPC Explorco to the Regent of Dagbon, Kampakuya Naa Yakubu Abukari II, at the Gbewaa Palace in Yendi following the death of the Overlord of Dagbon.

The delegation was led by GNPC chief executive Kwame Ntow Amoah, who is also a board member of GNPC Explorco, and Explorco managing director Samuel Opoku Arthur. Other members included senior executives from both institutions and GNPC Foundation managing director Helga Boadi.

Although the immediate purpose was to express condolences, the engagement inevitably extended into the relationship between Dagbon and the emerging exploration programme.

Speaking on behalf of the Regent, Zangbalun Naa Dr Jacob Yakubu II urged GNPC and Explorco to ensure that their operations create tangible employment and capacity-building opportunities for young people in Dagbon.

He also called for strong environmental protection, direct benefits for communities through meaningful social investment and consistent communication between the companies, traditional leaders and people living within the project area.

The palace further requested corporate support for the continuing construction of the historic Gbewaa Palace. Press Release - GNPC and GNPC Explorco Pay Condolence Visit to Regent of Dagbon.docx

The Regent’s demands should not be treated as ceremonial requests attached to a traditional engagement. They represent the foundations of the social licence that GNPC will require if exploration is to proceed without creating community resentment or unrealistic expectations.

GNPC and Explorco are preparing to drill the TUA-1X exploratory well at Chegu in the Mion District. The programme will move the Voltaian Basin campaign from years of seismic surveys and geological interpretation into direct subsurface testing.

Preparatory works are expected to include construction of a 13.5-kilometre access road, a drilling pad, a base camp and other infrastructure needed for the safe mobilisation of a rig.

Even before drilling starts, such works will affect land access, local transport, employment expectations, procurement relationships and interactions between technical teams and host communities.

This is why the palace’s demand for communication is consequential. In resource exploration, an information vacuum can quickly be filled by speculation.

The arrival of earth-moving equipment, contractors and drilling machinery may be interpreted by residents as confirmation that oil has already been discovered. Land values may change. Individuals may rush to acquire property near the site. Local businesses may borrow or expand in anticipation of a petroleum economy that does not yet exist.

Political actors may also present an exploratory programme as a development breakthrough before the geological evidence supports such a conclusion.

GNPC has therefore been careful to emphasise that the drilling of a well does not amount to the discovery of oil or gas.

Mr Ntow Amoah said the exploratory well was intended to determine whether hydrocarbons were present and, if so, whether they possessed characteristics capable of supporting commercial development.

“An exploratory well does not mean oil or gas has already been found,” he said during an earlier engagement on the project.

That warning is more than technical caution. It is essential expectation management.

A well may encounter no hydrocarbons. It may encounter traces that are too small, too difficult or too expensive to develop. Even a technically successful discovery would still require appraisal, economic evaluation, regulatory approvals, infrastructure planning and substantial investment before production could begin.

GNPC must therefore communicate two ideas simultaneously: the Voltaian Basin could represent a significant opportunity, but the TUA-1X well remains an experiment designed to answer a geological question.

The Regent’s emphasis on jobs and capacity building also raises an important policy issue. Local content cannot be postponed until a commercial discovery is announced.

The exploration stage already creates demand for civil works, logistics, catering, transport, accommodation, security, environmental monitoring and other support services. Not every role will require specialised petroleum qualifications.

GNPC and Explorco should identify which immediate contracts can be performed competitively by businesses in the operational area and publish transparent qualification requirements. Local participation should be designed around capability and value rather than reduced to political allocation or token recruitment.

At the same time, the companies must avoid promising that every local demand can be met through direct employment. Exploration campaigns are capital-intensive and technically specialised, but they do not necessarily generate large numbers of permanent jobs.

A better approach would combine short-term employment with deliberate capability building. Residents and local businesses should be trained for services that remain valuable even if the well is unsuccessful, including construction, road maintenance, occupational safety, environmental sampling, equipment support and general logistics.

This matters because a local-content policy tied exclusively to a petroleum discovery creates a dangerous dependency. If drilling does not produce a commercial result, communities may be left with disappointed expectations and few transferable benefits.

The quality of the project’s local-content strategy should therefore be measured not only by how many people are hired, but by how many workers and businesses become more capable after the exploration phase.

The Voltaian Basin is an onshore exploration area. Unlike Ghana’s producing offshore fields, activities will take place close to farms, settlements, roads, water resources and traditional landholding systems.

That proximity changes the environmental and social risk profile.

Access-road construction and site preparation can disturb land, alter drainage patterns, generate dust and affect farming activity before the drill penetrates the ground. Drilling itself creates additional requirements involving waste management, water use, chemicals, noise, emergency response and restoration of the site.

The Regent’s request for strict environmental protection should therefore translate into a disclosed management framework covering the entire exploration cycle.

Communities should know how land will be acquired or temporarily accessed, how compensation will be determined, how grievances can be submitted, how water quality will be monitored and what will happen to the site if the well is unsuccessful.

The baseline condition of water, soil, vegetation and livelihoods should be documented before major construction begins. Without baseline data, it becomes difficult to establish whether subsequent changes were caused by project activities or unrelated developments.

GNPC and Explorco should also define their rehabilitation obligations at the start. A dry well is not the end of corporate responsibility. Roads, drilling areas and temporary facilities must either be restored or formally transferred for agreed community use.

The project’s environmental credibility will rest less on declarations that operations will be sustainable and more on the publication of measurable standards, monitoring results and corrective actions.

The palace also requested direct community benefits through social investments.

This creates both an opportunity and a risk. Carefully selected investments can strengthen healthcare, education, water access, skills and local economic participation. Poorly structured corporate social responsibility can instead become a collection of discretionary donations with limited long-term effect.

GNPC Foundation’s involvement offers a route for aligning social investment with broader development priorities. However, projects should emerge from structured community-needs assessments rather than informal requests alone.

The strongest investments would complement district development plans and address constraints connected to the exploration programme. These could include vocational training, maternal healthcare, potable water, local road safety, agricultural productivity and support for young enterprises seeking to participate in supply chains.

Traditional leaders, district authorities, community representatives, women’s groups and young people should participate in deciding priorities. That process would reduce the risk that benefits become concentrated among politically or socially influential groups.

The palace’s request for support towards the Gbewaa Palace is understandable given the institution’s historical importance. Any such support should nevertheless be transparently separated from statutory compensation, local-content expenditure and wider community-development commitments.

Clear classification would protect both GNPC and the traditional authority from perceptions that cultural support is being exchanged for consent to exploration.

The TUA-1X programme is also an institutional test for GNPC Explorco.

Ghana’s petroleum sector has historically depended heavily on international oil companies for exploration, field development and operations. A state-led onshore campaign offers GNPC an opportunity to demonstrate that it can move beyond holding interests in projects towards building technical and operational capacity of its own.

The immediate objective of the well is to collect subsurface information. Even if it does not produce a commercial discovery, the data could improve understanding of the Voltaian Basin’s geology and guide future exploration decisions.

That means success should not be defined solely as finding oil.

A technically sound well, safely delivered within a defensible budget and accompanied by high-quality geological data, could still advance Ghana’s knowledge of the basin. Conversely, even a hydrocarbon indication would be undermined by cost overruns, environmental damage, weak procurement or damaged community relationships.

The economics of frontier-basin exploration require particular discipline because uncertainty is high. Each stage of expenditure must be justified by the information it is expected to produce.

GNPC should therefore disclose enough information for the public to understand the project’s milestones, without compromising commercially sensitive geological data. Relevant disclosures could include procurement progress, environmental approvals, community agreements, site-development milestones, safety performance and high-level expenditure categories.

Transparency would help prevent the project from becoming another public-sector venture surrounded by large expectations but limited public accountability.

Mr Opoku Arthur thanked the Regent, traditional authorities and communities for the cooperation extended to technical teams working in the area.

“As we move forward, maintaining this relationship through open communication and continuous engagement will be critical to the successful delivery of the project,” he said.

That statement correctly recognises that community trust is not a public-relations accessory. It is an operational asset.

A project with strong community relations is more likely to secure access, resolve grievances early, protect infrastructure and maintain continuity. A project characterised by secrecy and unmet expectations can face opposition, delays and escalating costs even before its geological prospects are known.

The condolence visit therefore represents more than corporate courtesy. It is part of the institutional relationship through which GNPC and Explorco must explain risk, negotiate expectations and demonstrate respect for traditional authority.

But goodwill will have to be converted into systems.

There should be permanent community liaison structures, regular public briefings, accessible grievance channels and clear reporting on commitments made during engagements. Communities should not have to wait for high-level visits to obtain basic information about activities occurring on their land.

The presence of Mion Member of Parliament Misbahu Mahama Adams and District Chief Executive Hamzah Azindow Moabalyn signals that both political and local-government institutions will be involved in the project’s social environment. Their participation can improve coordination, but it also makes transparency essential to prevent local benefits from being politicised.

The Voltaian Basin programme could eventually broaden Ghana’s petroleum map beyond the offshore western corridor. If commercial resources are discovered, the implications for investment, infrastructure, employment and national energy planning could be significant.

But that outcome remains uncertain.

The first meaningful measure of success will therefore not be the quantity of oil or gas encountered. It will be whether GNPC and Explorco can execute a technically credible exploration campaign while respecting communities, protecting the environment and managing public expectations.

Dagbon’s traditional leadership has already stated the terms on which it expects that relationship to proceed: jobs, skills, environmental safeguards, visible development and honest communication.

GNPC has responded by promising responsible operations and continuous engagement. The real test begins when construction equipment arrives, contracts are awarded, land is accessed and the effects of exploration become tangible.

If those commitments are honoured, the TUA-1X campaign could build both geological knowledge and confidence in Ghana’s national oil company.

If they are treated as ceremonial assurances, GNPC may discover that the hardest risk in the Voltaian Basin is not buried beneath the ground. It is the loss of trust above it."

representative.title: An Heir in Cetera
representative.author: Nathan Thornburgh

snapshot.title: An Heir in Cetara
snapshot.evidenceText: In an ancient village on the Amalfi Coast, one family has made colatura the same slow way since 1950. Now the question is who comes next. This place, Cetara, is old. Not like Paris old or Edinburgh old. Far older. So old that it served, for the ancient Greeks, as a sort of Here Be Dragons part of the world just on the edge of their maps. The Greeks feared the people who lived there—even as they were trying to colonize them—and processed that fear into some of their greatest stories. Not far from here are the three small islands that Strabo called the Sirenuse, home to the half-woman, half-bird enchantresses who lured sailors to their deaths, until Odysseus outsmarted them. The siren song remains strong here in Cetara. The village is well hidden from the crowds that choke the rest of the Amalfi Coast, with a little bobbing fishing fleet in the harbor and a pocket beach guarded by a sixteenth-century stone watchtower. Ask chef Pasquale Torrente, and he will gladly tell you about how the village (with the help of some fried fish and a couple bottles of wine) finally soothed a very hungover Anthony Bourdain, who filmed with him there for a 2011 episode of No Reservations . “By the end of the shoot,” says Torrente, “Anthony said he would buy that tower and live there for the rest of his life.” You can mark Cetara’s age in its most famous product: colatura di alici , the concentrated essence of salted anchovies, splashed on spaghetti or stirred into broth. It’s a medieval descendant of the garum that Romans were making on this spot two thousand years ago. At the Fabbrica Nettuno workshop up on the hill, the process remains unbroken from the Middle Ages: stack anchovies and salt in a wooden barrel, press them, age them, and collect the extract that seeps out from the bottom. snapshot.title: K. Star: Attempts to stir tensions in Hasakah, Our people must remain vigilant
snapshot.evidenceText: Two children injured over bomb explosion in Homs countryside Vienna protest demands constitutional recognition of Kurdish Language Bakur Kurdistan delegation visits Institutions and YPJ in Hasakah Israeli forces detain 3 shepherds in Quneitra Kongra Star stresses unity against attempts to sow discord Mano Khalil prepares new film about Kurds in Rojava Jal Agha meeting condemns international plot against Ocalan North Kurdistan delegation meets Hasakah governor Mazloum Abdi stresses importance of uniting region’s components Protesters block Damascus–Baghdad highway with burning tires in Dumayr Return convoy for displaced families from Serêkaniyê postponed until Tuesday Acts of vandalism targeted Martyrs’ Families Council headquarter in Tel Tamer Delegation from North Kurdistan meets with Mazloum Abdi Martyrs of 12 March stadium prepares to host Syrian premier league matches after renovation Kongra Star has warned against attempts to stir discord in Hasakah, saying that internal and external actors are seeking to fuel conflict in Syria amid tensions that have gripped the city over the past two days. In a statement issued in Kurdish on Saturday and translated into Arabic by ANHA agency, Kongra Star said developments in Hasakah coinciding with the anniversary of the October 9 international conspiracy point to deliberate attempts to provoke tensions, stressing that the timing is no coincidence. The statement said escalating tensions, interference affecting civilians and attempts to target Kurdish neighborhoods threaten peaceful coexistence and regional security. It also warned of the consequences of armed groups moving toward Hasakah from al-Shaddadi, Deir ez-Zor and Raqqa, saying that failure to stop their movements increases the risk of conflict between the region’s communities. Kongra Star stressed Hasakah’s strategic and historical importance as a city home to Kurds, Arabs and other communities, noting that its residents had previously suffered under Arabization policies. It also recalled the city’s role in the fight against ISIS mercenaries, particularly on the fronts of Hasakah, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and al-Shaddadi. The statement said the current developments target the forces and political parties that contributed to defeating ISIS mercenaries and seek to undermine relations among the region’s communities. It stressed that the situation in Hasakah cannot be viewed as merely a local crisis, but is linked to policies pursued by internal and external actors seeking to expand their influence in the region. It warned against attempts to revive Baathist policies based on dismantling social cohesion and fueling divisions among peoples through armed groups and social unrest. Kongra Star called on the various communities in Hasakah to adopt a united position against provocations and continue democratic and organized activities. It stressed that preventing armed conflict is not the responsibility of Kurds or Arabs alone, but of all the region’s communities. Kongra Star also called on Syrian officials to fulfill their responsibilities in maintaining security, protecting civilians and controlling the movements of armed groups. It urged them to investigate how armed groups from al-Shaddadi and Deir ez-Zor reached Hasakah, identify those who allowed them to move and explain why they were not prevented from advancing toward Kurdish neighborhoods. Concluding its statement, Kongra Star called on the peoples of Rojava, democratic forces in Syria, women’s organizations and civil society organizations to act responsibly against attempts to incite discord and hostility, and to work to prevent any potential conflict in Hasakah from escalating or spreading to other parts of Syria. representative.title: Illegal sand extraction rampant in Bishwambharpur, threatening settlements with erosion
representative.author: Staff Reporter, Sunamganj

snapshot.title: Illegal sand extraction rampant in Bishwambharpur, threatening settlements with erosion
snapshot.evidenceText: Following the plundering of sand from the Morachela river and Jadukata in Sunamganj's Dowarabazar upazila, an organised group has now been accused of illegally extracting and transporting sand through various roads from unleased canals and rivers in Bishwambharpur upazila. Sand is being hauled day and night using trolleys, noshimons, and pickups. The unchecked extraction is changing the natural landscape of canals and adjacent land, leaving homesteads, croplands, and roads at risk of erosion. A journalist was also allegedly harassed while filming the transport of sand. Local residents alleged that an influential syndicate has long been extracting sand from the Kapna canal and the Dhopajan river. Those who protest are intimidated, leaving many afraid to speak out publicly. The upazila administration, however, maintained that it remains vigilant in curbing illegal sand lifting, while police said they have no information regarding the matter. Visits to different parts of Bishwambharpur upazila over the past few days and conversations with local residents revealed that sand is being transported via the roads of Chalban, Baghber, Mathurkandi, Kapna, and Karer Bazar. Traffic of sand-carrying vehicles increases significantly at night, with local sources saying over 50 vehicles move sand under the cover of darkness. A syndicate reportedly extorts Tk 200 from each vehicle. Local sources said a young man named Rumel from the Karer Bazar area leads this group. He could not be reached for comment regarding the allegation. A small trader from the Karer Bazar area, speaking on condition of anonymity, said many sand-laden trolleys move via Mathurkandi at night. "A syndicate is behind this. Locals suspect they are extracting sand in collusion with administration officials. No one dares to protest out of fear," he said. The trader added that a journalist was harassed a few days ago for filming the sand-carrying trolleys, and anyone protesting faces threats. The role of local public representatives has also come under scrutiny. Shafiqul Islam, a member of Palash Union Parishad, said some sand trolleys ply at night, but none of the representatives are involved. He said he had heard reports of a journalist being detained and harassed over filming a few days ago, claiming the matter was later settled through discussions. Asked who was involved in the extraction and transport, Shafiqul could not name anyone specifically, saying only that some local youths occasionally bring sand. Locals have accused several individuals of involvement in the illegal extraction and transport, identifying them as Mizanur, Hafiz, Suleman, Shahjahan, Deen Islam, Billal, Younus, Sabuj, Julhas, and Saddam, among others. Their comments could not be obtained. In the Mathurkandi and Kapna areas of the upazila's Salukabad union, sand extraction was witnessed firsthand. Residents alleged that prolonged extraction has altered the natural contours of canals and adjacent land, leaving houses in a cluster village and the Mathurkandi road at risk of collapse. Locals fear that continued extraction will cause further damage to homesteads, agricultural land, and road communication. They alleged that many hesitate to protest publicly due to fear of influential figures, and attempts to film the transport are met with obstacles. Frustration is mounting in the area, but no effective remedies have been taken, they added. Repeated calls to the mobile phone of Rumel for comments went unanswered. Bishwambharpur Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Sakina Akter visited the affected areas to stop illegal sand lifting. She said the administration remains alert regarding sand theft and is trying to raise awareness among locals. "However, those involved in sand extraction are often not found when we reach the spot. Cooperation from all is needed in this regard," she said. Bishwambharpur Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Ahad Ullah Bhuiyan said police had no information regarding sand plundering via roadways, adding that action would be taken if specific details about those involved were provided. Eisteddfod A SHORTAGE of cockles has forced a historic south Wales shellfish business to suspend production and lay off eight workers, highlighting the pressure on an industry that has supported coastal communities for generations. Parsons Pickles, which has been based in Burry Port since 1948, mothballed its Ashburnham Works factory in August after a sharp reduction in the quantity of cockles being landed. Its parent company, Lenger UK, described the season as among the most challenging in living memory. It said several beds had closed sooner than anticipated and harvesting volumes had fallen to exceptionally low levels. Cockles account for about 60 per cent of the company’s activities, leaving its traditional processing operation particularly exposed when supplies fall. Eight production workers were made redundant, although managers and some key staff were retained. The company said it hoped to restart production when conditions allowed it to operate sustainably. The suspension was not described as a permanent closure. Official figures make clear that the difficulties are not uniform across Wales. The Welsh Government’s August 2026 survey of the Three Rivers cockle fishery, covering beds around Llansteffan, Ferryside, Llanybri and St Ishmaels, estimated a total stock of 7,632 tonnes, down from 9,216 tonnes in August 2025. The estimated harvestable surplus was 1,307 tonnes, compared with 1,781 tonnes a year earlier — a reduction of about 27 per cent. The figure is calculated after allowing for minimum landing sizes and leaving sufficient shellfish to support feeding birds. The August 2026 assessment was a spot-check survey, so the comparison should be treated with that qualification. The Gwendraeth cockle bed remains closed until further notice, while the Llansteffan, Llanybri, Ferryside and St Ishmaels beds have been open under permit conditions since July. Nine frequency bands are used in the UK to deliver 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G coverage. Lower frequencies travel further but offer slower speeds, while higher frequencies have less range but are faster. The application shows that 2100MHz coverage would improve across much of Tenby and the surrounding area. representative.title: Still wielding a chainsaw at 85: the Australians restoring nature in retirement | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
representative.author: Rosamund Brennan

snapshot.title: Still wielding a chainsaw at 85: the Australians restoring nature in retirement
snapshot.evidenceText: For a growing band of older Australians, retirement has become an unlikely second act, spent rewilding mountains, counting sea slugs and coaxing damaged country back to life When Susan Downes stepped into the hallway of an old farmhouse for sale in York, Western Australia , she felt an oddly certain sense of knowing. “Oh, this is my house,” the retired GP remembers thinking. There was just one problem: it came with 200 hectares. Widowed and with her children grown, Downes, then in her 60s, was finally able to act on a long-held wish to move to the countryside. She had imagined something modest: an old house with “a little bit of garden and stuff”. Two hundred hectares was rather more than she had in mind, no matter how charming she found the high ceilings. “I thought, the house is lovely, but I can’t possibly do that.” But the property had gotten under her skin. Returning for another look two weeks later, she discovered Mount Mackie, a 295-metre hill at the back of the farm where ancient York gums and wandoos had survived about 150 years of grazing. Almost all of the understorey had disappeared. “These magnificent old trees” were all that remained. “I felt a great connection to the land,” she says. Downes, now 76, bought the property and slowly began restoring it. She started with a small local grant to control foxes and feral cats. Then she applied for another, and was awarded 24,000 trees over three years. “I thought, OK, I can start doing this,” says Downes, who began her career as a botanist. “This is what I really want to do.” Today, about 45,000 native seedlings have been planted, while a further 45 plant species have reappeared naturally from the seed bank. The restoration now spans 120 hectares of Downes’ working farm, which she is placing under a conservation covenant so it can never again be cleared. The work is supported by Friends of Mt Mackie, a volunteer group with a core crew of about eight alongside more than 80 volunteers who join organised planting and seed-collecting days. Downes’ days are spent rebaiting live traps, weeding and planting, and dealing with what she jokingly calls “all this bloody admin”. But the payoff is considerable. “Some of the trees are now taller than I am,” she says proudly. “You can see them from two or three kilometres away.” Downes is part of a large cohort of Australians spending their spare time repairing the natural world. The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics data suggests roughly 290,000 Australians volunteer through environmental protection or animal welfare organisations. Retirement brings more time, he says, but also a chance to reassess priorities and think about what will be left for children and grandchildren. “The sort of stirring song of the Australian bush calls to them,” he says. What brings her the most joy is “seeing people love the place … having people share it with me”.

representative.title: California restored former grazing land at Dutch Slough into tidal marsh; between 2020 and 2025 Marsh Wren density jumped from 0.15 to 18.47 birds per hectare, an increase of more than 12,000% - The Times of India
representative.author: TOI Science Desk

snapshot.title: California restored former grazing land at Dutch Slough into tidal marsh; between 2020 and 2025 Marsh Wren density jumped from 0.15 to 18.47 birds per hectare, an increase of more than 12,000%
snapshot.evidenceText: California’s efforts to restore wetlands in the Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta are showing measurable benefits for marsh-dwelling birds, with a newly published study documenting a dramatic rise in Marsh Wren numbers after tidal flows were reintroduced to former agricultural land. According to the journal Restoration Ecology on June 8, 2026, the research by Jason Riggio and colleagues tracked bird populations from 2020 to 2025 at restoration sites managed by the California Department of Water Resources (DWR). The findings build on the state agency’s Dutch Slough Tidal Marsh Restoration Project, which converted former grazing and dairy land into freshwater wetland habitat. The study found that Marsh Wren density at Dutch Slough rose from 0.15 birds per hectare in 2020 to 18.47 in 2025, an increase of more than 12,000%. Other marsh-associated species, including Song Sparrows and Common Yellowthroats, also recorded substantial gains as vegetation developed and the restored landscape became more suitable for wetland wildlife.How wetland restoration changed the landscapeThe Dutch Slough project is located near Oakley, at the western edge of California’s Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta. According to the DWR, the site covers 1,187 acres of former grazing and dairy land acquired as part of broader efforts to protect water quality and restore habitat in the Delta.The first phase of restoration involved reshaping the land to suitable tidal elevations, planting native vegetation and opening sections of the site to natural tidal exchange. The agency reported in November 2021 that more than half of the property had been restored, with the completed phase allowing daily tides to flow through the wetland.The work included planting more than 40,000 trees, shrubs, flowering plants and grasses, alongside approximately 25,000 tule plugs. These plants helped establish the vegetation needed to support a range of wetland species. The project was designed to deliver several benefits beyond wildlife habitat, including helping reverse land subsidence, improving environmental conditions and providing a buffer against flooding. It also serves as a living laboratory for scientists studying how restored freshwater tidal wetlands develop over time.Marsh birds responded within a few yearsThe research team analysed 1,258 bird surveys conducted between 2020 and 2025 across 26 sites at Dutch Slough, Sherman Island and Twitchell Island. The sites included restored tidal wetlands, managed freshwater marshes and unrestored pastureland, allowing researchers to compare bird communities under different habitat conditions.The results showed that several marsh-dependent species colonised the restored wetland quickly. Marsh Wren numbers rose sharply, while Song Sparrow density increased from 5.09 to 16.37 birds per hectare and Common Yellowthroat density climbed from 0.77 to 5.08 per hectare between 2020 and 2025.American Bitterns, which were not detected in the restored tidal marsh in 2020, reached an estimated density of 0.86 birds per hectare by 2025. Pied-billed Grebe density also increased, from 0.10 to 0.47 birds per hectare. These changes suggest that tidal reconnection and the development of emergent vegetation created suitable nesting and feeding conditions for species associated with freshwater marshes. Within one to four years, several marsh specialists reached densities comparable to or higher than those in established managed wetlands.Restoration also changed which birds thrivedNot every species benefited equally. As vegetation spread across the restored marsh, birds that favour open water and exposed ground became less common. Black-necked Stilt density fell from 2.47 birds per hectare in 2020 to none detected in 2025, while Killdeer numbers dropped from 1.55 to 0.10 per hectare. Mallard density also declined by 83%.The pattern reflects a natural shift in habitat as wetlands mature. Open-water areas and exposed mud can attract waterfowl and shorebirds during the early stages of restoration, while growing stands of marsh vegetation create more suitable conditions for species that nest and forage among dense plants.The research also found that restored tidal marsh supported a greater variety of waterbird species than managed marshes or pastureland. By 2025, tidal marsh sites averaged seven waterbird species, compared with 3.8 in managed marshes and 1.8 in pastureland. However, overall bird species richness remained relatively stable throughout the study period. The findings suggest that restoration changed the composition of bird communities rather than simply increasing the total number of species present.Why the findings matter for future restorationThe Dutch Slough project demonstrates how restoring natural water movement can help re-establish wildlife habitat in a heavily modified landscape. The Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta has undergone extensive changes through agricultural development, land drainage and the construction of levees, leaving much of its original wetland ecosystem altered.According to the researchers, continued monitoring will be important to establish whether the early gains persist as vegetation matures. Maintaining different habitat types across the wider landscape could also help support species with contrasting needs, including birds that depend on open water and exposed ground. The study, published in Restoration Ecology, adds evidence that large-scale wetland restoration can produce measurable ecological benefits within a relatively short period. At Dutch Slough, the sharp rise in Marsh Wren density offers one of the clearest examples of how wildlife can respond when a landscape is reconnected to its natural tidal processes.

representative.title: Rescued turtles return home as hundreds of eggs incubate at Dubbo zoo - ABC News
representative.author: Zaarkacha Marlan

snapshot.title: Turtles found buried in metres of mud returned to rejuvenated wetland
snapshot.evidenceText: Paul Keyte releasing turtles into the Gingham Wetlands. ( Supplied DCCEEW ) The first turtles rescued from a dried-out Gingham Waterhole in the Gwydir Wetlands near Moree are back in the wild. Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo helped rehabilitate the rescued turtles and is now incubating more than 250 eggs laid by the reptiles. The remaining adult turtles will be progressively released, while hatchlings are expected to be returned to the wild by the end of next year. The first turtles rescued from a dried-out wetland in north-west NSW are back in their natural habitat, with a new generation of turtle hatchlings expected to join them later this year. Ten broad-shelled turtles and three Murray River turtles were released at Gingham Waterhole in the Gwydir Wetlands in September by the NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW). They were among 39 rescued from the waterhole after it dried out in April, and taken to Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo for rehabilitation. Turtles covered in mud, saved from the Gwydir Wetlands by UNE ecologists in April 2026 ( Supplied: Debbie Bower ) Senior keeper James Witcombe said seeing the first reptiles return to a refilled wetland after months in care was a significant moment. "It's the kind of moment that we as zookeepers and conservationists live for, to see something that's a pretty devastating reality turn into a much better future," he said. "To see that first group of 13 returning to their wetland and seeing photos of the wetland full of beautiful water and invertebrates returning to that space, it really is a special moment." The 13 turtles were returned to Gingham Waterhole as part of a staged release in September. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) The turtles were found burrowed deep in the mud, after Water NSW temporarily suspended environmental water flows to the wetlands earlier this year. Mr Witcombe said the 39 reptiles arrived in Dubbo covered in thick mud and underwent comprehensive health assessments, while keepers quickly adapted the purpose-built platypus conservation centre to accommodate them. "They were all covered in dense, filthy mud, so we set up a bit of a production line to get them all cleaned off and identified," he said. Keepers and veterinarians monitored the turtles' recovery, regularly weighing them and providing plenty of food to improve their condition after they experienced stress in the drying wetland. Once the turtles were healthy enough, keepers lowered the water temperature to mimic winter conditions and provided UV lamps and basking areas to give the light they needed. The rescued turtles spent several months in care at Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) The initial health checks also revealed 14 female broad-shelled turtles were carrying eggs. Because broad-shelled turtles usually lay their eggs during rainy conditions, keepers instead induced egg-laying. Now more than 250 turtle eggs are sitting in an incubator at the Dubbo zoo. Most of the female broad-shelled turtles arrived at the zoo carrying eggs. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) "We will still see a very large percentage of those make it to hatching stage," Mr Witcombe said. The hatchlings could provide an important boost to the population, with foxes and other feral pests known to dig up the subterranean turtle nests at the Gingham Waterhole. The young turtles are expected to be released into the wild by the end of next year. Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Environmental flows resumed in late May and refilled Gingham Waterhole, allowing the staged return of the turtles to begin. DCCEEW executive director of conservation programs Ingrid Emery said the reptiles were being selectively released. "They are being returned progressively over the coming months as the conditions allow and as they're healthy enough to do so," she said. "We are seeing the ecosystem recover out there," she said. Environmental water deliveries had been suspended earlier this year amid concerns about inundation of neighbouring private property. Wildlife specialists rescued the turtles as Gingham Waterhole dried out earlier this year. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) Ms Emery said the department was working with landholders and an environmental water advisory group to plan future water deliveries. "We're planning to use our environmental water to maintain refuge habitat, because we know we are going into a dry period," she said. The released turtles will not be individually tracked, but Ms Emery said ongoing ecological monitoring would help the department assess the health of the wetland and plan future water management. representative.title: ICE secretly tracked protesters
representative.author: Nick Penzenstadler USA TODAY, Leah Millis, Reuters, File 2026

snapshot.title: ICE secretly tracked protesters
snapshot.evidenceText: Michael Khalili always suspected his work tracking federal immigration officers in Minneapolis would land him on the federal government’s radar. The photos agents took of his car and face had to go somewhere. Those fears became real when his status with Global Entry, a pre-screened flyer program, was revoked a day after an exchange in March with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He then faced secondary airport screening when returning to the United States from an international trip this fall. USA TODAY sued ICE under the Freedom of Information Act and obtained a St. Paul, Minnesota, field office database that reveals what legal observers feared: Protesters are being tracked and logged into a secret database for what they argue is exercising protected First Amendment speech. The document, titled simply "Agitator Log," contains 60 instances of ICE officers in Minneapolis logging their interactions with protesters and legal observers around the Whipple Federal Building in the spring of 2026. "I am in no way surprised. It was clear they were tracking us and trying to find reasons to crack down on us," Khalili told USA TODAY. "I try to keep this in perspective. Published - October 10, 2026 12:53 pm IST - HYDERABAD Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul from Hyderabad has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course, after clearing all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results. Photo: Special Arrangement There were days when Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul struggled to find food. Estranged from her family after coming out as a transgender woman, she spent years trying to make ends meet, searching for jobs while refusing to give up on her dream of becoming a doctor. When the path to postgraduate medical education was blocked by the absence of clear admission procedures for transgender candidates, she turned to the courts. On Saturday (October 10, 2026) her perseverance culminated in a milestone. Dr. Ruth John Paul cleared all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results, completing her postgraduate degree in Emergency Medicine at the ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar, Hyderabad, where she studied during the 2023-26 academic session. She has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course. “I am feeling very happy. It is a matter of pride for me and my community. It is a great achievement in my life,” she said. The youngest of three siblings, Dr. Ruth John Paul hails from Khammam district and grew up in a family with limited financial means. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was raised by her mother. She completed her schooling and intermediate education in her native district before clearing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and pursuing undergraduate medical education. She came out as a transgender woman during her undergraduate years. This led to her family rejecting her, leaving her separated from them for nearly six years. The period that followed was marked by financial insecurity and the struggle to survive independently. “There were times when I did not even have food. I struggled to survive and looked for jobs,” she said. In 2021, she found part-time work at Mitr Clinic (now Sabrang Clinic), which is India’s first transgender clinic. She worked there for around two years while continuing to prepare for postgraduate medical entrance examinations. Clearing the entrance examination was not the end of her struggle. Dr. Ruth John Paul said she encountered difficulties during postgraduate medical counselling because there were no clear protocols for accommodating transgender candidates. With the assistance of transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, she approached the Telangana High Court seeking relief. The legal proceedings continued for nearly two years. An interim order from the High Court eventually enabled her to proceed with admission. In 2023, she secured a seat in Emergency Medicine at ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar. Her admission marked a turning point, but the challenges did not end there. She said she continued to encounter stigma and apprehension from people who were unfamiliar with transgender individuals. Working in a clinical environment brought its own challenges. As an emergency medicine trainee, she had to interact with patients during some of their most vulnerable moments, while also navigating the prejudices that transgender people can face. She recalled how some people were initially hesitant or uncomfortable around her. “Initially, some people were scared and did not know how to respond. But when I interacted with patients and treated them with care, they began to appreciate me. People who were initially apprehensive have now become comfortable with me,” she said. Now that she has completed her postgraduate course, Dr. Ruth John Paul wants to use her medical training to help people in need, particularly transgender individuals who require emergency and critical care. “I want to serve everyone, especially transgender people who face critical medical emergencies. I want to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity or sexuality,” she said. Terms & conditions | Institutional Subscriber Comments have to be in English, and in full sentences.
