representative.title: Flydubai investigation: 7 findings that change what we know about attempted terror attack | Khaleej Times
representative.author: Sahim Salim

snapshot.title: Flydubai co-pilot attack plot: 7 key findings from UAE investigation
snapshot.evidenceText: Sun, Oct 11, 2026 | Rabi al-Thani 29, 1448 | Fajr 04:58 | DXB 30.7 °C An attempted suicide attack targeting an airport terminal, two earlier flights used for reconnaissance and a pilot whose suspicions helped thwart the plot: The UAE's latest investigation into flydubai flight FZ1073 has revealed significant new details about the September 30 incident that nearly ended in disaster. The findings, announced by UAE Attorney-General Dr Hamad Saif Al Shamsi on Friday, October 9, establish what the 29-year-old Omani co-pilot allegedly intended to do, how he prepared for the attack and how those aboard the aircraft prevented it. Here are seven key findings and how they change what was previously known. In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the co-pilot was accused of attempting to crash the aircraft. Early reports suggested he intended to use the plane as a weapon against a target in Israel, with Ben Gurion Airport and a high-rise building in Tel Aviv mentioned as possible targets. The UAE investigation has now identified a specific intended target: the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport. According to prosecutors, the co-pilot planned to seize control of the aircraft and carry out a suicide attack designed to cause the "greatest possible loss of life". The suspect's motives were among the biggest unanswered questions in the initial days of the investigation. Early reports raised different possibilities, including terrorism and mental health issues, while later accounts pointed to extremist beliefs and radical online activity. The UAE investigation now traces the first signs of his radicalisation to 2017, when he was studying in Australia. Prosecutors said he was influenced by takfiri ideology through extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks. The investigation adds a significant new detail: the suspect admitted drawing inspiration from the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States. The findings establish a much longer history of alleged radicalisation and planning than was previously known. Earlier reports suggested the co-pilot had planned a similar attack in July but abandoned it at the last moment. Some accounts claimed he changed his mind because someone he knew was aboard. The UAE investigation found that he used two earlier flights to Tel Aviv specifically to familiarise himself with the route and Ben Gurion Airport as part of his preparations for the terrorist plot. The findings establish that the earlier journeys were used for reconnaissance, but neither confirm nor reject claims that he had planned an earlier attack and abandoned it because he knew someone aboard. Earlier reports suggested Oman Air had removed the suspect from flying duties over concerns about his beliefs and assigned him to an administrative role. According to UAE prosecutors, he worked for Oman Air between 2020 and 2024, followed by a period at Royal Air Maroc in 2025, before joining flydubai in January 2026. Investigators examined flydubai's recruitment procedures and found that the suspect had met the professional and security requirements for employment. These included holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks. None of these procedures revealed his extremist beliefs or intentions, prosecutors said. The nature of the assault was initially unclear, with early witness accounts describing a stabbing and raising questions about whether a knife or another weapon had been used. The UAE subsequently established on October 3 that the co-pilot had attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe. The latest investigation adds forensic evidence to that finding. According to prosecutors, the captain's injuries were concentrated on his head, a vital area where such injuries could have been fatal. The forensic findings were consistent with the accounts of the suspect, the injured captain and witnesses. Who actually landed flydubai flight FZ1073 after its captain was seriously injured in the cockpit? The question sparked conflicting accounts, with some early reports suggesting that an Israeli plumber with no flying experience had helped bring the aircraft down safely. The UAE investigation has now clarified the roles of professional pilots aboard the aircraft, whose actions were crucial to stopping the attacker and bringing the plane safely to the ground. According to prosecutors, a pilot assigned to operate the aircraft's return flight was near the cockpit when he noticed its door opening and closing repeatedly. Suspecting something was wrong, he approached and attempted to enter using the access code. After gaining entry, he witnessed the co-pilot attacking Captain Machchhar with an emergency axe. He immediately intervened, assisted by a cabin crew member and several passengers, who together rescued the injured captain and restrained the attacker. The captain assigned to the return flight and his co-pilot then regained control of the aircraft, diverted it to Saudi Arabia and landed safely at Tabuk Airport. The investigation establishes their crucial role in saving the aircraft and those aboard, although the two pilots have not been publicly identified. In the days after the attack, questions emerged about whether the co-pilot had acted independently or had connections to terrorist organisations or foreign actors. Earlier investigations had not established links to an organised terrorist group, although speculation about outside involvement continued. The UAE Public Prosecution has now obtained a detailed confession from the suspect in the presence of his lawyer and with the required legal safeguards. Prosecutors said he admitted acting alone, without the involvement of others. However, investigators have not treated that claim as conclusive. The Public Prosecution is continuing to examine evidence, investigate possible accomplices and other connections, and review recordings and technical reports. snapshot.title: Flydubai co-pilot attack plot: 7 key findings from UAE investigation
snapshot.evidenceText: Sun, Oct 11, 2026 | Rabi al-Thani 29, 1448 | Fajr 04:58 | DXB 30.7 °C An attempted suicide attack targeting an airport terminal, two earlier flights used for reconnaissance and a pilot whose suspicions helped thwart the plot: The UAE's latest investigation into flydubai flight FZ1073 has revealed significant new details about the September 30 incident that nearly ended in disaster. The findings, announced by UAE Attorney-General Dr Hamad Saif Al Shamsi on Friday, October 9, establish what the 29-year-old Omani co-pilot allegedly intended to do, how he prepared for the attack and how those aboard the aircraft prevented it. Here are seven key findings and how they change what was previously known. In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the co-pilot was accused of attempting to crash the aircraft. Early reports suggested he intended to use the plane as a weapon against a target in Israel, with Ben Gurion Airport and a high-rise building in Tel Aviv mentioned as possible targets. The UAE investigation has now identified a specific intended target: the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport. According to prosecutors, the co-pilot planned to seize control of the aircraft and carry out a suicide attack designed to cause the "greatest possible loss of life". The suspect's motives were among the biggest unanswered questions in the initial days of the investigation. Early reports raised different possibilities, including terrorism and mental health issues, while later accounts pointed to extremist beliefs and radical online activity. The UAE investigation now traces the first signs of his radicalisation to 2017, when he was studying in Australia. Prosecutors said he was influenced by takfiri ideology through extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks. The investigation adds a significant new detail: the suspect admitted drawing inspiration from the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States. The findings establish a much longer history of alleged radicalisation and planning than was previously known. Earlier reports suggested the co-pilot had planned a similar attack in July but abandoned it at the last moment. Some accounts claimed he changed his mind because someone he knew was aboard. The UAE investigation found that he used two earlier flights to Tel Aviv specifically to familiarise himself with the route and Ben Gurion Airport as part of his preparations for the terrorist plot. The findings establish that the earlier journeys were used for reconnaissance, but neither confirm nor reject claims that he had planned an earlier attack and abandoned it because he knew someone aboard. Earlier reports suggested Oman Air had removed the suspect from flying duties over concerns about his beliefs and assigned him to an administrative role. According to UAE prosecutors, he worked for Oman Air between 2020 and 2024, followed by a period at Royal Air Maroc in 2025, before joining flydubai in January 2026. Investigators examined flydubai's recruitment procedures and found that the suspect had met the professional and security requirements for employment. These included holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks. None of these procedures revealed his extremist beliefs or intentions, prosecutors said. The nature of the assault was initially unclear, with early witness accounts describing a stabbing and raising questions about whether a knife or another weapon had been used. The UAE subsequently established on October 3 that the co-pilot had attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe. The latest investigation adds forensic evidence to that finding. According to prosecutors, the captain's injuries were concentrated on his head, a vital area where such injuries could have been fatal. The forensic findings were consistent with the accounts of the suspect, the injured captain and witnesses. Who actually landed flydubai flight FZ1073 after its captain was seriously injured in the cockpit? The question sparked conflicting accounts, with some early reports suggesting that an Israeli plumber with no flying experience had helped bring the aircraft down safely. The UAE investigation has now clarified the roles of professional pilots aboard the aircraft, whose actions were crucial to stopping the attacker and bringing the plane safely to the ground. According to prosecutors, a pilot assigned to operate the aircraft's return flight was near the cockpit when he noticed its door opening and closing repeatedly. Suspecting something was wrong, he approached and attempted to enter using the access code. After gaining entry, he witnessed the co-pilot attacking Captain Machchhar with an emergency axe. He immediately intervened, assisted by a cabin crew member and several passengers, who together rescued the injured captain and restrained the attacker. The captain assigned to the return flight and his co-pilot then regained control of the aircraft, diverted it to Saudi Arabia and landed safely at Tabuk Airport. The investigation establishes their crucial role in saving the aircraft and those aboard, although the two pilots have not been publicly identified. In the days after the attack, questions emerged about whether the co-pilot had acted independently or had connections to terrorist organisations or foreign actors. Earlier investigations had not established links to an organised terrorist group, although speculation about outside involvement continued. The UAE Public Prosecution has now obtained a detailed confession from the suspect in the presence of his lawyer and with the required legal safeguards. Prosecutors said he admitted acting alone, without the involvement of others. However, investigators have not treated that claim as conclusive. The Public Prosecution is continuing to examine evidence, investigate possible accomplices and other connections, and review recordings and technical reports. snapshot.title: Trump Is Reopening the Middle East’s Deadliest Sectarian Fault Lines

The violent sectarian era that followed the U.S. invasion of Iraq and peaked with the rise of the Islamic State more than a decade ago may feel distant in Washington, but in the Middle East the wounds remain fresh. Just this past spring, Iraqi forensic teams uncovered the remains of more than 30 Kurdish Peshmerga fighters, Iraqi security personnel, and Yazidi women and children in an Islamic State mass grave near Mosul. From Lebanon, still living in the long shadow of its civil war, to Syria and Iraq with more recent civil wars of their own, sectarian tensions permeate the region. The violent sectarian era that followed the U.S. invasion of Iraq and peaked with the rise of the Islamic State more than a decade ago may feel distant in Washington, but in the Middle East the wounds remain fresh. Just this past spring, Iraqi forensic teams uncovered the remains of more than 30 Kurdish Peshmerga fighters, Iraqi security personnel, and Yazidi women and children in an Islamic State mass grave near Mosul. A week earlier , across the Syrian border in eastern Deir Ezzor, another mass grave was uncovered , one of at least 18 such sites documented in Syria this year. Last year’s massacre of more than 1,400 Syrian Alawites, a religious minority to which Assad belonged, in March, and sectarian killings of Druze in Suwayda in July threatened to unravel the new Syrian state. From Lebanon, still living in the long shadow of its civil war, to Syria and Iraq with more recent civil wars of their own, sectarian tensions permeate the region. Eminent Syrianist Joshua Landis calls it the “ Great Sorting-Out ,” the violent unwinding of the post- Sykes-Picot order , where Sunni transnational tribes, pockets of Abrahamic and non-Abrahamic religious minorities, and orphaned ethnonationalists were folded into newly drawn states across the Levant. This order, established by the Western powers at the end of World War I, is coming to a violent end as communities across the region retreat into rigid ethnic and sectarian enclaves. Few places have paid a higher price for that unwinding than Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon. Enter U.S. President Donald Trump. Fresh from firing Nate Swanson , one of the few officials in his administration who deeply understood Iran and Shiite politics, his White House has rolled out a set of policies that invite a new unraveling. By proposing that Syria’s president, and former al Qaeda commander, Ahmed al-Sharaa’s forces could “take care of Hezbollah,” while simultaneously pushing to disarm Shiite armed factions that helped lead the campaign against the Islamic State in Iraq, Washington is playing fast and loose with forces it does not understand, with potentially catastrophic consequences. In 2003, Washington invaded Iraq knowing so little about the sectarian fault lines involved that some of its top policymakers seriously floated installing a Sunni Hashemite king to smooth the transition. The last Hashemite ruler of Iraq was shot and dragged through the streets in 1958. The new U.S.-led regime also disenfranchised a sizable and armed Sunni minority, which had held positions of power under Saddam Hussein, almost overnight. A decade of gruesome sectarian civil war later, Iraq had gone from a country where Sunni and Shiite neighborhoods blurred into one another to a patchwork of hardened cantons and governorates, enclaves that functioned, depending on which sect you belonged to , as either haven or sundown town. Sectarian resentment, compounded by American and Gulf support for poorly vetted Sunni extremist factions in the Syrian civil war, helped incubate the Islamic State. The caliphate swallowed a third of Iraq within months, taking Mosul and most of Anbar province, before the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) and other ground troops, backed by U.S.-led coalition air power, clawed the territory back and dismantled the Islamic State’s territorial state. Washington’s long campaign against post-revolutionary Iran has done little to dispel the regional image of the U.S. as an engine of regional sectarianism. In the 1980s the United States backed Saddam through his eight-year war against Iran. Decades later, Washington stood by as Saudi troops helped crush a Shiite uprising in Bahrain before backing Riyadh again in 2015 with bombs, intelligence, and midair refueling as it launched its war against the Zaydi Shiite Houthi movement in Yemen. Each of these conflicts had drivers that went well beyond sect. But time and again, Washington chose partners and policies that reinforced a single regional narrative: a U.S.-backed Sunni order squaring off against Shiite challengers. Washington is now leaning on Ali al-Zaidi, Iraq’s new, Trump-favored prime minister, to disarm the very forces that grew out of the last round of sectarian violence with an initial deadline of the 30 th of September. That day has come and gone, and the militias refused to disarm. Zaidi is himself Shiite, but Iraqi Shiite politics is deeply divided between Iran-aligned factions and more nationalist currents that are suspicious of Tehran and willing to work with Washington. He belongs to the latter, and although has pushed the disarmament deadline to June 2027, he has also stated that disarmament is non-negotiable. Now the factions have entered what amounts to a standoff: the disarmament of militias that answer more to Iran than Iraq and don’t trust Washington’s ties with the current Iraqi government or the consolidation of state security control under the authority of an al-Zaidi-lead Iraqi state. The PMF—an umbrella organization that includes Iran-aligned factions such as Badr, Kataib Hezbollah, and Harakat al-Nujaba, alongside Iraqi state-aligned units—was formed in 2014, after Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, a powerful Iraqi Shiite figure, issued a “defensive jihad” fatwa calling on all Iraqis to defend against the Islamic State. The PMF was formally folded into Iraq’s security forces two years later. Sistani, who turned 96 in August, has never rescinded that fatwa, but he has also never said what becomes of it once he is gone or what it should mean politically, a succession question that hangs over the entire disarmament debate. PMF leaders point to that founding history as proof of both the organization’s legitimacy and the state’s limits. As spokesperson Mouhanad al-Oqabi put it , Iraq’s security would “crumble in an instant” if the group abandoned the thousands of positions it held across Iraq. The militias have plenty of reasons for their skepticism, and most of them predate Trump. They point to the likelihood that U.S. personnel will simply be rebranded as trainers consultants and contractors and return in one form or another. They point to Turkey’s footprint in the north, to a persistent Islamic State threat, and to Damascus, now led by Sharaa. Finally, militia leaders also have material reasons to resist disarmament: Their weapons sustain patronage networks, salaries, contracts, and political leverage that would shrink if they demobilized. That distrust stems from something deeper than regional power politics that’s restricted to the modern era. Shiite political culture carries with it a powerful sense of mazlumiyah , the memory and consciousness of the Shiite having been wronged, ranging in time from the martyrdom of Hussein ibn Ali, the Prophet Muhammad’s grandson, in 680 to the brutal repression of the Saddam regime and the massacres committed by the Islamic State. Recognizing that is not to reduce Shiite politics to culture, any more than Confucianism explains every Chinese state policy. But this mazlumiyah still helps explain why images of Shiite under attack in Iran or Lebanon resonate so strongly in Iraq, and why a demand to disarm, arriving at precisely this moment, rings differently in Baghdad than it does in Washington. In July, U.S. and Saudi aircraft struck PMF positions across Iraq, claiming the attack responded to drones launched from Iraqi territory against Saudi oil facilities. Several factions prepared retaliatory strikes on Saudi Arabia and U.S. bases before Hadi al-Amiri, leader of the Badr Organization, one of Iraq’s largest and oldest Shiite political-military movements, talked them down. Weeks later, Iraqi authorities arrested Abbas al-Yaqoubi, a senior militia leader who held a PMF intelligence post, as the disarmament push intensified. Iraqi leaders, former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki among them, have repeatedly warned that forcing the issue could trigger an internal confrontation that spills into neighboring countries. The situation is even more combustible in Lebanon, where political power is formally divided among 18 recognized religious communities. Few states can function indefinitely with an armed movement, answerable to no one, running a parallel government a few miles from Beirut’s center. Hezbollah’s secretary-general, Naim Qassem, has repeatedly insisted that the fate of the group’s weapons cannot be dictated by Washington or Israel. “Nobody outside Lebanon has anything to do with the weapons,” he said in May, calling them an “internal Lebanese matter.” He has also said Hezbollah is prepared to discuss folding its arsenal into Lebanon’s national defense once an agreement exists and the south is genuinely protected from further Israeli incursions—which seems a long way off. Hezbollah was born out of Israel’s 1982 invasion and occupation of southern Lebanon, and its pitch to Lebanese Shiite has barely changed in four decades: It remains the only thing standing between the south and the next invasion, whenever the state cannot. Qassem has turned that argument directly against Lebanese President Joseph Aoun’s government, accusing it of “serving Israel” rather than Lebanese sovereignty. He called the U.S.-brokered framework tying Israeli withdrawal first to Hezbollah’s disarmament a surrender dressed up as diplomacy. Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam retort that there can be no real sovereignty while Hezbollah independently controls questions of war and peace. Israeli forces still occupy large parts of southern Lebanon, which makes the government’s promise that the Lebanese state can replace Hezbollah as protector of the south a considerably harder sell. Across the border, Washington has pushed Sharaa’s Sunni Islamist-led government to “take care of Hezbollah” in Lebanon, despite Syrian officials reportedly fearing that such a move could ignite sectarian tensions in both countries. In northern Lebanon’s Sunni-majority city of Tripoli, Sharaa’s government has received a hero’s welcome , with many Sunnis seeing Damascus as a potential counterweight to Hezbollah’s power. Over the other border, Iran-aligned Iraqi Shiite factions warned Sharaa that any move against Hezbollah or Lebanon’s Shiite “resistance environment” would amount to a declaration of war and could draw a military response from Iraq. A Syrian intervention would therefore risk mobilizing Lebanese Sunnis behind Damascus while pulling Iraqi Shiite factions into the fight. Across the Gulf, the war in Iran has destabilized fragile Sunni-Shiite ties. Bahrain, whose Sunni monarchy rules over a large Shiite population, imposed new restrictions on Shiite religious observances, arrested clerics , and barred public mourning of Iran’s late supreme leader. Kuwait has also tightened restrictions around Shiite religious gatherings, revoked thousands of citizenships, and prosecuted people accused of “inciting sectarian strife.” And now Yemen’s hitherto frozen civil war has reignited. A four-year truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed southern government has broken . In the last few weeks, the Iran-backed group has taken most of the country’s western coast and now fully controls the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Verified footage from the Saudi-backed Giants Brigades showed fighters running over Houthi fighters with armored vehicles while calling them “dogs” and rawafidh , a sectarian slur for Shiites. The force itself grew out of ultra-conservative Sunni religious networks in Saudi Arabia. Earlier this month, Sunni clerics accused the Houthis of attacking Mecca, even though the group said it had targeted Aramco facilities instead. The consequences of another sectarian conflagration would fall first on people with the least control over any of it. Shiite civilians would again risk being treated as Iranian proxies, Sunnis as jihadis or Gulf clients, Alawites as extensions of a fallen regime. Smaller communities, Yazidis, Christians, Druze, would again find themselves squeezed between larger armed camps. This fire has already been lit. In the first weeks of the latest regional war, roughly a million people fled their homes in Lebanon; more than 200,000 crossed into Syria in March alone, according to the U.N. Refugee Agency. Another round of communal violence across Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon would mean more mass graves, more room for the Islamic State and other opportunistic extremists to rebuild, and another wave of refugees moving through Jordan and Turkey, and eventually toward Europe. Washington should start by rebuilding the expertise it has stripped. More officials who understand Iraqi Shiite politics, Lebanese sectarian dynamics, Syrian minorities, and the region’s religious institutions might better identify the multitude of trip wires this administration is now barreling toward. That expertise should inform a more restrained policy: Stop treating disarmament as something that can be imposed on a deadline from Washington, avoid using one regional actor to coerce another, even as a threat, and give Iraqi and Lebanese institutions the space to negotiate coherent, sustainable arrangements that their own communities can actually sustain. representative.title: ‘A culture of corruption’: One voter card, many polling options; Brampton candidates question how City Hall plans to stop duplicate voting | The Pointer
representative.author: Adrian Peries

snapshot.title: ‘A culture of corruption’: One voter card, many polling options; Brampton candidates question how City Hall plans to stop duplicate voting
snapshot.evidenceText: Brampton residents hoping to vote in the October 26 municipal election should have received their voter cards detailing their respective polling locations. This is nothing out of the ordinary, as elections allow voters to cast a ballot ahead of time, should they not be able to make it on election day. This year, a rarely used system has prompted Brampton residents to voice concerns over the glaring holes in the widely criticized way the city’s officials have chosen to run the voting process. On their polling cards, there is a list of multiple locations, in some cases more than a dozen, where eligible residents can turn up and vote within their ward. People, including candidates, are asking, how would the City know if one resident votes multiple times? “Confidence in the integrity of the election has to come first,” says candidate Monica Singh Soares. “These are not accusations…they’re basic election integrity questions.” Wards 7 and 8 councillor candidate Monica Singh Soares says confidence in the election is key. (Submitted) Prabh Gill is running to be the next mayor of Brampton and recently sent a letter to City Hall that he shared with The Pointer. “Dear City Clerk, I am a registered candidate for Mayor in the 2026 Brampton municipal election. I am writing to ask for information about the voting and vote-counting equipment that will be used in this election. I want to be clear that I am not alleging wrongdoing by the City, its staff or any supplier. My purpose is to make sure residents and all candidates have the same clear information before voting begins.” Gill is seeking clarification about the process that was used to acquire the electronic voting machines that are being used, and what accountability is in place to ensure the integrity of the system. “The City's Bids and Tenders page for NRFP2025-347, Lease of Election Tabulation System and Electronic Voting System, lists the bid as awarded on January 9, 2026. The same page shows no awarded vendor and no contract value.” Brampton mayoral candidate Prabh Gill has questions about the integrity of the electronic vote counting machines being used in the election. (Supplied) The Pointer also sent questions to City staff about steps that are being taken to ensure voting integrity and what can be done if any irregularities crop up. There was no response. The City of Brampton website reports that the municipal Voters' List identifies people who are eligible to vote in the municipal election, by name, qualifying address, school support and residency.” “The Voters' List is live and when a voter attends a voting location, they are marked as having voted. This information is updated immediately and all other voting locations will see the same information.” There is very little information on the voting page that explains what safeguards are in place to ensure voting integrity. “Our online tool will allow you to confirm or provisionally update or add your information to the Voters' List. Soares said she was told by City officials that a live voters’ list will record each vote and all other polling locations will be able to see it. The Pointer asked how such safeguards would actually work and what protocols are in place to ensure the integrity of the live voters list. It’s unclear how a volunteer or worker at one voting station would know that someone who appears to cast a ballot has already voted somewhere else. City staff did not explain why the usual system that has been in place in Brampton, restricting voters to one designated polling station where they are registered to cast a ballot, was not used this year, and why the city is not doing what other municipalities across the country do. Many residents, including candidates, think a live voters list is not enough to ensure fair elections, and are questioning why the City changed the usual system used in Brampton and across the country, which tells voters which specific nearby polling station they have to show up at to cast one single ballot, after scrutineers cross them off the list for that specific location, the only one they are able to vote at. Soares, a candidate for councillor hoping to represent Brampton’s Wards 7 and 8, is not accusing anyone of cheating; she is concerned about safeguards and the loss of trust in the system that residents are raising. She said voters have no idea what safeguards are in place to prevent someone from voting up to a dozen times. The City’s position effectively relies on the honour system, putting the onus on voters not to break the rules. Soares says a live voters list allows someone to be marked as having voted at a site once they cast a ballot. But what happens if they do the same at another polling station? She wants to know how a duplicate vote is flagged, and how it would be reconciled afterward. “The government should be going above and beyond what they can, not simply saying ‘trust us’”. She is especially concerned about the choice to move away from the usual system after years of controversy at City Hall, which she described as having a “culture of corruption.” “There’s a culture of corruption,” she said. “And people are nervous. And I think that’s what may be an elephant in the room that people are not talking about.” One of the voter cards in Brampton, for the 2026 municipal election, with multiple listed locations a resident can choose to vote at in their ward, instead of the usual system across the country that gives voters only one location where they are registered to cast their ballot. Candidates are worried about fraud. (Submitted) Soares said being outside of City Hall’s politics, she calls out potential corruption when she sees it. Soares also raised concerns over the identification that can be used. “A voter notice itself is also not identification,” she said. A publicly-sourced review of ballot counting machines in Brampton, or EVMs (electronic voting machines) dated October 5 has been spreading across the internet, raising concerns about who controls the vote counting process. It is a closed system in Brampton, with City Hall entirely in charge of taking the voting data from the machines and recording the results. It is possible that in the hands of unethical City Hall leaders those responsible for the voting machines could easily manipulate the results to favour certain candidates. Only a complaint under provincial rules could trigger an external review, and even then it’s not clear how a sophisticated vote rigging scheme could be exposed. The document claims that the American company ES&S was the 2022 election supplier for voting tabulator machines . The City of Brampton leased DS200 tabulators and 15 ExpressVote accessible units. A 2026 staff report says the old contract had expired, and a Request for Proposals (RFP) was being developed. The public document also raises serious issues over ten years. For example, in 2023, a coding error on ExpressVote XL machines in Northampton County, Pennsylvania, made printed summaries appear to flip judicial retention votes, and ES&S acknowledged fault. On the City of Brampton’s voter FAQ page, the use of voter machines is addressed. “The City has established procedures and safeguards governing the use of voting and vote-counting equipment to protect the accuracy, security and integrity of the election. Each piece of voting equipment undergoes rigorous testing ahead of an election. The technology does not eliminate a paper ballot. All votes processed by vote tabulators have a corresponding paper ballot. The use of voting and vote-counting equipment is permitted under Ontario's Municipal Elections Act and is commonly used by municipalities across Ontario.” There is no information about independent, external oversight of City Hall staff. Mayor Patrick Brown was asked about concerns regarding the change to allow multiple voting locations and if there is an independent, external auditor monitoring the use of voting machines so no manipulation takes place. He did not respond. Gill sent ten questions to Brampton’s City Clerk regarding the integrity and transparency of the voting system: 1. Who is the final awarded supplier for NRFP2025-347, and what legal entity signed the agreement? 2. What is the total contract value, including lease, software, support, licensing, training, ballot services, accessibility units, maintenance, peripherals, optional work and taxes? 3. Who submitted bids, and what was the final scoring matrix? 4. Why does the public tender page say Awarded but also show No Awarded Vendors? 5. Does Brampton use any modem, cellular, wireless, VPN, remote support or internet based transmission for election night results? If yes, when is it active and what safeguards exist? 6. Are final official results physically uploaded and cross checked with printed tapes and paper ballots before certification? 7. What independent testing, logic and accuracy testing, cybersecurity testing, vulnerability scanning, DGSI compliance review and accessibility review will be completed before advance voting? 8. Will candidates be allowed to observe equipment demonstration, testing, sealing and post election tabulation certification? 9. Have all conflict of interest declarations been signed by vendors, evaluators, staff, consultants and elected officials where applicable? 10. Will the Clerk publish an incident reporting protocol for tabulators and accessible voting devices before Election Day? Soares said, “Technology isn’t inherently the problem, transparency is the issue.” The Pointer also sent questions to the City Clerk’s office and elections coordinator Roger Wilson, asking if the system being used this year is open to fraud, and what the City is doing to protect the voting machine process and the ballot casting process from fraud, including the possible hiring of an independent external oversight auditor. representative.title: Myanmar’s Leaders Tried to Erase My Rohingya Identity 11 Years Ago – The Diplomat
representative.author: Shwe Maung

snapshot.title: Myanmar’s Leaders Tried to Erase My Rohingya Identity 11 Years Ago
snapshot.evidenceText: In July 2015, I was invited to the residence of U Aung Thaung, a senior and influential leader of Myanmar’s Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP), in Naypyidaw. We discussed the approaching general elections and parliamentary nominations for the constituencies in northern Rakhine state. What happened during that meeting has remained outside the public record for more than 11 years. I want to disclose it now because the political question at its center – the recognition of Rohingya identity and rights – remains unresolved. It is also relevant to how ASEAN engages with Myanmar’s military leadership today. I was elected to Myanmar’s house of parliament, the Pyithu Hluttaw, from Buthitaung township of Rakhine state in November 2010 as a USDP candidate. In the summer of 2015 I was preparing to secure my office for another term. But, during our private conversation, U Aung Thaung proposed a condition that went far beyond ordinary electoral politics. As I recall it, he told me that he, the USDP leadership, President U Thein Sein, and then Commander-in-Chief Min Aung Hlaing did not accept “Rohingya” as an ethnic identity. He urged me to stop advocating for that identity and to persuade my constituents to identify themselves as “Bengali” instead. He presented this change as a pathway toward obtaining citizenship documentation and restoring political participation. He also advised me to give a media interview stating that “there is no Rohingya but Bengali,” without mentioning our private meeting and his name. My parliamentary nomination, he indicated, depended on my willingness to support that position. I refused. I could not ask my constituents to surrender their identity in exchange for the possibility of receiving documents, voting rights, or another parliamentary term. Political representation should protect the rights of a community, not become an instrument for bargaining those rights away. U Aung Thaung encouraged me to consult my constituents and reconsider. I subsequently informed community leaders and constituents about the conversation. They supported my position and we were all on the same page. I did not disclose the meeting to the media at that time because of the political consequences of making such an account public while living in Myanmar. During my visit, I saw large portraits of President Thein Sein, Min Aung Hlaing, and nationalist Buddhist monk U Wirathu in an office at the residence. An assistant told me that the office also served U Wirathu whenever he comes to Naypyidaw. These are my recollections of what I saw and I was told 11 years ago. The statements about Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing were made to me by U Aung Thaung. I cannot claim that I heard either man personally authorize the proposal. But U Aung Thaung confirmed the proposal with Union Immigration Minister U Khin Yi, today’s USDP chairman and speaker of Pyithu Hluttaw, over the phone in front of me. The central proposition was unmistakable: I was being asked to abandon public advocacy for the identity of the people I represented as a condition of continuing my political career. On August 4, 2015, I resigned from the USDP. Two days later, I applied to contest the upcoming Pyithu Hluttaw election as an independent candidate for Buthitaung. On August 22, the Maungdaw District Election Subcommission rejected my candidacy. Its decision concluded that my parents had not been Myanmar citizens at the time of my birth in 1965. I appealed, together with concrete documents, to the Rakhine State Election Subcommission, which upheld the rejection on September 1, 2015. The Union Election Commission subsequently affirmed the decision, communicating its ruling in a letter dated September 6, 2015. This outcome presented a profound contradiction in my political life. The same Union Election Commission had formally recognized me as an elected member of parliament following the November 7, 2010 election. Its recognition certificate, dated January 10, 2011, identified me as the elected representative of Buthitaung and recorded my citizenship card. Five years later, election authorities found me ineligible to stand for the same parliamentary seat because they now considered the evidence of my parents’ citizenship insufficient. The State Election Subcommission acknowledged that my father possessed a national registration card, which serves as a primary document for full citizenship, and that my maternal grandparents also held national registration cards. Nevertheless, it concluded that those records did not adequately establish the citizenship qualifications required under the election laws. I maintained that I had submitted the same family citizenship documentation in both electoral processes. The surviving recognition certificate and 2105 rulings represent contrasting official outcomes, although a complete comparison of the underlying applications would require examination of the original 2010 candidate file. I believe the circumstances of my exclusion cannot be separated from the political pressure I experienced over my Rohingya identity. But the official election decisions do not themselves establish that my refusal of U Aung Thaung Thaung’s proposal caused my disqualification. In November 2015, I publicly described the disenfranchisement of Rohingya voters and candidates in an opinion article for the New York Times. What I did not reveal then was the private conversation that had proceeded my departure from the USDP. I am revealing it now not simply to revisit my personal experience, but because it illuminates a continuing political problem. For decades, Rohingya identity has been contested by successive Myanmar authorities, often through the characterization of the community as “Bengali” migrants. Questions of citizenship, documentation, and political participation have been intertwined with that dispute. The consequences extended beyond elections. The mass atrocities committed against Rohingya in 2017 drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people into Bangladesh and intensified international demands for accountability. The Myanmar military coup in February 2021 subsequently plunged the country into wider political and humanitarian crisis. Today, the Rohingya question cannot be treated as an isolated refugee-management problem. It is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order in which citizenship and fundamental rights are protected without discrimination. This why ASEAN’s diplomatic engagement with Min Aung Hlaing deserves close scrutiny. Regional governments have legitimate reasons to maintain channels of communication concerning humanitarian access, armed conflicts, migration, and regional security. Diplomatic contact is not necessarily equivalent to recognition or endorsement. But engagement must be judged by what it achieves for people affected by Myanmar’s crisis. For Rohingya, discussions of repatriation are incomplete unless they address the conditions that forced people to flee and the rights they must be able to exercise upon return. A refugee cannot be expected to regard return as durable when questions of identity, citizenship, personal security, and political belonging remain unresolved. ASEAN should therefore make these issues substantive elements of its discussions with Myanmar’s authorities. They include equal citizenship rights, recognition of the right to self-identification, meaningful political participation, protection against further atrocities, accountability for grave violations, and conditions for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return. The wider realities of Myanmar’s conflict must be taken into account. The aspirations of people resisting military rule, the safety of civilians across the country, and political future of ethnic communities cannot be separated from efforts to resolve the Rohingya crisis. My experience in 2015 taught me how readily the question of identity could become a condition imposed upon political participation. The documents from my parliamentary career show that official recognition in one election offered no assurance of eligibility in the next. Eleven years later, I remain convinced that Rohingya rights cannot depend on whether individuals agree to relinquish the name by which they identify themselves. ASEAN cannot settle Myanmar’s political future on its own. But it can insist that engagement address the rights and security of the people whose lives are at stake. A sustainable future for Myanmar requires more than meetings among political leaders. It requires a political order in which no community must choose between its identity and its rights.

Diplomatic contact is not necessarily equivalent to recognition or endorsement. But engagement must be judged by what it achieves for people affected by Myanmar’s crisis. For Rohingya, discussions of repatriation are incomplete unless they address the conditions that forced people to flee and the rights they must be able to exercise upon return. A refugee cannot be expected to regard return as durable when questions of identity, citizenship, personal security, and political belonging remain unresolved. ASEAN should therefore make these issues substantive elements of its discussions with Myanmar’s authorities. They include equal citizenship rights, recognition of the right to self-identification, meaningful political participation, protection against further atrocities, accountability for grave violations, and conditions for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return. The wider realities of Myanmar’s conflict must be taken into account. The aspirations of people resisting military rule, the safety of civilians across the country, and political future of ethnic communities cannot be separated from efforts to resolve the Rohingya crisis. My experience in 2015 taught me how readily the question of identity could become a condition imposed upon political participation. The documents from my parliamentary career show that official recognition in one election offered no assurance of eligibility in the next. Eleven years later, I remain convinced that Rohingya rights cannot depend on whether individuals agree to relinquish the name by which they identify themselves. ASEAN cannot settle Myanmar’s political future on its own. But it can insist that engagement address the rights and security of the people whose lives are at stake. A sustainable future for Myanmar requires more than meetings among political leaders. It requires a political order in which no community must choose between its identity and its rights.

representative.title: Yemeni government’s military says its forces advancing against Houthis
representative.author: Al Jazeera

snapshot.title: Yemeni government’s military says its forces advancing against Houthis
snapshot.evidenceText: Saudi-backed forces say 1,150 Houthis killed in operations against the Iran-aligned group over the past 24 hours. How much worse can Yemen's humanitarian crisis become? The military of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has killed hundreds of Houthi fighters in targeted operations over the past 24 hours. Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemeni government forces, said at least 1,150 Houthis were killed in almost 2,000 targeted operations across the country as part of operation “Dawn of Yemen”. He said the army had destroyed Houthi ammunition dumps and at least 180 combat, transport and supply vehicles operated by the Houthis, adding that ground forces “continued to advance their assault”. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the information. An attack on King Khalid International airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, on Saturday killed and injured several people and led to flights being cancelled. When asked if the United States would join strikes against the Houthis after the attack, President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he “will make a decision soon”. Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen on Saturday, said the Houthis had yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack. But the Iran-backed group has warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target. Mawry said the Houthis were preparing to fight the war on multiple fronts, including against the participation of international actors, such as Pakistan. “The Houthis say that if Pakistan engages in any military activities against them on behalf of Saudi Arabia, then they will be treated in the same fashion as the Saudis are currently being dealt with,” Mawry said. There are plans to launch ballistic missiles towards Pakistan and attack Pakistan-flagged vessels in the Red and Arabian seas, he added. “The fighting is spreading on multiple fronts, but it is a situation that will keep escalating,” Baraa Shiban, an associate fellow in international security and Yemen expert at the London-based Royal United Services Institute think tank, told Al Jazeera, adding that the violence will not be “dying down” anytime soon. “There is no mediation happening this time – there [are] no regional or local mediators that are able to cool down the situation,” he said. The Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea. Battles are now raging around the strategic southern Yemeni cities of Mocha and Dhubab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides claim control of the shipping lanes.

representative.title: Alert: Reports: Armed Saboteurs Cross From Belarus Into Latvia,…

snapshot.title: Alert: Reports: Armed Saboteurs Cross From Belarus Into Latvia,…
snapshot.evidenceText: Published: Sun, 11 Oct 2026 05:03:18 GMT · Severity: WARNING · Category: Breaking Severity: WARNING Detected: 2026-10-11T05:03:18.364Z A report filed at 04:14 UTC claims armed, masked intruders entered Latvia from Belarus and carried out sabotage, pointing to a deliberate cross‑border operation against a NATO state. If verified and traced to Belarusian or Russian backing, this shifts the confrontation line from rhetoric to kinetic hybrid action on EU territory, with direct implications for NATO posture and European risk assets. A 04:14 UTC report states that armed, masked intruders crossed into Latvia from Belarus and conducted sabotage before the incident was publicized. The brief account, citing an article on “Armed, masked intruders enter Latvia from Belarus and carry out sabotage,” alleges a cross‑border operation rather than a routine criminal act. There are no immediate details on the specific target, casualties, or damage, and no official Latvian or NATO confirmation yet. But even as a preliminary claim, this marks a qualitatively different category of incident: armed sabotage teams allegedly transiting directly from Belarusian territory into a NATO member state. The information so far is limited: we know only that the intrusion route is described as ‘from Belarus’, that the personnel were armed and masked, and that their activity is labeled ‘sabotage’. Source confidence is medium‑low at this stage pending corroboration from Latvian authorities or independent reporting. However, the framing strongly suggests more than smuggling or ordinary border crime, and places the event squarely in the domain of hybrid or irregular warfare. For people on the ground in Latvia’s border regions, this type of incursion translates into immediate insecurity: rail lines, power substations, communications nodes, or local government assets are the typical targets of sabotage. Border communities may face tighter controls, increased military and police presence, and potential restrictions on cross‑border trade and transit. For governments in Riga, Vilnius, Warsaw, and Brussels, a confirmed sabotage team entering from Belarus would force decisions on border fortification, rules of engagement, and potential attribution to Belarusian or Russian security services. Militarily and in security terms, the allegation points to an escalation in hybrid pressure on NATO’s eastern flank. Even a small sabotage cell can probe for weaknesses in surveillance, response times, and political tolerance for ‘gray zone’ activity. If Minsk is found complicit—or if Russia is judged to have directed or enabled the operation—this becomes a test case of NATO’s response to sub‑Article‑5 hostile acts, potentially triggering stepped‑up deployments, intelligence sharing, and special operations activity along the Belarusian border. Markets will read any confirmation of Belarusian or Russian involvement as an incremental rise in European geopolitical risk. Direct kinetic action on EU/NATO soil, however deniable, tends to support safe‑haven flows into US dollar, Swiss franc, and gold, while adding modest pressure on the euro and Central/Eastern European currencies. European defense names could see renewed buying on expectations of additional spending on border security, ISR (intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance), and special forces capabilities. Broader European equity indices are unlikely to move sharply on this alone, but escalation or repeated incidents could start to weigh on sentiment toward CEE assets and banks with exposure to the Baltics and Poland. Over the next 24–48 hours, key watch points include: (1) official statements from the Latvian government detailing the nature of the sabotage, any casualties, and whether the intruders were captured or neutralized; (2) public attribution—does Riga explicitly blame Belarusian services, Russian operatives, or treat this as an isolated criminal act; (3) any coordinated response by NATO, such as emergency North Atlantic Council consultations or visible force posture adjustments in the Baltic region; and (4) evidence of follow‑on or copy‑cat incidents along the Latvia–Belarus and Lithuania–Belarus borders. A move from a single alleged incursion to a pattern would materially raise the strategic and market stakes. MARKET IMPACT ASSESSMENT: If confirmed as Belarusian or Russian-backed action, expect modest safe-haven bid into Bunds, USD, and gold, mild pressure on EUR and CEE FX, and incremental support for European defense equities. Escalation or confirmation of state involvement would raise regional risk premiums and could weigh on broader European equities. representative.author: Isabella Rossi

snapshot.title: FT: Estonia moves troops closer to Russia over threat of invasion and buys weapons with a range of 300 km – Babel.ua – EUROP INFO
snapshot.evidenceText: Estonia has intensified its defensive posture amid escalating regional tensions, relocating troops closer to its border with Russia and acquiring new weaponry with an extended range of up to 300 kilometers. This move comes amid growing concerns over a potential Russian invasion, signaling Tallinn's commitment to bolstering national security as geopolitical pressures mount. The strategic deployment and enhanced armament underscore Estonia's response to the shifting security landscape in Eastern Europe, a development closely monitored by NATO and international observers. Estonia Enhances Military Presence Near Russia Amid Heightened Invasion Threat In response to escalating tensions along its eastern border, Estonia has intensified its military deployment by repositioning additional troops closer to the Russian frontier. This strategic move is aimed at bolstering the country's defense capabilities amid credible intelligence pointing to a potential invasion threat. The Estonian Defense Forces have also accelerated their procurement of advanced weaponry, including missile systems with a striking range of up to 300 kilometers , significantly enhancing their ability to respond swiftly to any hostile actions. Analysts emphasize that the newly acquired armaments, combined with the troop reinforcement, mark a decisive shift in the Baltic nation's defense posture. Key elements of Estonia's upgraded arsenal include: Long-range missile batteries capable of precise strikes deep into adversarial territory Enhanced surveillance drones for real-time intelligence gathering Advanced anti-aircraft defenses designed to counter aerial threats effectively Equipment Range Deployment Status RS-300 Missile System 300 km In deployment Reconnaissance Drones Up to 150 km Operational Surface-to-Air Missile (SAM) 100 km Enhanced coverage Strategic Arms Acquisition Boosts Estonia's Defense Capabilities with Extended Range Weapons Estonia has significantly enhanced its defense posture by acquiring advanced weaponry capable of striking targets up to 300 kilometers away. This move not only extends the operational reach of its armed forces but also sends a strategic message amid rising tensions in the region. The newly procured systems include precision-guided artillery and missile platforms designed to reinforce border security and improve rapid response capabilities. Military officials emphasize that these acquisitions are crucial for deterring potential aggression and ensuring Estonia's sovereignty in an increasingly volatile geopolitical landscape. Alongside the extended range weaponry, Estonia is repositioning its troops closer to the Russian border, signaling a prepared and proactive defense strategy. Key features of this military upgrade include: Enhanced mobility for rapid deployment Modern targeting systems for improved accuracy Integrated command and control networks The strategic combination of upgraded hardware and tactical troop movements aims to create a robust deterrent capable of countering multiple threat vectors. Capability Details Weapon Range 300 km Deployment Zones Closer to Eastern border Systems Integrated Artillery & missile platforms Purpose Deterrence & defense readiness Recommendations for Strengthening Regional Security and Diplomatic Engagements Enhancing regional stability demands a multipronged approach that balances military preparedness with robust diplomatic initiatives. In light of Estonia's strategic troop movements and acquisition of long-range weaponry, neighboring countries should prioritize establishing regular security dialogues to prevent misunderstandings and reduce escalatory risks. These forums could facilitate transparent communication on defense postures and foster collaborative threat assessments, ultimately strengthening trust across borders. Coordinated diplomatic efforts must also extend to multilateral institutions where shared security challenges, such as hybrid warfare and cyber threats, can be addressed collectively. Key recommendations include: Implementing joint training exercises to enhance interoperability among Baltic and Nordic forces Expanding intelligence-sharing agreements to monitor potential provocations in real time Increasing diplomatic outreach to Moscow to establish clear red lines and conflict de-escalation mechanisms Investing in regional resilience programs to safeguard critical infrastructure and civilian populations Recommendation Objective Expected Impact Regular Security Dialogues Build trust and transparency Reduce miscalculations Joint Military Exercises Enhance cooperation and readiness Improve response times Intelligence Sharing Monitor and deter threats Increase situational awareness Regional Resilience Initiatives Protect critical infrastructure Mitigate impact of hybrid attacks To Conclude As tensions in Eastern Europe continue to mount, Estonia's decision to reposition troops nearer to the Russian border and invest in long-range weaponry signals a significant escalation in its defensive posture. This move reflects growing concerns over regional security and the perceived threat of invasion. Analysts will be closely watching how Russia responds to these developments, which could further influence the fragile balance in the area. The coming months will be critical in determining whether diplomatic efforts can ease tensions or if military preparations will lead to a more entrenched standoff.

representative.title: Zaporizhzhia Bombing Death Toll Reaches 20 as Rescue Ends
representative.author: Tymur Dubovyk

snapshot.title: Zaporizhzhia Death Toll Climbs to 20 Dead as Rescuers Conclude Search
snapshot.evidenceText: In brief: Search and rescue operations in Zaporizhzhia concluded on Sunday, Oct. 11, following a Russian guided aerial bomb strike that killed 20 people, including four children, and injured 17 others. Emergency workers cleared 320 metric tons of debris, with canine units from Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk regions aiding the operation as municipal authorities declared a day of mourning and transitioned to site recovery. Search and rescue operations in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia concluded following a Russian guided aerial bomb strike on a residential building on Saturday, Oct. 10, bringing the final death toll to 20, including four children. According to the State Emergency Service of Ukraine , another 17 people sustained injuries in the strike, including three children. Emergency crews dismantled collapsed structural sections of the damaged residential building and removed approximately 320 metric tons of concrete and masonry debris during the operation. Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Specialized search teams deployed canine units from the Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk regions to assist in locating victims beneath the rubble. With rescue operations officially terminated, municipal maintenance departments and utility services transitioned to clearing the perimeter and conducting structural stabilization work. A municipal day of mourning was declared across Zaporizhzhia on Sunday, Oct. 11, to honor the victims of the bombardment. The Saturday morning aerial assault caused extensive destruction across urban neighborhoods, collapsing an entire entrance section of a multi-story residential structure while damaging adjacent buildings and detached homes. Search and recovery operations continued without pause throughout Saturday, with rescue workers operating through shifting debris. Following eight hours of continuous excavation, emergency personnel extracted an adult woman alive from the rubble before transferring her to medical personnel for treatment. The bombardment was executed using tactical aircraft deploying high-explosive guided aerial bombs (KABs), which are released from standoff ranges outside the engagement perimeter of Ukrainian short-range air defense networks. President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the attack on the regional capital , characterizing the deadly strike as Moscow’s response to recent diplomatic moves easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports. representative.title: Transport unions adopt global principles to put workers at the heart of AI | World Ports Organization
representative.author: Akira Nakamura

snapshot.title: Transport unions adopt global principles to put workers at the heart of AI | World Ports Organization
snapshot.evidenceText: Launched today in Colombo, Sri Lanka, Seizing Control: Transport Workers’ Principles for Artificial Intelligence sets out the conditions that employers, technology providers and governments must meet when AI affects transport workers. They establish that no AI system in transport can be responsibly conceived, assessed, deployed or governed without the workers it affects and the unions that represent them. As the global alarm bells on AI get louder – with even industry leaders now calling for regulation and for development to slow –debate is converging around the need fortransparency, independent scrutiny and the human control of AI. “The ITF Principles turn those demands into enforceable workplace rights,” said Frank Moreels, incoming ITF President and member of the ITF Future of Work Advisory Group. “This must include the right to know what systems are being introduced, to assess their impact, to negotiate before deployment, to challenge AI-driven decisions and to retain human authority in such safety-critical operations.” AI is already allocating work, monitoring drivers, setting fares, running signalling systems and shaping decisions on hiring, pay and discipline across transport. Transport workers and their unions understand best how operations work and are often the first to identify when technology creates risks to safety, rights or working conditions. The Principles establish worker and union involvement as an essential part of assessing, introducing and monitoring AI. Moreels said: “Every company introducing AI into transport has a responsibility to know what that system will do to the people working under it. The tech giants selling AI into transport will tell you everything their systems can do –and nothing about what happens when they fail.” “Workers are the first to see when a system gets it wrong: when a sensor misreads a driver, when a roster pushes crews past safe limits, when an algorithm discriminates, when a worker is killed when systems fail. That is why unions are not an obstacle to AI, we are essential to getting it right and improving both operations and jobs.” Horacio Calculli, Chair of the ITF Future of Work Advisory Group, said: “The question is not whether AI will be used in transport, but who controls it, who benefits from it and whose interests it serves? AI in transport must serve the workers who keep the world moving and the public they serve,not shareholders and tech giants.” “These Principles give transport unions, responsible employers and governments a common platform to responsibly assess, deploy and govern AI in transport. What we have agreed is a common floor, the rights every transport worker must hold whatever the system is called and whichever country they work in.” Grounded in ILO standards and consistent with the UN Guiding Principles and OECD Guidelines, the Principles make clear that engaging workers and their unions is a core part of due diligence on AI, from conception to rollout across operations. Companies serious about the risks posed by AI now have a clear route to engage with transport unions. “Governments and technology companies are debating how to keep AI under human control. For transport workers, that is not a future or theoretical question, it is about who allocates their work, assesses their performance, determines their pay and discipline, and makes decisions affecting safety,” said Baker Khundakji, ITF Future of Work Lead. “The first step is information. Employers must disclose what AI systems are being introduced, what data they use, how they work and which decisions they influence. Workers cannot negotiate over a system they have not been told exists. Without transparency, there can be no meaningful consultation or collective bargaining.” “Rules on AI are urgently needed. Transport unions will take these Principles to the bargaining table and to their governments to demand binding, enforceable regulation, including ratification of ILO Convention 193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy,” said Khundakji. The conference committed the ITF to building a cross-border and transport-widepicture of how AI is being deployed across multinational companies and supply chains, developing practical bargaining, information-request and impact-assessment tools for affiliates, and coordinating advocacy for binding regulation. This will include campaigning for the ratification and implementation of ILO Convention 193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. 01 Human Rights, Labour Rights and Democracy by Design Human rights, labour rights, equality and worker dignity must be at the heart of AI in transport. 02 Mandatory Information, Consultation and Negotiation Unions must have enforceable rights to be informed and consulted – and able to negotiate – before AI systems that impact transport workers are introduced or modified. 03 Human Oversight and Decision-Making Authority Workers must have the right to challenge AI-driven decisions. And in safety-critical transport operations, humans must remain in control. 04 Occupational Safety and Health and the Precautionary Principle Workers must have the right to stop work when AI creates unsafe conditions. The burden of proof to show AI systems make a workplace safer lies with employers, not workers. 05 Data Rights, Transparency and Algorithmic Accountability Data generated by workers is a product of their labour. They must have rights over it – informed consent, compensation, control over personal data and limits on surveillance. 06 Equality, Gender Justice and Youth Protection AI must not deepen inequalities affecting women, young and older workers, migrants, workers with disabilities or other marginalised groups. Those most exposed to its effects must have a voice in how AI shapes their work. 07 Corporate and Supply Chain Accountability Companies must be accountable for labour standards and due diligence across their entire supply chain – not just where AI regulation is strongest. 08 Fair Distribution of Productivity Gains AI-driven productivity must deliver workers better pay, shorter hours with no loss of pay, better jobs and opportunities for training and reskilling. The Principles were adopted by delegates at the close of the ITF Transport Workers’ Conference on Artificial Intelligence, held 15–18 September 2026 in Colombo, Sri Lanka –a conference that brought together union leaders, negotiators and workers from across transport including aviation, ports, shipping, rail, road transport, warehousing, urban transport and the platform economy. Seizing Control: Transport Workers’ Principles for AI is available at The Principles are grounded in international labour standards, including the ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work, ILO Convention 190 on Violence and Harassment, ILO Convention 193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy, the ILO Centenary Declaration for the Future of Work, and the ILO Tripartite Declaration concerning Multinational Enterprises. About the ITF The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) is a democratic, affiliate-led federation of over 760 transport unions in 150 countries, representing more than 16.6 million transport workers. Founded in 1896, the ITF works to protect and improve the lives and futures of transport workers worldwide. Photo credit: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect
