representative.title: New Lancet Commission provides roadmap to protect economies, security and global stability from catastrophic threats to health and human survival | Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation

snapshot.title: New Lancet Commission provides roadmap to protect economies, security and global stability from catastrophic threats to health and human survival | Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation
snapshot.evidenceText: Global experts warn that today’s decisions across health, finance, climate, defense and security sectors will determine how many years of good health future generations gain – or lose – to preventable illness and early death by 2100. Sunday 11 October, Berlin – The health of the next generation will be shaped not by one defining crisis, but by a set of 17 interlinked catastrophic threats spanning disease, social and economic conditions, environmental change, technology and conflict, finds a new Commission published in The Lancet and launched at the World Health Summit 2026 in Berlin. For the first time, it provides decision-makers with a common framework to understand these threats and target action. Drawing on historical evidence and new risk analysis covering 204 countries and territories from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), authors of The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health examined hundreds of possible threats. Of those, the authors identified 17 that pose the greatest danger to human health and survival between 2025 and 2100 – and that governments, funders and industry have a realistic route to act on through policy change, funding decisions and innovation. The Commission identifies two threats as having extinction-potential: The catastrophic threats to health also include: “The striking finding is not only the scale of these threats, but that humanity still has the agency to act. Across all 17 catastrophic threats, the decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation. But delaying action will only serve to shift and increase the costs into the future.” These threats extend far beyond health alone, jeopardizing global prosperity, security and stability. The Commission’s forward-looking assessment provides three recommendations for leaders across the health, finance, defense, climate and security sectors and beyond to address these risks before they escalate into crises: build threat-ready health systems, accelerate investment in breakthrough innovation, and strengthen the monitoring of emerging risks to better protect societies and economies. For each threat, the Commission modelled a plausible best-case and worst-case future. The gap between them – measured in amenable disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), or the number of years in good health that are lost due to sickness, disability or premature mortality that could be avoided with targeted action – show decision-makers where investment and innovation can make the greatest difference. A threat was identified as catastrophic if it met three key criteria: it could account for at least one billion DALYs by 2100, there is sufficient data to model the threat, and where there is sufficient scope for policy action. Commission co-chair Professor Christopher JL Murray, Director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington, says: “The striking finding is not only the scale of these threats, but that humanity still has the agency to act. Across all 17 catastrophic threats, the decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation. But delaying action will only serve to shift and increase the costs into the future.” Co-Chaired by Dr. Murray and Dr. Natalia Kanem, Former Executive Director of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the Commission was informed by the expertise of 35 leaders spanning health, economics, security, governance, and technology, offering a globally relevant perspective. If current trends continue, the 17 catastrophic threats collectively could account for tens of billions of years of lost health. While the scale varies by threat and region, every country faces significant risks. Within each country, the health harms will also be distributed unequally, with people in resource-limited settings and marginalized communities bearing the greatest burden, compounded by existing inequalities. Dr. Murray adds: “The estimates highlight how much health loss could be avoided in each area. Some are already imposing substantial health burdens today, while others carry a real danger if they materialize. Crucially, all 17 threats are interconnected, which is why they must be addressed together, not in isolation.” • While the likelihood of nuclear conflict and the malicious use of AI remain low, they present consequential threats because of their potential for extinction. Accounting for both their potential impact and probability, the Commission’s assessment finds action to prevent nuclear conflict could avert an estimated 133 million deaths and 9.35 billion DALYs by 2100, while action to reduce the risk of malicious AI could avert an estimated 10.4 billion DALYs. • Climate change is already a catastrophic and urgent threat to health and human survival. The Commission finds that limiting global warming to around 1.8°C (rather than letting it reach 4.4°C) could prevent 1.89 billion years of healthy life from being lost to causes like extreme heat and air pollution. The true burden is likely even greater, as this estimate only captures direct harms we can measure today, excluding harder-to-quantify effects such as displacement, drought and mental health impacts. Without sharp cuts to emissions, these losses will continue to compound beyond 2100 and increasingly intensify other threats, such as migration, in ways not yet reflected in these numbers. • 16.1 billion DALYs are amenable to improvements in educational attainment , with women and children in sub-Saharan Africa facing the greatest potential burden of associated health loss. Faster progress on education will substantially improve health outcomes and reduce mortality rates among educated mothers’ children, while indirectly contributing to slower population growth over the longer term. • Income inequality could impose an amenable health burden equivalent to 25 COVID-19 pandemics by 2100, accounting for an estimated 13.8 billion DALYs. • Obesity is a significant and growing health burden that is forecast to compound over time, contributing to 23.1 billion potential DALYs by 2100 that could be avoided through policies to reduce obesity risk. • Sub-Saharan Africa is forecast to bear around 70% of the amenable health burden linked to a collapse in development assistance for health . Dr. Richard Horton, Editor-in-Chief of The Lancet adds: “This Lancet Commission offers a radical conceptual shift in the way we think about future threats to human survival. It invites us to expand the array of dangers facing humanity, moving from single issues to a broader and more complex landscape of threats, which demands a much more extensive framework for coordinated action. The jeopardies that face us are multiple. Our solutions need to match that reality.” Proven and emerging solutions for most of the threats to health already exist and are ready to be scaled up and implemented – from medicines and health technologies to proven public policies – while others require targeted investment and innovation to reach their full potential. For the first time, the Commission gives decision-makers a common framework to inform action before harm becomes embedded, with a clear three-part agenda: Without action, each of the 17 catastrophic threats presents significant risks requiring timely attention. Many of the threats are also interconnected and should not be viewed in isolation. The Commission’s framework is meant to help decision-makers identify opportunities for collaborative, cross-sectoral action that can build stronger societies that are resilient to global threats. Commission Co-Chair Dr. Kanem notes: “Recent global events show us just how quickly stability can give way to crisis, and how costly it is to respond only after disaster strikes. And the global threats to health risk amplifying existing inequalities, with the greatest burden falling on the most vulnerable communities. Yet the future is not inevitable. The Commission makes a compelling case for reshaping the future by embedding foresight into decision-making. Governments and communities must act decisively starting today, to protect health and build a fairer, more peaceful and more secure future for the coming generations.” An accompanying Lancet Editorial says: “It is important to be clear about what this Commission is and what it is not. The Commission does not present a fixed ranking of threats or policy priorities. On the contrary, the report emphasises that its analysis should be seen as a dynamic process - its findings will probably change as new evidence and data are accrued…We believe this Commission can catalyse international, regional, and national actions to protect and strengthen the future of health and humanity. Doing so will require all of us to think much more broadly about where the biggest threats lie.” Join us for the Launch of the Findings from the Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health October 11, 2026, 05:00–06:30 PT / 14:00–15:30 CEST All our datasets are housed in our data catalog, the Global Health Data Exchange (GHDx). snapshot.title: UN Geneva Press Briefing - 09 October 2026
snapshot.evidenceText: Press Conferences | UNHCR , UNICEF , IFRC , OHCHR , UN WOMEN , IOM , OCHA , WHO Recovery and preparedness in Nepal James Elder, for the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), speaking from Kathmandu, said that more than 32,000 children in Nepal had been affected by floods that had begun when a mountain of glacial ice and rock collapsed into a Himalayan river in late August. Parts of towns and villages still looked like war zones. Scientists warned that, as the Himalayas warmed, this kind of disaster was becoming more likely, and the countries that had done least to cause it were being left to pay for it. Mr. Elder stressed that this problem reached far beyond Nepal. The Hindu Kush Himalaya held more ice than anywhere on Earth, outside the polar regions. Two hundred and forty million people lived in these mountains. Another 1.65 billion lived downstream and relied on the rivers this ice fed, which was nearly two billion people – about a quarter of humanity. That system was now being pushed out of balance. Faster melting brought more water and more flood risk now, and serious shortages later as the glaciers disappeared. Both were driven by a heating planet. Nepal produced only around 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet children, who were least responsible for the climate crisis, were among those bearing its heaviest consequences. This disaster had not begun when the waters rose. Before the floods, more than half a million children in Nepal had been already exposed to at least multiple overlapping climate and environmental hazards. On a positive side, the response from Government, communities and the UN was comprehensive, with new bridges built just weeks after a mountain of water and rock ripped through such infrastructure. However, unless the world acted to reduce climate risks, we would keep returning to the same valleys after the next flood and the next landslide, and yet again find children once paying the highest price. That was true in Nepal, across Asia and the Pacific, and around the world, concluded Mr. Elder. Caroline Holt, Director for Disasters, Climate and Crises at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), had just returned from Nepal and shared what she had seen. She had witnessed stories of both loss and resilience. Ms. Holt provided an example of a teacher who had reacted quickly and warned his 900 students, making sure no child in his school lost a life. This teacher had been trained on disaster preparedness by the Nepal Red Cross. Investment in early warning and preparedness mattered and saved lives, stressed Ms. Holt. Now, the focus was shifting from immediate life-saving assistance to recovery. The Nepal Red Cross was the first organization to provide cash assistance, which allowed people to continue their lives with dignity. In the hardest-hit locations families faced numerous obstacles, and people now needed confidence in the future, which required planning. Sustained, reliable resources were very much needed as the recovery efforts were getting underway, concluded Ms. Holt. Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde, Director of the Regional Bureau for West and Central Africa at the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), who had just returned from the region, said that UNHCR was increasingly concerned about the deepening displacement crisis in the Central Sahel, with nearly four million people uprooted across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, including more than 818,000 refugees and asylum-seekers. This was roughly twice the number recorded in October 2020. The crisis was being compounded by continued attacks affecting civilians, climate-related shocks and severe humanitarian funding shortfalls. Together, these pressures were forcing more families to flee, eroding livelihoods and limiting opportunities for displaced people to rebuild their lives, contributing to further movements within and beyond the region. In Mali, the vast majority of refugees were from neighbouring Burkina Faso. In Koro, in the Bandiagara region, the refugee population was now approaching the size of the local host community, placing mounting pressure on already scarce land and water resources, overstretched health services and limited livelihood opportunities. Climate-related shocks were adding another layer of pressure to communities already struggling with displacement and insecurity. In Koro, agricultural cooperative initiatives bringing together Burkinabè refugees and host-community members had helped expand cultivated land from 21 hectares in 2025 to 45 hectares in 2026, improving food production and household incomes. representative.author: Heather Stewart

snapshot.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns
snapshot.evidenceText: UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned. Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”. “Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said. Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt. Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East. The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures. But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs. “What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said. “We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.” Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs. De Croo said: “The cost today for bond financing for developing countries, it’s 9%. That is really, really high.” He added that the situation was expected to deteriorate between now and the spring. “For each of the three things that we mentioned – fuel prices, El Niño and the bond markets – unfortunately for each of those at the moment, we don’t see any light at the end of the tunnel.” His warning chimes with the findings of separate research published on Sunday by the campaign group Debt Justice, underlining the social impact of high debt servicing costs. It shows that low-income countries classified by the IMF as either in, or at risk of, debt distress have cut their education budgets by an average of 8% since 2019, and wider public spending by 2%. Heidi Chow, the executive director of Debt Justice, said: “High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education.” Debt Justice is calling for the outright cancellation of some of the most burdensome debts, and overhaul of the IMF-administered common framework for debt restructuring. Chow said: “We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders.” De Croo said the UNDP did not oppose efforts to secure debt relief for some of the hardest-hit countries – but argued it would take many months to negotiate, and instead called for more urgent action. “We urge the international community – multilateral lenders, donors, and partners – to step up access to affordable finance so countries can sustain support for their most vulnerable households,” De Croo said. He praised the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva’s recent call for spending restraint in developed countries, in the hope of taming bond yields. But he said: “We also need to have a coordinated policy for developing countries. representative.author: Heather Stewart

snapshot.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns
snapshot.evidenceText: UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned. Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”. “Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said. Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt. Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East. The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures. But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs. “What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said. “We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.” Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs. representative.title: UNICEF Warns Impending El Niño Threatens Education, Health, and Safety for Millions | Inter Press Service
representative.author: Oritro Karim

snapshot.title: UNICEF Warns Impending El Niño Threatens Education, Health, and Safety for Millions
snapshot.evidenceText: A mother and her child stand in the wreckage of their destroyed home in Toamasina, Madagascar, following a devastating cyclone. Credit: UNICEF/Tsiory Ny Aina Andriantsoarana UNITED NATIONS, Oct 9 2026 (IPS) - New figures from the United Nations Children’s Fund ( UNICEF ) project that the impending 2026-2027 El Niño cycle could be one of the strongest on record. Marked by unusually wet and dry conditions, this cycle is forecast to trigger a host of extreme weather events, threatening the health, security, education, and development of over 347 million children worldwide. “For children, El Niño is far more than a weather pattern. It can mean increased displacement, malnutrition, water shortages, and disease outbreaks. Children are also at risk of schools closing, while families could experience added financial hardship,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell, emphasizing that anticipatory action is critical in protecting communities from climate shocks in the coming months. Nearly half of the world’s children—roughly 1.1 billion—are already exposed to at least three overlapping climate hazards, including droughts, extreme heat, and floods. The impending El Niño cycle could affect children and communities across nearly 100 countries and territories between October and December 2026. Rohini Sampoornam Swaminathan, UNICEF Statistics and Monitoring Manager, tells IPS that children are uniquely vulnerable because of their early developmental stage and dependence on essential services and caregivers. This significantly limits their ability to withstand climate shocks, especially as basic services begin to disappear when extreme weather hits. “Communities may not have fully recovered from one shock before another one strikes, causing the impacts to compound over time,” she said. The Asia-Pacific region is projected to face the heaviest toll, with roughly 190 million children estimated to be at risk. Substantial populations are also critically vulnerable across East and Southern Africa, with 41 million children vulnerable to climate shocks, alongside another 41 million in Latin America and the Caribbean. Approximately 22 million children are similarly vulnerable in Europe and Central Asia, followed by 20 million in the Middle East and North Africa, and 20 million in West and Central Africa. El Niño’s regional impacts are expected to vary significantly and could compound pre-existing humanitarian crises. Swaminathan underscored that climate shocks that are manageable in some areas can become pronounced humanitarian crises in others. Tropical nations—such as Colombia, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, and the Philippines—are forecast to face unusually dry conditions, driving weaker agricultural outputs and severe water scarcity. This, in turn, could elevate rates of acute malnutrition and adverse health outcomes among children. Conversely, communities in the Greater Horn of Africa could face alarmingly high levels of rainfall, particularly in Somalia, where there is a greater risk of riverine and flash flooding. Children in this region are especially vulnerable to outbreaks of water-borne diseases. Between 2016 and 2023, weather-related disasters displaced more than 20,000 children daily. Swaminathan stressed to IPS that regions facing wetter climates could experience exacerbated displacement as floods push more communities far from their homes and into crowded, temporary shelters, which amplifies protection risks. In protracted conflict or crisis zones such as Chad and Afghanistan, El Niño poses a direct threat to survival for children. Already bearing the burdens of extreme hunger, displacement, and an overwhelming lack of access to essential services such as protection, these children have no safety net when climate shocks ravage their communities, as they are already on the brink of collapse. Beyond physical hazards, UNICEF’s findings highlight that disruptions to schooling are among the most alarming consequences of the impending cycle. Severe droughts and floods threaten widespread school closures, declining attendance, and rising dropout rates. In 2025 alone, extreme weather patterns interrupted education for an estimated 171 million students globally. Swaminathan warned that climate-induced disruptions to schooling carry profound risks for children’s safety, exposing them to heightened risks of violence, exploitation, and child marriage. Girls bear the brunt of these impacts, often taking on family caregiving roles that can lead to compromised health and nutrition, as well as limited access to essential services. “When girls leave school, they are often less likely than boys to return,” she noted. UNICEF estimates show that every US $1 invested in disaster risk reduction and prevention efforts can yield up to $15 in saved recovery costs. Yet less than 1 percent of humanitarian funding is allocated for anticipatory action, even with months of warning and massive projected losses. The agency continues to call on governments, donors, and partners to invest in lifesaving anticipatory intervention before peak impacts hit vulnerable communities. UNICEF highlights building climate resilience, securing essential services, and guaranteeing humanitarian access as key priorities in its response. Swaminathan underscored that children with disabilities, who already face persistent barriers in education, healthcare, and nutrition, must be considered in disaster preparedness. She emphasized that inclusive planning is essential in addressing structural inequalities and ensuring every region is adequately prepared. “Despite efforts to plan for disasters, most resources are mobilized only after the damage occurs, and the focus is often on the immediate response phase of a crisis,” said Swaminathan. “With forecasts providing months of warning, UNICEF is urging governments, donors, and partners to act before needs escalate by investing early and before impacts peak. Building resilience is not only about infrastructure and early warning systems, but also about strengthening the services and institutions children rely on and addressing the inequalities that make some communities far more vulnerable to climate shocks than others.”

representative.title: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment | Global health | The Guardian
representative.author: Kat Lay

snapshot.title: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment
snapshot.evidenceText: Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists Humans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment. They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition. The experts behind The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health said all the threats interact, meaning they must be addressed together – but stressed that there was “a realistic route to act” on each. “Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” said Prof Christopher Murray, commission co-chair and the director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington. To create its list, the commission modelled how many years in good health might be lost due to sickness, disability or early deaths due to each threat, based on current trajectories – a measure known as disability-adjusted life years (Dalys). “Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the report said, adding that while their likelihood remained low, they had the potential to end humanity in the case of nuclear conflict by injecting enough particles into the upper atmosphere to block sunlight and cause famine, or via AI-created biological weapons. An accompanying Lancet editorial, published alongside the report, warned: “The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.” Other risks that could cause more than 1bn cumulative Dalys, and therefore deemed “major catastrophic threats”, included air pollution , antimicrobial resistance , childhood malnutrition and climate breakdown, as well as conventional conflict, declining overseas aid , high alcohol use , high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics , obesity , poor mental health , smoking and unhealthy ageing . To be included on the list, threats not only had to potentially cause a high number of lost healthy years, but also to have potential solutions. Ibrahim Abubakar, commission member and professor of infectious disease epidemiology at UCL, said: “We are not starting from a point of view of ‘oh look, we want to scare you – we’ve got X many threats facing humanity’. We’re starting from the premise that if you are a policymaker today, whether at the global multilateral level or at the national level, these are the potential threats that you could face, and this is the magnitude by which, if you act, you can actually make a difference.” Action to limit global heating to about 1.8C (3.2F) rather than letting it reach 4.4C could prevent 1.89bn years of healthy life being lost, according to the report, which modelled best and worst case scenarios for each threat. In higher income regions, non-communicable diseases such as obesity and poor mental health were the dominant threats, while in lower income regions health loss was driven by issues such as low educational attainment. Many major donor nations, including the US and UK, have announced large cuts to aid spending over the past year. The potential collapse of, or steep reduction in, international health aid could cause up to 1.5bn Dalys before 2100, the commission found, nearly 70% of which would be in sub-Saharan Africa. The region also bears the brunt of child malnutrition. The commission was made up of 35 experts, and its findings will be shared on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated annually to re-evaluate the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging hazards. The authors urged leaders to address the risks before they escalated into crises, including via investment in technological innovations and by strengthening health systems. “We started this process three years ago, thinking that there were three big threats: conflict, climate, and pandemics,” said Murray. “There’s a much larger number of threats that we need to worry about, and governments really need to dedicate some money and staff to the task of anticipation, prevention and preparation for this more diverse set of threats.”

representative.title: Gaza: Ceasefire Anniversary Marks Year of Failed Promises | Human Rights Watch

snapshot.title: Gaza: Ceasefire Anniversary Marks Year of Failed Promises
snapshot.evidenceText: No Reconstruction; Acute Humanitarian Needs; Killing Continues Share this via Bluesky Share this via Facebook Share this via X Share this via WhatsApp Share this via Email More sharing options Share this via LinkedIn Share this via Reddit Share this via Telegram Share this via Printer (Beirut) – Israeli forces continue to kill and wound civilians and deny sufficient food, aid, and water to Palestinians in Gaza one year after a ceasefire agreement took effect on October 10, 2025, Human Rights Watch said today. Israel’s acts of genocide and crimes against humanity , including forced displacement and extermination, have persisted throughout the ceasefire. Other countries should take immediate measures to protect civilians and ensure that rights-based reconstruction begins. The Board of Peace, authorized under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803, is tasked with assessing parties’ compliance with the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. Promises of humanitarian relief and the restoration of essential civilian infrastructure are central to the plan. Yet, a year on, aid volumes remain far below required levels , critical humanitarian access routes have been repeatedly obstructed, and reconstruction has not yet begun. Continuing Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,400 Palestinians and wounded 4,881 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, bringing the death toll since October 2023 to over 74,000, including over 21,000 children. “The outside world may be under a dangerous illusion that life in Gaza is returning to normal, but reality tells a very different story, ” said Sarah Sanbar , acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch. “There is nothing normal about living in a tent under bombardment, without enough food or drinking water for your family.” With winter approaching, families living in an Israel-engineered shelter crisis face preventable deaths and suffering affecting key human rights such as the rights to housing, health, and education. Ninety-four percent of Gaza’s population lacks adequate shelter, the Palestine Shelter Cluster reported based on a survey of nearly 2,000 households across Gaza. Nearly two-thirds of housing units have been destroyed , and many of those still standing are damaged and unsafe. The survey showed that over half of the nearly 2,000 households are living in tents. In September 2026, a damaged building housing about 100 people collapsed , killing 21, including 12 children. Gaza’s education and health sectors remain shattered. The new academic year began last month with 93 percent of schools destroyed or damaged. The World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 56 attacks on health care in Gaza between January and August 2026, with just 35 of Gaza’s 57 hospitals and field hospitals partially functional and not one fully operational. Meanwhile, humanitarian organizations report an increase in disease due to the living conditions in overcrowded camps and shelters, including poor waste management, sewage overflow, and rodent infestation. The risks of famine and acute food insecurity loom over Gaza, as the entry of humanitarian aid remains limited and inconsistent , and people in Gaza are unable to produce their own food due to Israeli forces’ widespread destruction of agricultural land and restrictions on fishing. In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC), the world’s foremost experts on food security, reported that 67 percent of the population—over 1.4 million people—are “expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026.” According to the European Union and UN, the recovery and reconstruction needs in Gaza are estimated at US$71.4 billion over the next decade. On September 23, the Board of Peace presented a “6-Month Gaza Recovery Program” ready to begin “the moment funding and access allow,” but one year on, no recovery efforts have begun. Israel continues to move the “ Yellow Line ,” the stated limit of the physical presence of Israeli ground forces under the ceasefire, westward beyond its agreed boundaries as Israeli officials call the line Israel’s “new border.” The area within the Yellow Line now amounts to about 64 percent of the Gaza Strip, and Israeli forces are displacing Palestinians as the line moves while preventing residents from returning to their homes beyond the line, corralling Gaza’s 2.1 million people into an ever-shrinking strip of land. In June, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs ( OCHA ) documented that 196 Palestinians had been killed near the Yellow Line and its westward movement is swallowing up water points and health facilities , further restricting Palestinians’ access to key services. Alongside these actions, Israeli officials continue to openly declare a goal of ethnically cleansing Gaza. For example, in September, Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir proposed the “ 710 Disengagement Plan ,” aiming to depopulate Gaza in seven years, and establishing a ministry of “voluntary emigration” for that purpose. According to Palestinian civil defense authorities, over 630 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble since November 2025, and they estimate that over 8,000 remain buried under the rubble. The UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory warned in September 2026 that the large-scale removal of rubble in areas of Gaza under Israeli military control should not become a way to erase traces of atrocity crimes. Finding the remains of those lost under the rubble is essential so that families can know what happened to their loved ones, offer them dignified burial, and start a long process of recovery and remedy, Human Rights Watch said. As world leaders discuss the future of Gaza, it is essential for them to urgently address the rights of Palestinians to rebuild their lives in Gaza, categorically reject all Israeli propositions of forced displacement and ethnic cleansing, and support all measures of accountability to put an end to the catastrophic situation for rights in Gaza. “Palestinians deserve a better future where their rights are respected and they can live in dignity, but none of this is possible unless the atrocities stop and justice and redress become a reality,” Sanbar said. For example, in September, Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir proposed the “ 710 Disengagement Plan ,” aiming to depopulate Gaza in seven years, and establishing a ministry of “voluntary emigration” for that purpose. According to Palestinian civil defense authorities, over 630 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble since November 2025, and they estimate that over 8,000 remain buried under the rubble. The UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory warned in September 2026 that the large-scale removal of rubble in areas of Gaza under Israeli military control should not become a way to erase traces of atrocity crimes. Finding the remains of those lost under the rubble is essential so that families can know what happened to their loved ones, offer them dignified burial, and start a long process of recovery and remedy, Human Rights Watch said. As world leaders discuss the future of Gaza, it is essential for them to urgently address the rights of Palestinians to rebuild their lives in Gaza, categorically reject all Israeli propositions of forced displacement and ethnic cleansing, and support all measures of accountability to put an end to the catastrophic situation for rights in Gaza. “Palestinians deserve a better future where their rights are respected and they can live in dignity, but none of this is possible unless the atrocities stop and justice and redress become a reality,” Sanbar said. representative.title: 139 migrants die after boat capsizes off Djibouti - Los Angeles Times
representative.author: Jamey Keaten, Claudia Ciobanu

snapshot.title: 139 migrants, including children, die after boat capsizes off Djibouti
snapshot.evidenceText: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday. At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Persian Gulf nations. The official death toll represents only those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by other migrants, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, the IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, told the Associated Press by phone. “What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation,” Coissac said. “They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened.” Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship Thursday night and it sank very soon after, close to the shore, “mainly because it was overcrowded.” “The local authorities did their best,” he said, “but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore.” He said authorities were bringing the survivors to the IOM rescue center in Obock, a Djiboutian port town, where they received medical assistance after swallowing seawater, and psychological support. “They're all in a state of shock,” said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday. “I tried to talk to some of them, but it's very difficult.” Some of the migrants in the IOM center are aware that family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive. The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said. The IOM, the Geneva-based United Nations migration agency, said the vessel had 305 people on board and noted that the death toll was expected to rise. Personal items probably belonging to passengers, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement. That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait. “This is a devastating loss of life,” said Coissac. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.” In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia. More than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project. “No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” IOM Director General Amy Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.” Keaten and Ciobanu write for the Associated Press. Ciobanu reported from Warsaw.

representative.title: Landslide-dam breach likely triggered Budhi Gandaki flash floods in Nepal: ICIMOD | International
representative.author: ANI

snapshot.title: Landslide-dam breach likely triggered Budhi Gandaki flash floods in Nepal: ICIMOD | International
snapshot.evidenceText: The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has identified the failure of a temporary landslide-induced river blockage as the probable cause of flash floods in Nepal's Budhi Gandaki river corridor. In a press release, the regional intergovernmental learning and knowledge sharing centre said the flash flood “may have been triggered by the failure of a temporary river blockage created by a landslide near Chumchet in Gorkha district, according to preliminary accounts from Nepal’s authorities…” In its preliminary assessment, ICIMOD estimated that the flooding began at around 4 am Nepal time on October 11, carrying mud, sediment and debris downstream through the Budhi Gandaki corridor. Recounting the early-morning evacuation, Kamala Duwadi, a resident of Arughat in Gorkha district, told ANI that she and other residents moved to higher ground after receiving warnings about the approaching flood. “In the morning, an alert was issued to us. I was inside my home and I came out hearing the sounds outside; the police were making public announcements for the evacuation. It was around 4:30 in the morning. I own a shop here and some of the workers who live upstream also called and warned about the incoming flood situation and explained that they also ran to higher ground for safety and asked us to move to safe ground. The fear of the Bhotekoshi Flood is still in mind; we quickly moved out from here to the higher ground up in the hills,” Duwadi said. Initial reports indicate that people are missing, houses have been washed away, bridges have been lost and riverside infrastructure has been damaged. Damage has also been reported at the 341 MW Budhi Gandaki hydropower site at Selleri, although the full extent of the losses remains under assessment. The latest incident comes shortly after the Gyirong-Rasuwa disaster, highlighting the risks posed by cascading mountain hazards, in which one event can trigger another and amplify the impact on communities and infrastructure. The latest flooding follows another major flood-generating event in the same valley in April 2024, when a massive ice avalanche from the snout of the Manaslu Glacier plunged into Birendra Tal, triggering a sudden overflow into the Budhi Gandaki River. A detailed ICIMOD-led assessment found that the event was caused by displacement of lake water following the ice avalanche, rather than a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF). “Together, the two events highlight the range of hazards capable of generating destructive floods in Himalayan river systems and the importance of monitoring multiple sources of risk,” ICIMOD stated. “Coming so soon after the Gyirong-Rasuwa disaster, this event is another reminder of how exposed mountain communities and river corridors remain to sudden, cascading hazards,” said Pema Gyamtsho, Director General of ICIMOD. “While response efforts must remain the immediate priority, understanding what triggered this flood will be critical for reducing future risks and strengthening resilience.” The Budhi Gandaki flood also highlights the vulnerability of settlements, transport networks, energy infrastructure and essential services located along mountain river corridors. As response efforts continue, understanding the interaction between slope instability, river dynamics and downstream exposure will be crucial for risk reduction, infrastructure planning and recovery efforts across the Himalayan region. “Current analysis points to the possible failure of a temporary landslide blockage that released a heavily sediment-laden flood downstream,” said Qianggong Zhang, Strategic Lead on Climate and Environmental Risks for ICIMOD. “Events like this demonstrate why monitoring and evaluating unstable slopes and river systems together is essential in steep mountain catchments, where hazards can develop rapidly and affect communities far downstream.” ICIMOD notes that future risk assessments, infrastructure planning and recovery efforts should account for multiple hazards, their triggering mechanisms and their cascading downstream impacts, particularly in river corridors where settlements, transport networks, energy infrastructure and essential services remain highly exposed to sudden-onset hazards. representative.title: Panama declares state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities | CBC News
representative.author: The Associated Press

snapshot.title: Panama declares state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: The government of Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours. Officials did not attribute any deaths to the quakes but reported damages in all 10 of Panama's provinces and two Indigenous territories. The 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes on Friday toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centered about 10 kilometres southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometres. Powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks Panama Presidential Minister Juan Carlos Orillac announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, health-care facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities. Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, told reporters the state had reports of 27 people with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate. Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos. The civil protection agency tallied roughly 420 homes and about the same number of public schools damaged. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes. In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64 kilometres northeast of the epicenter, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government's guidance on what to do next. Canadian in Panama experiences aftershock live on air | Hanomansing Live "We've been here since 1 p.m. yesterday; we haven't moved," Tony Jimenez, whose home partially collapsed, said while sitting with relatives under a tent. "It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense — truly intense." The collapsed Church of San Atanasio was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a Latin American region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months. Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela's La Guaira state in June, killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people. The notably lower toll in nearby Panama may have been due to the country's strict building codes, especially governing construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdes, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage. On Isla Cana, off the Pacific coast of Los Santos, approximately 300 people were evacuated because of rising sea levels and rough surf. Meanwhile, in the city of Penonome, around 150 kilometres from the capital, a shelter was housing 13 people, including five children. The earthquakes caused a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district's main square, as well as damage to the governor's office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. In Panama City, one of the water treatment plants supplying the area operated at 20 per cent capacity on Saturday, and tent facilities with cots were set up at six hospitals. Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region's busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday but reopened hours later. Powerful earthquake hits Panama, triggers tsunami warnings But hundreds of travellers on major Panama-based airlines like Copa Airlines were left stranded in airports around the region. Their connections through Tocumen — one of the biggest travel hubs in the region — were cancelled or delayed. In Mexico City's airport, airline employees scrambled as families with babies were sleeping on the floor Saturday while one woman from Venezuela shouted in panic that the flight through Panama was one of the only ways she could return home to Caracas. The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage. The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica, killed 23 people, injured 559 and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region. A vehicle lies crushed beneath a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Penonome, Panama, on Friday. (Aris Mariota/The Associated Press) Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates. Panama lies along the "Ring of Fire," a 40,000-kilometre arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world's earthquakes occur. Messages of support and offers of assistance flooded in from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others. The U.S. Department of State on Saturday said it mobilized a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The U.S. government also pledged $5 million US for humanitarian assistance. U.S. Southern Command also said two helicopters supported by the State Department's drug-control bureau had delivered 2,000 pounds of food to Panamanian communities affected by the earthquakes. representative.title: Isaias brought flooding, wind and tornadoes to the Southeast
representative.author: Jennifer Gray, Miriam Guthrie, Rob Shackelford, Jonathan Erdman, Jonathan Belles

snapshot.title: Isaias brought flooding, wind and tornadoes to the Southeast
snapshot.evidenceText: Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the late evening of Oct. 9 in the Florida Panhandle at Category 2 strength. Wind gusts over 110 mph were clocked in several panhandle locations, along with storm surge flooding. Over 700,000 customers are without power in its wake. Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, Friday evening with sustained winds of 105 mph, a Category 2 hurricane. That was the first hurricane to landfall in the mainland U.S. in exactly two years, since Milton slammed into western Florida on Oct. 9, 2024. A rarely-issued extreme wind warning was issued Friday evening for the western Florida Panhandle, including Pensacola and Destin, for the likelihood of wind gusts over 115 mph ahead of the eyewall of Isaias. The highest gust recorded was 116 mph in Santa Rosa Sound, Florida, where sustained winds of 91 mph were also measured. Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value. Pensacola reported a 102-mph wind gust earlier Friday evening. Gulf Breeze, Florida, located across Pensacola Bay from Pensacola, reported a wind gust of 97 mph and sustained winds of 83 mph. Early observations show water levels surpassed 4.0 feet above normally dry ground in Destin and 5.6 feet in Panama City, Florida, and were likely higher in the western Panhandle. One caveat with these storm surge totals is they are measured relative to the Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) and this number includes tide influences so they should not be interpreted as storm surge heights alone. The highest wind gust reported was an impressive 117 mph three miles east-southeast of Oriole Beach. Two miles west southwest of Pensacola, at City Hall, a gust of 102 was reported. There was a roof blown off the Rest and Relax Inn on Plantation Road in Pensacola. Multiple collapsed gas station canopies were reported in Pensacola (Blue Angel Parkway and Mobile Highway) and also in Crestview. Trees were uprooted, one of which crushed a business on Fort Walton Beach. There were also multiple RVs blown over, including one onto US 98 between Gulf Breeze and Navarre. representative.title: CJP at Jantar Mantar: Delhi braces for more protests as 'Cockroach' group's arrested leaders freed - BBC News
representative.author: Geeta Pandey

snapshot.title: CJP at Jantar Mantar: Delhi sees more protests as freed 'cockroach' group's leaders vow to continue fight
snapshot.evidenceText: Hundreds of protesters continued to be detained in Delhi on Sunday India's Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has vowed to continue its protest seeking the resignation of top election official even as the nation's capital sees demonstrations for a second day, with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded. Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders were arrested on arrival in Delhi on Saturday. They were freed on Sunday. Dipke said "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated" in his first comments after his release. Media reports said 7,000 protesters were detained and released on Saturday, with hundreds detained on Sunday. The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections. It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied. On Sunday morning, Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were set free by a magistrate's court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year", police said. After his release, Dipke posted on X: "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India." He said he was going to his village to attend the funeral of his grandmother, who died around the time of his arrest. He added that "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated". Ranka and Das later told a news conference that the condition did not mean they could not protest. "Peaceful protest is our constitutional right and Jantar Mantar is a desginated protest site, so this doesn't mean we can't do peaceful protest," Ranka said. "Breach of peace is done by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and CEC Gyanesh Kumar," he said, adding that the CJP will continue to protest. Saturday saw dramatic scenes as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed. 'Cockroach' leaders say they have been detained ahead of march For a second day in a row on Sunday, much of central Delhi had roads barricaded, offices, shops and restaurants shut and internet services curtailed. In Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest shopping and entertainment hubs, there were rows upon rows of bright yellow police barricades, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel. Protesters were vastly outnumbered by security personnel and the BBC has witnessed many detentions. Some were put onto buses before being driven away. Some could be seen peering through the windows, others trying to push their way out while shouting "Gyanesh must go!" At one point, an entire bus reverberated with similar chants. Every now and then, small groups of protesters managed to slip past the barricades and sprint through the streets, with police personnel chasing after them. Within moments, they were surrounded, detained and, in some instances, dragged across the road, before being bundled into waiting buses. The most dramatic moment came during the detention of activist Neha Bora , external , who was chased by police personnel before being caught and detained. Some protesters also said they were feeling a little uncertain. One of them told the BBC that the absence of the CJP's top leadership on the ground was beginning to affect the movement's momentum. "Without them, we're feeling a little lost," the protester admitted, before quickly adding: "But that doesn't mean we'll stop our fight." Security forces have been deployed across Delhi The CJP had called for a protest on Saturday at Jantar Mantar - the road that the demonstrators had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms. Police had refused them permission and the city was in a virtual lockdown with unprecedented curbs in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue. At least 45 metro stations were closed and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route. Internet was also curtailed in central Delhi for the entire day. After the police detained the CJP leaders and other activists, lawyers and students leaders, the CJP called for more protests on Sunday. On Sunday, the Indian Supreme Court held a special hearing to deal with complaints of shutdowns and detentions. The court ordered the government to restore the internet, and ensure that metro and rail services functioned normally, unless there were a disturbance to public order. The court also said that free movement of people should be permitted and there should be no illegal detention. Watch: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi The row centres on a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide. The commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters. At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed. The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated. The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this. The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms. Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he wrote on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?" Chief Justice Surya Kant says his cockroach comments were misinterpreted. But Dipke's post went viral and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability. Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister. representative.title: Arab News | Israeli forces enter southern Syrian valley, block farmers
representative.author: Arab News

snapshot.title: Israeli forces enter southern Syrian valley, block farmers
snapshot.evidenceText: LONDON: Israeli forces entered a valley near the village of Abidin in southern Syria on Sunday, preventing farmers from working their land, Syria’s state-run news agency SANA reported. The force, traveling in three military vehicles, advanced into the Yarmouk Basin in western Daraa province before withdrawing toward Jamla and returning to occupied territory through the Tal Abu Al-Ghaithar gate, according to SANA’s reporter. An Israeli soldier also damaged a farmer’s motorcycle during the incursion, the reporter said. The operation followed an incursion on Saturday into Al-Mushayrifah village in Quneitra province and along the road to Durbul in the Damascus countryside, where Israeli forces searched pedestrians, vehicles and homes, Syrian media reported. The incursions are part of a reported pattern of Israeli military operations in southern Syria, including raids, arrests and shelling. Syria says such actions, along with the leveling of land, violate the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. Damascus has repeatedly demanded a full Israeli withdrawal from Syrian territory, calling Israel’s actions illegal under international law and urging the international community to help secure its withdrawal. The operations come amid growing concern over the impact of Israeli military activity on civilians in southern Syria. On Oct. 9, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk expressed concern about the continuing toll on civilians. Open-source monitoring recorded about 280 incidents involving armed Israeli incursions in September, the highest monthly total since the start of the year. Reported actions included raids on homes, movement restrictions, harassment, intimidation, arbitrary detention and destruction of livelihoods. OHCHR Spokesperson Shabia Mantoo said in a statement that the agency received reports on Wednesday that Israeli forces had shot and temporarily detained a farmer with a disability during an incursion into Jubbata Al-Khashab in northern Quneitra. According to those reports, the farmer tried to leave the area because he was frightened by the soldiers’ presence. Israeli forces then shot him in the leg and detained him while he was bleeding. He was released about 90 minutes later and taken by Syrian Civil Defense personnel to Al-Golan Hospital in Quneitra for treatment and surgery, OCHA said. Damascus says Israeli incursions, including raids, arrests, shelling and the leveling of land, violate the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. It has repeatedly demanded a full Israeli withdrawal from Syrian territory, called Israel’s actions illegal under international law and urged the international community to help secure that withdrawal. Meanwhile, Israel says its military presence in southern Syria is intended to prevent attacks on Israeli communities. Stay on top of the issues that matter to you the most.

representative.title: Syrian Security Forces Step Up anti-ISIS Operations, Pursue Former Regime Loyalists
representative.author: Souad Jarous

snapshot.title: Syrian Security Forces Step Up anti-ISIS Operations, Pursue Former Regime Loyalists
snapshot.evidenceText: Syrian Security Forces Step Up anti-ISIS Operations, Pursue Former Regime Loyalists Syrian security forces have intensified operations against ISIS cells following a deadly September bus attack near Masyaf in central Syria, while separately pursuing former regime operatives accused of crimes against civilians. Within a week, authorities announced the dismantling of an ISIS cell in Homs province, following the arrest of the group’s alleged military commander there. Seven former regime suspects were also detained as part of transitional justice efforts. The Internal Security Forces announced that raids in the Houla area of northern Homs, conducted with the General Intelligence Directorate, had dismantled an ISIS-linked cell and foiled planned attacks on places of worship and security patrols. Two suspects were arrested and two explosive devices were seized. Preliminary investigations indicated that the detainees had received and transported explosives and monitored potential targets as part of plans to incite unrest and undermine security. One suspect was caught attempting to plant an explosive device on a railway track, authorities reported. Investigations are continuing to identify other cell members and their connections. The operation followed the arrest about three days earlier of Khaled Raed Bayrouni, known as Abu Hassan Doshka, in Hujayra, near Damascus. The Interior Ministry described him as ISIS’s operational arm in Homs and the group’s overall military commander in its so-called Homs province. Bayrouni is accused of planning and overseeing bombings and sectarian attacks, including an explosion at an Alawite mosque in Homs that killed eight people in late 2025. Authorities also launched raids and arrests following a Sept. 27 attack on a bus transporting workers near the Masyaf bypass bridge, on the road linking Masyaf and Homs, that killed seven civilians. Despite ISIS’s territorial defeat in Syria and Iraq, its small cells remain a security threat, exploiting instability and security gaps, particularly in remote areas. In early October, the international coalition against ISIS pledged more than $75 million to support Syria’s counterterrorism efforts, including measures to address security vulnerabilities and dismantle dormant cells. Separately, the Defense Ministry reported Saturday that a Syrian army soldier had died of wounds sustained in a shooting by unidentified gunmen Tuesday evening in Buqrus, eastern Deir Ezzor province. Two customs patrol members were also wounded when unidentified attackers opened fire near Izraa bridge in Daraa province as officers escorted a transit convoy, the General Authority for Ports and Customs announced Saturday. In a parallel operation, security forces detained seven former regime suspects in Masyaf, Hama province, accusing them of serious abuses against civilians. Nabil Adnan Ismail and Ghazi Mohammed Ismail allegedly commanded groups within militias affiliated with the former Air Force Intelligence Directorate and participated in kidnappings, looting and massacres, including violence in Aqrab village. They also face extortion allegations. Brothers Taher Youssef al-Mohammed and Talal Youssef al-Mohammed, who served in Air Force Intelligence and the Scientific Studies and Research Center, are accused of repression, arrests and exploiting access to detainees’ files to extort their families. Faisal Badour, nicknamed “Tiger Cub” for his alleged brutality toward civilians, joined armed militias in 2012 and participated in former regime military operations in Hama and Aleppo provinces. Another detainee, Assef Salameh, served as a noncommissioned officer at defense factories until 2018. Authorities had earlier arrested Shaheen Hamdan al-Shaheen, a founder of the Air Force Intelligence-linked Shaheen Regiment militia. He is accused of involvement in massacres in eastern Hama and along the Athriya–Raqqa road in 2017. His militia allegedly committed killings, arrests, torture and destruction in Palmyra and Deir Ezzor province through 2019. Washington Targets Hezbollah’s Alternative Funding Networks The United States is stepping up efforts to track alternative financing channels used by Hezbollah as tighter sanctions threaten its traditional sources of funding, particularly Iranian money that has long underpinned the group’s military and security capabilities and political influence in Lebanon. Washington’s campaign extends beyond restricting Iranian transfers to tracing foreign funding networks and cross-border commercial activities that Hezbollah could use to compensate for any decline in Tehran’s support. A Reuters report last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million in cash from Iran the previous month to assist tens of thousands of families displaced by the war prompted a response from the US State Department. The department expressed doubt that the money had reached Hezbollah but reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining pressure on the group’s funding sources through sanctions, while supporting the legitimate Lebanese government’s efforts to rebuild southern Lebanon. Sami Nader, director of the Middle East Institute for Strategic Affairs, described the measures as part of a new round of US sanctions aimed at tightening financial pressure on Iran and its regional affiliates. “The issue is not specifically Hezbollah, but primarily Iran,” Nader told Asharq Al-Awsat, pointing to a recent US announcement describing Hezbollah as an integral part of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps. Nader said Tehran had developed alternative channels to circumvent financial restrictions, particularly through gold and cryptocurrencies. He described an expanding network of such activities across the region, with links to Iran and Hezbollah. The latest sanctions are designed to target these alternative mechanisms, he explained. Nader added that if cryptocurrency offices linked to these networks are found to exist, Lebanese authorities would likely be asked to shut them down and take action against them, while also tightening oversight of gold transactions. Hezbollah has long relied on multiple funding sources, particularly under previous Lebanese administrations that turned a blind eye to billions of dollars reaching the group, including through official border crossings. Economist Antoine Farah identified four principal sources of financing: The first was direct Iranian support, provided through regular transfers from Tehran. The second involved illicit activities, particularly drug smuggling and the Captagon trade, which Farah said Hezbollah had engaged in both inside Lebanon and abroad, notably in several Latin American countries. The third consisted of substantial donations from Shiite financiers and supporters around the world. The fourth was a network of front businesses established to generate additional revenue, launder money and conceal the origins and destinations of funds. Farah told Asharq Al-Awsat that Hezbollah’s ability to draw on most of these sources had declined considerably, while the group faced mounting pressure from legislative and regulatory measures being strengthened in Lebanon. Farah highlighted amendments being introduced to Law No. 44 on combating money laundering and terrorist financing, particularly provisions requiring the identification of the ultimate beneficial owners of companies and commercial enterprises. Identifying who ultimately benefits from commercial activities, while tracing the origins and destinations of funds, would help restrict the operations of front businesses established by Hezbollah, he explained. Farah also pointed to measures being taken by Banque du Liban, Lebanon’s central bank, to regulate currency exchange dealers and money transfer companies. He said the measures were making it increasingly difficult to exploit these sectors to transfer money and channel financing to Hezbollah. Abbas Calls for Palestinian Presidential, Legislative Elections in September 2027 Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has issued a decree calling for simultaneous presidential and legislative elections on Sept. 11, 2027, canceling a legislative vote scheduled for Nov. 28, 2026, after his Fatah movement and other Palestinian factions agreed to postpone it. The widely anticipated decision sets a new date for Palestinians to elect both their president and lawmakers amid concerns over Israeli restrictions and the security situation in Gaza and the West Bank. The decree calls on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza Strip to participate in free, direct presidential and legislative elections to choose the president of the State of Palestine and members of the Palestinian Legislative Council, in accordance with the law. snapshot.title: Israeli forces enter southern Syrian valley, block farmers
snapshot.evidenceText: LONDON: Israeli forces entered a valley near the village of Abidin in southern Syria on Sunday, preventing farmers from working their land, Syria’s state-run news agency SANA reported. The force, traveling in three military vehicles, advanced into the Yarmouk Basin in western Daraa province before withdrawing toward Jamla and returning to occupied territory through the Tal Abu Al-Ghaithar gate, according to SANA’s reporter. An Israeli soldier also damaged a farmer’s motorcycle during the incursion, the reporter said. The operation followed an incursion on Saturday into Al-Mushayrifah village in Quneitra province and along the road to Durbul in the Damascus countryside, where Israeli forces searched pedestrians, vehicles and homes, Syrian media reported. The incursions are part of a reported pattern of Israeli military operations in southern Syria, including raids, arrests and shelling. Syria says such actions, along with the leveling of land, violate the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. Damascus has repeatedly demanded a full Israeli withdrawal from Syrian territory, calling Israel’s actions illegal under international law and urging the international community to help secure its withdrawal. The operations come amid growing concern over the impact of Israeli military activity on civilians in southern Syria. On Oct. 9, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk expressed concern about the continuing toll on civilians. Open-source monitoring recorded about 280 incidents involving armed Israeli incursions in September, the highest monthly total since the start of the year. Reported actions included raids on homes, movement restrictions, harassment, intimidation, arbitrary detention and destruction of livelihoods. OHCHR Spokesperson Shabia Mantoo said in a statement that the agency received reports on Wednesday that Israeli forces had shot and temporarily detained a farmer with a disability during an incursion into Jubbata Al-Khashab in northern Quneitra. According to those reports, the farmer tried to leave the area because he was frightened by the soldiers’ presence. Israeli forces then shot him in the leg and detained him while he was bleeding. He was released about 90 minutes later and taken by Syrian Civil Defense personnel to Al-Golan Hospital in Quneitra for treatment and surgery, OCHA said. Damascus says Israeli incursions, including raids, arrests, shelling and the leveling of land, violate the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. It has repeatedly demanded a full Israeli withdrawal from Syrian territory, called Israel’s actions illegal under international law and urged the international community to help secure that withdrawal. representative.author: Nada Salam

snapshot.title: Iraq to truck crude to Syria's Mediterranean coast from mid-October
snapshot.evidenceText: Iraqi crude is set to move overland to a Mediterranean port by lorry starting in mid-October, under a route Syria has agreed to provide, Bloomberg reported Friday. Yousef Qiblawy, chief executive of state-owned Syrian Petroleum, said the agreement between Baghdad and Damascus is almost complete and that exports should begin as soon as possible. Trucking crude is slower and costlier than tanker shipping, so the mid-October convoys read less as a commercial upgrade than as insurance: Iraq is building a second outlet for a revenue stream that is 90 per cent of the budget and almost entirely routed through one strait. The Baniyas fuel oil and petrol flows show the corridor already works in both directions. Watch whether the first truck convoys reach Syria by mid-October and whether Baghdad and Damascus formally sign the agreement.
