representative.title: Naidiri village, Fiji: 18,000 corals and a no fishing zone since 2009
representative.author: Nicole McMahon

snapshot.title: Naidiri village, Fiji: 18,000 corals and a no fishing zone since 2009
snapshot.evidenceText: Naidiri is 32 households on Fiji's Coral Coast. Since 2009 it has kept a stretch of its own sea closed to fishing, and in one year planted 18,000 corals and 10,000 mangroves. Now its youth group wants the protected line pushed further out. Drive the Queens Road along the south coast of Viti Levu and you pass Naidiri without noticing it: a village of fewer than 150 people in Nadroga, with the reef flat right there beyond the beach. Sixteen years ago that reef was in trouble. "We saw overfishing, and we were restoring fish," says Manoa Duwai, who co founded what is now the Naidiri Biodiversity Park. "There was no coral and no juvenile fish. We thought, if this is the case, what will our children ever have? That was when we came up with the idea of a marine protected area." In 2009 the village declared a tabu, a traditional no fishing zone, along about 3.6 kilometres of its shoreline, and left it alone. Two years later its young people formed a youth group to look after it, the first of its kind among the 22 villages of Nadroga. In 2023 alone the community planted 18,000 corals on frames in the lagoon and 10,000 mangroves along the shore. Last year the park took first prize in its category at the OceanLove Innovation Awards in Barcelona, chosen from 260 entries from 64 countries. Waisea Nasokia of the Fiji Sun visited this week and found the fish back, the frames full, and the young people asking for more. Read the full story: Naidiri youths protect ocean for next generation, by Waisea Nasokia, Fiji Sun . More, in Naidiri, means further. Joseva Kungado, the village youth leader, told the Fiji Sun that the tabu must continue and its boundary should be extended out to sea, because the pressure on the reef has not gone away. Storm surges have smashed coral frames and the cages where giant clams are grown, and each time the youth group has rebuilt them. "We don't want our future generation to say our parents and our forefathers did not give something to us," Kungado said. "We want to leave something for them." On Monday a group of visitors planted coral with them at Naidiri Bay, among them Brianna Fruean, the Samoan Pacific leader, and Kal Glanznig, a young Australian ocean champion, who said it was "fascinating to see such incredible work by the youths of Naidiri." It is the simplest conservation there is, and it is the kind that works best close to shore, where the people who gave the water its rest can wade out and watch it heal. Our short take: the full story is by Waisea Nasokia for the Fiji Sun (6 October 2026). Enjoyed this? Every new edition is free, straight to your inbox. Subscribe free In Tla-o-qui-aht waters off Tofino, guardians, scientists and a kelp grower are raising baby kelp on four long lines under the sea and planting it out so young salmon and herring have a forest again. About 1,500 sea otters, back after the fur trade, are helping. At Long Nanny on the Northumberland coast, National Trust rangers kept watch over the dunes day and night all summer, and 126 pairs of little terns nested there, more than double the 1994 record. At Blakeney Point, a thousand pairs of sandwich terns came back after two years away. Voting is open in the ABC's Australian Insect of the Year, a tortoise shelled ladybird is in the final six, and the reigning champion is a dragonfly with painted wings. Good news for a living planet. representative.title: In UP SIR, ECI Software Auto-generated 85,854 Forms to Delete Voters Without a Reason
representative.author: Sumedha Mittal, Ayushi Kar, Shubhangi Derhgawen, Edited by : Furquan Ameen

snapshot.title: In UP SIR, ECI Software Auto-generated 85,854 Forms to Delete Voters Without a Reason
snapshot.evidenceText: New Delhi: The Election Commission of India (ECI) forced officers in Uttar Pradesh to sign deletion forms for 85,854 voters without giving any reason during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in the state. All these deletion forms were submitted after the legally mandated deadline. The deletion requests came en masse from election officers during the claims and objections period of the SIR in Uttar Pradesh (UP), between January 6, 2026, when the draft voter list was published, and April 10, when the final voter list was released. The Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (UP CEO) displayed all the deletion forms, officially called Form 7 objection requests, on its website. More than 4.3 lakh such forms were submitted. Working with a team of data analysts, The Reporters’ Collective scraped all the Form 7 disclosures from the UP CEO’s website. We found that 20 percent of these removal requests were submitted directly by the ECI’s own assembly-level officers. But the officers did not fill the forms. The ECI’s own software, ERONET automatically generated these forms, when officials deleted voters during the SIR hearings. The auto-generated forms came loaded with the officers’ digital signatures and were sent up for approval by their seniors. The job of these election officers is to adjudicate such claims of deletion. But in these cases they were acting as both the prosecutor and the judge. Under the law, citizens filing objections are required to put down specific reasons for requesting the deletion of voters. The ECI rules are clear on this. Applicants submitting Form 7 to seek deletions are required to select one of the justifications mentioned in the form. The reasons can be: the person is dead, underage, absent/permanently shifted, already enrolled or not an Indian citizen. In our investigation, we also found that a total of 1,10,476 voter deletion requests were submitted by individuals and accepted by the ECI after the legally mandated deadline. Out of 4.3 lakh Form 7 applications, in two assembly constituencies in UP, people with the same name filed hundreds of requests almost exclusively against Muslim voters. In Tarabganj and Pilibhit assembly constituencies, 90 percent of the deletion requests filed were against Muslims. In Tarabganj, 188 objections were raised under one name ‘Reshma’. When we dug further we found that all were filed on the same date against people from the same booth. The pattern repeats across the state. However, the ECI data does not provide identity details, beyond the name, of those who have proposed the deletions. Therefore citizens cannot independently verify or identify them. We sent detailed questions to UP Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa as well as to the ECI in Delhi. They had not replied by the time of publication. We analysed the scraped data and spoke to four election officials at the assembly level. We learnt that the Form 7 requests were automatically generated when officers removed voters during the SIR hearings they conducted. All the forms already had the official’s digital signature, leaving them no choice but to send them up the chain for approval. While 3.43 lakh individual objectors followed the process and specified the reasons for seeking a voter's removal, election officers failed to provide any reasons. We know that the ECI was auto-generating Form 7 requests through its software earlier during the enumeration process, as well. These were being submitted by booth-level officers (BLOs) who found voters to be absent, shifted, dead, or duplicate (ASDD) during enumeration. The BLOs had to specify one of the six reasons while filing deletions that would later be determined by election officers in each assembly, the electoral registration officers (EROs) and assistant electoral registration officers (AEROs), before they were put on the ASDD list. But we have now found that the ECI’s software compelled EROs and AEROs, who have quasi-judicial powers under the Representation of People Act, 1950 to both file and approve the deletion of voters after the SIR hearings were over. This goes against the ECI’s rules for SIR hearings. They explicitly state that a reason must be given or put on record for the voter to be removed. This change in procedure violates the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The rules say that election authorities must outright reject any claim or objection that is not submitted in the prescribed manner, including specifying a clear reason. But, changes in the software forced election officers to sign off on unlawful forms anyway. UP was one of the 12 states and union territories to conduct the second round of the SIR exercise. It ran in three broad phases. In the first phase, starting November 4 , 2025, BLOs were tasked with distributing and collecting enumeration forms from every voter listed in the state electoral roll as of October 2025. Voters whose forms could not be collected were placed on the ASDD list for deletion. For this step, the ECI’s central software, ERONET, automatically generated a Form 7 that the BLO was required to sign with a specified reason. Of the 15.44 crore voters originally registered in UP, 2.89 crore names were placed on the ASDD list. On January 6, the state CEO published its draft electoral roll. In the following claims and objections phase, hearings were conducted for voters who were flagged as doubtful by the ECI algorithm but placed on the draft list. The ECI marked 3.26 crore electors as doubtful due to ‘logical discrepancies’ or for being ‘unmapped’. Assembly-level officers, including EROs and AEROs, summoned these flagged voters for hearings to prove their identity. If officers failed to verify them, they were struck off the final rolls. On April 10, UP published the final voter roll with 13.4 crore electors. At the press conference , UP CEO Navdeep Rinwa did not specify the number of voters removed during these SIR hearings. But we spoke to four EROs about the en masse Form 7 deletions our investigation found. They claimed the forms were submitted to delete unverified voters during the SIR hearings. The ECI rules for the SIR define the window between the publication of the draft and final rolls – the claims and objections phase – as the period for receiving addition and deletion requests from voters. Draft rolls allow citizens to first inspect who has been wrongfully included or marked under ASDD so that they can submit Form 7 deletion or Form 6 addition requests. The fact that a significant portion of the deletion requests at the time, more than 20%, were filed by election officers raises suspicion. Our analysis of the data scraped from the ECI’s website shows that 85,854 (98.5 percent) of the 87,127 requests filed by EROs and AEROs have no reason mentioned for deletion. For 62 of those, only letters such as ‘A, N, H, E’ had been mentioned as the reason. In 1,211 forms, “absent/shifted” is mentioned as the reason for deletion. All the 87,127 requests by EROs and AEROs were filed within 19 days, between March 15 and April 2, 2026. The four EROs we spoke to claimed these deletion requests were initiated for voters flagged for logical discrepancies or for being unmapped. “As an ERO, whenever we did not approve a voter during a hearing, the system automatically generated a Form 7 on our behalf,” one ERO told The Collective . He clarified that since the mechanism for approving voters in the app was accessible only through their credentials, “it was bound to bear my signature.” We reviewed the ECI’s rules for SIR hearings, which were circulated only to officials and were never made public. They require that, after issuing a suo motu notice, officers put down an explanation for why a person is being removed from the roll. However, UP’s electoral officials claimed the ECI’s software had been tweaked in such a manner that they were left with no option but to become signatories to the deletion of thousands across the state. The EROs suggested the process had been turned on its head in the SIR. Hearings were held first and notices for the deletion of voters were generated next. Sumedha Mittal is an independent journalist based in New Delhi. She is drawn to stories about Indian elections and the functioning of the Election Commission of India. Even in her free time, you will find her chasing stories. Ayushi leads data investigations into India’s political economy for The Reporters Collective. She previously worked as a tech and telecom reporter for The Hindu BusinessLine. She studied at the University College London and writes fiction in her free time. Shubhangi Derhgawen is a freelance investigative journalist who reports on governance, and public policy with a focus on how state decisions shape people’s lives. She was previously with Deutsche Welle and NDTV India. Furquan is a journalist and the managing editor for The Reporters' Collective. He has written at the intersections of politics, identity, conflict and social exclusion for prime Indian and global news outlets such as The Telegraph , IndiaSpend, Hindustan Times, The Caravan and Al Jazeera. His last stint was with Land Conflict Watch, where he led the editorial and product initiatives. Furquan has also worked as a researcher with the International Center for Journalists and been a fellow at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, University of Oxford. He has presented his research at several academic conferences including the International Journalism Festival in Italy, at the UNESCO Press Freedom Day celebration in Ethiopia and at the Kabul University. The Reporters’ Collective collaboratively produces investigative journalism. In many languages and mediums. We report truthfully and bring out facts that the powerful prefer to keep hidden from citizens. Besides courage and integrity, such reporting requires resources. We need your support. We need citizens to donate to keep us going and keep our work free to read for those who can’t afford to pay. Your donations will help us remain independent and work without fear. The tax authorities have revoked our non-profit status claiming our journalism does not benefit the society. The order has severely choked the funds we need to carry out investigative journalism. If you believe the government and the powerful in the country need to be held accountable to citizens. If you believe our journalism does so, please donate to keep the Collective alive. snapshot.title: A 75-Year-Old Nalanda Cobbler, Who Mended Shoes All His Life To Help His Children Stitch A Bright Future
snapshot.evidenceText: Nalanda: Once upon a time, Kedar Mochi was repairing shoes on the pavement near JP Market on Ranchi Road. It was that spot which remained the only constant in his life, and the only means to earn a living, that helped him pay for his children s education and upbringing. Now past 75, Kedar has left behind his mud house and lives in Sabanhua Dihpar tola in Ward 5 of Harnaut Nagar Panchayat in Bihar’s Nalanda district, in a single-storey pucca house, that his children built for him and the family. Bringing up six children was not easy for Kedar but he ensured their education never took a back seat. Today, he proudly says that his elder son Sanjar Ravidas, also known as Manoj Kumar, is a school headmaster, younger son a rozgar sevak under MGNREGA and and two of his four daughters work in community healthcare."I am happy to see that my hard work paid off. All my children are doing well in life. The only reason of worry for me is my old-age pension which I have not received since last four months, says Kedar.Between mending shoes and polishing a few, Kedar reminisces, how he would take time out to read the newspaper. He also remembers how the discussions between customers influenced him and helped him develop a broad outlook. Politicians and educated people who stopped at my pavement shop there often stayed to talk. For me those conversations opened a world beyond daily earnings. I started questioning why poor families were denied ration, why students did not receive scholarships and what could be done about it, explains Kedar, who had completed matriculation level education.He began taking those grievances to the block office. He also understood how important is education for the children. With my limited earning I grew aware that apart from the worries of the next meal, my children s education should be the immediate priority, he says.His younger son, Ranjan Ravidas, recalls how old customers later on came not only have their shoes repaired or polished, but also to meet his father. The shop became a meeting point of old friends and acquaintances. "My father stitched shoes on the pavement but he also fought against injustice. If a ration dealer refused someone their ration, or anyone was denied their rights, he openly opposed it and confronted the officials," Ranjan says, recalling his father’s dealings with block development and circle officers.Poor students waiting for scholarships and families struggling to obtain ration found someone willing to accompany them and argue their case. Such encounters sharpened Kedar’s understanding of politics and made him a familiar figure among local residents.Although he never contested an election himself, he encouraged his wife, Kesari Devi, who had received no formal education, to enter public life. She was elected a ward member twice from Sabanhua panchayat. In 2006, Ranjan became a ward member, while Kesari served as a panch in the gram kachahri, the village-level dispute resolution body."We helped get work done for people in the village and educated our children, Kesari recalls on how she entered politics. At home, however, there was little money to spare. Kesari remembers the mud house and days when arranging two meals was difficult. Kedar continued to put the children’s education ahead of his own needs."We earlier had a mud house to live in, and at times even two meals a day were a struggle. But he never bothered about his own needs. He spent every rupee he earned on educating our two sons and four daughters," she says.Sanjar completed master’s degrees in sociology and English, along with a BEd, and became a teacher in 2007. In 2025, he cleared the Bihar Public Service Commission selection process for headmasters. He now serves in Triveniganj in Supaul district.Ranjan completed a master’s degree in history and joined MGNREGA as a rozgar sevak in 2008. He is currently posted in Hajipur.Kedar also ensured that all four daughters studied up to Class 10. All are now married and two work as ASHA and Mamta workers under the health department. His daughter Mamta Kumari, an ASHA worker in Khabra panchayat in Muzaffarpur, remembers how different their circumstances once were."Papa repaired shoes by the roadside but it was his hard work that ensured that our circumstances change. We all studied and that improved our condition later," she said.Kedar’s encouragement to participate in public life extended to his daughters-in-law. Pooja Devi, Sanjar’s wife and a graduate, contested the district council election from Harnaut in 2011 though she lost by just 200 votes."My father-in-law was involved in politics and he encouraged me to contest. He would go to the block office to help people get their ration and I was motivated with his way of dealing with people s issues. I therefore contested the district council election from Harnaut," Pooja says.His younger daughter-in-law, Shobha Devi, also contested a municipal election in Harnaut in 2023. The family said she received 5,500 votes but lost. Shobha said contesting elections required money that the family did not have. Her hopes now centre on the children’s education - she wants them to become doctors and engineers.Kedar s house now has a kitchen and a toilet and the uncertainty that once surrounded their daily meals has eased. Age and ill health have, however, confined Kedar largely to the house. I fought for people s issues but I have been deprived of my own old age pension since months. Occasionally even obtaining ration becomes difficult, rues Kedar.His children’s livelihoods offer some comfort, but those complaints remain unresolved. For a man who spent years arguing that poor families should receive what was due to them, the wait has become too personal now. But I am hopeful things will change and I will get my due. I have always taken up the cudgels for others, so, I believe, my concerns will be addressed, says Kedar with a faint smile.Also Read:After Laying Down Arms, Bastar s Arjun Clears Class X In First Division, Sets Target To Become An Education Ambassador 5 Doctors In The Making: This Poor Tribal Family From Kandhamal Village In Odisha Has All Children Studying Medicine

representative.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine - BBC News
representative.author: Sarah Rainsford

snapshot.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
snapshot.evidenceText: Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022 Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children. Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks. But German police were already closing in on him. After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany. Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine". Both he and his country have denied any involvement. Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov. Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea. There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas. Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers. They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda. Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat. As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow. Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure. But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise. The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services. In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich. That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy. He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks. But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected. Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him. By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert. Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs. None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions. But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them. "Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that." Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe. That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it. Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution. "Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out. The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution. Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence. "At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained. Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned". Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far. Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August. He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation. Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him. Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning. He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver. Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him. In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war". As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more." The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg. After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop. It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv. It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone. When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that". This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further. "I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully. He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did." Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial. Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated. He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023. His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing. And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either. His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up. I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot. snapshot.title: A century after it was taken, ancestral tipi cover returns to Kawacatoose First Nation
snapshot.evidenceText: Cree community in Saskatchewan brings home their Ancestor sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted fabric from Smithsonian in ‘Washington, D.C.’ Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter Those were okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn’s words when he first touched the tipi cover connected to his great-great-great-grandfather, sîpiskwêsîkan. After a century away from Kawacatoose First Nation , the ancestral item has returned to the Cree community. Community and family members gathered around the tipi cover after it was brought back from the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of the American Indian in “Washington, D.C.” “When I first touched it, I just felt so emotional,” Dustyhorn said. “I was thinking of all those that are gone on before me.” He thought about his parents, grandparents and ancestors — who preserved the history of the item through generations. He prayed for them to be present as the community finally brought home a piece of their history. “I told all of them, ‘Come with us, come and attend with us,” Dustyhorn recalled. “I know they were in between all of us — and they were here, too.” The tipi cover remained in the community for four nights before being temporarily housed at the Royal Saskatchewan Museum in oskana kâ-asastêki (Regina). Until the First Nation can build a permanent museum or cultural centre to house it safely, they plan to bring it home each year. The return followed a reparation process that lasted almost three years. Andrew Miller, an associate professor at the First Nations University of Canada, helped the Dustyhorn family locate the item and communicate with the Smithsonian. Miller described the tipi cover’s return as a meaningful example of reconciliation in action. “One of my friends from the Royal Saskatchewan Museum said, ‘Congratulations, you’ve just realized reconciliation,’” Miller said. “That’s what this is.” But for Miller, reconciliation means more than merely acknowledging past injustices. It also requires returning ancestral belongings and supporting communities as they restore cultural teachings. Dustyhorn said the return also highlights the need for stronger support from governments and museums — for all Indigenous communities hoping to recover what was taken away from them. “They talk about truth and reconciliation,” he said. “They splash that all over the news for a few years. “But where’s their help? How can we get the stuff back that was taken from us, too?” Miller and Dustyhorn said the tipi cover was taken during an era when museums and governments declared that Indigenous cultures were disappearing and needed to be archived. That view justified an urgent push to collect ceremonial belongings and other ancestral items from Indigenous communities worldwide. “They were wanting to capture the disappearing Indian,” Dustyhorn said. Miller said museums particularly sought items connected to regalia, ceremonies, and other cultural practices as part of that colonial narrative. “They were targets,” Miller said, describing sacred belongings as part of the “vanishing Indian culture” narrative. But, Dustyhorn emphasized, “We’re still here.” Miller first learned about the tipi cover from a former student, Andrea Dustyhorn. Years later, while researching ethno-ornithology — the relationships between people and birds — he found the tipi cover in the Smithsonian’s catalogue. “You should see this,” he told the chief. “What do you want to do?” Together they began an arduous process to bring the cover home. Dustyhorn’s family provided genealogical information and oral histories connecting it to his great-great-great-grandfather. During one meeting, he recounted Smithsonian representatives asking how he knew the tipi cover actually belonged to his community. Their question, he said, reflected what he called a big difference between written museum records and Cree ways of preserving history: through oral stories, saved for generations. “Everything is handed down orally,” Dustyhorn told them. “Let me tell you a story.” Dustyhorn began sharing the history passed down through his family about the tipi cover — and the person who took it. As he described the collector’s journey from Alaska through Saskatchewan, the Smithsonian representatives recognized details that matched their own written archival records. “They said, ‘Did you know he started in Alaska?’” Dustyhorn recalled them asking about information he already knew. “And I’m like, ‘Really?!’” The exchange connected the community’s oral history with the Smithsonian’s documentation, which to the museum established the family’s claim to the cover. According to archival records, the item was taken in Saskatchewan in 1926. Although the National Museum of the American Indian has since deleted its record of the tipi cover, an archived version of its webpage states it was obtained by museum staffperson Donald Cadzow — who it notes was a “non-Indian.” “Collected from Dusty Horn (sîpiskwêsîkan, Plains Cree, b. ca. 1863),” the record states. Cadzow was hired seven years before he took sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted fabric, promising payment the community says never came. “He made four field trips north,” the Smithsonian Institution states, “and collected over 2,000 objects from northern Athapaskan and Plains peoples.” It was later transported through Winnipeg, “Toronto” and “New York City”— before finally reaching “Washington, D.C.” A century later, last June, the Smithsonian notified the family it had deemed the cover was ready to return. At the time he was travelling to “Regina” when he got the email. “I just started pumping my fist,” he remembered. “Yeah, it’s the tipi,” he replied. “It’s ready to come home.“ In August, a group from Kawacatoose First Nation finally travelled to “Washington, D.C.” to repatriate the tipi cover. On the journey back, Dustyhorn said the weather changed as they approached the border. Rain, hail and lightning surrounded the vehicle. “It started raining really hard,” Dustyhorn said. “It was raining and lightning happening all around us… it started hailing.” He saw the weather as a sign that the tipi cover was leaving behind the painful history connected to its removal. “It’s washing the negativity — the 100 years of negativity that it is carrying … leaving it in the States,” he said. Miller also remembered that storm — but also the clear skies that emerged soon after they crossed into “Canada.” The travelers placed tobacco down, seeing the brightening weather as a meaningful part of the tipi cover’s return journey home. Yolanda Dustyhorn, the community’s cultural co-ordinator, described the item’s return as an emotional and historic moment. “Words can’t describe,” she said. “It’s very touching to have it come [back home]. She also spoke about the item’s condition after so many decades away. “The way it’s preserved, it’s 100 years old … yet we were able to still erect it,” she said. “It’s amazing.” She hopes having the tipi cover available in Saskatchewan will help younger generations learn about their history, culture and traditional teachings. “We gotta bring our culture back,” she said. “I want them to see this and to realize we gotta bring our culture back.” She plans to incorporate the returned tipi cover into programs for Youth. Her work includes teaching traditional medicines, ribbon skirts, belts and other cultural practices. “I’m targeting the Youth and the children,” she said. “We are gonna start bringing culture back.“ Miller said the loss of cultural belongings continues to impact many Indigenous communities a century later. “It impacts the present generation to this day.” He said the removal of ceremonial belongings like the tipi cover significantly disrupted cultural education, language and traditional practices. “This was involved in ceremony,” Miller said. But there are countless more ancestral belongings from Indigenous Peoples still held in museums and archives around the world. “There’s a lot out there,” he said. “Pipes, rattles, regalia, medicine bundles.” Reflecting on his correspondence with the Smithsonian, Dustyhorn said he felt there were unnecessary delays throughout the repatriation process. “We’d wait months for a reply,” he said, and they kept setting up more and more meetings. Although they were ultimately successful, Miller argued that museums should be willing to participate more proactively in repatriating communities’ cultural belongings — “to give back the things that are requested,” he said. For Kawacatoose’s leader, despite the hurdles he had to jump through, the return of his great-great-great-grandfather’s tipi cover proved what communities can accomplish when they keep fighting for their belongings. He encouraged other First Nations hoping to recover ancestral belongings to be persistent. “Start the process and finish the process,” Dustyhorn recommended. “Keep going forward — one foot in front of the other everyday — until they get it home. “I want all the other communities to get their stuff, to bring pride back to their Nations.” His First Nation is now working to bring home additional belongings, he said, estimating that about 900 artifacts connected to the community are held at the Glenbow Museum in otôskwanihk (Calgary). The community is also preparing for the return of objects from the Field Museum in “Chicago.” Miller said that collection could include roughly 60 items. For the Nation and the Dustyhorn family, the return of sîpiskwêsîkan’s tipi cover is both a homecoming — and a renewal of their profound cultural pride. “I want all our kids to be proud,” the chief said. “Walk with your head held high.” Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter Brittany Boschman is of Swampy Cree-German heritage, born and raised in Brandon, Manitoba, with strong ties to her home community of Pimicikamak Cree Nation. Brittany holds a Bachelor of Arts in Indigenous Studies and Indigenous Communications Arts (INCA) from the First Nations University of Canada, with minors in Cree and Kinesiology. In her spare time, she loves all things sports. And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter. Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect. representative.title: 'Home' documentary from 'Degrassi' co-creator explores complexities of Ontario encampment
representative.author: News Staff

snapshot.title: 'Home' documentary from 'Degrassi' co-creator explores complexities of Ontario encampment
snapshot.evidenceText: TORONTO — When tents started popping up on the lawn in front of a sprawling provincial property in Cobourg, Ont., television producer Linda Schuyler wondered who the people living in the encampment were. “I started to go in and get to know them,” said Schuyler, a filmmaker and producer who is best known as the co-creator of the “Degrassi” television series. “As Torontonians, we have been very aware of the homeless crisis for a long period of time. And I always felt kind of helpless about it. It seemed like such a big problem. I didn’t know what I could do to help,” said Schuyler, who splits her time between Toronto and a community near the southern Ontario lakeside town. She teamed up with filmmaker Will Bowes to explore the inner workings of the encampment and the complex individual circumstances of its residents. The result is a new documentary, titled “Home,” set to premiere on TVO on Saturday, coinciding with World Homeless Day. The film introduces audiences to several unhoused people who settled at Brookside, a vacant property owned by the province that had previously been home to Cobourg’s elite and later became a youth detention centre. It details the myriad reasons how someone can end up without a home, from executives and business owners losing their livelihoods, to those who faced abusive partners, the death of loved ones and the challenges of addiction and mental health. The filmmakers said they first entered without filming equipment and simply listened to people’s stories. Once they formed relationships, the filmmakers asked if people were comfortable speaking on camera. If they did, they’d receive a Tim Hortons gift card to acknowledge their time. Schuyler said they’d also ask people if they would give them a tour of their tents or structures. “And without a doubt, they would all say, ‘Oh, just a minute. Let me tidy up a bit,” she said. “They really took pride in building little gardens and little pathways to get to their homes,” Bowes added. “It was remarkable what they were able to accomplish.” Along with highlighting the people inside the encampment, the film, which collected around 60 hours of footage over about a year, also shared the perspectives of people in the local community. That included the town’s mayor as well as social workers, community advocates and concerned citizens who had reservations about the proximity of the encampment to local schools. “Even though we wanted to get to know the people in the encampment, we did want to be fair to the community and give some of the local people an opportunity to talk about it from their perspective,” Schuyler said. The documentary does not, however, include any narration, a deliberate choice because “narration can be leading and it can be judgmental,” Schuyler said. “It’s a principle that we had way back in ‘Degrassi.’ We really wanted to give our young people an authentic voice and we really wanted to look at whatever issue we were dealing with from multiple sides. And that approach spilled over into this documentary,” Schuyler said. “Without getting too political about it, we wanted to just show that it’s a multi-faceted story,” she said. Bowes said the experience of making the documentary forced him to acknowledge the biases he had formed around homeless people. “I also felt like if you end up in an encampment, that is a result of years, if not decades of bad decisions (and) definite substance abuse,” Bowes said. “But that couldn’t be farther from the truth. Many people are there because they had a really terrible time during COVID.” Making this film also showed him how the journey of homelessness is not linear. For example, at one point, the documentary follows a few people who moved into a motel after the encampment was dismantled following the sale of Brookside. However, their motel stay was temporary and soon after they arrived, they had to leave. “Sometimes you’re getting ahead and then the rug gets pulled out from under you, and that was really frustrating for us obviously as filmmakers, who are trying to put together a narrative, and you want the narrative to progress and get better and see someone start thriving or at least start taking the steps to,” Bowes said. “But unfortunately that just wasn’t possible,” he said. The filmmakers said the goal isn’t for the documentary to provide a clearcut answer for how to solve the issue but rather for audiences to walk away having to mull it over for themselves. “We are so rich with resources, both land and otherwise, I find it embarrassing as a Canadian that we cannot treat our unhoused better,” Schuyler said. “I hope that that sentiment somehow will arouse in people who watch the documentary.” Bowes said he also hopes the film leads to more empathy for homeless people. “A little bit more understanding for the human being that you might have otherwise walked past or put a label on,” he said. representative.title: 'Home' documentary from 'Degrassi' co-creator explores complexities of Ontario encampment
representative.author: News Staff

snapshot.title: 'Home' documentary from 'Degrassi' co-creator explores complexities of Ontario encampment
snapshot.evidenceText: TORONTO — When tents started popping up on the lawn in front of a sprawling provincial property in Cobourg, Ont., television producer Linda Schuyler wondered who the people living in the encampment were. “I started to go in and get to know them,” said Schuyler, a filmmaker and producer who is best known as the co-creator of the “Degrassi” television series. “As Torontonians, we have been very aware of the homeless crisis for a long period of time. And I always felt kind of helpless about it. It seemed like such a big problem. I didn’t know what I could do to help,” said Schuyler, who splits her time between Toronto and a community near the southern Ontario lakeside town. She teamed up with filmmaker Will Bowes to explore the inner workings of the encampment and the complex individual circumstances of its residents. The result is a new documentary, titled “Home,” set to premiere on TVO on Saturday, coinciding with World Homeless Day. The film introduces audiences to several unhoused people who settled at Brookside, a vacant property owned by the province that had previously been home to Cobourg’s elite and later became a youth detention centre. It details the myriad reasons how someone can end up without a home, from executives and business owners losing their livelihoods, to those who faced abusive partners, the death of loved ones and the challenges of addiction and mental health. The filmmakers said they first entered without filming equipment and simply listened to people’s stories. Once they formed relationships, the filmmakers asked if people were comfortable speaking on camera. If they did, they’d receive a Tim Hortons gift card to acknowledge their time. Schuyler said they’d also ask people if they would give them a tour of their tents or structures. “And without a doubt, they would all say, ‘Oh, just a minute. Let me tidy up a bit,” she said. “They really took pride in building little gardens and little pathways to get to their homes,” Bowes added. “It was remarkable what they were able to accomplish.” Along with highlighting the people inside the encampment, the film, which collected around 60 hours of footage over about a year, also shared the perspectives of people in the local community. That included the town’s mayor as well as social workers, community advocates and concerned citizens who had reservations about the proximity of the encampment to local schools. “Even though we wanted to get to know the people in the encampment, we did want to be fair to the community and give some of the local people an opportunity to talk about it from their perspective,” Schuyler said. The documentary does not, however, include any narration, a deliberate choice because “narration can be leading and it can be judgmental,” Schuyler said. “It’s a principle that we had way back in ‘Degrassi.’ We really wanted to give our young people an authentic voice and we really wanted to look at whatever issue we were dealing with from multiple sides. And that approach spilled over into this documentary,” Schuyler said. “Without getting too political about it, we wanted to just show that it’s a multi-faceted story,” she said. Bowes said the experience of making the documentary forced him to acknowledge the biases he had formed around homeless people. “I also felt like if you end up in an encampment, that is a result of years, if not decades of bad decisions (and) definite substance abuse,” Bowes said. “But that couldn’t be farther from the truth. Many people are there because they had a really terrible time during COVID.” Making this film also showed him how the journey of homelessness is not linear. For example, at one point, the documentary follows a few people who moved into a motel after the encampment was dismantled following the sale of Brookside. However, their motel stay was temporary and soon after they arrived, they had to leave. “Sometimes you’re getting ahead and then the rug gets pulled out from under you, and that was really frustrating for us obviously as filmmakers, who are trying to put together a narrative, and you want the narrative to progress and get better and see someone start thriving or at least start taking the steps to,” Bowes said. “But unfortunately that just wasn’t possible,” he said. The filmmakers said the goal isn’t for the documentary to provide a clearcut answer for how to solve the issue but rather for audiences to walk away having to mull it over for themselves. “We are so rich with resources, both land and otherwise, I find it embarrassing as a Canadian that we cannot treat our unhoused better,” Schuyler said. “I hope that that sentiment somehow will arouse in people who watch the documentary.” Bowes said he also hopes the film leads to more empathy for homeless people. “A little bit more understanding for the human being that you might have otherwise walked past or put a label on,” he said. representative.title: Archaeologists found possibly 13,000-year-old Clovis sites at 9,500 feet near Yellowstone; the discovery challenges what scientists thought about ancient glaciers | - The Times of India
representative.author: TOI Science Desk

snapshot.title: Archaeologists found possibly 13,000-year-old Clovis sites at 9,500 feet near Yellowstone; the discovery challenges what scientists thought about ancient glaciers
snapshot.evidenceText: Imagine standing at 9,500 feet in rugged mountains where, according to long-held scientific thinking, a thick cap of ice should have blocked almost all life thousands of years ago. Now imagine finding stone tools there, left by some of the earliest widespread people in the Americas. A Montana archaeologist and his team report exactly that, and the discovery has sparked excitement, caution, and a lot of questions. If confirmed, it could change how we understand ancient glaciers, hunting, and mountain life. Read on to learn what was found, why it surprised experts, what remains unproven, and why Indigenous voices matter.How archaeologist Scott Dersam found Clovis stone tools at 9,500 feetThe story begins with archaeologist Scott Dersam, who, according to a Mountain Journal, has spent years searching the Beartooth Mountains near Yellowstone National Park. Dersam earned his doctorate in 2022 and runs the nonprofit Alpine Ecosystems Research Institute with his wife, Sari. His interest was sparked by Vern Waples, a former game warden whose collection of more than 2,000 artefacts from the Beartooth and Pryor Mountains was donated to the Custer Gallatin National Forest and is described as the largest and densest high-elevation stone tool collection in North America. Earlier archaeologists who retraced Waples's steps found little, and Dersam says that failure drew him in. Working at about 9,500 feet, he now says he has found the highest, and potentially oldest, human habitation sites known anywhere in North America.Why evidence of Clovis people in the Yellowstone high country defies the Pinedale glacier timelineTo see why scientists are surprised, it helps to know who the Clovis people were. The report explains that they persisted across the continent roughly 13,000 years ago, left the first consistent and widespread trace of human presence in the Americas, and specialised in hunting mammoths and other giant animals thought to roam mostly on the plains. Thousands of Clovis artefacts have been found, overwhelmingly at low elevations. The mountains, meanwhile, were believed to be locked under ice. The Pinedale Glacier blanketed nearly all of Yellowstone National Park and peaked about 20,000 years ago, so animals lacked forage and people likely stayed away. Yet Dersam reports soil tests showing sediment that saw sunlight between 17,000 and 22,000 years ago, when ice should have been deepest. That is why he says the sites should not exist under current understanding.The intact ancient hearth and buried Clovis point base that excited the research team after four yearsThe most dramatic moment came this summer. While digging a small pit to collect soil, not artefacts, Dersam brushed away dark carbon that did not fit a forest fire and uncovered what appeared to be part of an ancient hearth. In the middle of it sat the base of a Clovis point. The team needed about an hour to calm down, according to the report. Dersam explains that a hunter likely tossed the broken stone into the fire about 13,000 years ago, pending testing, and that it probably never moved since. Other high-elevation Clovis points had all been scattered on the surface, so an intact buried example is unprecedented, he says. Over four years, he has found six more Clovis sites at high elevations, five in the Beartooths. Montana's only widely accepted Clovis site remains Anzick.How a 2022 flood, shifting glaciers, and narrow corridors in the ice may explain the discoveryWhy now? A torrential rain-on-snow event in June 2022 blasted the remaining spring snowpack from the Beartooths and unleashed floods across Greater Yellowstone, churning sediment that had been buried for thousands of years. When Dersam returned that August, sites with hundreds of flakes suddenly had thousands, and he found two clearly identifiable Clovis points. He offers possible explanations for how people reached such heights. Perhaps scientific understanding of glaciation paints with too broad a stroke, and this basin never iced up, or narrow corridors in the ice let animals and their human pursuers pass. He also theorises that melting glaciers and permafrost allowed meat storage, and that mammoths followed the spring green wave upward, as Yellowstone bison do today. These ideas remain hypotheses until laboratory testing and peer review are complete.Why Indigenous tribes, off-site archaeology, and peer review matter before the claims are confirmedResponsible research matters as much as the discovery itself. Dersam practises what he calls off-site archaeology, leaving most findings in place and recording notes, photographs, and coordinates, removing only points that passersby might otherwise take. The report notes that seven to ten tribal historic preservation officers and elders voiced support at a Forest Service meeting this year. The history is delicate. A Clovis boy known as Anzick-1, buried about 12,600 years ago and found near Wilsall in the late 1960s, was reburied in June 2014 with help from Shane Doyle of the Crow Tribe. Dean Nicolai of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes says artefacts are alive and removing them can disturb a spiritual context. Dersam hopes to submit his findings for publication, and the results will depend on lengthy laboratory work.

representative.title: Mayoral candidate Dixon’s name is misspelled Dixion on Inglewood mail ballots | Inglewood Independent

snapshot.title: Mayoral candidate Dixon’s name is misspelled Dixion on Inglewood mail ballots | Inglewood Independent
snapshot.evidenceText: The City Clerk says every vote marked for the misspelled name will count for Fre'Drisha "Sha" Dixon, who has asked a judge to order corrections. Inglewood's Nov. 3 mail ballots list mayoral candidate Fre'Drisha "Sha" Dixon as Dixion. The City Clerk says those votes count for her, the county says it printed what the city certified, and Dixon has gone to court seeking corrections and notices to voters. If you plan to vote for Fre’Drisha “Sha” Dixon, mark the line that reads Dixion: the City Clerk has put in writing that every one of those votes counts for her, whatever a judge decides about reprints or notices. Mail ballots for Inglewood’s Nov. 3 mayor’s race spell one candidate’s last name wrong . Fre’Drisha “Sha” Dixon appears as Dixion, with an extra letter i, second from the top of the six names in the race. The same spelling shows up on her candidate statement on the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s website. Dixon learned of the error on Saturday, Oct. 3, when a campaign volunteer texted her a photo of a mail ballot, and by then ballots were already in some voters’ hands. Inglewood had more than 66,000 registered voters as of Sept. 4. The Inglewood City Clerk’s office verifies how local candidates’ names are spelled and sends them to the county registrar, which prints ballots and candidate statements, registrar spokesperson Mike Sanchez has said. Sanchez said the clerk gets ballot proofs to approve before anything is printed, and that the city signed off on them before production. In writing, he said the name on the ballot “matches the information certified to our office by the City.” Dixon’s name was spelled correctly when she ran for mayor in 2022, and city materials posted through at least Aug. 21 also had it right. Copies of the filings she submitted to the City Clerk, the county registrar and the California Secretary of State spell it correctly as well. No explanation of how the extra letter got in has been made public. In an email to Dixon on Monday, Oct. 5, City Clerk Aisha Thompson apologized for what she called a misprint of the last name. Thompson wrote that she asked the county whether the name could be fixed on the voting machines and was told no, because two versions of the last name could confuse voters. In a separate statement, Thompson wrote that “every vote cast for Ms Dixon (Dixion) will count in her favor.” Dixon has filed a writ of mandamus, a request that puts the question before a judge, who will decide whether and how the city and county offices must fix the error. She is asking the court to order corrections to election materials not yet sent out, updated in-person ballots, and written and digital notices to voters about the mistake. Dixon has said she does not believe the misspelling was an honest mistake and worries voters will think the name she has campaigned under for months is missing from the ballot. No ruling on her petition has been made public, and no office has been found at fault. The misspelling has already traveled beyond the ballot: a newspaper Q&A with the candidate carries the Dixion spelling in its headline, while her campaign site uses Dixon. representative.title: Teachers Restore Butcherknife Creek to Create Outdoor Classroom | The Slope
representative.author: The Slope Team

snapshot.title: Teachers Restore Butcherknife Creek to Create Outdoor Classroom
snapshot.evidenceText: The Yampa Valley Stream Improvement Charitable Trust finished a full restoration of Butcherknife Creek near Strawberry Park Elementary School. The work is done. Students are already using it. The project revived trout habitat and aquatic insect life in a channelized creek bed. Fly Water Inc., a Fort Collins-based design firm, built the site. The trust funded it in full. They partnered with Trout Unlimited’s local chapter and the Yampa Valley Fly Fishers. This wasn’t a city initiative or a state grant. It was two teachers who got tired of the status quo. Bennett Colvin, a Steamboat Springs High School teacher, and Jeff Ruff, the trust president and retired social studies teacher, came up with the idea in August 2024. Both taught at Steamboat Springs Middle School then. Both are avid fishermen. They asked a simple question: what if there was a viable fishery right outside the classroom doors? Colvin serves as the youth coordinator for the Yampa Valley Fly Fishers. He and Ruff approached their organizations for money. They got it. Now, the creek is an outdoor classroom. Colvin takes his students there at least once a week. They examine water quality, river animals, riparian habitat, and birds. He calls it studying "what it takes to study a river." They also test the restoration’s effectiveness. They look for what else needs fixing. Colvin wants his students to think like watershed scientists. He sees this as a pathway into natural resources careers. Courtney Wiedel, who teaches at Steamboat Springs Middle School, uses the space for her sixth-grade class. She runs ecology lessons there. Her students observe the habitat and build food webs. The creek is a "thriving riparian habitat" at her doorstep. Wiedel also runs a fly-tying club that meets every Friday morning. She uses the creek for inspiration. Students collect samples of insect life from the water. They mimic what they see in nature when they tie flies. The class also does a math and science lesson focused on macroinvertebrates. They collect data on the types and quantities of bugs in the creek. That data determines water quality. Sometimes, Wiedel said, they just go to the creek to "nature bathe" and meditate. The physical changes are specific. The project increased and deepened water-holding areas. It added trees and vegetation to create a habitat that supports trout. The creek bed was channelized before this work. Now it functions as a living ecosystem. The partnership structure matters here. The charitable trust provided the funding. The local chapters of Trout Unlimited and the Yampa Valley Fly Fishers provided the expertise and community connection. The school district provided the location and the students. No one is claiming this solves all environmental issues in Steamboat Springs. But it puts a functional, healthy stream within walking distance of students who might otherwise never see one up close. Colvin and Ruff started with a question in August 2024. They now have an answer that students touch, measure, and study every week. The restoration is complete. The classroom is open.

representative.title: A Mississippi couple spent 20 years rebuilding a forest on their property, and this summer conservation agents arrived with 500 rare frogs from the United States to release them. - Evidence Network
representative.author: Dr. Kyle Muller

snapshot.title: A Mississippi couple spent 20 years rebuilding a forest on their property, and this summer conservation agents arrived with 500 rare frogs from the United States to release them. - Evidence Network
snapshot.evidenceText: More than 20 years ago, Jim and Laura Currie began reclaiming a degraded piece of land on their property in Mississippi, United States. Their goal was to help a protected species that already lived in the area: the gopher tortoise. What they could not imagine then is that this work would end up turning their property into a new home for one of the most endangered frogs in the country. In June 2026, conservation teams arrived at Woodland Cottage in Hancock County with a very special mission: release nearly 500 dusky gopher frogs ( sevosa frog ) bred in captivity. The event, documented by the US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), represents a new step in the recovery of a species that was once reduced to a single known population. For 20 years they recovered a forest that was very degraded The story of these frogs began long before the first specimens arrived on the property. Jim and Laura Currie had been working for more than two decades with the Partners for Fish and Wildlife program of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service, Wildlife Mississippi and the US Department of Agriculture to recover the ecosystem of their land. Part of the area had previously been used for grazing and had also suffered logging. The landowners began replanting longleaf pines, a species characteristic of these forests in the southeastern United States, in addition to recovering the communities of native herbs and plants that grow under them. They also began to use prescribed burning, a fundamental tool to maintain the natural characteristics of this type of ecosystem. The initial goal was to benefit the gopher tortoise, but the restoration ended up having a much broader scope. The recovered forest began to provide the necessary conditions for numerous species, including migratory birds, pollinators and other animals. And among them was a particularly strange frog. The frog that once had a single population known throughout the world The dusky gopher frog is a small amphibian associated with longleaf pine forests and certain temporary ponds. Its situation is especially delicate because it needs a very specific set of conditions to survive and reproduce. For decades, the loss and fragmentation of its habitat, changes in land use and the suppression of natural fire deteriorated the ecosystems on which it depended. The decline became so pronounced that between 1988 and 2004, only one surviving population was known, located in a single pond in the De Soto National Forest, in southern Mississippi. The species is listed as federally endangered in the United States. One of the keys to its survival is precisely in the relationship between the forest and wetlands. The frog uses temporary ponds to reproduce, while the terrestrial ecosystem that surrounds them must maintain adequate conditions for the specimens to survive. Plus, there’s another surprising connection: Burrows dug by gopher tortoises can be used by more than 300 different species, including the dusky gopher frog itself. Therefore, the work that the Curries began thinking mainly about turtles ended up also creating a suitable habitat for frogs and more species. Then almost 500 captive-bred frogs arrived. The turning point came in June 2026. Conservation teams moved nearly 500 dusky gopher frogs bred in captivity by the Memphis Zoo to Woodland Cottage. The specimens were released into several ponds on the property, already restored and prepared to host a new population. It was not just any liberation. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, this event created the only known population of this species in Hancock County and also marked the first release of dusky gopher frogs on private working lands as part of this recovery program. The project brings together several organizations, including the FWS itself, the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks, the Memphis Zoo and Wildlife Mississippi, as well as the landowners. The release thus represents much more than the arrival of hundreds of amphibians to some ponds: it is an attempt to ensure that a species that was on the verge of disappearing can once again occupy part of its historical territory. The goal now is to get the frogs to form a stable population Releasing the animals is just the beginning. Conservation of the dusky gopher frog requires creating new populations and maintaining different breeding groups to reduce the risk that a single problem could affect the entire species. Efforts over the past few years have already established new reintroduction sites in Mississippi. The Woodland Cottage case also has special significance because it demonstrates the role that private land can play in the recovery of threatened species. For more than two decades, the Curries slowly restored a landscape that had lost much of its original features. When they started, their goal was to help a turtle. Now, that same work has opened the doors of his property to hundreds of frogs that desperately need new places to live. The result shows the extent to which recovering an ecosystem can have effects that go far beyond a single species. A forest grows again, ponds regain their function and, two decades later, almost 500 small amphibians have a new opportunity to return to nature. And this time, the future of one of the rarest frogs in the United States also depends on that restored forest functioning again as a complete ecosystem.
