snapshot.title: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say : NPR - Theamericanhabit
snapshot.evidenceText: @2022 - All Right Reserved. Designed and Developed by Kaniz Fatema A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants. ROXBURY, N.J. — On a warm morning on Sept. 4, masked immigration agents rolled into Dover, N.J. Footage of the raids rippled across social media, sent people into hiding and reignited rumors that had been circulating for months: Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were taking people to a nearby warehouse. The warehouse in Roxbury was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants as part of President Trump’s mass deportation efforts. That plan to convert warehouses into detention centers faced fierce backlash and legal challenges from residents and immigrant advocates. It was largely abandoned, and in several sites, including Roxbury, the government is legally forbidden by a court order from converting them to a detention facility, pending environmental assessments. But an NPR investigation has found signs that the New Jersey facility is being used. And the state’s Office of the Attorney General says it is looking into similar reports. In early 2026, Homeland Security bought 11 warehouses to turn into ICE detention facilities. They spent about a billion dollars on these. NPR spoke to an official at a government contractor whose company was approached to convert several of the warehouses into ICE facilities. He spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation from the government. “No one that we spoke to at DHS was for this idea whatsoever. The deputy director told us point-blank that they had pushed back very hard on it. Everybody knew warehouses are horrible places to put people,” he says. At a meeting with a deputy director at DHS, he says, his company proposed an alternative: FEMA-style camps in Texas that would be more humane. He says that idea was swiftly shot down. While White House adviser Stephen Miller was not at the meeting, they were told that this was not what Miller wanted. The contractor says his understanding from that meeting was that “Miller did not want the facilities that were comfortable. He did not want facilities that were humane. We were told point-blank that that was not what the administration wanted.” “Steve Miller certainly seemed to make that point to everyone that he wanted it to be cruel. This was what Miller had stated to the DHS at that time, to the DHS director and deputy director. What surprised me was just how adamant the people were that it was going to happen. Damn the consequences. I would say in 25 years of working with the U.S. government, I’ve never been in that position before.” In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the contractor’s comments were “false hearsay allegation(s) from someone who has never even met or talked with Stephen Miller.” Bis also said that Miller “has never made any remarks to anyone about wanting illegal aliens to have worse detention facility conditions. It simply isn’t true and this is defamatory.” The White House did not respond to repeated requests to speak to Miller directly. Early on, the warehouse plan was met with protests in both conservative and liberal towns. Several state attorneys general filed lawsuits to halt construction, based on environmental concerns. “It very quickly became an absolute boondoggle,” says Michael Wriston, a former military intelligence analyst who co-founded Project SaltBox, a watchdog group that tracks ICE’s expansion. “It was really about the optics of people being kept in these cages and these large warehouses. They wanted a lot of what they called B-roll to play on social media, but they didn’t do any due diligence of making sure that they conformed with environmental policy or that the construction wouldn’t disturb local water tables.” A DHS official who served during Trump’s first term, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared government retaliation, says that while they were not in the meeting the contractor described to NPR, they had often heard higher-ups in the administration wanting to make a point of showcasing difficult conditions immigrants were being held in. Then, with the departure of DHS Secretary Kristi Noem in March, there was a shift: Her replacement, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, sought to do less showy immigration crackdowns. Today, Homeland Security is selling several of the warehouses. But they’re still holding on to a few, including in Hagerstown, Md. , Surprise, Ariz., and Roxbury, N.J. “ These locations are very critical to ICE’s deportation agenda,” says Wriston, “because they fill in the gap in places where ICE does not have a robust detention network. They don’t have a lot of jails there.” They are also located in areas where there are no partnerships with the police who can house detainees in local jails. In Maryland , Arizona and New Jersey , following lawsuits from each of the state attorneys general, DHS has either agreed or been ordered by a judge to halt the conversion of the warehouses into detention centers, pending environmental impact assessments. But throughout the summer, in the towns surrounding the Roxbury warehouse, rumors started to bubble. Over the summer, there was a historic surge in ICE arrests: around 100,000 people in July and August. In New Jersey, the rumor mill started churning. The Roxbury warehouse is located in a wooded area, on a road right off Route 46. Project NINJA (No ICE in North Jersey Alliance), a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, says several neighbors reported vehicles, often in a caravan, speeding up the road. Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner in Dover, N.J., on Sept. 17. “They’re holding people in that warehouse,” one woman says in a WhatsApp group in the town of Dover, which is about 15 minutes from Roxbury. “I have a co-worker who was taken there. They hold them there and at night they take them somewhere else.” The message was forwarded to NPR by Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner. “But, you know, it’s like third- and fourth-hand accounts,” says Wittner. “It just didn’t seem probable at the time because of the court order. But it kind of made you scratch your head a little bit.” A woman says she was driving to work when she saw a raid taking place in Dover. She decided to follow the car carrying people who were detained. “I just needed to know, is he going to Roxbury?” She took video as she trailed them up Route 46. She asked that NPR not use her name because what happened next made her fearful of what the government might do. She says the car she was following turned onto the woodsy road that leads to the warehouse. She says she waited to see if there was any more movement. “And then maybe five minutes after that, a white Dodge Durango started kind of circling around me,” she says. “And then on his last loop, he started filming me. He had a yellow case on his cellphone. After that, a black Tahoe started doing the same thing. I was on a public sidewalk, and it was intimidating. It was really intimidating. I’m scared. But I am more scared for our community.” Councilwoman Wittner says she strongly suspects ICE is using the Roxbury warehouse: “The immigration enforcement activity happened in Dover between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m.” Wittner points to the woman who was able to follow the vehicle up Route 46: “The last vehicle entered the warehouse road at 8:25 a.m.” Meanwhile, footage of the raid started circulating on social media. Back in Dover, another woman says she saw the videos as she got her kids ready for school. NPR viewed the videos and confirmed their authenticity. In one of them, a worker is cornered against a wall by two masked agents. She says she was thunderstruck. She asked that we not use her name because she fears being targeted. At 8:25 a.m., she says, she got a call from her father. He’s 59, she says, and he sounded disoriented. He told her he was handcuffed in some kind of jail. She found it strange, she says, because the Roxbury warehouse would be the only place he could have been taken in that short a time span. She also discovered a friend of hers had been picked up. She hasn’t been able to speak to her father since then, and neither has NPR. But NPR located her friend in Honduras, where he’s been deported. He requested anonymity, because he fears repercussions for his loved ones who are still in the U.S. “I was picked up on my way to work, on Friday, Sept. 4. The agents loaded me into a van. They took us to Roxbury,” he said. He says he and the other people detained were handcuffed and held in the parking lot for several hours. He counted nine other men with him. “I just went into a state of shock,” he says. “I signed my deportation papers. The next morning I regretted it. But I was scared. Eventually, they transferred us to a real facility.” In a statement to NPR, DHS did not respond to a question about whether it was holding people at the Roxbury location. But it did give NPR a statement it has previously sent about ICE detention, saying DHS upholds strict standards and that immigrants can choose to leave detention by being deported. A member of Project NINJA, a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, in Roxbury on Sept. 17. The activists at NINJA say ICE’s actions violate the legal order. The order lists several actions ICE can take with the site — mainly upkeep — but nowhere on that list is detention an acceptable action, they say. Harvard professor Andrew Mergen, a former attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice Environment & Natural Resources Division, says ICE may technically not be violating the court order, which stipulated it would not convert the place into a detention center pending an environmental assessment. Ultimately, Mergen says, the situation shows the limitations of using environmental claims. “The community is acting here to prevent people from being detained,” says Mergen. “And the administration seems to have cleverly elided that intention, by sort of saying, ‘Well, we’re not going to build this facility, but we’re going to use this space in furtherance of detention.'” He says he understands the frustration: “It’s just infuriating if what you are trying to do is say ‘No. Not here. Not here.’ “ Wittner says since the raid, she’s heard from other close relatives or close friends of two men who were picked up that day, who say they were inside the Roxbury warehouse. She says the situation is unacceptable: “We need our Congress members to conduct an oversight visit yesterday, quite honestly. We need our state to aggressively pursue this investigation and demand to get inside.” She says DHS has had time “to go in and clean up their mess if they, in fact, got caught doing something that they shouldn’t have.” Meanwhile, in Dover, the streets where the raid happened remain deserted. At an empty diner at lunchtime, a waitress who did not want to be named because of the climate of fear in town says one of the workers who was taken used to come here for a bite. Then she leans over and asks: “Do you know where they took those men?” Save my name, email, and website in this browser for the next time I comment. @2025 – All Right Reserved. snapshot.title: Paraguayan Educator Lilia Piatti Earns Doctorate At 93 Years Old
snapshot.evidenceText: Sorry, this product is unavailable. Please choose a different combination. At 93 years old, Paraguayan educator Lilia Piatti reached a milestone she had spent years pursuing: a doctorate in Education. Piatti defended her thesis at the National Institute of Higher Education ( Instituto Nacional de Educación Superior, or INAES ) in Asunción. Her journey, however, was about more than earning another academic title. After personal loss and technological challenges, Piatti turned both experiences into motivation to keep learning. Piatti focused her doctoral research on adult learning and digital technology. Specifically, her thesis examined the impact of the digital divide on adult university students using video platforms. The subject became personal during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Piatti encountered difficulties with new technologies. Consequently, her own experience inspired academic questions about technology and adult education. During the pandemic, Lilia Piatti took language courses as a way to stay mentally active. However, adapting to digital tools presented challenges during her studies. That experience later became the foundation for her doctoral research. Her work therefore explores difficulties that can emerge when technology becomes central to learning. snapshot.title: The outlaw bear that captured Asheville • Asheville Watchdog
snapshot.evidenceText: She knew the name might annoy people — that it could strike them as gimmicky, craven, even exploitative. The first time she mentioned it to a friend, he told her: That’s a terrible idea. But it had come to her almost involuntarily, and now she couldn’t stop thinking about it. Was it so unusual? Neighborhood bears are named all the time. They pick up monikers like they do ticks or briars. One bear might have a different name from each house on the street. This bear, though, was unusual. Everyone was talking about her. She was wanted by the state. She had developed a taste for cat food, which she realized could be found inside houses; had several times broken into homes in a north Asheville neighborhood; and, on Aug. 18, had injured the occupant of one of those homes as she tried to escape. Wildlife officials planned to capture her, euthanize her, and relocate her cubs. Depending on who you asked, the bear was either a menace to public safety or a victim of human negligence. Hannah Furgiuele was not the only person — and certainly not the only person in Beaverdam Valley — with strong feelings about the bear’s apparent fate, but she would become the neighbor with the most sway over it. The name was an inflection point. Some of Furgiuele’s less sympathetic neighbors called the bear “Baddie Patty,” but another idea had been kicking around Furgiuele’s head. America’s most beloved country singer had just died, and Furgiuele had been reading about her conservation advocacy, her love of her mountain home. It felt right, not just because of the pun embedded in the name but also because of how it turned the story on its head — what if the villain of the story could be seen in the light of someone who, everyone agreed, was a saint? Soon there were signs all around the neighborhood, a website, a petition. Thousands of people signed it, then tens of thousands. There was a new rallying cry: Pardon Dolly. All of this was possible because the story didn’t have an ending. Dolly, as so many people suddenly knew her, didn’t disappear. She didn’t even stop trying to break into houses. But she also didn’t get caught. Beaverdam Valley is the kind of neighborhood that would look good on an Asheville real estate brochure. In a city unceasingly described as being nestled among the Blue Ridge Mountains, the valley really is suspended between two worlds: A few minutes in one direction stand the restaurants and supermarkets lining Merrimon Avenue; in the other, the Craggy Mountains and Blue Ridge Parkway. One might, beginning a quick jaunt to Trader Joe’s, have to stop their car to let a herd of deer or a flock of wild turkeys cross the street. This liminal, pastoral quality casts a sense of serenity over the community. It’s not unusual for neighbors to leave their windows open and doors unlocked. The same features have also made Beaverdam Valley a site of frequent meetings between human and ursine residents. Sometimes, these encounters reify the neighborhood’s splendor. “If you are around a mother bear and her cubs, you will fall in love,” Reb Haizlip, a retired children’s-museum architect who lives there, said, “It’s impossible not to see the beauty and playfulness in those animals — the love that exists between a mother and her cubs, the way they play and work together.” The human-animal relationships can also be more frictive. Bears’ lives center on finding food; they’ll take it wherever they can get it, and once they locate a reliable source, they’ll go back for more. Chris Todd, the president of the Beaverdam Valley Neighborhood Association, said that the bear-resistant trash can he acquired through a city program worked well for a while, until the bears figured out that tossing it in the air and letting it crash repeatedly would do the trick. Now he has bear-proofing straps on his bear-proof can. Between May and September of this year, the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission received more than 800 bear-related reports from Buncombe County — nearly half the statewide total. Seventy-one of them involved a break-in. And no community had more than Beaverdam Valley. One evening in August, a houseguest returned to the home where she was staying on Spooks Branch Road — one of many streets named for the area’s streams and coves — to find a mother black bear and her cubs playing in the twilit back yard. The homeowner and her guests usually entered through the back door. But so did the bears: Multiple times this summer, the mother had let herself in and absconded with bags of cat food. The entries had left the back door broken. The visitor gave them a wide berth, went through the front door, then came back out to clean up some lawn clippings. When she turned around, she saw the cubs playing on the front porch but no sign of the mother. Then she realized the front door was open. Inside, the homeowner woke to the sound of her guest banging on her bedroom window. She exited her room, saw the bear, and tried to shield herself behind her front door. The bear swatted at the homeowner, walked out of the house, and departed with her cubs. Within the hour, Ashley Hobbs, a biologist with the Wildlife Resources Commission, was en route to Mission Hospital, where the injured woman was taken by ambulance. Hobbs found her alert and talkative, with a pair of gashes along the upper right side of her face — “relatively speaking, in terms of bear attacks, pretty minor,” Hobbs said. (This account of the attack is drawn from a WRC incident report; the victim declined to be interviewed for this story.) Hobbs spends much of her time talking to homeowners and government officials in and around Asheville, trying to convince them to adopt habits and policies to keep people and bears safe from each other — stowing food and locking doors, issuing bear-resistant trash cans and developing ordinances to punish intentional feeding. She’s also the person who responds when a particular bear becomes a nuisance or, worse, a threat. That nobody else in the wildlife agency has a job like Hobbs’ one-place-one-animal gig is one of many indications that Asheville is a crucible of human-bear relations. Plenty of residents live harmoniously with the creatures. But Asheville is also full of tourists and transplants who have never seen bears; of residents who fail to secure their dog food or bird seed; of people who have either never heard the adage that “a fed bear is a dead bear” or who are foolish enough to think it doesn’t apply to them; and of trash cans and dumpsters and garage fridges not designed for a world full of hungry, persistent, 400-pound animals who want what they have. Of the 18 injuries caused by bears statewide since 2017, 11 have taken place in Buncombe. That night in the hospital, the victim told Hobbs everything that had happened: the pattern of cat food theft, the unlocked doors, how just that morning the same mother bear and her cubs had gotten into her trash. They would talk again in the morning; for now, she told Hobbs, she didn’t want the bear killed. What happened next would not be so uncomplicated. Most of the 9,000 or so black bears in western North Carolina’s mountains don’t become nuisances, and even most bears that do — the kind that can often be found feasting on the contents of overturned trash bins — don’t become so dangerous that they leave wildlife managers only one option. But by the morning after the Beaverdam Valley incident, it had become clear to state wildlife officials that this bear had crossed the threshold. In the hours after the attack, it had broken into another home nearby and tried to enter a third. Hobbs had also identified it as matching the description of a bear that had forced its way into a different home several times this summer. Hobbs and that resident had worked together to bear-proof the house, she said, “but obviously it didn’t dissuade this bear from doing it in other parts of the community.” In short, the bear was habituated: Now that it knew it could acquire food by breaking into houses, it was unlikely to stop. On Aug. 19, a day after the attack, the WRC announced that it would seek to trap the mother and her cubs. Urban cubs get bigger than their rural counterparts, thanks to the preponderance of food in developed areas, and these cubs were “very vigorous,” said Hobbs, who had seen them on the cameras she’d set up. They were also “following mom and investigating.” Hobbs worried that if they weren’t moved soon, they’d adopt their mother’s foraging habits. Cubs do well with relocation; at about eight months old, these would have the combination of instinct and learned behavior to find food and a den for the winter after being dropped at an undisclosed location on national forest land. But researchers have found that adult bears have high mortality rates when relocated, and those that survive tend to find their way back or replicate the same dangerous behavior in new places. The mother, wildlife officials said, would be “humanely dispatched,” a term of art for euthanasia. The plan would be to trap her, load her into a truck, and take her to an offsite facility. She would be shot — gunshot is recognized as the quickest, least painful method of large-mammal euthanasia — then undergo a necropsy, wherein biologists would examine her stomach contents, collect DNA, and pull a tooth to estimate her age. Her body would be buried. This sequence of events, however tragic, is not uncommon in this area. As Hobbs would later point out, this wouldn’t be the first bear euthanized this year under similar circumstances. In May, wildlife officials shot and killed a half-dozen bears in Black Mountain and in Asheville’s Haw Creek neighborhood. The WRC had intervened in an effort to avoid fatal outcomes — Hobbs had been working with the Black Mountain neighbors for a year — but people continued to leave their doors unlocked and their trash accessible and, in some cases, kept feeding bears directly. The cullings made the news but passed with few ripples. The Beaverdam case was different. Local news outlets picked up the WRC’s news release. On social media, the story quickly elicited outrage, tinged with a misanthropic sense of humor. Facebook commenters invented alibis for the bear. “Run, mama, run!” became a rallying cry. “I live somewhere off beaverdam rd and saw her earlier,” one Reddit user commented. “I ain’t no snitch.” The overwhelming sentiment: This bear had been marked for death not because it acted outside the norms of its species, but because our kind had failed to adapt to its presence. We were the bad neighbor. Furgiuele, who lives near the house where the bear swatted the homeowner, couldn’t shake the story. She heard of the euthanasia plan the morning she left for a family vacation. That night, snuggled in bed with her 4-year-old son, she couldn’t sleep. She unlocked her phone and started typing. “This bear has young cubs,” she wrote. “Euthanizing her doesn’t help people learn to coexist in bear country.” Furgiuele first lived in Beaverdam Valley in her 20s. Bears were a regular presence then, too; her cat, Puma, had a knack for befriending cubs who visited her yard. After several years in Barnardsville, she looked to move back to Asheville last year and was happy to find a place in the valley that she describes as her “mullet house” — city in the front (charming curb appeal), country in the back (plenty of room for enclosures for goats and pigs). She quickly came to see the neighborhood’s many bears as part of her community, subject to her respect and wonder but not control. Sometimes a family of them would join her in her yard, at a distance, as she tended to her plants or built a wooden pirate ship for her son to play in. After one found its way into her backyard pen and fatally mauled a beloved goat, Bernie, she added a pair of Great Pyrenees to her flock. She could get frustrated with neighbors who were careless with their trash or birdseed but also knew how easy it was for a bear to take advantage of a momentary lapse: She once left a car door open while unloading groceries and returned to find a 40-pound bag of dog food had disappeared with only a trail of kibble left behind. “It almost feels like all of those different pieces came to a head with this story, because this bear is in my yard every day,” she said. “It was really personal to me. I’ve been looking — not looking for something else to do; I don’t need anything else to do — but needing to do something to make a difference, wanting my kid to see me fighting for something I believe in.” A friend who’s a longtime environmental advocate and journalist told her: Get the media’s attention . The first thoughts of helplessness and outrage she jotted down that night at the beach became a brief letter to the editor published in the Raleigh News and Observer . The next week, she submitted a longer piece to Asheville’s Citizen-Times , mourning the relocation of two of the cubs — “The devil is screaming behind my house,” a neighbor had texted her, describing the sound they believed to be the mother bear’s reaction — and grappling with her desire to lay blame. (Furgiuele took to calling the remaining cub Wendell, after another late hero, the environmental writer and activist Wendell Berry.) She could direct her anger at the WRC or at her neighbors, she wrote, but ultimately, this was a “systematic failure.” The bears were only adapting to their surroundings. Humans’ inability to adapt in turn had doomed them. Why are we drawn to animal outlaws? Captive animals who escape confinement, wild ones that upend our sense of social order — their sagas often become a mirror for the way we live, how we treat one another and our environment. They also make for entertaining news stories. Sometimes the creatures become local causes célèbres, like Chance the Snapper, an American alligator who took up residence in Chicago’s Humboldt Park lagoon, or Kenneth Allen, AKA the Hairy Houdini, a Bornean orangutan who garnered a fanbase in the 1980s for his repeated escapes from his San Diego Zoo enclosure. A rhesus macaque dubbed the Mystery Monkey of Tampa Bay captivated Floridians, on and off, for more than a decade. “Maybe there’s some muddled metaphor for America in (it),” the essayist Jon Mooallem wrote of the Mystery Monkey’s escapades in a 2012 New York Times Magazine story . “Or maybe it’s only tempting to look for one because there’s such hunger for a hint of any way forward. Maybe it’s not a metaphor. Maybe we’re on our own. Maybe it’s just a macaque.” Bears are prolific within this subgenre. There’s Tripod, a Florida bear who went viral after stealing White Claw hard seltzers from an outdoor fridge. There was Pedals, a New Jersey black bear who walked on his hind legs due to front paw injuries (and who was killed in a 2016 bear hunt, despite a widespread campaign to have him moved to a sanctuary). In early 2022, California wildlife developed a plan to trap, and possibly euthanize, Hank the Tank, a 500-pound black bear that had been linked to more than two dozen home break-ins near Lake Tahoe. Perhaps predictably, the bear’s name and rotund appearance elicited the internet’s delight. A grassroots campaign blamed Hank’s food habituation on unsecured garages and a local policy banning bear boxes and advocated for his humane relocation. Like so many American legends, Hank’s was a product of human conflation and misapprehension. DNA testing revealed that at least three separate bears had committed the home invasions. And when the bear in question was finally captured, it turned out to be a female, later renamed Henrietta. But the story got its happy ending: An agreement between state governments allowed Henrietta to be moved to the Wild Animal Refuge, a sanctuary spread across 10,000 acres in remote southeast Colorado, including nearly 250 acres of black bear habitat. Bears tend to fare poorly in zoos and other close-quarter confines — researchers have found patterns of abnormal behavior and self-mutilation — but the Refuge is a rare place that can hem them in while giving them the things they need most: sustenance (including salmon, crab, and fresh produce, much of it donated by grocers) and room to roam. “Life’s easy when they have food,” Pat Craig, the founder of the Refuge and its parent facility, the Wild Animal Sanctuary, said. “We have a lot of bears that come up to our habitats and look at it like they’re going to knock on the door.” Last month, Craig answered a cold call from Furgiuele, who had come across the saga of Hank in her efforts to find Dolly an escape route. She hardly expected Craig to pick up the phone, much less his immediate response when she explained the situation: Sure , he said, we’d be glad to take her . He also emphasized that the gambit would be a longshot. The vast majority of inhabitants at the Wild Animal Sanctuary and Refuge are born into captivity — bred and eventually rescued from “Tiger King people,” Craig said. State laws put strict limits on transfers of wild animals to sanctuaries, and moving those animals between states is even harder. And Craig wouldn’t have to look far to find a wild bear marked for death; as of early September, Colorado wildlife officials had euthanized nearly 300 this year. Over the past decade, Craig has been able to accept only five or six wild bears, he said. When he does, it’s almost always the result of a public pressure campaign that captures government attention. (Colorado Gov. Jared Polis was a vocal proponent of the Hank the Tank transfer.) “It probably has 100% to do with social media and how much traction someone’s post gets,” Craig said. Furgiuele’s campaign was already gaining traction with the public, with tens of thousands of people signing her petition. It also caught the eye of state officials. Soon after her conversation with Craig, Furgiuele got a call from Brad Howard, the chief of the WRC’s wildlife management division. The conversation was mutually respectful, she said, but it left her pessimistic about the Colorado option. “I could sort of tell by his voice that he was telling me no without telling me no,” she said. She recalled Howard telling her that Dolly was clearly not predatory — that “if she was truly aggressive, she’d be dead by now.” The bear’s adaptation to freely available food and her defensive reaction in the close-quarters encounter on Spooks Branch Road were responses to scenes in which humans were the actors. Yet the agency was wary of making an exception for this bear; it didn’t want people to think they could treat a symptom, bear habituation, without addressing the problem of human behavior. (The WRC declined to make Howard available for an interview.) She told him she’d call back with another idea. Furgiuele pursued every angle she could find. She met with Hobbs at the Western North Carolina Nature Center’s Bears and Brews event. Though some supporters of the Pardon Dolly campaign saw the WRC as the opposition, Furgiuele said she treats Hobbs as an ally, someone trying to solve the same problem from the opposite end of the spectrum: Neither wants dead bears, and both want to force people to confront their role in the destabilization of wildlife. Hobbs said that the increasingly common conflicts involving humans and bears energized her. “I’m pretty much a can-do kind of person,” she said. Furgiuele has a handful of political connections, people she knows both from her past environmental activism and through her father, a former town attorney and councilmember in Boone. She made regular calls to Gov. Josh Stein’s office and to his western residence , which sits atop Town Mountain, an area rife with bears. (The first time she tried to reach Stein, a confused receptionist transferred her to the office of clemency, where a functionary told her, “We don’t pardon bears in our office.”) Failing to get a call back, she started asking other officials to intervene on her behalf. The WRC had intervened in an effort to avoid fatal outcomes — Hobbs had been working with the Black Mountain neighbors for a year — but people continued to leave their doors unlocked and their trash accessible and, in some cases, kept feeding bears directly. The cullings made the news but passed with few ripples. The Beaverdam case was different. Local news outlets picked up the WRC’s news release. On social media, the story quickly elicited outrage, tinged with a misanthropic sense of humor. Facebook commenters invented alibis for the bear. “Run, mama, run!” became a rallying cry. “I live somewhere off beaverdam rd and saw her earlier,” one Reddit user commented. “I ain’t no snitch.” The overwhelming sentiment: This bear had been marked for death not because it acted outside the norms of its species, but because our kind had failed to adapt to its presence. We were the bad neighbor. Furgiuele, who lives near the house where the bear swatted the homeowner, couldn’t shake the story. She heard of the euthanasia plan the morning she left for a family vacation. That night, snuggled in bed with her 4-year-old son, she couldn’t sleep. She unlocked her phone and started typing. “This bear has young cubs,” she wrote. “Euthanizing her doesn’t help people learn to coexist in bear country.” Furgiuele first lived in Beaverdam Valley in her 20s. Bears were a regular presence then, too; her cat, Puma, had a knack for befriending cubs who visited her yard. After several years in Barnardsville, she looked to move back to Asheville last year and was happy to find a place in the valley that she describes as her “mullet house” — city in the front (charming curb appeal), country in the back (plenty of room for enclosures for goats and pigs). She quickly came to see the neighborhood’s many bears as part of her community, subject to her respect and wonder but not control. Sometimes a family of them would join her in her yard, at a distance, as she tended to her plants or built a wooden pirate ship for her son to play in. After one found its way into her backyard pen and fatally mauled a beloved goat, Bernie, she added a pair of Great Pyrenees to her flock. She could get frustrated with neighbors who were careless with their trash or birdseed but also knew how easy it was for a bear to take advantage of a momentary lapse: She once left a car door open while unloading groceries and returned to find a 40-pound bag of dog food had disappeared with only a trail of kibble left behind. “It almost feels like all of those different pieces came to a head with this story, because this bear is in my yard every day,” she said. “It was really personal to me. I’ve been looking — not looking for something else to do; I don’t need anything else to do — but needing to do something to make a difference, wanting my kid to see me fighting for something I believe in.” A friend who’s a longtime environmental advocate and journalist told her: Get the media’s attention . The first thoughts of helplessness and outrage she jotted down that night at the beach became a brief letter to the editor published in the Raleigh News and Observer . The next week, she submitted a longer piece to Asheville’s Citizen-Times , mourning the relocation of two of the cubs — “The devil is screaming behind my house,” a neighbor had texted her, describing the sound they believed to be the mother bear’s reaction — and grappling with her desire to lay blame. (Furgiuele took to calling the remaining cub Wendell, after another late hero, the environmental writer and activist Wendell Berry.) She could direct her anger at the WRC or at her neighbors, she wrote, but ultimately, this was a “systematic failure.” The bears were only adapting to their surroundings. Humans’ inability to adapt in turn had doomed them. Why are we drawn to animal outlaws? Captive animals who escape confinement, wild ones that upend our sense of social order — their sagas often become a mirror for the way we live, how we treat one another and our environment. They also make for entertaining news stories. Sometimes the creatures become local causes célèbres, like Chance the Snapper, an American alligator who took up residence in Chicago’s Humboldt Park lagoon, or Kenneth Allen, AKA the Hairy Houdini, a Bornean orangutan who garnered a fanbase in the 1980s for his repeated escapes from his San Diego Zoo enclosure. A rhesus macaque dubbed the Mystery Monkey of Tampa Bay captivated Floridians, on and off, for more than a decade. “Maybe there’s some muddled metaphor for America in (it),” the essayist Jon Mooallem wrote of the Mystery Monkey’s escapades in a 2012 New York Times Magazine story . “Or maybe it’s only tempting to look for one because there’s such hunger for a hint of any way forward. Maybe it’s not a metaphor. Maybe we’re on our own. Maybe it’s just a macaque.” Bears are prolific within this subgenre. There’s Tripod, a Florida bear who went viral after stealing White Claw hard seltzers from an outdoor fridge. There was Pedals, a New Jersey black bear who walked on his hind legs due to front paw injuries (and who was killed in a 2016 bear hunt, despite a widespread campaign to have him moved to a sanctuary). In early 2022, California wildlife developed a plan to trap, and possibly euthanize, Hank the Tank, a 500-pound black bear that had been linked to more than two dozen home break-ins near Lake Tahoe. Perhaps predictably, the bear’s name and rotund appearance elicited the internet’s delight. A grassroots campaign blamed Hank’s food habituation on unsecured garages and a local policy banning bear boxes and advocated for his humane relocation. Like so many American legends, Hank’s was a product of human conflation and misapprehension. DNA testing revealed that at least three separate bears had committed the home invasions. And when the bear in question was finally captured, it turned out to be a female, later renamed Henrietta. But the story got its happy ending: An agreement between state governments allowed Henrietta to be moved to the Wild Animal Refuge, a sanctuary spread across 10,000 acres in remote southeast Colorado, including nearly 250 acres of black bear habitat. Bears tend to fare poorly in zoos and other close-quarter confines — researchers have found patterns of abnormal behavior and self-mutilation — but the Refuge is a rare place that can hem them in while giving them the things they need most: sustenance (including salmon, crab, and fresh produce, much of it donated by grocers) and room to roam. “Life’s easy when they have food,” Pat Craig, the founder of the Refuge and its parent facility, the Wild Animal Sanctuary, said. “We have a lot of bears that come up to our habitats and look at it like they’re going to knock on the door.” Last month, Craig answered a cold call from Furgiuele, who had come across the saga of Hank in her efforts to find Dolly an escape route. She hardly expected Craig to pick up the phone, much less his immediate response when she explained the situation: Sure , he said, we’d be glad to take her . He also emphasized that the gambit would be a longshot. The vast majority of inhabitants at the Wild Animal Sanctuary and Refuge are born into captivity — bred and eventually rescued from “Tiger King people,” Craig said. State laws put strict limits on transfers of wild animals to sanctuaries, and moving those animals between states is even harder. And Craig wouldn’t have to look far to find a wild bear marked for death; as of early September, Colorado wildlife officials had euthanized nearly 300 this year. Over the past decade, Craig has been able to accept only five or six wild bears, he said. When he does, it’s almost always the result of a public pressure campaign that captures government attention. (Colorado Gov. Jared Polis was a vocal proponent of the Hank the Tank transfer.) “It probably has 100% to do with social media and how much traction someone’s post gets,” Craig said. Furgiuele’s campaign was already gaining traction with the public, with tens of thousands of people signing her petition. It also caught the eye of state officials. Soon after her conversation with Craig, Furgiuele got a call from Brad Howard, the chief of the WRC’s wildlife management division. The conversation was mutually respectful, she said, but it left her pessimistic about the Colorado option. “I could sort of tell by his voice that he was telling me no without telling me no,” she said. She recalled Howard telling her that Dolly was clearly not predatory — that “if she was truly aggressive, she’d be dead by now.” The bear’s adaptation to freely available food and her defensive reaction in the close-quarters encounter on Spooks Branch Road were responses to scenes in which humans were the actors. Yet the agency was wary of making an exception for this bear; it didn’t want people to think they could treat a symptom, bear habituation, without addressing the problem of human behavior. (The WRC declined to make Howard available for an interview.) She told him she’d call back with another idea. Furgiuele pursued every angle she could find. She met with Hobbs at the Western North Carolina Nature Center’s Bears and Brews event. Though some supporters of the Pardon Dolly campaign saw the WRC as the opposition, Furgiuele said she treats Hobbs as an ally, someone trying to solve the same problem from the opposite end of the spectrum: Neither wants dead bears, and both want to force people to confront their role in the destabilization of wildlife. Hobbs said that the increasingly common conflicts involving humans and bears energized her. “I’m pretty much a can-do kind of person,” she said. Furgiuele has a handful of political connections, people she knows both from her past environmental activism and through her father, a former town attorney and councilmember in Boone. She made regular calls to Gov. Josh Stein’s office and to his western residence , which sits atop Town Mountain, an area rife with bears. (The first time she tried to reach Stein, a confused receptionist transferred her to the office of clemency, where a functionary told her, “We don’t pardon bears in our office.”) Failing to get a call back, she started asking other officials to intervene on her behalf. representative.title: ‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine — Meduza

snapshot.title: ‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine — Meduza
snapshot.evidenceText: Since 2022, residents of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region have lived under occupation. In 2023, the city was flooded after the Kakhovka dam was blown up: the flooding destroyed dozens of residential blocks and all of its infrastructure. In the fall of 2026, Oleshky found itself cut off. There’s a humanitarian catastrophe there: the city has no electricity, food, or medicine. Every way out is mined and blocked by Russian troops. Meduza spoke to people who have miraculously managed to stay in touch with those who remain in Oleshky. Here’s what they told us. Svitlana (not her real name), a former resident of Oleshky who fled the city in 2022 because of the war, smiles as she recalls her garden — and the compliments her friend Nina used to pay it. Before the full-scale war, Nina used to bring her homemade milk every Thursday. “I had [about a third of an acre] of land, and I planted peony bushes all along the perimeter. The scent was intoxicating!” Svitlana says. “Nina asked why I didn’t take the flowers to market. But how could I sell something so beautiful?” Svitlana’s yard brimmed with flowers until autumn, and hers wasn’t the only one. “It was as if the townspeople were competing over whose front garden was more lavish. Oleshky bloomed and smelled wonderful.” Svitlana calls the land she lived on for three decades “rodiucha,” which translates from Ukrainian as “fertile”: Stick a branch in the ground and it will sprout. Everyone had everything: tomatoes, cucumbers, orchards… I grew 14 varieties of grapes, three varieties each of apricots and peaches. There was so much of a harvest that there was nowhere to put it: I sold some and canned the rest. I shared preserves with people displaced from Donbas — I’d send volunteers whole crates of it. On weekends, Svitlana liked to spend time along the Kinska River, a left tributary of the Dnipro. The Kinska had a beach and good fishing spots, and from its pier you could catch a pleasure boat or a passenger ferry to Kherson, about 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) away by water. Russian cell service in Oleshky, which has been under occupation since the first days of Russia’s invasion, operates with severe disruptions. But because the city is close to Kherson, Ukrainian mobile networks can still be picked up at random spots around town. That is how Svitlana stays in touch with her neighbors Olha and Dmytro (not their real names), the people closest to her who remain in Oleshky. These days, Svitlana hears little from her neighbors. She says the constant risk of a drone strike keeps them in the basement most of the time. In the spring, Olha wrote to her on Viber: “We just need to survive.” Mykyta (not his real name), another resident who also fled the city in 2022, keeps in touch with Oleshky through Ukrainian mobile networks. He calls his mother, Tamara (not her real name), every day, and to reach him, she has to go out into the yard, find a signal, and stay put wherever she finds it. Sometimes the call cuts off mid-sentence. “My mother runs from drones. She hears a sound in the sky and rushes straight into the house, where the signal disappears,” Mykyta explains. “Every day I hear explosions over the phone.” Mykyta spent six months living under occupation: he didn’t want to leave right away, thinking “it would all be over quickly.” “But then [representatives of the occupation authorities] came to search my place and beat my legs so badly that I couldn’t walk normally for two months. That’s when I realized nothing was going to end quickly, and I left.” Tamara and her husband, Borys (not his real name), stayed in Oleshky. According to Mykyta, his father refused outright to leave the city — he didn’t want to abandon the household. “Dad used to say, ‘Let’s just sit tight, maybe things will get better.’ Nothing got better. He got seriously ill, and that’s when my mother said they were staying — Dad wouldn’t have survived the trip. She’s already buried him.” After her husband’s death, Tamara kept putting off leaving because she didn’t want to abandon her two dogs. But both dogs died this year, Mykyta says: My mother tried hard: she wouldn’t cook anything extra for herself, she’d give it to them instead. But she had to feed them whatever she could. A lot of people in Oleshky now eat purslane — it’s this fatty grass. My mother added it to the dogs’ food. They ate tomatoes, cucumbers, honey, pasta — whatever supplies were left. I think that’s what did them in. The humanitarian crisis in Oleshky began in 2023. After the Kakhovka dam was blown up, the city was flooded by 90%, and its infrastructure was severely damaged. Since then, there has been no electricity or gas. Only people with their own wells have drinking water. But pumping water from a well requires a pump, running the pump without electricity requires a generator, and the generator needs fuel. The last fuel delivery to the city coincided with the final food supplies , in late spring 2026. Kseniia Arkhipova, a police officer in Oleshky before the invasion, tells Meduza this. In 2022, during the occupation, she began volunteering to help local residents, which angered the pro-Russian authorities. After they detained her, she left her hometown for Ukrainian-controlled territory. Since getting out of Oleshky, Arkhipova has coordinated help for her fellow residents remotely, helping deliver food and medicine, taking part in organizing evacuations, and keeping a list of people who have died in the city during the war. By August 30, she had confirmed 136 deaths since the start of the invasion. As far as the volunteer knows, no one has managed to bring food into Oleshky since spring 2026: vehicles that have tried have come under fire and been forced to turn back. The Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda has reported that by the end of summer it had become impossible to enter the city: Russian and Ukrainian drones clashed in the skies over Oleshky every day. The occupation administration itself accuses the Ukrainian military of blockading the city and claims that Ukrainian drones attack convoys carrying humanitarian aid. In May and June, people in Oleshky still had supplies, then the harvest came in from their gardens: grapes, tomatoes, potatoes, zucchini. But the supplies ran out, and people started sounding the alarm — there’s no food. Mothers write to me: “Ksyusha, my child has nothing to eat, what do I do? He’s hungry all the time.” It’s like 1933 all over again, “wonderful Russian culture” in all its glory. Kseniia is referring to the Holodomor , which killed nearly 4 million residents of the Ukrainian SSR. Ukraine’s official position , backed by 29 countries (Russia is not among them), holds that the Holodomor was a deliberate genocide of the Ukrainian people by the Soviet government. Mykyta says that, just as in Soviet times, Ukrainians are dying of hunger because of Russia: “It doesn’t fit in my head that something like this could happen in this day and age. This is an actual Holodomor.” In July, the occupation authorities in the Kherson region denied there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they had acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, and that utility crews weren’t making repairs because of the shelling. On September 21, Putin’s press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, called the situation in the Russian-occupied city “critical.” “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to hinder deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops continue working to resolve the situation,” he said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also addressed the crisis in Oleshky. In one of his evening addresses in May, he said : “The situation specifically in this part of the occupied territory is extremely difficult, and it’s very hard to carry out evacuations. It’s important that international organizations — everyone able to help with this — are engaged and take decisive action.” Residents of Oleshky have very few ways to get food: Ukrainian authorities say the city is under a complete blockade. Tetiana Hasanenko, who heads the Oleshky city military administration from Ukrainian-controlled territory, said in comments to Ukrainska Pravda that Russian troops have mined every route out of Oleshky: People have two options: either die from starvation, or come under drone or artillery fire and be killed. There is no third option. At the same time, Yevhen Voronetskyi, a serviceman with the 34th Independent Marine Brigade “Borysfen” of the Ukrainian armed forces, told Ukrainska Pravda that Ukrainian troops have mined some routes out of Oleshky to prevent Russian forces from bringing in weapons. Voronetskyi said Ukraine’s military keeps the main road out of the city clear so civilians can leave, even helping people make their way along it and sometimes guiding them with drones along a relatively safe route. In 2023, Russian forces mined the fields around the city out of fear of a Ukrainian military landing on the left bank of the Dnipro. There is no confirmation that the Russian army has continued mining the main roads around Oleshky. Each side blames the other. Petro Andryushchenko, a former adviser to the mayor of Mariupol who now heads the Center for Occupation Studies, said in an interview with the Ukrainian outlet NV that Russian forces are using the city’s residents as human shields: “This is a real humanitarian catastrophe, and one created entirely by the Russians as cover for military operations.” The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported on June 25 that “thousands of civilians trapped in frontline communities in southern Ukraine are facing a deepening humanitarian crisis.” Oleshky became a front-line city in the fall of 2022, when the Russian army, under pressure from Ukrainian forces, retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson. Since then, the occupation authorities say, Ukrainian attacks have hindered their efforts to rebuild Oleshky — including after the 2023 flooding — and to deliver food and medicine to the city. As FPV drones became more common on the battlefield, Oleshky, like Kherson on the opposite bank, grew increasingly dangerous. The front line runs right between the two cities, along the river, and it takes drones only a few minutes to cross the Dnipro and reach a target. But drones aren’t the only threat in the city and its surrounding area. The area around the city has been mined so heavily that by early 2026, entering or leaving it had become very difficult. That, said Tetiana Hasanenko, who is trying to stay in touch with the city’s residents, is precisely what led to the sharp deterioration of the situation in Oleshky. Vegetable gardens in Oleshky have turned into a deadly obstacle course. Neighbors told Mykyta that the plot around his house, which he abandoned in 2022, is “littered with mines,” including antitank mines and “petal” mines . According to Mykyta, the areas around the city are unsafe too: “The riverbanks were mined, and after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam], the water scattered those mines who knows where.” “Oleshky is closed off on all sides,” Kseniia Arkhipova sums up. “There are about 1,500 people caught in this trap.” Since the start of the Russian invasion, the city’s population has shrunk nearly 15-fold: according to figures from the Oleshky city military administration, 22,000 people lived in Oleshky before 2022. Some residents risk their lives to walk to Radensk, a nearby village, in search of food. Like Oleshky, it’s under Russian control. The roughly 20-kilometer (12-mile) route is extremely dangerous: the road is mined, and the open terrain is exposed to drone fire. Some still manage to get food, which is sold at an improvised market in Oleshky. Mykyta learned the prices there from his mother: “I’m in shock. A sack of potatoes costs 7,000 rubles! A can of sprats costs 1,000 rubles, compared to 60 in Radensk.” Mykyta says a friend of his mother’s advised her to turn to “some religious people.” He doesn’t know who they are, but he’s heard from his mother that they have more food than many other residents. Through these people, his mother Tamara was able to get “a couple of kilograms of buckwheat, some pasta, canned meat, oil, flour — a little of everything.” Mykyta has been trying to arrange food deliveries to his mother through charitable organizations in nearby cities, but so far without success. The Ukrainian military sometimes sends humanitarian cargo into the blockaded city. Since March, Ukrainian forces have used drones capable of carrying up to 10 kilograms (22 pounds) of cargo, dropping boxes of canned meat, flour, crackers, oil, and grains directly onto Oleshky. But this isn’t regular supply, and not every resident gets a package. “A ten-kilo package is enough for one family for a week. And then what?” Kseniia Arkhipova adds. On September 27, the Ukrainian military dropped its largest shipment of food into Oleshky to date, delivering about four tons (4.4 tons) of food at roughly 100 pre-selected locations. Arkhipova afterward received many grateful messages from locals, and she shows Meduza one of them: “A huge, huge thank you to the guys. God bless them, a deep bow to them!” Overnight on October 4, the Ukrainian military carried out another operation delivering four tons (4.4 tons) of humanitarian aid to Oleshky by drone. According to figures from Ukrainska Pravda, no evacuation of Oleshky has ever been officially organized in four years of occupation. In the spring, the occupation authorities promised for the first time to move Oleshky residents to safer towns. Hoping that would happen, Arkhipova, the volunteer, began coordinating people in a Telegram chat. Svitlana, the Oleshky resident who left her blooming garden behind in 2022, followed Arkhipova’s messages in the chat. On March 5, she wrote to a neighbor: “Olechka, the question of evacuating Oleshky residents is being decided at the highest level. They’re compiling lists of people so they know exactly how many buses are needed.” Kseniia recalls how “everyone hoped the Red Cross would come and evacuate everyone”: Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said , without specifying dates, that Kyiv had agreed on “clear mechanisms” for evacuation with Russia, backed by the International Red Cross. But Russia, he said, has stalled the process: “For a long time now, after the talks that were held, the Russian side has not confirmed its readiness to carry out a humanitarian mission to evacuate people.” Kseniia Arkhipova said that by believing the rumors about the Red Cross and an organized evacuation, people missed their last real chance to leave: “Most of those 200 people are still in Oleshky. In the end, only 67 risked leaving on foot.” Volunteers coordinate on-foot evacuations from Oleshky remotely, Kseniia says. They put together a plan based on information residents share with them whenever they manage to get in touch. The last “window of opportunity” for evacuating on foot opened on September 10 and lasted about two weeks, Arkhipova said. That was when Russian troops cleared mines from a stretch of one of the roads leading out of the city. The first thing residents do is make their way to nearby Radensk (also occupied by Russia). After making the trip, some are “completely unable to move,” Kseniia continues: They arrive dirty, emaciated, with nothing. Sometimes they weigh less than 50 kilograms (110 pounds), just skin and bones. No clothes, no shoes, no money — no home. Recently an 87-year-old woman was brought out on a cart. When she saw bread, she took out a handkerchief, wrapped a crust in it, pressed it to her chest and said, “I won’t give it up, this is my bread.” In Radensk, refugees from Oleshky are housed with volunteers willing to take them in, and “they just rest for a few days,” Kseniia says. Some are put up in empty, nonresidential spaces, like stores. Then those who are able make their way to free Ukrainian territory — through Russia and Europe. About 30 Oleshky residents have left the occupation since the start of September. The volunteer says that among those who left, everyone who initially didn’t want to evacuate “regrets, without exception, staying stuck for so long.” “I yell at them: ‘I told you to leave a year ago, two years ago, three years ago!’ And they answer: ‘Ksyusha, it’s hard to leave everything behind. You’re young — you just turned around and left. We can’t do that.’” Among those Arkhipova has helped leave are also refugees who for a long time didn’t believe they were really in danger. She said they decided to evacuate only after someone close to them had been killed. After being rescued from occupation, Oleshky residents can count on support that Ukraine provides to evacuees and internally displaced persons (IDPs). ”[But] while they fill out the paperwork and wait for that measly 2,000 hryvnias [about 40 euros or 3,800 rubles], what are they supposed to do in the meantime?” Kseniia says. From time to time, she manages to persuade Ukrainian charitable foundations and Russian antiwar organizations to help refugees from Oleshky. The “window of opportunity” for evacuation has now closed again, Arkhipova says. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman, is convinced that an evacuation of Oleshky’s residents could realistically be carried out in a single day. All that’s needed is to clear the road of mines and send in, roughly speaking, four big buses [into the city]. People will come out on their own, and those who can’t move will be wheeled out on carts. Loading everyone up and driving them out — the whole operation would take three hours! Why isn’t this being done? Because Russia can’t be negotiated with. In late September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha spoke about the crisis in Oleshky in an address to the UN and the International Red Cross. At Ukraine’s request, the OSCE called on Russia to give international organizations access to Oleshky, supply residents with food and medicine, and allow them to leave the city safely. Vladimir Saldo, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region, gave an interview to the television channel Vesti on September 28. Asked whether a full evacuation of Oleshky was possible and necessary, he said: Of course such a possibility exists. But let’s try to understand the residents who are there. Taking them and forcibly removing them right now would probably be wrong and unfair. Those who wanted to leave have already left. There are no restrictions for anyone there. Saldo then added: “We need to do everything so that they [the local residents] can get everything they need to live there: fuel, food, medicine, communications.” Two days after Saldo’s interview aired, Kseniia Arkhipova learned that several Oleshky residents had again tried to walk to Radensk for food. She posted a notice in the city chat warning that four people had been injured by landmines along a certain route that day and urging anyone heading to Radensk to avoid that stretch of road: Regardless of Saldo’s statements, many Oleshky residents genuinely don’t want to, or can’t, get out. For instance, Mykyta’s mother isn’t willing to abandon her home, he says: “She says if she leaves, everything will be looted. ‘And who needs us there [outside our hometown] anyway?’” Kseniia Arkhipova also described the fear that residents still in Oleshky feel toward looters. From her conversations with residents, she learned that Russian troops rotated through Oleshky around mid-September: “The ones who came in now are polite — they might come ask for food, [saying] ‘you leave us alone, and we’ll leave you alone,’” Kseniia recounts from her acquaintances’ stories. “But before that there were ones who took everything. Or they’d kick people out of their homes and onto the street because they had solar panels, which meant they had electricity.” Among those who can’t leave the city are the people Arkhipov
