He calls his mother, Tamara (not her real name), every day, and to reach him, she has to go out into the yard, find a signal, and stay put wherever she finds it. Sometimes the call cuts off mid-sentence. “My mother runs from drones. She hears a sound in the sky and rushes straight into the house, where the signal disappears,” Mykyta explains. “Every day I hear explosions over the phone.” Mykyta spent six months living under occupation: he didn’t want to leave right away, thinking “it would all be over quickly.” “But then [representatives of the occupation authorities] came to search my place and beat my legs so badly that I couldn’t walk normally for two months. That’s when I realized nothing was going to end quickly, and I left.” Tamara and her husband, Borys (not his real name), stayed in Oleshky. According to Mykyta, his father refused outright to leave the city — he didn’t want to abandon the household. “Dad used to say, ‘Let’s just sit tight, maybe things will get better.’ Nothing got better. He got seriously ill, and that’s when my mother said they were staying — Dad wouldn’t have survived the trip. She’s already buried him.” After her husband’s death, Tamara kept putting off leaving because she didn’t want to abandon her two dogs. But both dogs died this year, Mykyta says: My mother tried hard: she wouldn’t cook anything extra for herself, she’d give it to them instead. But she had to feed them whatever she could. A lot of people in Oleshky now eat purslane — it’s this fatty grass. My mother added it to the dogs’ food. They ate tomatoes, cucumbers, honey, pasta — whatever supplies were left. I think that’s what did them in. The humanitarian crisis in Oleshky began in 2023. After the Kakhovka dam was blown up, the city was flooded by 90%, and its infrastructure was severely damaged. Since then, there has been no electricity or gas. Only people with their own wells have drinking water. But pumping water from a well requires a pump, running the pump without electricity requires a generator, and the generator needs fuel. The last fuel delivery to the city coincided with the final food supplies , in late spring 2026. Kseniia Arkhipova, a police officer in Oleshky before the invasion, tells Meduza this. In 2022, during the occupation, she began volunteering to help local residents, which angered the pro-Russian authorities. After they detained her, she left her hometown for Ukrainian-controlled territory. Since getting out of Oleshky, Arkhipova has coordinated help for her fellow residents remotely, helping deliver food and medicine, taking part in organizing evacuations, and keeping a list of people who have died in the city during the war. By August 30, she had confirmed 136 deaths since the start of the invasion. As far as the volunteer knows, no one has managed to bring food into Oleshky since spring 2026: vehicles that have tried have come under fire and been forced to turn back. The Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda has reported that by the end of summer it had become impossible to enter the city: Russian and Ukrainian drones clashed in the skies over Oleshky every day. The occupation administration itself accuses the Ukrainian military of blockading the city and claims that Ukrainian drones attack convoys carrying humanitarian aid. In May and June, people in Oleshky still had supplies, then the harvest came in from their gardens: grapes, tomatoes, potatoes, zucchini. But the supplies ran out, and people started sounding the alarm — there’s no food. Mothers write to me: “Ksyusha, my child has nothing to eat, what do I do? He’s hungry all the time.” It’s like 1933 all over again, “wonderful Russian culture” in all its glory. Kseniia is referring to the Holodomor , which killed nearly 4 million residents of the Ukrainian SSR. Ukraine’s official position , backed by 29 countries (Russia is not among them), holds that the Holodomor was a deliberate genocide of the Ukrainian people by the Soviet government. Mykyta says that, just as in Soviet times, Ukrainians are dying of hunger because of Russia: “It doesn’t fit in my head that something like this could happen in this day and age. This is an actual Holodomor.” In July, the occupation authorities in the Kherson region denied there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they had acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, and that utility crews weren’t making repairs because of the shelling. On September 21, Putin’s press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, called the situation in the Russian-occupied city “critical.” “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to hinder deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops continue working to resolve the situation,” he said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also addressed the crisis in Oleshky. In one of his evening addresses in May, he said : “The situation specifically in this part of the occupied territory is extremely difficult, and it’s very hard to carry out evacuations. It’s important that international organizations — everyone able to help with this — are engaged and take decisive action.” Residents of Oleshky have very few ways to get food: Ukrainian authorities say the city is under a complete blockade. Tetiana Hasanenko, who heads the Oleshky city military administration from Ukrainian-controlled territory, said in comments to Ukrainska Pravda that Russian troops have mined every route out of Oleshky: People have two options: either die from starvation, or come under drone or artillery fire and be killed. There is no third option. At the same time, Yevhen Voronetskyi, a serviceman with the 34th Independent Marine Brigade “Borysfen” of the Ukrainian armed forces, told Ukrainska Pravda that Ukrainian troops have mined some routes out of Oleshky to prevent Russian forces from bringing in weapons. Voronetskyi said Ukraine’s military keeps the main road out of the city clear so civilians can leave, even helping people make their way along it and sometimes guiding them with drones along a relatively safe route. In 2023, Russian forces mined the fields around the city out of fear of a Ukrainian military landing on the left bank of the Dnipro. There is no confirmation that the Russian army has continued mining the main roads around Oleshky. Each side blames the other. Petro Andryushchenko, a former adviser to the mayor of Mariupol who now heads the Center for Occupation Studies, said in an interview with the Ukrainian outlet NV that Russian forces are using the city’s residents as human shields: “This is a real humanitarian catastrophe, and one created entirely by the Russians as cover for military operations.” The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported on June 25 that “thousands of civilians trapped in frontline communities in southern Ukraine are facing a deepening humanitarian crisis.” Oleshky became a front-line city in the fall of 2022, when the Russian army, under pressure from Ukrainian forces, retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson. Since then, the occupation authorities say, Ukrainian attacks have hindered their efforts to rebuild Oleshky — including after the 2023 flooding — and to deliver food and medicine to the city. As FPV drones became more common on the battlefield, Oleshky, like Kherson on the opposite bank, grew increasingly dangerous. The front line runs right between the two cities, along the river, and it takes drones only a few minutes to cross the Dnipro and reach a target. But drones aren’t the only threat in the city and its surrounding area. The area around the city has been mined so heavily that by early 2026, entering or leaving it had become very difficult. That, said Tetiana Hasanenko, who is trying to stay in touch with the city’s residents, is precisely what led to the sharp deterioration of the situation in Oleshky. Vegetable gardens in Oleshky have turned into a deadly obstacle course. Neighbors told Mykyta that the plot around his house, which he abandoned in 2022, is “littered with mines,” including antitank mines and “petal” mines . According to Mykyta, the areas around the city are unsafe too: “The riverbanks were mined, and after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam], the water scattered those mines who knows where.” “Oleshky is closed off on all sides,” Kseniia Arkhipova sums up. “There are about 1,500 people caught in this trap.” Since the start of the Russian invasion, the city’s population has shrunk nearly 15-fold: according to figures from the Oleshky city military administration, 22,000 people lived in Oleshky before 2022. Some residents risk their lives to walk to Radensk, a nearby village, in search of food. Like Oleshky, it’s under Russian control. The roughly 20-kilometer (12-mile) route is extremely dangerous: the road is mined, and the open terrain is exposed to drone fire. Some still manage to get food, which is sold at an improvised market in Oleshky. Mykyta learned the prices there from his mother: “I’m in shock. A sack of potatoes costs 7,000 rubles! A can of sprats costs 1,000 rubles, compared to 60 in Radensk.” Mykyta says a friend of his mother’s advised her to turn to “some religious people.” He doesn’t know who they are, but he’s heard from his mother that they have more food than many other residents. Through these people, his mother Tamara was able to get “a couple of kilograms of buckwheat, some pasta, canned meat, oil, flour — a little of everything.” Mykyta has been trying to arrange food deliveries to his mother through charitable organizations in nearby cities, but so far without success. The Ukrainian military sometimes sends humanitarian cargo into the blockaded city. Since March, Ukrainian forces have used drones capable of carrying up to 10 kilograms (22 pounds) of cargo, dropping boxes of canned meat, flour, crackers, oil, and grains directly onto Oleshky. But this isn’t regular supply, and not every resident gets a package. “A ten-kilo package is enough for one family for a week. And then what?” Kseniia Arkhipova adds. On September 27, the Ukrainian military dropped its largest shipment of food into Oleshky to date, delivering about four tons (4.4 tons) of food at roughly 100 pre-selected locations. Arkhipova afterward received many grateful messages from locals, and she shows Meduza one of them: “A huge, huge thank you to the guys. God bless them, a deep bow to them!” Overnight on October 4, the Ukrainian military carried out another operation delivering four tons (4.4 tons) of humanitarian aid to Oleshky by drone. According to figures from Ukrainska Pravda, no evacuation of Oleshky has ever been officially organized in four years of occupation. In the spring, the occupation authorities promised for the first time to move Oleshky residents to safer towns. Hoping that would happen, Arkhipova, the volunteer, began coordinating people in a Telegram chat. Svitlana, the Oleshky resident who left her blooming garden behind in 2022, followed Arkhipova’s messages in the chat. On March 5, she wrote to a neighbor: “Olechka, the question of evacuating Oleshky residents is being decided at the highest level. They’re compiling lists of people so they know exactly how many buses are needed.” Kseniia recalls how “everyone hoped the Red Cross would come and evacuate everyone”: Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said , without specifying dates, that Kyiv had agreed on “clear mechanisms” for evacuation with Russia, backed by the International Red Cross. But Russia, he said, has stalled the process: “For a long time now, after the talks that were held, the Russian side has not confirmed its readiness to carry out a humanitarian mission to evacuate people.” Kseniia Arkhipova said that by believing the rumors about the Red Cross and an organized evacuation, people missed their last real chance to leave: “Most of those 200 people are still in Oleshky. In the end, only 67 risked leaving on foot.” Volunteers coordinate on-foot evacuations from Oleshky remotely, Kseniia says. They put together a plan based on information residents share with them whenever they manage to get in touch. The last “window of opportunity” for evacuating on foot opened on September 10 and lasted about two weeks, Arkhipova said. That was when Russian troops cleared mines from a stretch of one of the roads leading out of the city. The first thing residents do is make their way to nearby Radensk (also occupied by Russia). After making the trip, some are “completely unable to move,” Kseniia continues: They arrive dirty, emaciated, with nothing. Sometimes they weigh less than 50 kilograms (110 pounds), just skin and bones. No clothes, no shoes, no money — no home. Recently an 87-year-old woman was brought out on a cart. When she saw bread, she took out a handkerchief, wrapped a crust in it, pressed it to her chest and said, “I won’t give it up, this is my bread.” In Radensk, refugees from Oleshky are housed with volunteers willing to take them in, and “they just rest for a few days,” Kseniia says. Some are put up in empty, nonresidential spaces, like stores. Then those who are able make their way to free Ukrainian territory — through Russia and Europe. About 30 Oleshky residents have left the occupation since the start of September. The volunteer says that among those who left, everyone who initially didn’t want to evacuate “regrets, without exception, staying stuck for so long.” “I yell at them: ‘I told you to leave a year ago, two years ago, three years ago!’ And they answer: ‘Ksyusha, it’s hard to leave everything behind. You’re young — you just turned around and left. We can’t do that.’” Among those Arkhipova has helped leave are also refugees who for a long time didn’t believe they were really in danger. She said they decided to evacuate only after someone close to them had been killed. After being rescued from occupation, Oleshky residents can count on support that Ukraine provides to evacuees and internally displaced persons (IDPs). ”[But] while they fill out the paperwork and wait for that measly 2,000 hryvnias [about 40 euros or 3,800 rubles], what are they supposed to do in the meantime?” Kseniia says. From time to time, she manages to persuade Ukrainian charitable foundations and Russian antiwar organizations to help refugees from Oleshky. The “window of opportunity” for evacuation has now closed again, Arkhipova says. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman, is convinced that an evacuation of Oleshky’s residents could realistically be carried out in a single day. All that’s needed is to clear the road of mines and send in, roughly speaking, four big buses [into the city]. People will come out on their own, and those who can’t move will be wheeled out on carts. Loading everyone up and driving them out — the whole operation would take three hours! Why isn’t this being done? Because Russia can’t be negotiated with. In late September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha spoke about the crisis in Oleshky in an address to the UN and the International Red Cross. At Ukraine’s request, the OSCE called on Russia to give international organizations access to Oleshky, supply residents with food and medicine, and allow them to leave the city safely. Vladimir Saldo, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region, gave an interview to the television channel Vesti on September 28. Asked whether a full evacuation of Oleshky was possible and necessary, he said: Of course such a possibility exists. But let’s try to understand the residents who are there. Taking them and forcibly removing them right now would probably be wrong and unfair. Those who wanted to leave have already left. There are no restrictions for anyone there. Saldo then added: “We need to do everything so that they [the local residents] can get everything they need to live there: fuel, food, medicine, communications.” Two days after Saldo’s interview aired, Kseniia Arkhipova learned that several Oleshky residents had again tried to walk to Radensk for food. She posted a notice in the city chat warning that four people had been injured by landmines along a certain route that day and urging anyone heading to Radensk to avoid that stretch of road: Regardless of Saldo’s statements, many Oleshky residents genuinely don’t want to, or can’t, get out. For instance, Mykyta’s mother isn’t willing to abandon her home, he says: “She says if she leaves, everything will be looted. ‘And who needs us there [outside our hometown] anyway?’” Kseniia Arkhipova also described the fear that residents still in Oleshky feel toward looters. From her conversations with residents, she learned that Russian troops rotated through Oleshky around mid-September: “The ones who came in now are polite — they might come ask for food, [saying] ‘you leave us alone, and we’ll leave you alone,’” Kseniia recounts from her acquaintances’ stories. “But before that there were ones who took everything. Or they’d kick people out of their homes and onto the street because they had solar panels, which meant they had electricity.” Among those who can’t leave the city are the people Arkhipov

representative.title: Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack | Houthis | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Al Jazeera Staff

snapshot.title: Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack
snapshot.evidenceText: Sanaa has come under intense bombing since the Yemeni government announced a campaign to take the capital from the Houthis. Sanaa, Yemen – At midnight on Tuesday, air strikes rattled the Yemeni capital Sanaa, a city that has been mostly spared bombing since a truce was announced between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis in 2023. The head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashid al-Alimi, had recently announced a new military offensive was being launched, named Operation Dawn of Yemen, to take Sanaa from the Houthis, who have held the city since September 2014. Government ground forces remain hundreds of miles away from the capital and embroiled in fighting with the Houthis on Yemen’s west coast and around Taiz. This means attacks on Houthi positions in Sanaa must come from the air, but the air campaign has caused civilian casualties. An air strike on Monday hit a location in the Sa’wan area of Sanaa governorate, killing a child and wounding seven other civilians. The Yemeni government has pledged to continue its attacks until it achieves its objectives, notably the recapture of Sanaa. Regardless of the political opinions of Yemenis in the capital, most fear their city, far from the front lines, will become a war zone once again. Strong memories remain of the Saudi-led coalition’s Operation Decisive Storm , launched against the Houthis in March 2015, which saw hundreds of civilians in Sanaa killed in air strikes. Since the start of the new Yemeni government offensive, dozens of strikes have hit the capital, including an attack on Sanaa’s international airport, which killed two workers. Both operations were aimed at Houthi sites. Ghamadan Abood, a 30-year-old courier and Sanaa resident, said the new wave of attacks on the city has heightened fear among residents. “When I learned about the new operation on Sunday, my feeling of security shrank,” he told Al Jazeera. “At any time and anywhere, air strikes may hit, and civilians could become the next casualties.” On Monday, Abood was travelling on his bike when air strikes hit Sa’wan, just two kilometres from where he was. With Houthi military facilities believed to be positioned in the city, and the government sometimes hitting residential areas, the bombing highlights the vulnerability of civilians in Sanaa. “The strikes could be aimed at missile launch pads, military equipment or facilities, but some of these facilities could be near neighbourhoods, farms or roads. So, innocent people could be killed, injured or left terrified,” Abood said. Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, has also come under repeated missile attacks by the Houthis, including two strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the latest on Saturday killing 12 people . On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said Sanaa, Saada, and Amran were among the primary sources of Houthi missile threats. The coalition has noted that ongoing military operations are aimed at curbing the group’s ability to launch missiles on the kingdom. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to the International Organization for Migration. Most of those forced to leave their homes have come from Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, where the most intense ground fighting between government and Houthi forces has taken place. Saleh Ayidh, a 50-year-old resident of Sanaa and father of five, fears the new air strikes will also force people from their homes in the north. “Today, we see Sanaa as a safe place and distant from the front lines. For me, no place is safe in Yemen, particularly in the north, and war can spread anywhere,” he told Al Jazeera. At the start of the Saudi-led coalition’s operation against the Houthis in March 2015, Ayidh’s family left the city for a home in the countryside. They lived there for six months, far from the assault on the Yemeni capital. “Now we do not know what will happen to us. We will decide whether we need to leave the city if the air strikes keep intensifying,” Ayidh said. “Without safety, life is hard.” The recent air strikes are widely viewed in Sanaa as a sign that war has returned to the capital, prompting residents to stock up on food and fuel. When Operation Decisive Storm began in 2015, the cost of goods and fuel rose due to disruption to logistics and panic buying. The same trend is being seen again in Sanaa after the recent resumption of hostilities. Grocery owner Nashwan, 24, has boosted his inventory of essentials such as rice, cheese, milk, biscuits, cooking oil and sugar, before they become too difficult to find. He also stocked up on petrol, buying 100 litres to use for his minibus if a fuel crisis hits the capital. “These commodities may become expensive in the coming days. If the war keeps escalating, buying them would cost me more,” Nashwan said. “I do not want to feel the impact of the war immediately.” Any road closures or a decline in imports caused by the war and a Saudi naval siege on Houthi areas will present major challenges for civilians. “Rising prices of food and fuel are a real worry for the entire population amid the war and will worsen the humanitarian situation in Yemen,” Wafiq Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, told Al Jazeera. Last week, the UN World Food Programme warned that three-quarters of families in parts of Yemen were going hungry. There are fears an escalation of the fighting will lead to a more intense food crisis across Yemen, which the WFP has already described as “absolutely devastating”. Despite the optimism of the internationally recognised government when announcing Operation Dawn of Yemen, few in Sanaa believe it has the ability to recapture the capital from the Houthis any time soon. Raiman al-Hamdani, a London-based Yemen analyst, said government forces are big on paper, but remain scattered across multiple fronts, while soldiers are using outdated gear. “They can hold their lines but can’t push the Houthis out of their mountain strongholds,” Raiman told Al Jazeera last week . Fuad Ali, 40, a university graduate in Sanaa, said the Saudi-backed government has lost the public’s trust, particularly its claim that it could capture the capital after it suffered a series of embarrassing military defeats in recent weeks on the coast . “The government has failed to seize the coastal Hodeidah province or Al-Jawf desert province. The fight there could be easier given the topography. How can it recapture the mountainous Sanaa?” Ali told Al Jazeera. Operation Dawn of Yemen will bring more “destruction to the country’s facilities and increase civilian casualties”, he added. Ali doubts the operation will return the government to Sanaa. But he also believes the government and Saudi-led coalition have learned their lessons from 2015, when huge civilian casualties from air raids drew international condemnation. “I am still optimistic that Operation Dawn of Yemen will not damage Sanaa as Operation Decisive Storm did,” Ali said.
snapshot.imageAlt: Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack

representative.title: Mexico votes to make platforms pull AI-altered voices - Voice Over Talent Industry News
representative.author: Marcus Delgado

snapshot.title: Mexico votes to make platforms pull AI-altered voices - Voice Over Talent Industry News
snapshot.evidenceText: Mexico already says you cannot clone a voice without written consent. On Tuesday its lower house voted to say what happens next: platforms that are told about a voice, image or recording “modified or altered without authorisation through artificial intelligence” must take it down fast, or face fines that reach into the millions of pesos. The opposition calls it the Anti-Meme Law. A radio announcer in León, whose cloned voice was selling a wine festival for the state government two weeks ago, is the case that shows what the vote is really about. The reform to the Federal Copyright Law, sent by President Claudia Sheinbaum, cleared the Chamber of Deputies on 7 October: 325 votes to 114 with one abstention in general, then 310 to 97 on the detail. It rewrites article 114 Octies and adds articles 114 Nonies and 232 Septies, and it now goes to the Senate. The core of it is a duty. Once an internet service provider has “certain knowledge of the existence of an alleged infringement,” it must remove the material “expeditiously and effectively,” in the wording Excélsior published from the bill. The material in question includes “works, images, voice, videograms or phonograms modified or altered without authorisation through artificial intelligence or other technological tools,” as Agencia Reforma summarised the text. Providers must publish a policy for cutting off repeat offenders, keep it in their terms of service, and run a notice mechanism. The fines are set by IMPI, the industrial property institute, in units called UMA: 1,000 to 40,000 of them, which Noroeste worked out as roughly 117,310 to 4.69 million pesos, with a further 100 to 500 UMA for each time a provider keeps ignoring a notice. A provider is not automatically liable for what its users post. Under the new article 114 Nonies it is on the hook only when it knew, took part, had the ability to control the content and drew a direct financial benefit from it. Sheinbaum says no article in the text mentions memes. The nickname stuck because the takedown duty applies to any altered image, and critics think platforms will remove first and ask later. Ariana Rejón Lara of the PRI asked from the rostrum whether this was really Mexico’s main problem. Her colleague Mario Zamora put it bluntly: “They’re taking away our parody, they’re taking away our criticism.” Gloria Núñez of Movimiento Ciudadano argued that “the excessive amount of these fines turns removal into a mechanism of censorship.” Kenia López Rabadán of the PAN accused the government of wanting to force providers to withdraw service “when the Government finds a piece of content inconvenient.” Ariana Rejón Lara of the PRI at the rostrum during the 7 October debate, a frame from the Chamber's live stream. Image: Cámara de Diputados Morena, which holds the majority, rejected all of it. “We are not imposing a gag,” said Claudia Selene Ávila Flores, who carried the bill, as Expansión reported, insisting the aim was to protect intellectual property, not restrict speech. Raúl Villaseñor, also of Morena, said the reform “guarantees a balance between the protection of those rights and the development of the digital economy.” Sheinbaum had got there first. At her morning press conference on 1 October, when the companion bill on government identity fraud passed the Senate, she said the so-called Anti-Meme Law “doesn’t prohibit any meme. What’s more, it’s the law for defending authors, copyright, that’s the law, and it has nothing to do with memes.” Her examples were AI videos of herself touting fake investments. Free-speech groups are not reassured. Artículo 19 warned before the committee vote that the reform “introduces responsibilities and sanctions that could lead internet service providers to monitor and restrict the activity of their users,” and that the vague test of whether a provider “contributes to, induces or causes” an infringement “could open the door to excessive surveillance.” On Imagen Radio on 8 October, Fernando Gutiérrez Cortés of Tecnológico de Monterrey’s digital media observatory said the risk was prior censorship of satire unless intent to deceive is defined precisely. On 25 September, Diego Carreto, a 26-year-old commercial announcer from León, posted a video with a wine-festival spot playing behind him. “This is my voice for a State Government advert,” he said. “The problem is that I didn’t record it.” The ad for Vendimias Guanajuato 2026 had been running on radio, on social media and on the Visit México platform. “I had no idea this agency existed,” he said of Creorama, the firm the state tourism secretariat had hired. “I’ve never worked with them, never signed with them, never recorded or had any kind of contact with them.” Diego Carreto in the video he posted on 25 September, as shown in Milenio Televisión's report. Image: Milenio The consent law was already four months old. It did not stop the spot being made, and it did not take the spot down. What did was pressure. Backed by AMELOC, the Mexican association of commercial announcers, Carreto demanded removal, compensation and a finding of who was responsible. On 29 September the tourism secretariat, Secturi, said it “did not authorise the cloning or the use of voices through artificial intelligence to produce this material,” ordered Creorama to document its permissions or “suspend and replace the material immediately,” and promised to write AI-voice checks into its supplier contracts. That is the gap the new reform is meant to close: the days between a performer hearing their own cloned voice and the moment a platform acts. Whether the duty is written carefully enough to catch a cloned announcer without also catching a cartoon of a governor is the whole Senate argument. “This is my voice for a State Government advert. The problem is that I didn’t record it.” Diego Carreto, commercial announcer, León, 25 September 2026 Three laws in one year Mexico’s dubbing and announcing professions have had an unusual year. In February the culture secretary announced the consent initiative had been drafted with the profession itself, and when the Chamber passed it in April, the dubbing actress Liliana Barba of the Mexican association of announcers told IMER that it “means they have to ask our permission to use my voice, they can’t just steal it like that.” That law was published on 14 May. Voice Over Herald covered what it does and does not do, including the broadcaster already dubbing with AI, in September . The Chamber of Deputies' page for the Federal Copyright Law, showing the reform published on 14 May 2026. Screenshot taken 11 October 2026. Image: Cámara de Diputados Then came the autumn package. On 30 September the Senate passed, with 72 votes in favour, a reform to the Federal Criminal Code and the industrial property law that makes imitating the government’s institutional identity to deceive people a crime, with one to five years in prison. And on 7 October the Chamber passed the platform duty described here. All of it is sold as one fight against digital fraud and piracy; all of it lands on the same platforms that host a dubbing actor’s demo reel and a politician’s parody account alike. For performers outside Mexico, the lesson is the order of operations. A consent right is the first law. A takedown duty is the second, and it is the one that decides whether the first can be enforced in a week or in a court case. Mexico is about to find out how far it can push the second before the memes push back. representative.title: How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice — Meduza

snapshot.title: How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice — Meduza
snapshot.evidenceText: On September 20, 2026, Ukraine launched another large-scale drone attack on the Moscow region. One drone hit a high-rise apartment building in Kotelniki, southeast of Moscow. Another had struck the same building in June. Neither strike killed anyone, but the attacks badly frightened many people in the neighborhood. Reporters from Bereg, a cooperative of independent journalists, visited the Novye Kotelniki residential complex to see how repairs were progressing after the two attacks and how residents had responded. Meduza is translating their report in full. Drivers struggle to find parking in this densely populated neighborhood in Kotelniki, outside Moscow. Shoppers wait in short lines at grocery store checkouts. It’s a warm, sunny weekend day, yet the courtyard of the Novye Kotelniki residential complex is unusually empty. On September 20, a Ukrainian drone struck one of the complex’s high-rise buildings for the second time. The first strike came on June 18, 2026. The drone crashed into almost the same spot on the courtyard side, in the upper third of the building, and exploded. A black scorch mark stands out against the beige-and-brown exterior, with a hole at its center. All that remains of the balconies on floors 19–22 is twisted metal and rebar. Some of the facade tiles have broken off. The few residents walking in the courtyard occasionally look up at the building and whisper to one another. Many decline to tell Bereg how the constant drone alerts have changed their lives. “What is there to say?” says a woman of about 40 in a black hijab, waving off the question, though she had just been discussing that very subject with a friend. Olga, a blonde woman in a trench coat, comes out of a neighboring building with her two-year-old daughter. She says this is their first walk in the courtyard since the recent attack. This time, she says, the property management company quickly cleared the broken glass and other debris from the courtyard. But she’s still scared: “You never know, she could pick up a piece of glass or something. You’re more scared for her than for yourself.” On the day of the attack, Olga woke to explosions at four in the morning. She woke her husband. At first, he thought she was imagining things, but then he heard the explosions, too. Deciding it wasn’t safe to stay in their apartment, they carried their sleeping daughter downstairs to the ground floor, where neighbors had already gathered. Olga stayed in the lobby until eight in the morning. Throughout that time, she could hear explosions outside. “It was a nightmare: People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up, and we were all looking for medicine for them,” she tells Bereg. “You feel like you’re in a war zone, and you can’t believe this is happening to you.” Olga missed the summer attack — her family was away. Perhaps that’s why, unlike many of her neighbors, she hadn’t put a “go bag” with documents, medicine, and other essentials in her entryway. Before the September attacks, she had felt less anxious than others. Afterward, she no longer felt safe. Still, her family’s daily routine hasn’t changed. She and her husband decided against moving their bed farther from the windows, figuring it wouldn’t save them. “Look at the size of that hole,” she says, gesturing toward the damaged high-rise. “You keep thinking: God, what if it happens again tomorrow?” Olga says. “I was on sedatives for two days. I definitely don’t feel safe here. I’m stressed every day.” Her family is considering moving, but unless the attacks become more frequent — “not once or twice, but practically every day” — she and her husband are unlikely to “seriously start looking into it.” Olga hopes things will “get back to normal” because “they [the Ukrainians] have already hit what they wanted to hit, and now they’ll calm down.” She means the Moscow oil refinery, the Ukrainian military’s target. But the high-rise stood in the path of the drones flying toward it. A few things help Olga manage her anxiety: She’s become even more absorbed in caring for her child and stopped reading the news, although she used to scroll through neighborhood chats even at night. “There’s so much noise now, so many planted stories, so much fake news,” she says. “Even the [real] news — there’s so much of it. You watch all this, and the whole situation keeps playing over in your head. What for?” Ruslan, who lives in the same complex as Olga, takes the opposite approach: He tries to read all the news. He says the drone attacks don’t make him anxious. “I knew there’d be an attack — the elections and all that,” Ruslan says. He says the neighborhood has only been quiet for the last few days. Before that, neighbors often heard air defenses in action at night and early in the morning. On September 20, Ruslan and his family counted “at least 40 explosions.” “We could see flashes in the sky from our window — almost like the ones over Israel !” he says excitedly. “There were about 10 a minute at one point.” He saw the drone crash into the neighboring building. He and his family were about to head out into the stairwell when they heard a loud noise outside the window and red light flooded the apartment. Like Olga, Ruslan doesn’t have a “go bag,” and he says he won’t be getting one. He sees no need, because “our air defenses have gotten better at their job.” “Yeah, there are screwups. Unfortunately, they can’t intercept everything. But overall, our guys are doing their job, and they’re doing it well,” Ruslan says. “Every day on my way home from work, I see the air defense systems changing locations.” He tells Bereg he believes there won’t be any more strikes on the neighborhood because they’re no longer worth it for Ukraine: “They launched so many, and the results were really poor . They understand it’s a waste of money.” With a smirk, Ruslan recalls wondering during the first attack whether the target might have been the apartment building rather than the refinery — “maybe some general lives here.” But he quickly dismissed the idea: First, it was a large-scale attack, and second, “what general would live here?” Ruslan believes Moscow and its immediate surroundings are now “very well protected” and that the authorities should focus on deploying air defense systems in other regions. That’s his only complaint about the security measures. “I think our government will take care of us, and everything will be fine. Our army will handle it,” he says. “Maybe I’m not that well informed, or maybe I’m too optimistic. But I think everything really is fine.” The next large-scale attack on the Moscow region came overnight on October 6. It struck communities northwest of Moscow, damaging private homes and nonresidential buildings in settlements in the Solnechnogorsk, Volokolamsk, Istra, and Domodedovo districts. Ukrainian Telegram channels that monitor attacks and the Russian outlet Astra also reported a fire at the Volodarskaya oil depot, southeast of Moscow. The Ukrainian strikes and Russian air defense operations killed two people and injured nine. Ruslan’s school-age daughter looks at him admiringly. They chuckle together as they recall a neighbor who panicked during the latest attack. “Run, run, we’re under attack!” Ruslan says, imitating her, though he quickly adds that “everybody’s different.” His daughter says that after the summer attack, one of her classmates transferred to another school — her family had decided to move. “They were renting [their apartment]. Maybe if we rented here instead of owning, we’d feel better about moving, too,” Ruslan says. “Plus, we’ve got a mortgage here — where are we gonna go?” A man in a black jacket, probably an employee of the property management company, walks through the courtyard with a ring of keys. He unlocks a door marked “Shelter” leading to the basement, looks inside, locks it again, and moves on to the next building. Each of the complex’s more than 20 high-rises has a shelter. Residents of Novye Kotelniki say the management company told them the basements are kept locked because they contain “technical equipment that the engineers are responsible for.” In the event of a real threat, residents are to call the dispatch office. A staff member will then come during the attack and unlock the basement door. The company promises this will happen quickly. But on September 20, residents of some buildings complained in the neighborhood Telegram chat that they hadn’t been able to get into the basements until after seven in the morning, although the large-scale attack began at four. Signs reading “Shelter” have been hung at the basement entrances, but the management company has done little to equip the rooms, residents say. Some have benches; others don’t even have those, leaving people to sit on the concrete or stand. Aleksandra, a resident in her mid-40s, is smoking near the entrance to one shelter. Asked how she feels about the increasingly frequent attacks, she says emphatically: “It’s really bad, really bad!” Aleksandra lives in the building that drones have struck twice. Or rather, she used to — after the recent strike, she realized she was afraid to stay in her apartment. “As they say, what happens once might never happen again, but what happens a second time…” she says. Aleksandra was home during both attacks. On June 18, she and her husband woke to repeated explosions and began getting ready to go to the shelter. As she was tying her sneakers, a drone crashed into the building. “I hear this huge bang — and plaster starts falling down in our apartment!” she tells Bereg. “I opened the door, and there was already smoke in the stairwell. We didn’t know if we’d be able to get downstairs.” No one opened the shelter, and neighbors crowded onto the ground floor. “It all ended around eight, and that’s when they opened the basement,” Aleksandra says indignantly. “Well, what’s the point of going down there once it’s all over?” On the day of the second drone strike, Aleksandra again heard “a lot of activity” as explosions kept going off. First, she went out onto the communal balcony to take a look. From there, she could see several fires near the Moscow oil refinery, the Mega shopping mall, and the Sadovod market. She was horrified. “I wake my husband up: ‘Get up, there’s a real war out there — everything’s burning, everything’s in flames!’” she says. To reach the stairs, Aleksandra and her husband had to pass through the communal balcony. As soon as they opened its door, there was a loud explosion, and a wave of heat hit them. “I knew it had hit the building,” she says. “Something went bang, and things started falling.” As we talk in the courtyard, there’s a crash in the distance, quiet but distinct. Aleksandra flinches and abruptly turns toward the sound. “I think something fell at the construction site.” “I react like that all the time now [to sudden noises],” Aleksandra says. “My nerves are completely shot. I went a week without proper sleep, even with Novo-Passit, glycine, and things to calm me down. I’d sleep for two hours, then be awake again.” On September 20, Aleksandra and her husband waited for the explosions to stop, went back up to their apartment, packed everything they needed, and left for their dacha. They’re staying there temporarily but return to their apartment in Novye Kotelniki every few days. “We’re living out of bags: one in the car, one at the dacha, and one here. We come back, wash up, do the laundry, hang it up, and head back out,” Aleksandra says. “We try to get everything done as fast as we can. They’ve just posted [on Telegram channels] again that apparently another large-scale attack is expected. Who knows?” But they can’t stay at the dacha for long: It has almost no amenities, and the trip to work takes three hours. Driving every day proved too expensive, so they switched to public transportation. Aleksandra took out a mortgage to buy her apartment. She has no other home and no relatives who can take her in. Now she’ll have to pay both her mortgage and the rent on a new place in a safer neighborhood. “I’ll be working to pay the rent. What else can I do?” she says with a sigh. “I don’t know what I’ll eat, but I’m just scared to live here.” “Looking at the windows, I could tell that lots of people had left — almost no one was still here,” she says. “Today we packed up a bunch of bags and took a heater. And everyone coming toward us had bags, too. People are leaving, and no one wants to come back.” Far fewer people go into the high-rise hit by the two drone attacks than into the other buildings. Many residents emerge carrying large bags — clearly, they’re leaving for a long time. The lobby has two entrances: one from the courtyard, the other from the road. The courtyard entrance is now cordoned off with barriers wrapped in red and white tape. The concierge warns that residents can’t leave through that door, either. A chair braces it shut from inside, and a sign on it reads: “No entry! Risk of death!” It doesn’t explain the danger. Another notice asks residents not to use the elevators between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. so they can be available to “construction workers repairing the building.” Residents ignore the request, and there are no workers in sight. Residents say that for the first few days after the attack, the elevators ran only in the evenings. Those with apartments on the upper floors of the 25-story building had to take the stairs or enter through the neighboring stairwell, use the elevator there, and cross the roof to reach their own building. The management company temporarily opened access to the roof for that purpose. The elevators are now running, and access to the roof has been closed off again. On many floors, boxes and bags of belongings are scattered about, along with plastic-wrapped crates of toys, black bags of construction debris, window frames, packages of building materials, and parts from household appliances. The smell of smoke still lingers on the fifth and sixth floors. On September 20, burning debris landed on a windowsill and started a fire. On the upper floors, it smells of burned plastic. The 21st floor suffered the worst damage. Workers had to remove the front panels from one elevator and the structure surrounding the shaft opening. A padlocked grille has replaced the door separating the elevator lobby from the apartments. The apartment the drone struck is on this floor. Georgy, whose name has been changed, was home in a neighboring apartment at the time. He and his wife, Yelena, whose name has also been changed, were about to head downstairs when he heard an unusual humming sound from the direction of the balcony. “I go over to the balcony and realize it [the drone] is getting closer, but I can’t see it. I can’t figure out where it’s coming from,” he tells Bereg. “I look down — and there it is, coming from the direction of the quarry, heading straight at me.” Georgy managed to shout to Yelena to run. He didn’t have time to get out of the way himself. The drone hit the neighboring apartment and exploded. The blast wave and a hail of fragments hit him. His arms and legs were badly cut. Bleeding heavily, he got dressed and pulled on his sneakers. His wife retrieved their cat, which had hidden under the bathtub. They grabbed a bag of documents and jewelry they had prepared in advance and ran downstairs. “If it had flown just a little higher, that would’ve been it — we wouldn’t be talking now,” Georgy says, visibly shaken as he looks at his bandaged wrists. “The explosion was unreal. I’d never experienced anything like it in my life. I wouldn’t wish that on anyone.” The couple went to the home of friends who lived nearby. From their friends’ window, Georgy saw an ambulance arrive at the complex. He went over to the medics himself for first aid and to have them “record [him] as one of the injured.” A few hours later, the couple returned to their apartment for belongings, then went back to their friends’ home. After that, they went to Yelena’s relatives’ home, where they’re now staying. Georgy shows photos of the wrecked apartment on his phone. The stretch ceilings have melted. The windows and balcony are gone, and everything is covered in soot. Furniture and appliances have toppled over, and fragments and pieces of the walls are scattered everywhere. After what he’s been through, Georgy tries to avoid going to Novye Kotelniki unless he absolutely has to. He arranged to meet Bereg’s reporter at a shopping mall in Moscow. “I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here,” Georgy says. It wasn’t until several days later, he says, that he fully realized “what could have happened.” It’s been hard to cope with. The other day, he went to get a haircut, and the buzzing of the clippers made him uneasy. “I barely slept for three nights. I asked my doctor to prescribe something to calm me down, but it’s still pretty tough,” Georgy says. “It’s okay, we’re strong, we’ll get through it. I think time heals.” Moscow regional authorities are working out how to repair the apartment and pay compensation, but Georgy is avoiding those subjects for now. Over the past week, he’s had to return to the apartment several times to let in specialists who are to assess the damage from the attack, as well as local administration representatives and officers from the Investigative Committee, Russia’s criminal investigation agency. representative.title: How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice — Meduza

snapshot.title: How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice — Meduza
snapshot.evidenceText: On September 20, 2026, Ukraine launched another large-scale drone attack on the Moscow region. One drone hit a high-rise apartment building in Kotelniki, southeast of Moscow. Another had struck the same building in June. Neither strike killed anyone, but the attacks badly frightened many people in the neighborhood. Reporters from Bereg, a cooperative of independent journalists, visited the Novye Kotelniki residential complex to see how repairs were progressing after the two attacks and how residents had responded. Meduza is translating their report in full. Drivers struggle to find parking in this densely populated neighborhood in Kotelniki, outside Moscow. Shoppers wait in short lines at grocery store checkouts. It’s a warm, sunny weekend day, yet the courtyard of the Novye Kotelniki residential complex is unusually empty. On September 20, a Ukrainian drone struck one of the complex’s high-rise buildings for the second time. The first strike came on June 18, 2026. The drone crashed into almost the same spot on the courtyard side, in the upper third of the building, and exploded. A black scorch mark stands out against the beige-and-brown exterior, with a hole at its center. All that remains of the balconies on floors 19–22 is twisted metal and rebar. Some of the facade tiles have broken off. The few residents walking in the courtyard occasionally look up at the building and whisper to one another. Many decline to tell Bereg how the constant drone alerts have changed their lives. “What is there to say?” says a woman of about 40 in a black hijab, waving off the question, though she had just been discussing that very subject with a friend. Olga, a blonde woman in a trench coat, comes out of a neighboring building with her two-year-old daughter. She says this is their first walk in the courtyard since the recent attack. This time, she says, the property management company quickly cleared the broken glass and other debris from the courtyard. But she’s still scared: “You never know, she could pick up a piece of glass or something. You’re more scared for her than for yourself.” On the day of the attack, Olga woke to explosions at four in the morning. She woke her husband. At first, he thought she was imagining things, but then he heard the explosions, too. Deciding it wasn’t safe to stay in their apartment, they carried their sleeping daughter downstairs to the ground floor, where neighbors had already gathered. Olga stayed in the lobby until eight in the morning. Throughout that time, she could hear explosions outside. “It was a nightmare: People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up, and we were all looking for medicine for them,” she tells Bereg. “You feel like you’re in a war zone, and you can’t believe this is happening to you.” Olga missed the summer attack — her family was away. Perhaps that’s why, unlike many of her neighbors, she hadn’t put a “go bag” with documents, medicine, and other essentials in her entryway. Before the September attacks, she had felt less anxious than others. Afterward, she no longer felt safe. Still, her family’s daily routine hasn’t changed. She and her husband decided against moving their bed farther from the windows, figuring it wouldn’t save them. “Look at the size of that hole,” she says, gesturing toward the damaged high-rise. “You keep thinking: God, what if it happens again tomorrow?” Olga says. “I was on sedatives for two days. I definitely don’t feel safe here. I’m stressed every day.” Her family is considering moving, but unless the attacks become more frequent — “not once or twice, but practically every day” — she and her husband are unlikely to “seriously start looking into it.” Olga hopes things will “get back to normal” because “they [the Ukrainians] have already hit what they wanted to hit, and now they’ll calm down.” She means the Moscow oil refinery, the Ukrainian military’s target. But the high-rise stood in the path of the drones flying toward it. A few things help Olga manage her anxiety: She’s become even more absorbed in caring for her child and stopped reading the news, although she used to scroll through neighborhood chats even at night. “There’s so much noise now, so many planted stories, so much fake news,” she says. “Even the [real] news — there’s so much of it. You watch all this, and the whole situation keeps playing over in your head. What for?” Ruslan, who lives in the same complex as Olga, takes the opposite approach: He tries to read all the news. He says the drone attacks don’t make him anxious. “I knew there’d be an attack — the elections and all that,” Ruslan says. He says the neighborhood has only been quiet for the last few days. Before that, neighbors often heard air defenses in action at night and early in the morning. On September 20, Ruslan and his family counted “at least 40 explosions.” “We could see flashes in the sky from our window — almost like the ones over Israel !” he says excitedly. “There were about 10 a minute at one point.” He saw the drone crash into the neighboring building. He and his family were about to head out into the stairwell when they heard a loud noise outside the window and red light flooded the apartment. Like Olga, Ruslan doesn’t have a “go bag,” and he says he won’t be getting one. He sees no need, because “our air defenses have gotten better at their job.” “Yeah, there are screwups. Unfortunately, they can’t intercept everything. But overall, our guys are doing their job, and they’re doing it well,” Ruslan says. “Every day on my way home from work, I see the air defense systems changing locations.” He tells Bereg he believes there won’t be any more strikes on the neighborhood because they’re no longer worth it for Ukraine: “They launched so many, and the results were really poor . They understand it’s a waste of money.” With a smirk, Ruslan recalls wondering during the first attack whether the target might have been the apartment building rather than the refinery — “maybe some general lives here.” But he quickly dismissed the idea: First, it was a large-scale attack, and second, “what general would live here?” Ruslan believes Moscow and its immediate surroundings are now “very well protected” and that the authorities should focus on deploying air defense systems in other regions. That’s his only complaint about the security measures. “I think our government will take care of us, and everything will be fine. Our army will handle it,” he says. “Maybe I’m not that well informed, or maybe I’m too optimistic. But I think everything really is fine.” The next large-scale attack on the Moscow region came overnight on October 6. It struck communities northwest of Moscow, damaging private homes and nonresidential buildings in settlements in the Solnechnogorsk, Volokolamsk, Istra, and Domodedovo districts. Ukrainian Telegram channels that monitor attacks and the Russian outlet Astra also reported a fire at the Volodarskaya oil depot, southeast of Moscow. The Ukrainian strikes and Russian air defense operations killed two people and injured nine. Ruslan’s school-age daughter looks at him admiringly. They chuckle together as they recall a neighbor who panicked during the latest attack. “Run, run, we’re under attack!” Ruslan says, imitating her, though he quickly adds that “everybody’s different.” His daughter says that after the summer attack, one of her classmates transferred to another school — her family had decided to move. “They were renting [their apartment]. Maybe if we rented here instead of owning, we’d feel better about moving, too,” Ruslan says. “Plus, we’ve got a mortgage here — where are we gonna go?” A man in a black jacket, probably an employee of the property management company, walks through the courtyard with a ring of keys. He unlocks a door marked “Shelter” leading to the basement, looks inside, locks it again, and moves on to the next building. Each of the complex’s more than 20 high-rises has a shelter. Residents of Novye Kotelniki say the management company told them the basements are kept locked because they contain “technical equipment that the engineers are responsible for.” In the event of a real threat, residents are to call the dispatch office. A staff member will then come during the attack and unlock the basement door. The company promises this will happen quickly. But on September 20, residents of some buildings complained in the neighborhood Telegram chat that they hadn’t been able to get into the basements until after seven in the morning, although the large-scale attack began at four. Signs reading “Shelter” have been hung at the basement entrances, but the management company has done little to equip the rooms, residents say. Some have benches; others don’t even have those, leaving people to sit on the concrete or stand. Aleksandra, a resident in her mid-40s, is smoking near the entrance to one shelter. Asked how she feels about the increasingly frequent attacks, she says emphatically: “It’s really bad, really bad!” Aleksandra lives in the building that drones have struck twice. Or rather, she used to — after the recent strike, she realized she was afraid to stay in her apartment. “As they say, what happens once might never happen again, but what happens a second time…” she says. Aleksandra was home during both attacks. On June 18, she and her husband woke to repeated explosions and began getting ready to go to the shelter. As she was tying her sneakers, a drone crashed into the building. “I hear this huge bang — and plaster starts falling down in our apartment!” she tells Bereg. “I opened the door, and there was already smoke in the stairwell. We didn’t know if we’d be able to get downstairs.” No one opened the shelter, and neighbors crowded onto the ground floor. “It all ended around eight, and that’s when they opened the basement,” Aleksandra says indignantly. “Well, what’s the point of going down there once it’s all over?” On the day of the second drone strike, Aleksandra again heard “a lot of activity” as explosions kept going off. First, she went out onto the communal balcony to take a look. From there, she could see several fires near the Moscow oil refinery, the Mega shopping mall, and the Sadovod market. She was horrified. “I wake my husband up: ‘Get up, there’s a real war out there — everything’s burning, everything’s in flames!’” she says. To reach the stairs, Aleksandra and her husband had to pass through the communal balcony. As soon as they opened its door, there was a loud explosion, and a wave of heat hit them. “I knew it had hit the building,” she says. “Something went bang, and things started falling.” As we talk in the courtyard, there’s a crash in the distance, quiet but distinct. Aleksandra flinches and abruptly turns toward the sound. “I think something fell at the construction site.” “I react like that all the time now [to sudden noises],” Aleksandra says. “My nerves are completely shot. I went a week without proper sleep, even with Novo-Passit, glycine, and things to calm me down. I’d sleep for two hours, then be awake again.” On September 20, Aleksandra and her husband waited for the explosions to stop, went back up to their apartment, packed everything they needed, and left for their dacha. They’re staying there temporarily but return to their apartment in Novye Kotelniki every few days. “We’re living out of bags: one in the car, one at the dacha, and one here. We come back, wash up, do the laundry, hang it up, and head back out,” Aleksandra says. “We try to get everything done as fast as we can. They’ve just posted [on Telegram channels] again that apparently another large-scale attack is expected. Who knows?” But they can’t stay at the dacha for long: It has almost no amenities, and the trip to work takes three hours. Driving every day proved too expensive, so they switched to public transportation. Aleksandra took out a mortgage to buy her apartment. She has no other home and no relatives who can take her in. Now she’ll have to pay both her mortgage and the rent on a new place in a safer neighborhood. “I’ll be working to pay the rent. What else can I do?” she says with a sigh. “I don’t know what I’ll eat, but I’m just scared to live here.” “Looking at the windows, I could tell that lots of people had left — almost no one was still here,” she says. “Today we packed up a bunch of bags and took a heater. And everyone coming toward us had bags, too. People are leaving, and no one wants to come back.” Far fewer people go into the high-rise hit by the two drone attacks than into the other buildings. Many residents emerge carrying large bags — clearly, they’re leaving for a long time. The lobby has two entrances: one from the courtyard, the other from the road. The courtyard entrance is now cordoned off with barriers wrapped in red and white tape. The concierge warns that residents can’t leave through that door, either. A chair braces it shut from inside, and a sign on it reads: “No entry! Risk of death!” It doesn’t explain the danger. Another notice asks residents not to use the elevators between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. so they can be available to “construction workers repairing the building.” Residents ignore the request, and there are no workers in sight. Residents say that for the first few days after the attack, the elevators ran only in the evenings. Those with apartments on the upper floors of the 25-story building had to take the stairs or enter through the neighboring stairwell, use the elevator there, and cross the roof to reach their own building. The management company temporarily opened access to the roof for that purpose. The elevators are now running, and access to the roof has been closed off again. On many floors, boxes and bags of belongings are scattered about, along with plastic-wrapped crates of toys, black bags of construction debris, window frames, packages of building materials, and parts from household appliances. The smell of smoke still lingers on the fifth and sixth floors. On September 20, burning debris landed on a windowsill and started a fire. On the upper floors, it smells of burned plastic. The 21st floor suffered the worst damage. Workers had to remove the front panels from one elevator and the structure surrounding the shaft opening. A padlocked grille has replaced the door separating the elevator lobby from the apartments. The apartment the drone struck is on this floor. Georgy, whose name has been changed, was home in a neighboring apartment at the time. He and his wife, Yelena, whose name has also been changed, were about to head downstairs when he heard an unusual humming sound from the direction of the balcony. “I go over to the balcony and realize it [the drone] is getting closer, but I can’t see it. I can’t figure out where it’s coming from,” he tells Bereg. “I look down — and there it is, coming from the direction of the quarry, heading straight at me.” Georgy managed to shout to Yelena to run. He didn’t have time to get out of the way himself. The drone hit the neighboring apartment and exploded. The blast wave and a hail of fragments hit him. His arms and legs were badly cut. Bleeding heavily, he got dressed and pulled on his sneakers. His wife retrieved their cat, which had hidden under the bathtub. They grabbed a bag of documents and jewelry they had prepared in advance and ran downstairs. “If it had flown just a little higher, that would’ve been it — we wouldn’t be talking now,” Georgy says, visibly shaken as he looks at his bandaged wrists. “The explosion was unreal. I’d never experienced anything like it in my life. I wouldn’t wish that on anyone.” The couple went to the home of friends who lived nearby. From their friends’ window, Georgy saw an ambulance arrive at the complex. He went over to the medics himself for first aid and to have them “record [him] as one of the injured.” A few hours later, the couple returned to their apartment for belongings, then went back to their friends’ home. After that, they went to Yelena’s relatives’ home, where they’re now staying. Georgy shows photos of the wrecked apartment on his phone. The stretch ceilings have melted. The windows and balcony are gone, and everything is covered in soot. Furniture and appliances have toppled over, and fragments and pieces of the walls are scattered everywhere. After what he’s been through, Georgy tries to avoid going to Novye Kotelniki unless he absolutely has to. He arranged to meet Bereg’s reporter at a shopping mall in Moscow. “I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here,” Georgy says. It wasn’t until several days later, he says, that he fully realized “what could have happened.” It’s been hard to cope with. The other day, he went to get a haircut, and the buzzing of the clippers made him uneasy. “I barely slept for three nights. I asked my doctor to prescribe something to calm me down, but it’s still pretty tough,” Georgy says. “It’s okay, we’re strong, we’ll get through it. I think time heals.” Moscow regional authorities are working out how to repair the apartment and pay compensation, but Georgy is avoiding those subjects for now. Over the past week, he’s had to return to the apartment several times to let in specialists who are to assess the damage from the attack, as well as local administration representatives and officers from the Investigative Committee, Russia’s criminal investigation agency. Those visits convinced him that he could no longer live in the complex, even if the building were fully repaired. “When you go back there, you start shaking — the atmosphere’s different, the aura’s different,” he says. “I’ve developed a phobia of the place, so I want to get everything sorted out as soon as possible and put this nightmare behind me.” Georgy’s neighbors are collecting signatures for a petition to the management company and the authorities. They’re demanding additional protection for the building that drones have now hit twice. “It feels unfair that they can’t keep our homes or our lives safe. You don’t feel very safe in your own capital,” Georgy says. He believes the air defenses can’t handle the number of drones flying toward Moscow. He sees only one way to guarantee an end to the attacks: It wouldn’t hurt to end this military operation. One decision — and it would all be over.
